And straight therewith Sir Loumor slew.

Then spake the babe, in cradle lay,
"I'll venge that deed some future day."
In cradle lay
"I'll venge that deed some future day."

"Thou'rt sprung, I know, from the same blood,
"To me thou never wilt be good."
"From the same blood
"To me thou never wilt be good."

She seiz'd the brat, "I'll stop thy boast,"
And dash'd its brains against a post.
"I'll stop thy boast"
And dash'd its brains against a post.

"And now that man for man I've slain
"I'll to my native land again."
"Man I've slain
"I'll to my native land again."

poems.title: Grimild's Revenge (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the stately Dame Grimild,
The mead she bade to brew,
And many a hero stout and bold
To banquet hall she drew.

She bade them come to deeds of war,
She bade them come to strife,
Where many a hero young and brave
Was doom'd to lose his life.

A champion, such as Hogen was,
Or Folker Spilleman, —
Find one such as those brothers were,
We surely never can.

But forward Hogen's mother stepp'd,
"It seem'd," Dame Bodil said,
"As in a midnight trance I lay,
"That all the birds were dead.

"And this is what the dream will say,
"If dreams ye understand,
"'Twill cost you many a hero's life
"To tread that heathen land."

But forward rode those gentlemen
To where the torrent swept,
And there they found a Merwoman,
As under a hill she slept.

"Wake up! wake up! thou Merwoman,
"Thou fair and lovely wife,
"And say if in the heathen land
"I'm doom'd to lose my life."

"O turn thee, Hero Hogen, turn,
"Thou gallant knight so bold,
"Thou hast at home on thine own land
'"So many a fort and hold.

"Wend homeward to thy grassy lands,
"Avoid the fray and strife;
"If to thy sister thou shalt come,
"That visit cos'ts thy life."

Then wax'd the Hero Hogen wroth,
His sword in haste he drew,
And struck the wretched Merwoman,
And cut her neck in two.

"Nay! rather thou it is shalt die
"Here on the glittering sand,
"And I so hale and hearty ride
"On to the heathen land."

Forward they rode, those gentlemen,
To where the torrents sweep,
And found th'unhappy Ferryman
Beside his wife asleep.

"Wake up! wake up! good Ferryman,
"And row me across the strait,
"And thee I'll give my ring of gold
"Full fifteen pounds in weight."

"Thyself retain thy ring of gold,
"For that I little care;
"To row and land thee at that place
"For three I should not dare.

"I never on that shore will land,
"Where waits me only woe;
"Against Dame Grimild's stern command
"Across I will not row."

So wroth the Hero Hogen wax'd,
So fierce was he of mood,
He lopp'd the honest boatman's head,
And round him reek'd the blood.

The gory bead he cast afar
Into the roaring Sound,
And after it the body threw
To join upon the ground.

Gunter and Gemot, gallant knights,
Steer'd off the boat from shore,
But, ere they half across were come,
A storm began to roar.

The oars with Folker's mighty stroke
Were broken both in twain,
But with his buckler Hogen steer'd
Across the boisterous main.

And as the knights their anchor cast
Out on the glittering sand,
'Twas he, the Hero Hogen's self,
The first debark'd on land.

It was the Hero Hogen's self
The first debark'd on shore,
And then came Folker Spilleman,
And many heroes more.

High on the tower the watchman stood,
Was pacing to and fro;
"Two highborn youths are hither come,
"And waiting stand below.

"Two warlike men are come to land,
"And bright their weapons glance,
"From head to foot in iron clad,
"And gay their horses prance.

"The one bears on his shield a hawk,
"All glittering bright with gold;.
"The other one a fiddle bears,
"A Duke's son he so bold."

Out stepp'd the stately dame, Grimild,
Could use the choicest word;
"His fiddle bears not he forsooth
"To serve a master's board.

"Two Duke's sons are those heroes both,
"That glance in bright array,
"And well they both are known to me,
"My father's sons are they."

There waiting stood the Dame Grimild
Array'd in verdant pall;
"Now saving Hogen, him alone,
"Be welcome hither all!

"Welcome, my friends, and take your seats
"Within the festive ring;
"But ne'er till death shall I forget
"Sigfrid the murder'd king."

Uprose the count, Sir Guncelin,
And thus to his men he cried;
"To day the Hero Hogen comes,
"Now let his strength be tried.

"We'll meet him hand to hand to day,
"We'll smite him till he's dead,
"And so his pleasant greenwoods gain,
"And all his gold so red."

But answer Hero Hogen made,
Where near the door he stood;
"Ready am I to try the chance,
"If ye but have the mood."

Out rush'd the band of faithful stains,
And up to battle sprung,
But ill they fared at Hogen's hand,
The old and eke the young.

Asunder broke in Folker's hand
His trusty blade of war,
But from the castle door he wrench'd
A heavy iron bar.

He heav'd a stroke, and on the ground
Seven gallant men were strown;
"Now God be prais'd" said Spilleman
"I've made my fiddle known.

"My fiddle I so hard have play'd.
"To make you dance and spring;
"From heavy work I am bathed in sweat
"Within my mail coat ring/'

Then stepp'd the county Sir Guncelin,
Up to the proud Grimild;
"Help us against these doughty foes,
"Or let the strife be still'd."

"Heave on, heave on, my gallant men,
"Who daily share my bread;
"Heave on, nor from the combat cease,
"Till Folker is lying dead."

"Hark thee, Grimild, bark, sister mine;
"Deep driven is my wound:
"That true thou never wast to me,
"Too well I now have found.

"Sev'n long and weary days I've watch'd
"Alike by night and day;
"Before I yield me up, and die,
"My death-wound I'll repay.

"My good and precious sword is gone,
"And snapp'd my bar of steel,
"But could I any weapon find,
"My pain I should not feel/'

Then answer'd him young Obbe Yern,
Who stood thereby so near;
"I'll lend thee a sword, the well tried blade,
"My brother held so dear.

"Methinks a gallant knight thou art
"And strong of limb and stark;
"How well thou wieldest fiddelbow,
"We've cause enough to mark."

"I thank thee much, thou man of worth,
"Thou brave young Obbe Yern,
"And well my brothers and myself
"Thy kindness will return."

So battled Folker Spilleman,
The clamour fill'd the sky;
Would rather perish like a man,
Than meanly skulk or fly.

poems.title: Grimild's Revenge (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the stately dame Grimild,
Let brew the wine and mead,
And sent for many a gallant man
Renowned for mighty deed.

"Go, bid them come to feats of war,
"And bid them come to strife;
"There's many a hero young and brave
"'Is doom'd to lose his life."

The Hero Hogen's mother dream'd,
She knew the purport well,
That, as his rider rode him out,
The foal slipp'd up and fell.

"Now what this dream betides, my son,
"I'd have thee well aware;
"Thy treacherous sister plots thy death;
"Of her designs take care."

The Hero Hogen, he it was,
Rode out along the strand,
And there he found a Merwoman,
Who bask'd upon the sand.

"Tell me, thou honest Merwoman,
"Tell me thou cunning wife,
"Shall I on When-isle slay my foes,
"Or shall I lose my life?"

"List, Hero Hogen, list to me,
"Thou gallant knight so bold,
"Here thou hast forts and castle towers,
"And silver too and gold:

"But if to When-isle thou shalt cross,
"And leave thy home so fair,
"Thou fallest slain by traitor hand,
"And buried stay est there."

Then wax'd the Hero Hogen wroth
At such ill-boding spell,
And smote the wretched Merwoman,
That on the earth she fell.

"There lie thou still, thou wretched wife,
"Stretch'd on the ocean sand;
"I well know how to make my way
"Back from the Whenish land."

Like lords they rode before the gate,
And bright their weapons, glanced,
In silken raiment they were clothed,
And high their horses pranced.

They beat the gate, till in the hall
Was heard the dinning knock;
"Up, Porter, up! why tarriest thou?
"Thy gate to us unlock."

"That dare not ?" the Porter said
With mantle-muffled chin;
"Without Grimild, my lady's, leave
"I let no stranger in."

He went and ask'd the proud Grimild,
Where at her board she sate;
"Two knights before the castle stand,
"And bid unbar the gate.

"There wait two lords before the door,
"And bright their weapons glance;
"In silken raiment they are clothed,
"And high their horses prance.

"The one he bears a fiddle bow,
"The other bears an em;
"That both are heroes stout and bold,
"That I can well discern."

"Surely they are my brothers both,"
The proud Grimild began;
"The Hero Hogen it will be,
"And Folker Spilleman."

And out went dames and maidens all
To view those champions' gait;
And slender were their belted waists,
Their persons tall and straight.

And went the stately dame, Grimild,
In scarlet robe array'd,
And courteously the stranger guests
To banquet table bade.

"But this is castle use and law,
"No sword may here be worn,
"Since traitor baud King Sigfrid slew,
"Whose death I daily mourn."

"Lady, 'twas I King Geffred slew,
"With this my hand and glaive;
"And I, who slew king Ottelin,
"So strong a man and brave

"Aye! camp'd before the walls of Troy
"I made those champions bleed,
"Tho' lost my trusty coat of mail,
"And gone my noble steed."

She led them into the banquet hall,
Where sat her men at board;
Against those two a hundred rose,
And brandish'd each his sword.

"Will one among ye, warriors,
"Who daily tat my bread,
"My brother Hogen dare to slay,
"And earn my gold so red?"

When that heard Folker ' Spilleman,
He sprang across the board,
He wrench'd the door from oft' its hinge,
He bared a fearful sword.

He seiz'd the heavy bolt of steel,
With glee he swung it round,
And fifteen champions at a blow
Laid lifeless on the ground.

"Bravo!" said Folker Spilleman,
"Now doth my fiddle sing;"
And then slew Hero Hogen too
His twenty at a swing

Up spake the stately dame Grimild,
Her breast with anger glow'd;
"'Twere better, had ye stay'd at home,
"When from your land ye rode.

"A hundred widows ye will leave,
"Before the fight is done."
"That" Hero Hogen answer'd her,
"Thyself thou hast begun,"

The Hero Hogen rais'd his helm
All burning off his brow;
"My flesh beneath the coat of mail
"With heat begins to glow.

"I feel with thirst and weariness
"My heart within mor sink;
"Would God in heaven I had at hand
"A horn of wine to drink!

He loos'd his helm, the raging thirst
With dead -man's blood to slake;
"In nomine Domini!" were the words,
The Hero Hogen spake.

Grimild's three hundred warriors all
Dead on the ground had lain,
By Hero Hogen's heavy hand
And by his brother slain.

"God help thee, Folker Spilleman,
"Who liest near me dead!
"Well has thy bar of steel today
"Serv'd thee in weapon's stead. "

Full four and twenty fell for one,
As there they stood in rank;
He like a champion mow'd them down,
Before, himself, he sank.

"If I live yet one other day,
"Ere it begin to wane,
"I'll make my sister rue thy death,
"I'll have her burnt or slain."

To her, Grimild, a fearful fate,
And day of reckoning came;
For Hogen's son closed in a cave
And starved that vengeful dame.

poems.title: Grimild's Revenge (C)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the stately dame Grimild,
The mead she bade to brew,
And gallant knights to share the feast
From every country drew.

She bade them come, and tarry not,
To battle-field and strife:
And there it was, so young and brave,
That Hogen lost his life.

The Hero Hogen, he it was,
He walked along the strand,
And there he found a Merwoman
Asleep upon the sand.

"Good luck to thee, clear Merwoman,
"Thou fair and cunning wife;
"Shall I on Whenild's land be safe?
"Or shall I lose my life?"

"Here thou hast forts and massive towers,
"With gold thy coffers fill'd;
"But if to When -isle thou shalt go,
"As surely wilt be kill'd."

The Hero Hogen, he it was,
His sword so hasty drew,
And struck the wretched Merwoman,
And cat her neck in two.

The dripping gory head he seiz'd,
And slung' into the Sound,
And after it the body toss'd,
To join upon the ground.

The Hero Hogen turn'd about
And walk'd along the strand,
And there he found a ferry man,
Was waiting on the sand.

"Hark thee, good honest ferryman,
"Row me across the strait,
"I'll give thee then my golden ring,
"Full fifteen pounds in weight."

"I will not row thee o'er the sound
For all thy gold so red,
"For if thou tread est Whenild's land,
"Thou fallest on it dead."

The Hero Hogen, he it was,
His sword so hasty drew,
And struck the wretched ferryman,
And cut his neck in two.

The golden bracelet off his arm
He gave the boatman's wife,
"See, take thou this as friendship's gift
"To pay thy husband's life."

Gunter and Gemot, gallant knights
From land the vessel drave,
But straight in fury rose the storm,
And boil'd the briny wave.

In fury rose the stormy sea,
And dash'd upon the shore;
Asunder brake in Hogen's hand
The massive iron oar.

ThaE iron oar in sunder brake
In Hero Hogen's hand,
But those two lords with gilded shields
Steer M on their boat to land.

As on the shore their troop debark'd,
They scour'd each man his blade,
And watching, what the strangers did,
There stood a gentle maid.

Her banded waist it was so small,
Her person tall and straight,
And yet her body duly short,
And maidenly her gait.

To Norborg then they march'd away,,
And towards the gate drew near;
"But where can now the Porter be, -
"Should aye be standing here?"

"Here 'tis the trusty Porter stands
"Hourly to watch and wake;
"If I but knew, whence ye are come,
"Your message I would take."

"Hither from kingdoms three we come,
"Both we and all our craw;.,
"For sister lady Grimild claim;
"The tale we tell is true."

In to the hall the Porter came,
And stood before the board;
A cunning man of speech was he
To choose the fittest word.

"There stand without before the gate
"Two men of noble mould
"The one of them a fiddle bears
"The one a helm of gold.

"The one a bow and fiddle bears,
"But not for master's fee;
"Come whence they may, these noble youths,
"Two duke's sons they must be."

It was the stately dame Grimild,
Her head wrapp'd in her cloak,
And went into the castleyard,
And thus to her brothers spoke:

"Now will you to the chamber go,
"And drink of mead and wine,
"Or rest your limbs on bed of silk
"With two fair ladies mine?"

Thus spake the stately dame Grimild,
In mantle wrapp'd her head,
And into the marble banquet room
To find her warriors sped.

"Here sit ye all, my men, at board,
"Sit sbiftking day by day;
"Now who will Hero Hogen face?
"My brother who will slay?

"If any here to earn a prize
"Can slaughter one so bold,
"Lord of my castles he shall be,
"And all my treasur'd gold."

Then up and spake a champion,
A chieftain o'er a land;
"It's I that will thy guerdon win
"With this my proper hand.

"'Tis I that will the guerdon win,
"And strike that hero dead;
"The lord of all thy castles be,
"And all thy gold so red."

Him answer'd Folker Spill em an
With massive iron bar;
"I'll surely leave my mark on thee,
"Before thou goest far."

A first and heavy stroke, he struck,
Laid fifteen champions low,
"Ha, Ha, so Folker Spilleman
"Can play his fiddlebow?

So many were the men he slew,
A bridge of them he built,
And broad and long I ween it was,
And much the blood he spilt.

Above were spread the wetted hides,
O'er rolling peas so small,
And forward Hero Hogen stepp'd,
And first was he to fall.

"The Hero Hogen turn'd about,
Would up again with speed;
"Stay, stay, my brother," cried Grim old,
"''Twas otherwise agreed.

"Stay there, my brother, keep thy word,
"As doth become a knight,
"If on the ground thou shouldest fall,
"No more to stand upright/'

The Hero Hogen kept his word,
As by his honour bound,
He fought awhile upon his knees,
And got his mortal wound.

Yet other champions three he slew,
None of the least were they,
And then to find his father's hoard
To Hammer took his way.

Still on the hero fortune smiled,
A lovely maid he won,
And with fair Whenild, so she hight,
Begat a worthy son.

Ranke that champion's name, and well
He venged a sire so brave;
For proud Grimild he starved to death
In Niding's treasure-cave.

And then away through Lombardy
He made his march to Bern,
And with his kindred Danish men,
Great glory did he earn.

His mother Whenild stay'd at home,
From her took When it's name;
To knights and gallant champions
Is known that island's fame.

poems.title: Samson
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Young Samson at court in service stood,
And there he his king's fair daughter wooed.

"Kirstin, now listen, fair maid, to me,
"And tell me, will you my trulove be?"

"Dear Samson, thy bride I gladly were,
"But thwart my father I do not dare."

The maid he wrapp'd in his mantle blue,
And up on his charger gently threw.

He hold her fast on his gallant gray,
And off to his home with her rode his way.

His hat he joyfully waved on high;
"And now then, king of the Danes, Good bye!"

The news to the king was quickly sped;
"Your daughter has e'en with Samson fled."

The king bade over his castle call,
"Up, troopers, and d'on your harness all!

"Up! up! my men, up! to horse! to horse!
"My daughter is carried away by force.

"Up, troopers! up, all! take spear and bow,
"In Samson ye'll find a dauntless foe.

"Ride, follow up hard on the villain's track,
"Till dead or living ye bring him back."

Nor were they tardy, his guardsmen leal,
But arm'd, and buckled their spurs on heel.

They rode, and as soon as they reached the mead,
Their horses urged to their utmost speed.

They rode and they came to Samson's gate,
Where Mette his stately mother, sate.

"Speak, Mette, lady so fine and fair,
"Where's Samson thy son? o tell us where."

US "My Samson yesterday rode away,
"And will not be back till Christmas day."

"We'll give thee heaps of the ruddy gold,
"To tell us where Samson has his hold."

"Right pleasant the sight of gold in store,
"But Samson is now at home no more.

"As gay as in chest are gold's bright hues
"'Tis painful an only son to lose."

They down on the grass a mantle spread,
And pour'd upon it the gold so red.

"A house is on yonder northward side,
"And Samson is there and his royal bride."

So false was his mother, she basely sold
Her only son for a heap of gold.

The troopers they rode to Samson's yard,
Were thinking to win a rich reward.

They batter'd the door with spear and shield,
"Out, Samson, and meet us upon the field!"

Young Samson he back the casement threw;
"Ye count so many and we so few;

"But wait) good troopers, sit down and rest,
Till I for the combat am duly drest."

To help him his lady did not fail,
But buckled about him his coat of on ail.

Well arm'd he sprang from his chamber door,
And thinn'd their ranks so close before.

He first slew four of them, then slew five,
Of thirty he left not one alive.

He hew'd them, till hew he could no more,
He trampled in thirty troop ors' gore.

"And now from his stall my charger bring,
"I'll mount him and ride to see the king/'

He stopp'd as he pass'd the homestead gate,
Where waiting his traitress mother sate.

He drew from his scabbard the reeking steel;
"My mother art thou, or its edge shouldst feel."

He drew from the sheathe his glittering knife,
"My mother art thou, or it cost thy life.

"The cruellest mother thou hast been,
"Hast sold my life to my foes yestreen.

"For yonder glittering heap of gold
"A mother her own son's life has sold!"

As Samson rode to the palace gate,
There stood the king in a robe of state.

"Hark, Samson, my man, and answer me,
"Where tarry the troopers I sent for thee?"

"Your troopers are all on my courtyard spread,
"Are wounded' some of them, some are dead:

"Some sick, some likely enough to die,
"And somE on the bier as corpses lie.

"So tell me, my king, so brave and fine,
"When "end you to fetch your mastfed swine?

"Let five of your baggage waggons come,
"And load them, and bring the slaughter'd home."

His sword from the scabbard Samson drew,
"And were you not king, this should you rue."

"Nay, gallant Samson, pat up thy blade,
"Thou pro vest thee worthy a royal maid.

"E'en take my daughter and sheath thy knife;
"I give her to thee to be thy wife."

He turn'd him about and homeward hied,
To visit in peace his royal bride.

He turn'd him, and gave his horse the rein,
And rode to his lovely bride again.

poems.title: Vidrick Verlandson and Giant Langbane
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of George Borrow (1826), titled "Vidrik Verlandson".
poems.text:
King Diderick he sits at home at Bern,
And boasts of his power and might,
Of wondrous feats he has done in war,
And many a humbled knight.

King Diderick is peering from castle tower
As wide as his eye can see;
"Would God, that a Hero so stout I knew,
"As dared to contend with me!"

Him answer'd the Master Hildebrand,
For travell'd had he so far;
"There dwells a champion at Birtingsberg
"Thou darest not meet in war."

"Now hark thee, good Master Hildebrand,
"So brave on the battle field!
"Ride foremost thou in the wood to day,
"And carry my royal shield."

"Nay" answer'd the Master Hildebrand,
For prudent as brave was he;
"I will not carry thy shield to day,
"Such honour becomes not me."

Then up and spake Vidrick Verlandson,
So hasty and warm of mood;
"'Tis I that will lead the band today,
"And march through Birting wood."

'Twas so spake Vidrick t Verlandson,
And rous'd himself to wrath:
"My sword is a finely tempered blade,
"Cuts iron as well as cloth."

Three hundred champions brave they were,
Came marching to Birting's ground,
And hunted the giant Langbane out,
And him in the forest found.

Then up and spake Vidrick Verlandson,
"Strange game it is we shall try;
"Let me to the wood first ride alone,
"If ye can on me rely."

And answer'd him Diderick thus, the king,
For jealous of fame was he;
"If Langbane the giant thou dost find,
"Conceal not the truth from me,"

He waited not, Vidrick Verlandson,
But off to the forest sped,
And there he a narrow footpath found,
That straight to the giant led.

As onward and onward Vidrick march'd,
O'er Birting's heath away,
He came to where, all so grim and black,
The giant Langbane lay.

The slumbering giant he rous'd from sleep
With thrust of his spear so rough;
"Awake thee, Giant! Wake, Langbane, wake!
Methinks thou hast slept enough."

On this wild heath for many a year
"I've rested me day and night,
"And never has one come here before
"To wake me from sleep to fight."

"But now it is Vidrick Verlandson
"With sword of the keenest steel,
"I'm come from dreaming to wake thee up,
"Its edge I'll make thee feel."

The Giant Langbane he turn'd him round,
And wink'd with his sleepy eyes;
"What paltry foolish young swain is this,
"A Giant like me defies?

"But hark thee, I will not fight with thee,
"Unless of a knightly race;
"So tell to me who and whence thou art,
"And all thy lineage trace."

"My father was Verland, the canning smith,
"And well he deserv'd his fame;
"My mother, the child of a king was she,
"Fair Bodild she hight by name.

"My shield's call'd Skrepping, and on its face
"Has many an arrow play'd;
"And this my helmet of steel, call'd Blank,
"Has broken many a blade.

"And Skimming is named my noble horse,
"Of wild mare foal'd in the wood;
"And Mimmering is call'd my trusty sword
"Well temper'd in hero's blood.

"Myself I am Vidrick Verlandson,
"And well I am clad in steel;
"And stirrest thou not thy lengthy legs,
"My strength thou wilt quickly feel.

"And further, thou Giant Langbane, hark!
"My message is quickly told,
"The king outside of the forest waits
"To take thy tribute of gold."

"As much as I own of treasur'd gold,
"I keep it in safety stored;
"And never will let it be told of me,
"That stable-boy won my hoard"

"As young and as little as I may seem,
"Thy strength I will surely break;
"From off its carcase I'll lop thy head,
"And all thy treasures take."

The Giant Langbane would fain in peace
A little while longer lie;
"Young hero, return in safety home,
"Unless thou art will'd to die."

Then rear'd him Skimming on both his legs,
And right on the Giant ran.
And seven of his ribs he broke at once,
The battle with that began.

All foaming with wrath the Giant rose,
And whirled his massy bar;
At Vidrick he aim'd it, but sped the steel
Away to the hill afar.

Full surely the Giant Langbane thought
To slaughter his puny foe,
But Skimming so nimbly had leap'd aside,
That Vidrick had miss'd the blow.

The Giant he gnash'd his teeth with rage,
And loudly began to wail;
"As firm in the hill-side sticks the bar,
"As hammer could drive a nail."

Nor longer did Vidrick then delay,
For wrathful of mood he grew;
"Turn, Skimming, about! and, Mimmering, ware!
"See thou, what thou canst do."

Sword Mimmering he took in both his hands
And straight at Langbane ran,
And down to his entrails through his breast
He clove that monstrous man.

The Giant Langbane had now from sleep
Woke up with the deadly pain,
And if he had only had the power,
Had paid it him back again.

A curse on thee, Vidrick Verlandson!
"A curse on thy trenchant blade!
"Such pain and anguish thy hand has dealt,
"So deadly a wound has made."

"I'll mince thee up into bits as small
"As leaves in an autumn wind,
"Unless thou tellest, where in this wood
"Thy treasure heaps I may find."

"Have mercy, good Vidrick Verlandson,
"Forbear thee to strike me dead;
"And I will show thee my treasure house,
"Its roof of the gold so red."

The Giant he crept, and Vidrick rode
So deep in the murky wood,
And found, where, shining as bright as fire,
The house with the gold roof stood.

"Now roll from the mouth that massy stone,
"And raise from its hinge the door,
"And more the gold than in all thy land
"Thou findest therein in store."

Vidrick could scarcely stir the stone,
Though he with his two hands strove;
But Langbane with ease the weighty mass
With only two fingers hove.

"Now turn thee homeward, my pretty page,
"And make me no more ado,
"For more than thou with both thy hands
"I carry with fingers two."

"Nay, nay," said Vidrick Verlandson,
"Thy cunning is too well known;
"No man that is wise will waste his strength
"In heaving a block of stone."

"A greater treasure of gold is here
"Than fifteen kings can show;
"Step down to it, Vidrick Verlandson,
"The foremost thou shalt go."

"Nay," answer'd him Vidrick Verlandson,
His crafty designs he knew,
"'Tie thou the foremost shalt enter in,
"As usual it is to do."

But while the giant was stooping low,
As in at the door he crept,
Vidrick with only a single blow
His head from his shoulders swept.

The bleeding carcase he lifted up,
And leant it against an oak,
And then to his friends rode back, again,
And thus of his combat spoke.

But first he smear'd with the Giant's blood
Himself and his gallant steed,
And rode up slowly before the King,
As tho' he were lamed indeed.

"And here ye are standing, good comrades, still,
"All under the shady leaf!
"The Giant today has worsted me,
"And heavy will be your grief."

"If fell upon thee today so hard
" "The blows of the Giant's hand,
"Then venture we not another life,
"But ride to our native land."

"Nay! nay! King Diderick, turn thee round;
"But turn thee and come with me;
"And all the treasure the Giant own'd,
"I'll show it in store for thee."

"If Langbane the Giant thou hast slain,
"Thy fame spreads over the land;
"Nor is there a champion born on earth,
"Thou mayest not well withstand."

King Diderick's heroes, and all his men,
The Giant they wish'd to see,
But stood afar off like laughing stocks,
Nor dared to approach the tree.

They fear'd he might stretch his giant legs,
And after their army run;
They stood aghast at his monster size,
And wake him there dared not one.

And much and heartily Vidrick laugh'd,
And ask'd in a merry vein;
"But how had ye faced the living man,
"And dare it not, now he is slain?"

He poked the corpse with his lance's shaft,
And down he toppled the head,
And truly it was, as all confessed,
A giant most stout and dread.

They dragg'd the glittering treasure out,
And parted the gold anon,
And Vidrick he claim'd the greater part
By dint of his valour won.

But hardly so much was Vidrick glad
Those treasures of gold to gain,
As for that himself he had all alone
So mighty a giant slain.

In triumph they homeward rode to Bern,
King Diderick joy'd the most;
He gave to Verlandson after him
The first and the highest post.

poems.title: The Tournament
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the versions of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Oh, Seventy-Seven Twice-Told Were They" and George Borrow (1826), titled "The Tournament".
poems.text:
A troop they were of seventy-seven,
As out from Hald they went,
And forth they march'd to Bratingsborg,
And boldly pitched their tent.

The king he stood on Bratingsborg,
And look'd around so far:
"Are yonder champions tired of life,
"That here they come to war?

"Now hark thee, Siward, Hasty swain,
"Thou wanderer far and wide,
"Go thou and view these warriors arms,
"Up off to their army ride."

Siward stepp'd in beneath the tent,
And duly greeted all;
"Is one among you, gallant knights,
"Will try with me a fall?

"Whoever rides a tourney best,
"Here's one that him defies;
"Our prowess let us fairly test,
"Our horses be the prize."

On table-board the dice were thrown,
And roird about so wide,
And on Childe Hummer fell the lot
A joust with him to ride.

To Verland's son Childe Hummer went
To help him in his need;
"Lend me to-day against a pledge
"Skimming, thy noble steed.

"Eight castles, all so strongly built,
"These will I give thee first;
"And then the sister I love the best,
"Of pledges not the worst. "

"Yon Siward he is a hairbrain knight,
"Sees not his weapon's end;
"If Skimming's hurt, not all thy kin
"Could make me due amend.

"For were these castles all of gold,
"And all their water wine,
"All would I not for Skimming take;
"Thank God! the horse is mine."

Vidrick his hand struck on the board;
"Four winters now are past,
"Since with a girth for battle fray
"I girded Skimming last."

Childe Hummer mounted upon his back,
Glad such a horse to ride;
It seem'd to Skimming wondrous strange,
When spurs stuck in his side.

The gold shone bright on Hummer's shield
As sun in summer 's heat;
"And now God help me, poor young swain,
"Firmly to keep my seat!"

Against him rode a gallant knight,
A hero stout and bold,
And both their shield-straps burst in twain,
And far their shields were roll'd.

"Young man, thy horse thou sittest well,
"And like a gallant knight,
"Dismount, I'll wait thy thrust awhile,
"Make thou thy saddle tight."

The second bout those heroes rode,
They proved their prowess well,
Childe Hummer's shield was struck so hard,
That. on the ground he fell.

"The good horse Skimming now is mine,
"From off his back thou'rt thrown;
"So now, brave youth, say, what the race
"Thou claimest for thine own.

"My mother is Lady Helwig call'd,
"And dwells at Lesen-eye;
"My father's name is Jensen Boe,
"And Hummer hight am I."

"If thou art Holmboe Jensen's son,
"My next of kin art thou;
"So take thy horse and go in peace,
"I knew thee not till now.

"But first with shield straps bind my arms,
"Bind me to yonder tree,
"And ride and tell King Diderick,
"That thou hast beaten me."

Childe Hummer stepp'd beneath the tent,
On table toss'd his blade;
"I've bound to an oak the stalwart knight,
"Who late such boasting made."

"Hark thee, Childe Hummer, Vidrick said,
"'Tis spoken but in joke,
"Or Siward with his own good will ff' /' "-. '.
"Was bound to yonder oak/'

Vidrick then took a little horse
And rode away to the wood;
He fain himself would see the place,
And learn how matters stood

As Siward there was standing bound,
And saw him on the way,
Up by the roots he tore the tree,
He dared no longer stay.

The king he stands on Bratingsborg,
And looks o'er dale and down;
"Hither conies Siward Hasty swain,
"And summer brings to town'

The Queen is looking far and wide,
From out her lofty bower;
"Siward has in the forest been,
"And brings us back a flower.

"But hark thee, Siward Hasty swain,
"What now, my son, I say:
"Where is the horse that thou hast won,
"And brought me home today?"

"That horse to one my next of kin
"I've given for friendship's sake,
"Nor hast thou here a knight, would dare
"That horse from him to take."

"Then tell me, Siward Hasty swain,
"For thou wast in their tent;
"What is their several shields' device?
"And what therewith is meant?"

"Blazon'd upon the first shield stands
"A lion stout and bold;
"And Diderick's that, the king's device,
"A lion crown'd with gold.

"Blazon'd upon the second stands
A lion and giant tall:
"And that is Master Hildebrand's,
"The bravest knight of all.

"Blazon'd upon the third shield stand
A hammer and pair of tongs;
"And that to one, no quarter gives,
"To Verlandson belongs.

"Blazon'd upon the fourth shield stand
"Two spurs with gold so bright;
"And those the Hero Hagen wears,
"That forward eager knight.

"Blazon'd upon the fifth shield stand
"A fiddle and fiddle-bow;
"And that bears Folker Spilleman
"To play them never slow.

"Blazon'd upon the sixth shield stand
"Two arrows clean and white;
"And that one claims Childe Wifferlin,
"Who never shrunk from fight.

"Blazon'd upon the seventh shield stands
"A linden all in leaf,
"And that bears Holmboe Jensen's son,
"Young Hummer, gallant chief.

"Blazon'd upon the eighth shield stands
"A table of gold so red,
"And that bears gallant Wolf of Yern
"A champion courtly bred.

"Blazon'd upon the ninth shield stands
"A lindworm's monster length,
"And that is bearing young Sir Orm,
"Who fears no mortal strength.

"Blazon'd upon the tenth shield sits
A hawk so swift of flight;
"And that childe Detloff bears, the Dane,
"So prompt of hand in fight.

"Blazon'd upon the eleventh shield,
"A naked sword-blade lies;
"And that the rich Sir Herman bears
"In every bold emprize.

"Blazon'd upon the twelfth shield stand
"A cowl and bar of steel;
"And that the stout monk Alsing bears
"And makes the foeman feel.

"And now as many as I have seen,
"Their shields I've truly told,
"And sooth to say, there carry them
"As many heroes bold."

The gladness spread through all the court,
Outside and in the hall;
The knights they parted best of friends,
And home went joyous all.

poems.title: King Diderick in Birtingsland
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The king rules over the castle tower,
And lords it over land,
And many a gallant champion leads
All arm'd and sword in hand.

Then let the peasant till his farm,
His horse. the trooper guide,
The king of Denmark, him alone,
O'er fort and tower preside.

King Diderick sits on Bratingsborg,
Looks over land and sea;
"I know not one in all this world,
"Dares match himself with roe/'

"And yet," said Brand of Wifferlin,
For he had wander'd far,
"There's one whom I could show thee, king,
"A match for thee in war.

"King Isak is that champion's name,
"He dwells in Birtingsland,
"And leads such warriors in his train,
"As can a wolf withstand.

"He leads such warriors in his train,
"As oft have fought the bear;
"The flesh and blood of Christian men
"His foul but only fare.

"Each morning, soon as dawns the day,
"Hell -food he loves to gnaw,
"Toads, vipers, efts and poisonous herbs
"To spice his fiendish maw."

In stepp'd to the hall a little page,
And stood before the board;
"The tribute fix'd a year ago
"'Tis time ye pay my lord."

"I'll nevermore the tribute give
"I hitherto have paid;
"Will rather march to Birtingsland,
"And there unsheathe my blade."

With joy rose Hwitting Helfred's son,
And laugh'd with all his heart;
"If you to Birtingsland will go,
"I'm here to take my part'

"Last year thou wast in Birtingsland,
"And there thy horse hast lost;
"'Twere best, I trow, to stay at home,
"Or dear thy game may cost"

"Rather than stay at Bratingsborg,
"I'd lose a foot and hand;
"Nay, if no horse I have to ride,
"On foot I'll join your band."

The troop that rode from Bratingsborg,
So solid was and great,
The stones were crushed, the trembling earth
Gave way beneath their weight.

Foremost of all king Diderick rode,
A lion upon his shield,
And on it shone the golden crown
Afar across the field.

With gleaming crown of ruddy gold
The royal Diderick rode,
And next him Vidrick Verlandson
His tongs and hammer show'd.

Next follow'd Siward, Hasty swain,
With brightly polish'd spear,
And then came Brand of Wifferlin
Who knew no sense of fear.

Next him the Hero Hogen rode
All blooming like a maid;
And then rode Folker Spilleman,
In hand his naked blade.

Next after them young Alf of Yern,
His horse a noble dan,
And then the young knight Homme rlom,
Sir Holmboe Jensen's son.

Bold Gynther next and Gemot rode
With arrows laid on bow,
And then rode Sonne Folkerson
With courage on his brow.

Next them the little Grimmer came
With burnish'd coat of mail,
And Seier, in battle field so prompt,
Was never seen to quail.

The next rode Master Hildebrand,
Who sat so well his steed,
And then the stout monk Alsing rode,
Had earn'd a champion's meed.

They went away from Bratingsborg
In full array and force;
Behind walk'd Hwitting Helfred's son,
For he had lost his horse.

So long ran Hwitting Helfred's son,
His face with anger glow'd;
He struck a warrior off his horse,
And mounted it, and rode.

The good king Diderick turn'd him round,
Was riding in the van;
"On horseback now I see the swain
"Who barefoot lately ran.

"But hark thee, Hwitting Helfred's son,
"And hear what I would say;
"'Tis thou shalt march to Birtingsland,
"And make them tribute pay.

"Aye!" answer'd Hwitting Helfred's son,
And laugh'd with hearty glee,
"And if I go to Birtingsland,
"We'll go but only three."

"Then take thee Vidrick Verlandson
"And Diderick, him of Bern;
"These are of all my gallant men
The last their backs to turn."

They mounted horse, those stalwart three,
And long the way they rode,
And, but the simple truth to tell,
Most fiery tempers show'd.

The watchman high on turret stands,
And looks around so far;
"Yonder I see three champions come,
"Methinks they're bent on war.

"The one is Hwitting Helfred's son,
A tried and stubborn foe;
"The same was here and lost his horse,
"'Tis now a year ago.

"The next is Vidrick Verlandson,
"His hammer and tongs withal;
"The third is Diderick, he of Bern,
"Three champions stout and tall.

Their horses in the yard they left
And into the castle strode,
And, truth to tell, without delay
Their ruthless spirit show'd.

The porter near the gate they seized
And chopp'd in morsels small,
And in they strode before the king,
Into the lofty hall

Isak, the king of Birtingsland,
He rose, and this his word;
"Now whence are come these desperate men,
"Who stand before my board?"

Up then the royal butler spake,
Who pour'd the wine and mead;
"Let us but take our spears in hand,
"We'll drive them back with speed."

But Helfred's son the braggart seiz'd
All by his shaggy beard,
And beat his head, till floor and wall
With reeking brains were smear'd.

Aye farther, Hwitting Helfred's son
A dismal jest to make,
He toss'd the body upon the board;
"Who broils for me the steak?"

Stepp'd forward Diderick, he of Bern,
And sword from scabbard drew,
King Isak in his navel stabb'd,
And ran his body through.

And on fWi'd Vidrick Verlandson,
And clear'd himself a ring;
He left fall forty champions dead
Around their slaughter'd king.

In tears king Isak's mother came,
And old was she and gray;
With her those heroes, truth to tell,
Strange games began to play.

In anger Hwitting Helfred's son
His sword upon her drew,
But she in sunder kiss'd the blade,
And shiver'd off it flew.

His trusty blade she kiss'd in twain,
In shivers made it fly;
But her he seiz'd by both her legs,
And whirl'd her up on high.

She changed her form to a screaming crane,
And off to the welkin flew,
But he drew on a feather dress,
And flew to the welkin too.

They flew all day, they flew for three,
Untired still on they went,
Till by her legs the crane he seized,
And into morsels rent.

And that day's pastime ending so,
All arm'd and sword in hand,
They left king Isak's warriors dead,
And rode from Birtingsland.

poems.title: King Diderick and the Dragon
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The good king Diderick mounted horse
And rode to Bern away,
And found a lion and lothely worm
In fierce and bloody fray.

One day they had fought, and eke the next,
And all the third as well;
At night the lion could no more,
And down on the green-sward fell.

In great distress the lion cried,
As near him rode the king;
"O good King Diderick, pity me,
"And speedy succour bring.

"Come to my aid, thou gallant king,
"Make good thy glorious name,
"Since blazon'd upon thy shield I stand
"All glowing like a flame."

King Diderick stood in anxious thought
Some little while aside;
"This noble lion help I must,
"Whatever may betide."

Thereon king Diderick spurr'd his steed,
And drew his trusty sword,
And with that lothely lindworm closed,
And deep the monster gored.

Right stoutly laid the king about,
He hew'd with might and main,
Till at the hilt by dint of blows
His good sword brake in twain.

Him grasp'd the worm beneath her tail.
His horse beneath her tongue,
And bare them into a mountain cave
As meat to feed her young.

The king she into a corner toss'd,
But gave her young the steed;
"There, children, eat that morsel up,
"I'll sleep before I feed.

"Content ye, children, while I rest,
"With this the coarser fare;
"The man, when I wake up again,
"With all of you I'll share."

Pent in that lothely lindworm cave
He search'd it round and round,
And found the sword call'd Adelring!
That famous sword he found!

He knew the finely temper'd blade,
He knew the gilded knife;
"Ha, Sigfred! rest thy soul in peace!
"Thou here hast lost thy life.

"In many a fight I've stood with thee,
"In many a long campaign,
"But never did I know before,
"That here my friend was slain."

With joy the king his weapon grasp'd,
Its temper sought to know,
And struck the cavern's flinty side,
Till all was in a glow.

As saw the lindworm's elder son
Their cavern flash with flame,
"Who now," said he, "in her own house
"The hostess puts to shame?"

With wrath that little lindworm boil'd,
And fierce and fiercer grew;
"Who dares in her own dwelling house
"The hostess harm to do?"

Then spake the other lindworm young,
That in the corner lay;
"Should but our mother wake from sleep,
"How thou wilt rue the day!"

In wrath king Diderick thus replied,
For fierce of mood was he;
"From sleep I'll quickly rouse her up,
"And cold her dream shall be.

"Thy dam a knight of noblest birth,
"The brave King Sigfred slew;
"His death I'll with a heavy hand
"Avenge on each of you."

Up then the mother lindworm woke,
And much she shook with fear;
"Who then is this, disturbs my rest?
"Who makes such clamour here?"

"'Tis I — king Diderick, king of Bern,
"A word with thee I crave,
"The same whom coil'd beneath thy tail,
"Thou broughtest to thy cave."

"O good king Diderick, slay me not,
"My heaps of treasure take;
"We'll here instead of useless strife
"A bond of friendship make."

"Full many a knight hast thou devour'd,
"Allur'd by crafty wile;
"But never more so shaft thou me
"Or other one beguile."

"O good king Diderick, hear my prayer,
"And deign my life to save,
"And I will show thee where thy bride
"Lies hidden in the cave.

"Above my head the keys are hung,
"Which lock her prison door,
"And at my feet thy trulove lies
"Beneath the cavern floor."

"Above and with thy lying head
"Shall be the work begun,
"And down below and at thy feet
"Thy slaughter first be done/'

He straight the mother lindworm slew,
And then the eleven young,
But through the venom fear'd to step,
That dripp'd from off her tongue.

Before -his feet he dug a trench
To drain away the blood;
For well he knew, with death was fraught
That boiling poisonous flood.

King Diderick loudly curs'd the lion,
And angry he be.came;
"Light every curse and foul reproach
"Upon that lion's name!

'"Twas he brought me to this distress,
"May God reward his deed!
"Had he not stood upon my shield,
"I had ridden out my steed."

His voice the noble lion heard,
For loud king Diderick cried;
"Now wait, good king; I'll with my claw
"Dig through the cavern's side.

The lion dug, King Diderick hew'd,
The cave was all ablaze;
The king but for the lion's help
Had ended there his days.

He now had fell'd his monster foe,
And all her young ones slain,
And arm'd with shield and coat of mail
Came out upon the plain.

But though from prison he was free,
He much bewail'd his steed,
For oft they had each the other help'd
In time of urgent need.

"Now hear me, Diderick, hear me, king,
"And cease thy grief and care;
"Up! mount thee on my shaggy back,
"And thee I'll gladly bear."

So over meadow, hill, and dale
Right gaily rode the man,
As homeward through the forest glades
The grateful lion ran.

And comrades were the lion and king
In every field of strife;
For each had proved the other's friend,
And saved each other's life.

Beside him, when he rode afield,
Would run the faithful beast,
And laid his head in Diderick's lap,
When sat the king at feast.

From this his name of 'Lion knight'
The brave king Diderick bare,
And lifelong true in war and peace
Remained that faithful pair.

poems.title: Vidrick Verlandson and Wolf of Yern
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Childe Wolf of Yern to sessions rode,
And stood before the King;
"O lend me men for a father's death
"A full revenge to wring."

"I'll freely lend thee a troop of men,
"Myself will with thee go,
"But pray thou Vidrick Verlandson
"To aid thy feebler blow.

"I lend thee troopers, mail clad all,
"My bravest men and best:
"Vidrick and Diderick the stout
"Bring low the loftiest crest.

"Two heroes they both strong and brave,
"Victors in many a fight;
"Their very names in every land
"The boldest fill with fright;'

In strode to the hall the Danish King
Bright as a burning flame;
Now who of you, ye Danish men,
"Will aid my kinsman's claim?"

The king came forward, where they sat,
A silver cup in hand;
"Who of my gallant troopers here
"Will join my kinsman's band?"

They answer'd naught, but to their lips
Their hoods in silence press'd,
Save only Vidrick Verlandson,
Who turn'd their fears to jest.

"For me' said Vidrick Verlandson
In tone of merry cheer,
"'Twould be like drinking a cup of mead,
"If once we cross'd a spear."

Diderick to hear what Vidrick said
So fierce and angry grew,
Their heads he lopp'd from troopers twain,
And at the King's feet threw.

"'Twere best," said Vidrick Verlandson
For glory all athirst,
"We steal not on them unawares,
"But send an envoy first."

That errand took young Helmer Gray,
And sped so fleet from town,
That dumb were all who saw him pass,
And every eye cast down.

The bold young Helmer Gray it was,
So bright with golden lace,
Whom neither hawk nor hound could beat,
Or hold him equal pace.

In came the bold young Helmer Gray,
And stood before the board;
A clever wight in parley he
To choose the fittest word.

"Hail, king of Brattens Vendel, hail!
"And Knights, who form thy train!
"Tomorrow comes Childe Wolf of Yern
"To venge a father slain."

"Wiser did Wolf to stay at home,
"And drive afield his kine,
"Than challenge send, and seek to match
"His puny strength with mine.

"Wiser would he, like some vile worm,
"Go creep beneath a stone,
"Than combat where a stouter man,
"His sire, was overthrown.

"Wiser did he to stay at home,
"And under brambles hide;
"His father stood me blows but nine,
"Still less will he abide."

"Hark! king of Brattens Vendel, hark!
"Keep teeth before your tongue;
"The whelp grows up with rending fangs,
"Remains not always young."

"There's not a man in all the world,
"For whom I need to fear,
"Save only Vidrick Verlandson,
"And he's not very near. M

"Ah not replied young Helmer Gray,
And struck the boaster dumb,
"'Tis even Vidrick Verlandson,
"Who with his men will come."

Then up and spake a trooper bold;
"Who that is, I can tell;
"His father was the famous smith,
"I know that champion well.

"Once on a time at Birtingsborg
"Our warriors all were met,
"And Vidrick play'd a wondrous game,'
"I never shall forget.

"Fifteen our stoutest men he fell'd
"With many a jest and jeer;
"I stood close by, and saw it all,
"And pale I was with fear."

"Now hark thee, good young Helmer Gray,
"A prayer I make to thee;
"What thou canst tell of Verlandson,
"Conceal it not from me."

"If Vidrick lay in his chamber sick,
"And could no longer ride,
"There's left to meet your force afield
"Enough brave men beside."

Then spake the Brattens Vendel king,
Spake like a man, did he:
"I'll meet him on the battle-field,
"If horse can carry me."

But up a trooper rose, and thus
His braggart speech begun;
"Vidrick! we'll never shrink from him,
"A low-bred collier's son."

Young Helmer Gray was standing near,
And, fired at what he said,
Struck him but once, and on the earth
Down fell the trooper dead.

"What!" said the Brattens Vendel king,
And spake in angry heat,
"What! strike my bravest champion dead
"Before my very feet!"

"My maxim", said young Helmer Gray,
"I need not seek to hide;
"I'll never bear that any man
"Vidrick or me deride."

Then said that bold young Helmer Gray
That raging thirst he found;
"So prithee, Brattens Vendel king,
"Let drink be handed round."

They brought him eighteen quarts of ale,
He drank them one by one,
And 'fore the king to fifty bits
He kick'd the empty tun.

Then off he ran, young Helmer Gray,
The news to his lord to bring;
"Now sharpen spear, and polish sword,
"Tomorrow comes the King."

Across the black and pathless heath
They rode in murk of night,
But from their armour, bright as day,
There gleam'd a guiding light.

They rode by night o'er Birting's plain,
They rode through Birting's moor,
Seven hundred warriors they were strong,
And costly armour wore.

Soon as they came to Birting's town,
Their men in ring they, drew,
And valiant Vidrick Verlandson
For captain chose anew.

A flag, whereon a lion gleam'd,
They raised on Birting's heath,
And doom'd was many a guiltless man
That day to meet his death.

They hack'd with sword, they shot with how,
They did not stint nor tire;
The crimson sweat ran off their limbs,
Their bucklers sparkled fire.

Then spake the Brattens Vendel king,
As through his helm he peer VI,
"What captain leads their troops today
"By all my men so fear'd?"

Thereto replied the little page
Who rode next at his side;
"There's none but Vidrick Verlandson,
"That fiery horse could ride."

Said one who knew the champion well,
One of the royal band;
"'Tis truly Vidrick Verlandson
"And Mimmering in his hand/'

Then look'd again the Vendel king
Through visor's narrow bar;
"Against that Tongs and Hammer shield
"'Tis useless waging war.

"I march to certain death today,
"Vidrick leaves none alive;
" Against that Tongs and Hammer shield
"It's vain for me to strive.

"Heathen or. Christian man alike
"To battle I defy,
"Save only Vidrick Verlandson,
"For him no match am I."

And off the Brattens Vendel king
Spurr'd fiercely o'er the down,
And Vidrick Verlandson assail'd,
And fain had overthrown.

His blows the Brattens Vendel king
Let fall so fast and hard,
That Vidrick nothing else could do,
Than stand awhile on guard.

"I've stood thee fairly eighteen blows,
"As fast as blows could fall;
"I charge thee on thy kingly name
'"To stand me one for all."

"If thou hast stood me eighteen blows,
"I'll do for thee the same;
"I'll stand unflinching eighteen blows,
"Nor stain my kingly name."

About his helmet bright with gold
A silken thread he bound;
"My bride hear not that hand of smith
"Dealt me the mortal wound!"

A word to Mimmering Vidrick spake,
"Now, Mimmering, do thy best,
"'Tis many years, since last the time
"I hew'd with equal zest."

He firmly clench'd his Mimmering's hilt,
With all his might he hove;
And the proud King from gilded helm
Down to his saddle clove.

Then shouted Vidrick Verlandson
Under the mountain side;
"Is none of all your troopers left
"A joust with me to ride?"

Dead lies the Brattens Vendel king,
His blood streams on the heath,
And glad at heart is Wolf of Yern
To've venged his father's death.

Around him o'er the battle-field
Young Helmer gazed his fill;
"These boasters lie. like sleeping mice,
"So mute they're all and still."

With Wolf rode home the King's men all,
And joy on every tongue,
That Vidrick for a father's death
A full revenge had wrung.

poems.title: Childe Orm and the Berm Giant
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the mighty Bermeriis,
A monster large and tall,
So mad was he, no strength of man
His fury held in thrall.

It was the mighty Bermeriis
Girt on his sword so bright,
And rode away to the royal court
A worthy foe to fight.

"Hail, Danish king! here then you sit,
"And at your board preside;
"Your daughter you shall give to me,
"And realm with me divide.

"Either your daughter you shall give,
"And kingdom with me share,
"Or find a champion bold enough
"A joust with me to dare."

"Neither my daughter shalt thou have,
"Nor yet the half my land,
"But e'en a bold and gallant knight
"To fight thee hand to hand."

It was the stately Danish king
Strode up his castle hall;
"Now who will win a lovely maid
"Among my warriors all?"

There sat those champions all so still,
None answer'd him a word,
Except childe Orm, the youngest swain,
And lowest at the board.

"Your daughter will you give to me,
"And share with me your land?
"Then here there stands the champion,
"Will meet him hand to hand"

It was the stately Danish king
Met him with scornful taunt;
"And who is then the puny mouse,
"Dares make this haughty vaunt?"

"It is no puny mouse I am,
"Tho' such the name you gave;
"For father I king Sigfred claim,
"Who perish'd in the cave."

"And is King Sigfred then thy sire?
"His features I can trace,
"But scarcely fifteen years, I ween,
"Have bronzed that beardless face."

At evening tide, the hour when swains
Their steeds to water bring,
It listed Orm, the youthful swain,
To wake the sleeping king.

So hard childe Orm, the youthful swain,
The tomb began to pound,
That all its massive marble walls
Were shaken to the ground.

"Who wakes me up before my time?
"Who dares disturb my bones?
"Can I not e'en repose in peace
"Beneath these heavy stones?"

"'Tis I wake thee before thy time,
"'Tis I this deed have done,
"But not to cause thee grief or pain,
"Childe Orm, thy youngest son."

"And is it thou art come, childe Orm,
"My youngest son so clear?
"And is it gold, or silver plate,
"Or coin, thou seekest here?"

"I want nor gold, nor silver plate,
"Nor coin from out thy grave,
"But all to win a lovely maid
"Sword Birting come to crave."

"Birting, my sword, thou shalt not get
"To win for thee the bride,
"Till thou hast venged thy father's blood
"In Iceland, where he died."

"And if I Birting cannot get,
"And win the boon I crave,
"With massive rock I'll pound thy tomb,
"And crush thee in the grave."

He gave him Birting from out his tomb,
The hilt into his hand;
"Grasp it with firm and dauntless mood,
"And thee shall none withstand."

Childe Orm it was, the youthful swain,
Girt on the sword so bright,
And strode into the castle hall,
And long'd his foe to fight.

Up went childe Orm, the youthful swain,
Before the board to stand;
"Where skulk those vaunting troopers now,
"Last evening were so grand?"

All mute those Danish courtiers sat,
Nor answered him a word;
But one, the mighty Bermeriis,
He sprang across the board.

Thus spake the mighty Bermeriis,
And this reply made he,
"Swear that sword Birting thou hast not,
"Before I fight with thee."

"Birting I swear I do not hold,
"Nor know that famous brand,
"Under his tomb my father lies,
"And grasps it in his hand."

They drew with two bright gilded shields
A circle on the mould,
And sooth were standing there to fight
Two champions stout and bold.

And on the pear-bush drizzled rain,
And rain on the pear-tree,
And he, that mighty Bermeriis,
Was cut across the knee.

"With many a knight and champion
"I've fought with stab and blow,
"But never yet was warrior law
"To strike a man so low."

"So short was I, and thou so tall,
"And thence the seeming breach,
"I struck no higher than thy knee,
"Nor higher could I reach/'

Childe Orm it was, the youthful swain,
To Iceland steer'd his snake,
Would for his father foully slain
A deadly vengeance take.

Childe Orm it was, the youthful swain,
Stepp'd out upon the strand,
And there he Gerd and Arland met
Walking upon the sand.

"Welcome ashore, thou brave young man,
"From off the stormy main!
"And tell us, is to manhood grown
"Childe Orm the youthful swain?"

"That Orm, the youthful swain, ye see,
"Sail'd hither o'er the brine;
"I come to venge a father's death,
"Or claim of you the fine."

Arland and Gerd with point of sword
Began to spirt the earth;
"Fine for thy father thou shalt get
"Never a penny's worth."

They drew with three bright gilded shields
A circle upon the mould,
And, sooth, were standing there to fight
Three champions stout and bold.

They fought a day, they fought for twain,
The third day even so,
And hold or vantage neither one
Could get upon his foe.

Then thus a friendly mermaid spake
Down in her ocean cell;
"Now hark thee, Orm, thou youthful swain,
"Thy sword is under spell.

"And hark thee, Orm, thou youthful swain,
"Thy sword in spell is bound,
"But swing it three times round thy head,
"And stick it in the ground."

He swung it three times round his bead,
And stabb'd it in the mould,
Heav'd then one blow, and at his feet
Both Gerd and Arland roll'd.

When so he had venged his father's blood
In Iceland, where he died,
He back to the royal court return'd
To claim his lovely bride.

And happy now the youthful swain,
That alt his toil is done;
He nightly sleeps in peace and bliss
With her his valour won.

Quit is Childe Orm, the youthful swain,
Of care and all alarm;
And sleeps, as pleased and glad as he,
His trulove on his arm.

poems.title: Rodengard and the Eagle
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the rich Sir Rodengard
In green-wood went to ride,
And met the eagle of Beedelund
At early morning tide.

"Now list, thou rich Sir Rodengard,
"Why ridest thou alone?
"Where is thy hawk, and where thy hound,
"And where thy followers gone?"

"Some are on land, and some at sea
"Are ploughing through the foam,
"And I myself to shoot the deer
"In green-wood forest roam."

"If these wild deer, that are my meat,
"Thou darest thus to slay,
"Right dearly, rich Sir Rodengard,
"Thy shooting thou shalt pay."

"I've beasts at home, both ox and cow,
"And foal, and fatted steed;
"Tis little, eagle of Beedelund,
"That I thy visit heed."

'Tis not for ox, 'tis not for cow,
"Or foal or steed I come;
"But trust me, rich Sir Rodengard,
"I'll visit thee at home.

"I'll on thy castle yard descend,
"I'll choose me out the best,
"And both thy handsome sisters too
"Shall have me there for guest."

"Those maids I've loved and cherish'd both,
"E'er since their father died;
"Forbid it heaven, that aught of ill
"Those blossoms should betide!"

"If with thy right good hearty will
"I cannot feed on these,
"Then on that mirror of womanhood,
"Thy trulove, I will seize."

So stoop'd the rich Sir Rodengard,
And on a linden rind
He wrote with skill the potent runes,
He long had borne in mind.

He bound the eagle of Beedelund
High on the linden bough;
"And so, fierce eagle, think no more
"To get my trulove now."

There sits the eagle of Beedelund,
And starving droops his wing,
And on rides rich Sir Rodengard,
And makes his charger spring.

There starves the eagle of Beedelund,
All sitting on the spray,
And glad is rich Sir Rodengard,
And holds his wedding day.

poems.title: Ravngard and Memering
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Dame Gunild, she dwells in Spire,
And her the great and rich admire,
The Dame Gunild.

To woo her suitors come from South
In rich array and prime of youth,
To Dame Gunild.

To woo her suitors come from West,
The wealthiest, bravest and the best,
To Dame Gunild.

To woo her suitors come from North,
Men of well-earn'd renown and worth,
To Dame Gunild.

To woo her suitors come from East,
For wealth and bravery not the least,
To Dame Gunild.

To woo her too Duke Henry came,
And fate decreed them woe and shame.
The Dame Gunild!

He woo'd and brought her home for wife;
Behind them followed storm and strife,
The Dame Gunild.

The Duke to war must march away,
And her to guard bade Ravngard stay,
The Dame Gunild.

"Of Brunswick, Sleswick, Spire take care,
"But chiefly watch my consort dear,
"The Dame Gunild."

As steer'd the Duke his ship from land,
Rode Ravngard off along the strand,
To Dame Gunild.

He round him wrapp'd his scarlet cloak,
And up to the lady went and spoke,
To Dame Gunild.

"Hear now, I pray, my lord's last word,
"And fetch me Adelring, his sword,
"My Dame Gunild."

"No such behest gave me the Duke,
"When lately leave from me he took.
Said Dame Gunild.

"Unless you give me Adelring,
"A charge against you I shall bring,
"My Dame Gunild."

"Lie as thou wilt, on thee the shame,
"For God will prove me free from blame/'
Said Dame Gunild.

The Duke from war march'd home again,
And Ravngard met the glittering train;
From Dame Gunild.

"How has it fared with Spire this year?
"And how is she, my wife so dear,
"The Dame Gunild?"

"Your land is in its wonted state,
"But ill has lived your wife of late,
"The Dame Gunild.' '

"Ravngard, thy charge I deem untrue,
"For faithlessness I never knew
"In Dame Gunild."

"'Tis what myself have seen with pain,
"Gunild has with th' Archbishop lain,
"The Dame Gunild."

"I'll smite her down with heavy hand,
"And none shall dare my wroth withstand,
"Her, Dame Gunild."

The Duke his scarlet mantle hent,
And up to his consort's chamber went,
To Dame Gunild.

Gunild, as near her door he drew,
Rose up to show him honour due;
The Dame Gunild.

"Welcome my noble Lord again!
"How fared you in your late campaign?"
Said Dame Gunild.

"Most lucky had I deem'd this year,
"Such deeds of thee did I not hear,
"My Dame Gunild."

"My gracious lord, oh, say not so;
"Of wrong or crime I nothing know."
Said Dame Gunild.

"It little boots to plead or feign,
"For with th' Archbishop thou hast lain,
"My Dame Gunild."

With ruthless hand he dealt the blows,
Nor one to help his lady rose,
The Dame Gunild.

None but two courtly dames would dare
To pray the Duke her life to spare,
The Dame Gunild's.

"My lord, be not this charge believ'd;
"With lying tale you've been deceived
"Of Dame Gunild."

"Let her then seek her out a knight,
"Who does a joust with Ravngard fight,
"The Dame Gunild."

Bare, head and foot, her garments rent,
From out her door in sorrow went
The Dame Gunild.

With tears she sought the banquet hall,
Where sat and drank the champions all,
The Dame Gunild.

Those knights, as towards the door she drew,
Stood up to show her honour due,
To Dame Gunild.

"Is here within a gallant knight,
"Will for an injured lady fight,
"For Dame Gunild?"

Her cause would no one undertake,
Mute all, till Memering rose and spake,
"O Dame Gunild!

"For fifteen years I serv'd your sire,
"Fed at his board, and took his hire,
"My Dame Gunild;

"But saw you never in such a plight,
"With thin and tatter'd raiment dight,
"My Dame Gunild;

"Never my master's child have seen
"Walk barefoot o'er the castle green,
"My Dame Gunild.

"To some the merchant coin he told,
"To some with caps he measur'd gold,
"My Dame Gunild;

"On Ravngard he the most bestow'd,
"The one who first has treason show'd
"My Dame Gunild:

"I've ever sat at table-end,
Whither good gifts are wont to wend,
"My Dame Gunild;

"And now for you I'll take the field,
"If Adelring to me you'll yield,
"My Dame Gunild."

"If thou wilt take the field for me,
"The sword I'll gladly fetch for thee."
Said Dame Gunild.

On the bare mould they drew a ring,
Where each his sword and shield should bring
For Dame Gunild.

"A solemn oath thou now shalt swear,
"That Adelring thou dost not wear,
"For Dame Gunild."

"So help me God! to me is known
"Above the ground its hilt alone."
The Dame Gunild!

"And now an oath thou too shalt swear,
"That thou sword Southwind dost not bear."
The Dame Gunild!

"So help me God from pain and woe!
"That Southwind sword I do not know."
The Dame Gunild!

The first blow Ravngard on him laid,
In twain he sunder'd Memering's blade.
The Dame Gunild.

"Now," said the Duke, "may all men see,
"How true is what is charg'd to thee:
"My Dame Gunild."

"The charge, my lord, is still untrue,
"The broke my champion's sword in two."
Said Dame Gunild.

The first blow Memering on him laid,
In twain he sunder'd Ravngard's blade,
For Dame Gunild.

"Hold up now, Memering, stand aside,
"And wait till I my shoe have tied."
The Dame Gunild!

Down to the greensward Ravngard bent
And so his good sword Southwind hent.
The Dame Gunild!

"This villain perjury thou shalt mourn;
"Thy guilty soul hast thou forsworn."
The Dame Gunild!

The first blow Ravngard on him laid,
In twain he sunder'd Memering's blade.
The Dame Gunild -

"Stay, Ravngard, now stand thou aside,
"And wait till I my shoe have tied."
The Dame Gunild!

Down to the greensward Memering bent,
And Adelring his sword he hent.
For Dame Gunild!

"This perjury thou too hast to mourn,
"Thy guilty soul hast thou forsworn,
"For Dame Gunild."

"Nay, for I sware to me was known
Above the earth its hilt alone."
The Dame Gunild!

The first blow Memering on him laid,
In twain he sunder'd Ravngard's blade;
For Dame Gunild.

Memering heav'd yet one other blow,
And headless fell his guilty foe
"Fore Dame Gunild.

"See there, my lord, thy champion's fate,
"And now thy groundless wrath abate."
Said Dame Gunild.

"For now, my lord, yourself may see,
"That Ravngard basely lied on me."
Said Dame Gunild.

Duke Henry tapp'd her cheek so fair,
"Forgive me, and be again as dear,
"My Dame Gunild."

The gallant Memering homeward sped,
With broken shins and bleeding head,
To Dame Gunild.

"Now, Lady, for thy father's soul
"My life long give me bread and bowl,
"My Dame Gunild."

"Memering, my champion, stout and leal,
"Fear not, thy wounds myself will heal."
Said Dame Gunild.

"And all thy days I'll give thee bread,
"And clothe thee too in scarlet red."
Said 'Dame Gunild.

poems.title: Memering
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The smallest man was Mimering
In all the realm of Karl the king.
My loveliest maidens.

Before him yet his mother bare,
Were made the clothes he was to wear.

Before he well could walk upright,
His limbs with coat of mail were dight.

Before he e'en began to ride,
He girt a broadsword on his side;

And soon as he the sword could wield,
He sallied out and took the field.

On battle bent he paced the strand,
Where lay the merchantmen at land.

He saw beneath the mountain side
A mailclad warrior towards him ride.

The stranger gallop'd up with speed,
And fierce as lion look'd his steed.

"List, knight, and say, dost thou desire
"To take in pay a faithful squire?"

"Methinks thou'rt yet too young and frail
"To bear my heavy coat of mail."

Enraged, and prompt to avenge a slight,
From off his horse he knock'd the knight;

Nor wrought him that disgrace alone,
But beat his head against a stone:

Then mounted horse, and long'd to fight
With some more brave and doughty knight

He reach'd a wood, and riding on
Encounter'd Vidrick Verlandson.

"Well met, brave knight, art thou in heart
"To fight and take thy lady's part?"

'Twas Vidrick Verlandson replied,
"Ready, and be thy valour tried."

They fought one day, aye did they twain,
But neither could the victory gain;

So swore they friendship, firm and pure,
That should till judgement day endure.

But how should they be friends for life?
And that same night renew'd their strife!
My loveliest maidens.

poems.title: The Bald-head Monk
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There lies a cloister behind a wood,-
Its vanes with gold ablaze;
And standing before it are champions twelve,
That cloister sworn to raze.

To plunder and raze those cloister walls
Twelve stalwart champions stood,
And seized and slaughter'd both ox and cow,
That serv'd the monks for food.

The bald-head Monk from his window look'd,
And rattled the beams and wall;
"What! are then our foes no more than these?
"I'll meet them and fight them all."

The Monk he call'd to his serving boy,
"Knave, fetch me my massive club;
"I'll up and off to the forest go,
"And yonder champions drub."

Fifteen were the men who brought it in,
As many they were, or more,
The Monk his club with his fingers two
As deft and as gaily bore.

The Monk he shouldered his massive club,
And off to the greenwood hied;
And waiting to seize him and bind his limbs
Twelve champions there espied.

They drew a ring on the heathy ground,
Sang each to the other a lay,
And doleful enough, to say the truth,
The measure they sung that day.

He first slew four, and he then slew five,
And all at a blow the rest,
And started away, the bald-head Monk,
Of worthier foes in quest.

It listed him then, the bald-head Monk,
To go on a wider tour,
And off to the wood he paced his way
So leisurely o'er the moor.

Away to the wood he boldly strode
O'er meadow and mountain fell,
And met there the lothly and vicious Trold,
The one call'd Sivard Giell.

"Now tell me, art thou the selfsame Monk,
"Who wrought on our champions woe?
"And wilt thou rather like craven fly?
"Or stand to me blow for blow?"

"In truth I am still that selfsame Monk,
"Who wrought on the champions woe,
"Nor will I rather like craven fly,
"But stand to thee blow for blow."

The Trold began, and he struck the Monk
So flat on his shaven crown,
That blood from his brawny shoulders burst,
And dripp'd from his garments down.

But now the Monk in his turn laid on,
And stretch'd the Trold at his length;
"O curses on thee, thou bald-head Monk!
"Too well do I feel thy strength.

"But stay thy hand, thou bald-head Monk,
"And strike me, I pray, no more;
"I'll heap thee with gold and silver too
"And coin that I have in store.

As tall as on foot the stalwart Monk,
Was down on his knees the Trold,
And, creeping, he show'd him a secret cell
With fifteen doors of gold.

He led him the road to a secret cell
With fifteen golden doors,
And all that the Monk could carry away,
He took of the treasured stores.

The gold to his cloister and silver too
Seven loads he carried away,
And bade them to send another one out,
Who better his club could play.

When daylight waned, and the cheerfull sun
To slumber had sunk below,
The Monk had still to his cloister home
Fifteen long miles to go.

The sun from out of the glowing west
Beneath the earth had sunk,
And yet the dish that the first was serv'd,
The Abbot's, — that took the Monk.

Because for the soup he had to wait,
Fifteen monks' heads he broke,
Because the fish was still in the pot,
Fifteen of them hung to smoke.

"Alas!" said aloud the serving boy,
While fetching the grits for soup,
"Whenever the Monk to cloister comes,
To this we shall have to stoop."

He struck the Abbot across the eye,
And knock'd it out of his head,
Because he was sitting beyond the time,
That folk should be gone to bed.

Up started the Abbot, and left the board,
No longer be dared to stay;
And great indeed was the grief and pain,
He bad to endure that day.

The morrow had dawn'd, and cloister bells
So merry began to ring,
But matins or lesson the bald-head Monk
Would neither read nor sing.

Among the monks and the nuns he went
All sitting in cloister quire,
Nor dared they one of them read or sing
For fear of that bald-head's ire.

At last the Abbot, good holy man,
Was forced to resign his stall,
And then was seated the bald-head Monk
As Abbot above them all.

That cloister for thirty years or more
He govern'd with pomp and pride;
Nor e'er has the like of the bald-head Monk
Been Abbot there, since he died.

poems.title: Sir Genselin
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the count Sir Genselin,
He thus to his mother cried;
"My manhood I would fain essay;
"I'll up the country ride."

"And wilt thou ride then up the land?
"Thy manhood there essay?
"I'll give thee a good and gallant steed,
"Men call him 'Carl the grey"

"Gird thee no sword upon thy side,
"Nor spur upon thy feet,
"Unless the champion Iver Blue
"Thou shouldest chance to meet."

It was the Count Sir Genselin,
Rode under a mountain side,
And there he met young Theedman Thinn,
And call'd and bade him 'Bide.'

"Well met! well met! young Theedman Thinn,
"What place have you rested at?"
"On Bratinsborg, where men at arms
"Were striking fire from hat."

Wrath was the Count Sir Genselin,
And crimson grew his cheek;
"I swear by heaven, young Theedman Thinn,
"Thy death-doom thou didst speak."

With that he drew his glittering sword,
And smote young Theedman dead;
That did the Count Sir Genselin,
And ill the youngster sped.

So rode he forth to Bratingsborg,
The gate with his spear-shaft beat;
"Is here a champion bold enough
"Me in a joust to meet?"

Then up and spake Sir Iver Blue,
A man so void of fear;
"Now help me God, but at the gate
"A champion's voice I hear."

So fierce did Count Sir Genselin
His hauberk on him fling,
That loud across three hides of land
His mother heard it ring.

The lady woke at midnight hour,
And loud to the Lord she pray'd;
"O heaven in mercy shield my son,
"In danger lend him aid!"

They rode and met, those champions two,
Rode both so firm and bold;
But off his horse Sir Iver Blue
Afar on the field was roll'd.

"Now listen, Count Sir Genselin,
"My life I prythee spare,
"I've e'en a handsome bride betroth'd,
"To thee I yield the fair."

"Keep thou thy bride, her need I not,
"I take not her to wife;
"Give me thy sister, Swollen-toe,
"I'll thank thee all my life."

So to the marriage feast they rode,
As best they found the way,
And ask'd the bravest champions,
That hands on they could lay.

They sent for Vidrick Verlandson,
Stout Diderick, him of Berne,
And Danish Olger, one whose heart
For fight did ever burn.

They sent for Master Hildebrand,
And Siward Hasty swain,
And twelve more mighty champions
To form the bridal train.

Thither the giant Langbane came
I'escort the gentle bride;
And thither young king Sigfred came,
And ill his grief could hide.

And there the lady Kfeem-molt stood,
And dress'd the bride with care;
She clad her legs in iron greaves,
Her hands in jewels rare.

Thither the lady Brynild came,
From off the northern wold,
And with her came to share the feast
A hundred champions bold.

To bridal house they led the bride,
She thought the hint was good;
She ate two whole ox-carcases,
And found them pleasant food.

Five tuns of ale the lady drank,
To swill the roast and broil'd,
And then a mess of porridge craved
In seven-tun kettle boil'd.

Into the hall they led the bride
Array'd in scarlet pall,
But, ere she through the door could pass,
Came down seven ells of wall.

The bride they led to her bridal bench,
And down thereon she sate;
Of marble stone the bench was built,
But crush'd beneath her weight.

Then up the bridegroom rose, and spake;
His brain began to reel;
"I never yet a bride have known,
"Could eat so large a meal."

They next a little dance began
Out on the grassy lea;
The smallest dancer there had ells
Fifteen below the knee.

Eighteen the tallest champions
Followed the dancing bride;
The rocks gave way, she trod upon,
As round she thought to glide.

Out on the field they mark'd a ring,
Where stood those champions bold;
They fain would for the bride do fight,
And tourney for her hold.

Up sprang the bride with heavy hand,
And partner meet she caught;
'Twas giant Langbane tripp'd with her,
And wondrous feats they wrought

For then it was the youthful bride
Began her pace to mend;
And fifteen champions dead she slew
With but her stay-lace end.

poems.title: Stout Diderick and Olger the Dane
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Holger Danske and Stout Didrik".
poems.text:
Stout Diderick up in Bermer land
With eighteen brothers dwelt;
And each of these twelve sons could boast,
Whose hand their foes had felt.

And twelve as stout and dauntless sons
His fifteen sisters bare;
Thirteen sons had the younger one.
Whom danger could not scare.

These champions stood before the cave,
And were so lofty each,
Their heads rose — 'tis the truth I tell —
Above the highest beech.

"For many a year, and far and wide,
"We've fought, and not in vain;
"In Denmark lives a worthier foe,
"King Olger, call'd the Dane.

"This Olger up in Jutland dwells,
"If true what we've been told,
"And dares to set our power at naught,
"And crown his head with gold."

Swerting, he seized a bar of steel,
"King Olger I despise;
"Myself I'd meet a hundred Danes,
"And drive them back like flies."

"Nay, Swerting, hark thee, swarthy wight,
"Deem not their prowess small,
"For well I know king Olger's men
"Are valiant heroes all"

Uprose the mighty Bermeriis,
And spake in all his pride;
"We'll thither march, and see if he
"Our onset dares abide."

With eighteen thousand mailclad men
They march'd from Bermer land;
They vow'd to be king Olger's guests,
And reach'd the Danish strand.

Stout Diderick straight an envoy sent,
And bade King Olger say,
If he would fight him on the field,
Or yearly tribute pay.

With scorn King Olger made reply,
"he could bear a taunt;
"Meet us thy braggart king afield,
"We'll make him rue his vaunt."

Olger to council call'd his men,
The case before them laid;
"Stout Diderick treads our Danish soil,
"And tribute will be paid."

Then thus replied his champions all,
And bold they spake and plain,
"If Diderick's men to Denmark come,
"They go not back again."

And these the names of Olger's men.
Folding, and Wolf of Yern,
Hogen and Vidrick Verlandson,
And Blue, and Koll the stern.

Olger the Dane and Diderick met,
Kings both so fierce of mood;
And round them, all athirst for fight,
Their countless champions stood.

They strove that day, for three they strove,
Would none to the other yield;
And sooth it was a stubborn strife,
And grim that battle field.

They met and fought with all their might
Out on the dingy heath;
And wrathful were those warriors all,
And fought for life and death.

The blood on hill and flowery vale
Ran bubbling like a stream;
The very sun look'd red with gore
Through clouds of dust and steam.

Then spake the lofty Bermeriis
In grief and sore dismay,
"We've scarcely a hundred left alive,
"How can we win the day?"

Stout Diderick took to his heels, and fled
O'er wooded hill and dale;
Swerting, at risk of neck and limbs,
Fled on his master's trail.

Stout Diderick call'd his scattered troops,
And look'd to the angry sky;
"My men, we find no shelter here,
"To" Berm land let us fly."

"Off then!" so spake young Wolf of Tern
Beneath the hill so green;
"'Tis little cause ye'll have to boast,
"That ye've in Denmark been."

Full eighteen thousand mail clad men
Had march'd from Berm away,
But five and fifty were the most,
Came from that deadly fray.

poems.title: Childe Norman's Riddle Rimes
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Childe Norman sat in ladies' bower,
With golden harp beguil'd the hour.
Look round about, Childe Norman.

He harp'd beneath his mantle skin,
Till came his mother stalking in.

'"Twere nobler game, methinks, to ride,
"And brunt of mounted champion bide;

"To venge a father foully slain,
"Than trill on lady's harp a strain."

Childe Norman belted sword to side,
And would in search of battle ride.

"When may I mix the wine for thee,
"And when expect thee back to me?"

"Soon as the stone shall take to flight,
"And grows the raven's feathers white."

"Never did stone take wing and fly,
"Or raven change his sooty die.

"True! stones were never wont to soar,
"And, mother, you see me no more."

"Here then with me I'll thee detain,
"Go thou shalt not, or go in vain.

"Ill luck thy every step betide!
"Ill luck thy sword in combat guide!"

He tapp'd his mother's lily cheek;
