"In kinder tone, dear mother, speak."

"I'll blessings on thy journey call,.
"And thee shall naught of ill befall;

"But victory to thy sword be bound,
"Thy horse with victory tread the ground."

He rode along, the mountain side,"
And there he saw a champion ride;

A lynx upon his shoulder hung,
A bear beside him stalk'd along.

"Hear, champion, what I say to thee,
"These creatures thou shalt change with me."

"No knight has dared my blow abide;
"Since at my hands King Carel died."

A bitter joy Childe Norman fill'd;
"Thou then it was; my father kill'd."

They fought that day, they fought for twain, "
And all the third they fought again;

As near its close the fourth day drew,
That doughty chief he fell'd and slew.

His sword to his side Childe Norman bound,
And journey'd forth to foreign ground.

Where first he reach'd a farmer's stead,
His flocks afield a shepherd led.

"Now hark thee, shepherd, what I say,
"The flocks thou drivest, — whose are they?

"Say what is rounder than a wheel,
"And where is spread the daintiest meal?"

"The sun's more round than any wheel,
"In Heaven is spread the daintiest meal."

"What is it fills these vallies all?
"And what sits robed in richest pall?"

"'Tis snow fills all the vales so white,
"And robed most richly sits the knight."

"What than a sloe can blacker stain?
"What louder sounds than voice of crane?"

"Blacker than any sloe is sin,
"Louder than crane the thunder's din."

"What bridge is't hath the broadest span?
"Whom thinkest thou the ugliest man?"

"Ice is the bridge with broadest span,
"The Dwarfking, he is the ugliest man.".

"Where doth the loftiest highway go?
"Where doth the foullest liquor flow?"

"To Heaven" the loftiest highway goes,
"In Hell the foullest liquor flows."

"Where is the fort with moated wall,
"Where champions drink in festive hall?"

"Here lies a fort with moated wall,
"Where champions drink in festive hall."

Childe Norman took a golden band,
And laid it on the shepherd's hand.

"Thine is the prize, and other none
"Aught from Childe Norman ever won."

Childe Norman belted sword to side,
Back to his mother's house to ride:

But when he reached it, near the gate
Fifteen the foullest witchwives sate.

His trusty sword Childe Norman drew,
And all those lothely witchwives slew.

But worst his mother fared of all,
Chopp'd to a thousand pieces small.

poems.title: Angelfyr and Helmer Kamp
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Alf, he dwelt at Otterscliff,
A man of wealth and fame;
And sons he had two gallant youths,
Had earn'd a champion's name.

Alf, he dwelt at Otterscliff,
And sons he had so bold,
The king's fair daughter they would woo
On Upsal's dreary wold.

Young Helmer Kamp his servants bade
His saddled steed to bring,
"We'll up the country, and claim for bride
"The daughter of Upsal's king."

Then rose and bade young Angelfyr
With speed his horse to girth,
"And we to Upsal too will ride,
"Beneath us crack the earth."

There, as within the court they come,
Their cloaks they round them fling,
And stride both into the lofty hall
Before the Upsal king.

In walk'd young Helmer Kamp the first,
And stood before the board;
"Sir, will ye me your daughter give?
"Deign me a gracious word."

Then up went haughty Angel fyr
Before the board to stand;
"King, thou shalt me thy daughter give,
"And quit, thyself, the land."

"Nay," so the king of Upsal spake
With stately mien and voice,
"To none will I my daughter give,
"But leave to her the choice."

"O hearty thanks, my father dear,
"That choose myself I can;
"Young Helmer Kamp will I betroth,'
"He is at least a man.

"But Angelfyr will I not have,
"I loathe his fiendish face,
"I loath his father and mother too,
"And all his heathen race."

Short answer made young Angelfyr,
Wroth at the maiden's slight;
"We'll down below to the castle yard,
"And settle that in fight."

Content the king of Upsal was,
And this for answer made;
"Their swords are sharp, the lads are hale,
"E'en let the game be play'd."

Alf listening stood at Otterscliff,
What sounds came o'er the hill,
And wafted heard in every breeze
The clank of swords so shrill.

Alf heard it over at Otterscliff,
As on the heath he stood;
"How have my sons then fallen out?
"And why so fierce of mood?"

He waited not a moment more,
But sprang on his horse so red
And rode across, and Upsal reach" d,
Before his sons were dead.

"Speak thou, and say, young Helmer Kamp,
"What is't, my dearest son,
"That pouring from thy wounded head
"These streams of blood should run?'"

Young Helmer Kamp his father heard,
And thus he spake in pain;
"That did my brother Angelfyr,
"The bride he could not gain.

"Fifteen my wounds, and death-wounds all,
"Stabb'd with a poison'd knife;
"With only one, for a single hour
"No art could save my life."

He turn'd him, Alf of Otterscliff,
And rooted up an oak,
And fell'd his son, young Angelfyr,
Dead with a single stroke.

Now buried lie those champions two
In the same grave at rest;
And the Upsal king to his daughter gives
The youth she loves the best.

poems.title: Habor and Signild (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Havbor and Signelil".
poems.text:
Habor and Siward, princely chiefs,
A deadly feud had they,
All for the gentle Signild's sake,
So fair that lovely may!

It was young Habor, royal Prince,
At midnight hour awoke,
And all in haste of his vivid dreams
He thus to his mother spoke.

"It seem'd I stood in heaven above,
"Was in the beauteous town,
"And held my trulove in my arms,
"And through the clouds fell down."

Her ladies heard the Prince's dream,
Nor gave it heed or thought,
But well his royal mother knew,
With fate that it was fraught.

"Now ride, my son, to yonder cave,
"No moment check the rein,
"And the Elfking's eldest daughter pray
"Thy dream to thee explain.

In left hand Habor, royal prince,
Held firm his trusty Made,
As off to the Elfin cave he rode
To see that graceful maid.

With fingers small in mantle roll'd
He gently tapp'd her cell,
She lay awake, the summons heard,
And knew his purpose well.

"Hail! Elf-king's daughter, peerless maid,
"Robed in thy pall of state!
"For God's sake tell what means my dream,
"And what shall be my fate.

"It seem'd I stood in heaven above,
"Was in the glorious town,
"And held my trulove in my arms,
"And through the clouds fell down."

"The maid, for that you've dream'd of heaven,
"Shall in your bosom lie;
"But falling through the cloud portends,
"That for her you must die.

"And if I once should have the bliss
"That lovely maid to gain,
"To suffer death for one so fair
"Will never give me pain.

Prince Habor let his hair grow long,
Got ladies' dresses made,
And so disguised to Siward's rode,
As though to learn to braid.

The Prince was dress'd in ladies' clothes,
Had all in ladies' style,
And up the land to "Siward's rode
His daughter would beguile.

There, as he cross'd the castle yard,
He d'onn'd his scarlet cloak,
And mounting up to the ladies' bower
To dames and maidens spoke.

"My greeting, Matrons all, and Maids!
"And dames of each degree!
"And you, the Princess, most of all,
"If you indeed be she.

"Your skill, fair Signild, royal maid,
"The silk to spin and throw,
"Prince Habor greets you and entreats
"To me you'll deign to show."

"And if Prince Habor sent you here,
"You're come a welcome guest;
"With all the skill that I can boast
"Shall you be soon possess'd.

"I'll teach you work in silk and gold,
"No secret from you keep,
"And at my table you shall dine,
"And with my maid shall sleep."

"With Princesses I am used to dine,
"And at their side to lie;
"If now with servants I must sleep,
"For sorrow I shall die."

"Fear not, sweet lady, lack of care
"For one so gently bred,
"With me at table you shall eat,
"And share with me my bed."

Around her sat her maidens all,
And each her needle plied;
But his laid Habor on his lip,
And sat awhile aside.

They broider'd stag, they broider'd doe,
That ran in woodland green;
The Prince, oft as the wine went round,
Drank out the goblet clean.

In sullen mood and ill-starr'd hour
Came in the spiteful maid;
"So fair a lady I never saw,
"Who could not weave or braid.

"So fair a lady I never saw,
"Who neither sew'd nor span;
"So fair a lady I never saw,
"So well could empt a can."

And aye she vented gibes and jeers
In still more bitter strain;
"So fair a lady I never knew
"Such draughts of liquor drain.

"With needle sews she not a seam,
"She keeps it 'tween her teeth,
"But rnipts at once, be it e'er so full,
"The cup that holds the meath.

"Was ever maiden known to gaze
"With eyes so bold and keen?
"Or with such hard and horny hand
"A noble lady seen?"

"Now list thee, maid, whoe'er thou art,
"Why scoffest thou at me?
"Was thy work wrongly done or right,
"I never chid at thee.

"Thy bitter gibes and foul affront
"No longer will I brook;
"Turn I mine eyes or in or out,
"Tis not at thee I look."

Then sate him down the royal prince,
And broider'd work began;
He pictured both the stag and doe,
And hounds that yelping ran.

He work'd the lily, work'd the rose,
And bird on leafy spray;
His skill those maidens much admired,
And begg'd him long to stay.

They stitch'd and broider'd all day long
Till twilight dusk of eve,
Then, rising, fain would all retire,
And ask'd their lady's leave.

So late the hour, that o'er the court
The dew was seen to sweep,
As Signild, rising too from work,
Herself would go to sleep.

Habor, the royal prince, would know,
Where he should rest him too;
"Up in the chamber you shall sleep
"Reclined on cushions blue."

Up stairs and round the balcony
The way fair Signild led;
Within himself Prince Habor laugh'd,
And follow'd her to bed.

The cheerful tapers there they lit,
And were so well inclined;
But came with ill designs at heart
The spiteful maid behind.

The lights burnt out; they seem'd alone;
The maid they thought was gone;
And then the Prince his kirtle doff'd,
And first his sword-blade shone.

So gently as he laid him down,
And on the cushions sank,
Was heard, and no mistaken sound,
His shirt of mail to clank.

Fair Signild wonder'd much and spake,
Her heart so ill at ease,
"I never knew so fair a maid,
"To wear so coarse chemise."

On Habor's breast so bright with gold
Her lily hand she laid;
"And why is not your bosom grown
"Like any other maid?"

"Because my country's mode requires.
"That when to court we go,
"We damsels ride in coat of mail,
"And so it cannot grow."

They lay the weary hours of dark,
The maid beside the knight,
And talk'd so long, and still to talk
They found so much delight.

"But now, dear Lady Signild, say,
"While here we're left alone,
"Whom would you rather choose to wed,
"Of all whom you have known?"

"To me no knight is half so dear
"Of all in court are bred,
"As brave young Habor, royal prince,
"And him I may not wed.

"Though true, as yet his graceful form
"Has never met mine eyes,
"I've heard him sound his golden horn
"In riding to th' Assize."

"And is the king's son, Habor, he
"That is to you so dear?
"Then Signild, turn, my sweetest maid,
Tis he beside you here."

"Can you the King's son, Habor, be,
"And put me thus to shame?
"Why ride not in with hawk und hound
"In court my hand to claim?"

"Within these walls with hawk and hound
"I've made for you request;
"And, sooth, your father spurn'd my suit
"With scorn and bitter jest."

But while they thought they lay alone,
And chatted hour by hour,
That base and treacherous waiting maid
Was listening near the door.

Foul shame befall the wicked maid
For woe, she caused that night!
She came, and stole away his sword,
And shirt of mail so bright.

She carried off his trusty sword,
His mail she stole away.
And went in haste to the upper room,
To where king Siward lay.

"Wake up! wake up! my Lord and King,
"Quick from your couch arise,
"For clasp'd in young Prince Habor's arms
"Signild your daughter lies."

"Tell me no falsehood: be 'tis not:
"Habor it cannot be;
"For off in th' East-land waging war
"And far away is be.

"Forbear, thou lying wicked jade,
"On her such charge to make,
"Or, ere the morning's light shall dawn,
"I'll burn thee at a stake."

"But if, my noble lord and King,
"You will not trust my word,
"Yet look at this, his coat of mail,
"And this, his glittering sword. "

In haste upstarted then the King,
And shouted fierce with rage;
"To arms! to arms! my household all,
"Hard fight is here to wage.

"With sword and shield strive each your best,
"And stand not one aloof;
"Habor, the Prince, a dauntless foe,
"Is now beneath my roof."

His voice the gentle Signild heard,
And wrung her hands for fear;
"Up! Habor, up! what means this noise?
"Give heed! There's danger near/'

"Be calm, my dearest, let them come,
"I've means their force to meet,
"Here at my head my trusty sword,
"My armour near my feet."

Up from his couch Prince Habor sprang,
To every corner flew,
But gone was both his trusty sword,
And gone his armour too.

In grief and anger Habor spoke,
As there he stood so bare;
"That traitress maid foul shame befall!
"'Tis she has laid the snare."

Against his door in tumult wild
They beat with sword and spear;
"Out! Habor, out to the tilting yard!
"Wake up, and d'on thy gear."

Now proved he him a gallant prince,
For manfully he fought,
Nor, while a bedpost yet was left,
To yield could he be brought.

With foot and hand he dealt his blows,
With table, bench, and stool;
Full thirty of Siward's bravest men
Lay in a gory pool.

In vain with new -forged iron bolts
They chain'd him feet and hands,
With ease, as though they'd been of lead,
He burst their strongest bands.

Then up and spoke the crafty maid,
Whose rede was aye for ill;
"Bind him with hair from Signild's head,
"And hand and foot are still."

From Sign i Id's head to tie his limbs
But two hairs did they take,
And, such the love he felt for her,
That band he could not break.

She spoke, and while she spoke, the tears
Kan down her cheeks so fair;
"Habor, you have my full consent,
"In sunder snap the hair."

They dragged him then, the royal prince,
Within the prison wall,
And men and maidens crowded round,
His trulove most of all.

His hands and feet, while there he lay,
In heaviest bonds were kept,
But to and fro Fair Signild went,
And bitterly she wept

"Habor," she said in saddest tone,
"My mother's sisters three
"Will of my father beg your life,
"If you to that agree.

"For firm is else his stern resolve
"To hear of no delay,
"But hang you straight on the highest oak,'
"Ere breaks the dawn of day."

"What?" answer'd Habor, gallant prince,
"And full of wrath was he,
"Think you it were so small disgrace,
"That women begg'd for me?

"Farewell, my Signild! one request —
"One proof of love I claim;
"When high you see me swing aloft,
"Your chamber set on flame."

And thus that gentle maid replied,
Tho' sorely did she weep;
"Habor, I pledge my word to this,
"And will my promise keep."

They led him forth, the royal prince,
Down from the castle gate,
And all the women sobb'd and wept,
And deeply mourn'd his fate.

But when to the open plain they came,
Where he was doom'd to die,
A little while he bade them stop,
Her love he wish'd to try.

"Hang up, I pray, my scarlet cloak,
"For first I wish to see,
"If yet perhaps the king regrets
"To hang me on the tree."

Fair Signild, when the cloak she saw,
More sad and desperate grew;
"What boots me now a longer life?
The worst is all too true."

With sullen grief and anger fill'd
She call'd her maidens near;
"We'll in our chamber a pastime find
"These weary hours to cheer.

"If there be any here with us
"For Habor's death to blame,
"I'll fearful vengeance take on all,
"And perish in the flame."

With that the brands she toss'd about,
Till all the chamber glow'd;
How stern that haughty woman's will,
To every eye she show'd.

Prince Habor turn'd him round to look,
Where stood his Signild's bower,
And saw the fierce and greedy flame
Its crumbling walls devour.

"Throw on the ground my scarlet cloak,
"Nor let it longer wave,
"For had I ten more lives to lose,
"Not one of them I'd save."

King Siward out of his window look'd,
Sad scene there met his gaze;
Prince Habor hanging on the oak,
And Signild's bower a-blaze.

"Oh! Had I known or heard before,
"That loveties were so strong,
"For Denmark and for Norway both
"Had I not done them wrong.

"Haste, ye, to save my daughter's life,
"If still alive she be,
"And ye to save Prince Habor too;
"No felon thief is he."

But when to Signild's bower they came,
She lay in the cinder red,
And when those others reach'd the tree,
Habor the Prince was dead.

Prince Habor's corpse they carried home
In fair white linen roll'd,
And at his trulove Signild's side
Laid him in Christian mould:

But seiz'd the maid by neck and hair,
And right the death she found,
They buried her, fit bridal bed,
Alive beneath the ground.

poems.title: Habor and Signild (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Havbor and Signelil".
poems.text:
Habor and Siward, princely chiefs,
A deadly feud had they,
All for the gentle Signild's sake,
So fair that lovely may!

Habor at silent midnight hour
With vivid dream awoke,
And sleepless lay his mother dear,
And listen'd, while he spoke.

"I dream'd that, as in Danish land
"On Ossey bridge I came,
"There blazed a taper in my hand,
"And then — went out the flame."

"The dream, my son, that thou hast dreamt,
"Implies some lady fair:
"I'll send a message after one,
"Its meaning will declare."

Beside his mother Habor sat,
And hasty message sent
To fetch a wife well skill'd in dreams
To tell him what it meant.

And it was she, the cunning wife,
Into the chamber came,
And up stood Habor, royal prince,
And told her all his dream.

"Doubtless 'tis in your fate, young Prince,
"To win that lovely maid,
"But heed you well, lest with your life
"The gaining her be paid."

Prince Habor got a lady's dress,
" And left his hair to grow,
To Denmark then a journey rode
To many charged with woe.

Prince Habor o'er his shoulders threw
A lady's scarlet cloak,
And straight to the upper chamber went
To Sinnelille, and spoke.

"My greeting, gentle Sinnelille,
"And every dame and maid!
"Prince Habor bade me come to you
"To learn the art to braid."

"That art, so much as I have learnt,
"To you I shall disclose,
"And at my table you shall dine,
"And with my maid repose."

"With Princesses I am used to eat,
"And at their side to lie;
"If with a servant I must sleep,
"For shame and pain I die."

"Nay, lovely maiden, hear me now,
"And fear no lack of care;
"At table you shall sit with me,
"May bed too you shall share."

There sat those graceful maidens all,
And each her needle plied;
His laid Prince Habor on his lip,
And silent sat aside.

There work'd those maids, and pass'd the hours
With many a merry word,
But still and silent Habor sat,
And sketch'd upon the board.

He sketched the nimble hart and roe
Bounding on wooded hill;
And then, with all the art he could,
The lady Sinnelille.

But up and spake the waiting maid,
Spake like a spiteful shrew;
"So fair a maid I never saw,
"Who less of broidery knew.

"No seam she sews, but idly keeps
"Her needle 'tween her teeth;
"Yet be it ne'er so large and full,
"She drains the cup of meath."

"Cease thou thy gibes, base serving maid,
"And jeer no more at me,
"For whether I go in or out,
"I little think of thee."

The day had now begun to wane,
And yield its place to night,
And Sinnelille her orders gave,
That tapers they should light.

Her maidens two wax-tapers lit
So neatly shaped and dress'd,
And Habor towards his chamber led
With Sinnelille to rest

"Now tell me, gentle Sinnelille,
"While no one else is here,
"If there is any, who to you
"Is more than other dear?"

"Knight, that I love, in all the world
"None other do I know,
"Except Prince Habor, him alone,
"And him I must forego."

"And is Prince Habor then the knight
"Who is to you so dear?
"Oh! turn, my gentle Sinnelille,
"He's resting with you here."

"But why then, Habor, royal prince,
"Why put me thus to shame?
"And not ride up in knightly guise
"At court my hand to claim?"

"That could I not," with courteous tone
Prince Habor answer'd so,
"Your father is so hasty a man,
"With him 'tis word and blow."

"Believe me, Habor, royal Prince,
"These hours with woe are rife,
"For when my father hears of it,
"This visit costs your life."

"Oh! calm your fears; behind my head
"There lies my trusty blade;
"And tho' there came here thirty men,
"Should I not be afraid.

"And at my feet there lies below
"A new-made coat of mail;
"Though come here thirty armed men,
"I neither fly nor quail."

Ah! little did Prince Habor think
But that they lay alone:
Outside there lurk'd the waiting maid,
And heard his every tone.

She came and stole the Prince's arms,
" Both sword and mail away,
And hasten'd off to th' upper room,
To where King Siward lay.

"Wake up, my King, wake, Siward, wake!
"Your slumber is all to deep;
"Your daughter lies this very night
"In Habor's arms asleep."

Up from his bed King Siward rose,
And loud was heard to call;
"Wake up, my faithful troopers, wake;
"And d'on your armour all.

"Wake up, wake up, my gallant men,
"Arm ye with sword and shield,
"For here is come Prince Habor's self,
"And will not feebly yield."

They pounded hard his chamber door
With sword and eke with spear,
"Up Habor, hie thee to the yard,
"And lie no longer here."

But when he grasp'd behind his head,
Gone was his trusty brand;
"Up now, my gentle Sinnelille,
"Stern business is on hand.

"But let me, gentle Sinnelille,
"One proof of friendship claim;
"As soon as you shall see me dead,
"Your chamber set on flame."

And out stepp'd Habor, royal prince,
And manfully he fought,
Nor while a bedpost yet was left,
To yield could he be brought.

In vain with slender cords of flax
They tightly bound his hands;
At once, with ease, the royal prince,
Asunder snapp'd their bands.

Then spake that old and crafty maid,
"rede so prompt to find;
"Take but one hair from Sinnelille
"His hands therewith to bind:

"Take from her head to bind his hands
"Only a single hair,
"And Habor, for his tender love,
"That band will never tear."

From Sinnelille his hands to bind
But one bair did they take,
And captive he must yield himself,
The band be could not break.

They carried Habor, royal prince,
Outside the castle pale,
And hang'd him on the gallows tree,
The theme of many a tale.

There Habor spake, the royal prince,
With sad and sullen look;
"Hang up my scarlet mantle first,
"And let me on it look.

"My mantle on the gallows hang,
"And let me only see,
"Whether my gentle Sinnelille
"Will glad or sorry be."

Then spake the lady Sinnelille
With firm and haughty mind;
"This day I'll die, and Habor yet
"In Paradise shall find.

"There's many a trooper here at court
"Of Habor's death is glad;
"III on their brides my vengeance take
"And make them all as sad."

With that at once in every nook
The fiery brands she threw,
And kill'd herself, the haughty maid,
Among the bolsters blue.

There came and spake the little page,
Clad in his red attire;
"Fair Sinnelille with all her maids
"Is in her bower on fire."

"Then take my scarlet mantle down,
"On th' earth it well may lie;
"Had I a hundred thousand lives,
"Not one redeem would I."

King Siward out of his window look'd,
Sad sight there met his gaze!
Blue flames burst from his daughter's bower,
And she was in the blaze.

"My Sinnelille haste ye to save,
"Off, off to the smoking pile!
"And ye to the Prince, and him too save
"From dying death so vile."

But when they to the gallows came,
Hung Habor on the tree;
And when they reach'd the ladies' bower,
To cinders burnt was she.

"O had I e'er before this day
"The strength of loveties known,
"For all my goodly Danish realm
"This deed had I not done."

Him they had hung, and she was dead,
Fate sad as e'er was told;
That traitress maid, they buried her
Alive beneath the mould.

poems.title: The Lombards
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There ruled a King the Danish isles,
King Snccd the name he bare,
And famine spread through all his land,
And death, and grim despair.

He call'd his wisest men to court,
And publish'd this decree;
That each third man throughout the realm
At once should slaughtered be.

In Seeland dwelt an aged dame,"
These tidings when she knew,
"Forbid," said she, "the God above,
"That you such deed should do!

"Ne'er heard I yet of loyal men
"So foully put to death;
"Beware how those you dare to kill,
"Whom God has given breath.

Tis I will give you better rede,
"Although a poor weak wife;
"Ye let these people sail abroad,
"And fight to save their life."

The King he muster'd all his men,
As bade that aged dame;
And sooth it was a gallant host,
That at his summons came.

The Seeland wife hight Ingeborg,
As tells the ancient tale;
And got them built so vast a ship,
That all therein could sail.

Her two bold sons were captains made,
Two proper.men and keen,
And dauntless each his duty did,
Where ever they were seen.

At Bleking went those troops on board,
Indeed a mighty crew;
The King and council stood on shore,
And bade them all adieu.

Soon as they ploughed the wide deep sea,
Their joy-song they begun,
And great the glory wealth and fame,
They on that voyage won.

They reached a port in Lombardy,
That off in Walland lies,
And there they slaughter'd all the men,
And made the women prize.

poems.title: Regnar and Kragelille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A strange report spreads far and wide,
Spreads over all the land;
"King Sigurd has his daughter lost,
"Borne off by robber hand.

King Sigurd takes his purple cloak,
And wraps his head withal,
And mounts, to where his knights and squires
Sit in the castle hall.

On checquer'd board the dice were cast,
And roll'd about so wide;
Till on Prince Regnar fell the lot
In search of her to ride.

He sought her all the winter long,
Sought her five winters round;
But nowhere could the stolen maid
In all these years be found.

On through the forest Regnar rode,
Till, where he cross'd a lawn,
There met him a little serving boy
About the morning dawn.

"Now hark, my little serving boy,,
"What I would say to thee!
"The fairest maiden thou dost know,
"The same point out to me."

"Then list, young knight so brave and fair,
"Nor be your anger stirr'd;
"The best and fairest maid I know,
"Is keeping Habor's herd.

"Her cloak is made of coarse grey wool,
"Her gown the skin of goats,
"But like spun gold the yellow hair,
"That on her shoulder floats."

He rode across the grassy mead,
And through the tangled thorn,
And found her where she watch'd the goats,
To keep them off the corn.

He drew her kindly within his arm,
And tapp'd her fair white cheek;
"Now tell me who thy father is,
"And truth, I prithee, speak."

"My father, now an aged man,
"Herds goats along the coast;
"Myself, they call me Kragelille;
"My birth I cannot boast."

Prince Regnar sternly eyed the maid,
And drew his glittering knife;
"Toll me thy father's name and thine,
"Or it shall cost thy life."

"King Sigurd and his Queen were once
"The parents I could claim.
"As child they call'd me Swanelille,
"And that is my proper name."

It Prince Regnar stay'd to hear no more,
But wrapp'd in purple weed
He gently rais'd the maiden up,
And set her on his steed.

And over grassy plain he rode,
And over furrow'd hill;
That old man running after them,
And calling 'Kragelille.

He gave him gold and silver too,
And sent him pleas'd away;
But safely back to her father's house
He brought that lovely may.

And now may Regnar, royal prince,
Lay all his cares aside,
And sleep in peace and wedded bliss
Beside his youthful bride.

And she the gentle Swanelille
No longer sighs or weeps,
But calls a royal prince her own,
And happy with him sleeps.

poems.title: Karl and Kragelille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Carl at his banquet table sat,
"Swains, hear me every one!
"Go search me out the fairest maid,
"That breathes beneath the sun.

"Go search her out through all the land
"And northern kingdoms three,
A maid of equal rank with mine,
"And bring her home to me.

"Is she but good and gently bred,
"For wealth I little care;.
"Ye find and bring me home a maid,
"Is fit my bed to share."

Away they rode, those faithful swains,
O'er land and realm so wide,
But nowhere could they find a maid,
Was fit to be his bride.

The faithful swains were riding on
O'er grassy field and wood,
And came where tending a farmer's herd
A fair young maiden stood,

Then turn'd and spake the elder swain,
In scarlet cloak array'd;
"I see beneath yon wooded cliff
"A fair and lovely maid."

He spurr'd his steed, that ancient swain,
And rode him down below,
And spake, and ask'd the fair young maid,
If with them she would go.

"And kindly tell me, gentle maid,
"The secret truth declare,
"Of what so noble race you're born,
"To be so passing fair?"

"My father, he is a simple herd,
"Keeps goats upon the moor;
"Myself — my name is Kragelille,
"Of humble race and poor."

Her clothes were fluttering in the wind,
So tatter'd, worn and old;
Her hair about her shoulders hung
Like glittering threads of gold.

Her cheek was like the rosebud red,
Her neck like ermine white;
Much wonder'd all those Danish men
To see her in such a plight.

But he, that good and ancient swain,
Wrapped her in scarlet weed,
And gently rais'd the maiden up,
And placed her on his steed.

"But in such haste I must away,
"So far with you to roam?
"Nay, let me here in the meadow stay
"To drive my cattle home."

"Fair maid, no sorrow shall you taste,
"No tear shall ever shed;
"We take you hence to a better land,
"A rich young knight to wed."

In silken gown of finest hue
And scarlet cloak array M,
Up to the bower, to young Sir Carl,
They led the lovely maid.

With graceful mien the young Sir Carl
Welcom'd his beauteous bride;
"Seat thee, fair maid, on cushion blue,
"Repose thee at my side.

"And while we're sitting here alone,
"The truth, sweet maid, declare,
"Of what so noble race you're born,
"To be so passing fair?"

"My father he was call'd Sir Carl,
"In snake -pen he was kill'd;
"Myself — my name is Adelrun,
"My mother's name Bryn-hilde.

"While I was yet a tender babe,
"The boors ray father slew,
"Down into a snake-pen dark and deep
"My noble father threw.

"They drave my mother from out the land,
"I know not if she's dead;
"But me since then, an orphan child,
"They've kindly nurs'd and fed."

Sir Carl he tapp'd her fair white cheek,
"Sweet maid, your grief forego,
"For now my bride, you never more
"Shall pain or sorrow know.

"And if please God, I have the power,
"As good is my desire,
"I'll venge you on those wicked boors,
"Who slew your gallant sire."

"If venge me on the boors you will,
"That shall I gladly see,
"But spare, I pray, the farmer's wife,
"For she was good to me."

Bravo, Sir Carl! a loyal knight
Will true to his word abide:
That day month was his wedding day,
And Adelrun his bride.

poems.title: The Fight with the Worm
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
As I was a little shepherd boy,
And sat on a mountain side,
I caught a playful and spotted snake
I saw in the rushes glide.

I wrapped it up in a mantle blue,
That snake so spotted and barr'd,
And off to Sir Helsing's daughter fair
I took it to Lundengard.

"O thanks, many thanks, little shepherd boy,
"My thanks for a gift so brave;
"And well I will pay thee, if e'er from me
"A boon thou comest to crave."

She cherish'd the snake the winter through,
She cherish'd it winters three;
It grew to as foul and fierce a worm,
As one in the world may see.

Sir Helsing he and his wife so fair
Were daily in tears and woe,
For now no more for the lothely worm
Could they to their daughter go.

Sir Helsing at court he made it known,
And over the land so wide;
Whoever should slay the lothely worm,
His daughter should have for bride.

Out spake Child Sivord Ingorson,
And bounded across the board;
"'Tis I will fight with the lothely worm,
"Sir Helsing, you keep your word."

They fought together the livelong day,
Till sun sank under the hill;
And then fell Sivord Ingorson,
And breathless he lay and still.

The message was brought to the ladies bower,
That Sivord was slain and dead;
And bitterly wept that gentle maid
All under the scarlet red.

Right bitterly matrons wept and maids
All under their scarlet red,
As lay in the cloister at Grimerslew
The gallant young Sivord dead.

So went that whole long winter by,
And after it winters two,
The while she sat in her lonely bower,
And none to her dared to go.

Sir Helsing he sent to the royal court,
His envoys he bade to say;
"He gives his daughter and all his wealth
To him, who the worm will slay.'

That heard young Peter Rimboldson,
And boldly he rose and spake;
"'Tis I will combat the lothely worm,
"And all for the maiden's sake."

A shirt, that was woven of finest silk,
He over his shoulders drew,
And buckled upon it a coat of mail,
That glitter'd with steel so blue.

His velvet jacket he then put on,
The gold on it gleam'd afar;
And then the hide of a grisly beast,
All dabbled in pitch and tar.

Eight trenches he dug, so broad and deep,
And full were they all with blood;
But he in the ninth, young Rimboldson,
Secure from the venom stood.

They strove till sank the evening sun,
Had striven the livelong day,
And then was beaten the lothely worm,
And dead on the grass it lay.

But great was the joy in Lundengard
To hear of the victory won;
Sir Helsing he gave his daughter's hand
" To gallant young Rimboldson.

And so has young Peter Rimboldson
Got over his toil and pain,
That fair and noble young lady won,
That lotheliest monster slain.

poems.title: The Sword of Vengeance
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "The Avenging Sword".
poems.text:
Sir Peter came to a castle gate,
As e'en there sat the king in state.

"Welcome, Sir Peter! friend well met!
"What! not avenged thy father yet?"

"I've gone to th' utmost bounds of South,
"Where scalds the sun a land of drouth;

"I've gone to th' utmost bounds of West,
"Where sinks the sun to nightly rest;

"I've gone to th' utmost bounds of North,
"Where frost unceasing chills the earth;

"And here in th' East my course I stay,
"Where kindles up the light of day;

"Yet none, though wide and far I go,
"Can me my father's murderer show."

"And what wilt thou on him bestow,
"Who doth thy father's murderer show?"

"I'll give him silver, give him gold,
"And merchant coin I'll not withhold;

"I'll give him these, I'll give him more,
"The boat that lies on yonder shore."

Then said the king with scornful leer,
"Thy father's murderer seest thou here.

"Aye" said the king with scornful leer,
"Thy father's murderer seest thou here.

"The Lord my God to me be true,
"As I for thee a father slew."

Sir Peter smote his heaving breast,
"Lie still, my heart, be thou at rest.

"Lie still my heart, not too much haste;
"Our vengeance, trust me, we will taste."

Sir Peter walk'd the castle yard,
And with his faithful sword conferr'd.

"Hark thee, my sword, so staunch and good,
"Canst thou bestir thyself in blood?

"My sword, say, wilt thou stand by me?
"No friend on earth have I but thee."

"But how can I then lend thee aid,
"Wrench'd from its hilt my trusty blade?"

Sir Peter a famous smithy knew,
And got his sword-blade fix'd anew.

They forged the hilt of silver white,
The pommel made of gold so bright.

"My sword, now wilt thou stand by me?
"No friend on earth have I but thee."

"O be but thou as keen of mood,
"As thou shalt find my temper good.

"Be thou as firm and staunch in fight,
"As I shall in my hilt be tight."

Sir Peter went to a grassy bank,
Where fast and hard the champions drank.

Sir Peter would his sword essay,
And slain at once eight champions lay.

Sir Peter's sword so wildly flared,
It neither maid nor mother spared.

Sir Peter hew'd with deadly swing,
And spared not, he, or prince or king.

Up spake the child in cradle lain,
"So vengest thou a father slain?

"The vengeance, thou hast wreak'd for thine,
"Grant God I live to take for mine!"

"I've well avenged a father dead,
"To vengeance thou shalt not be bred."

With that the threatening brat he slew,
With one blow cut him through and through.

"Still thee, my pretty sword so brown;
"For God's sake keep thy choler down."

Then spake the sword in sullen mood,
"Thee would I slay and taste thy blood.

"Hadst thou by name not call'd on me,
"I would at once have slaughtered thee."

Back to the smith Sir Peter paced,
And got himself in iron cased.

He bade them case him foot and hand,
For he would march and leave the land.

He came where lay the buried king,
And off fell band and iron ring.

poems.title: Grimmer (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Brave sons Sir Erick Grimmer had
And keen for battle fray;
They never went, but sword in hand,
To either feast or play.

They never went to ladies' dance,
But with their naked sword;
Nor ever, but in coat of mail,
Would sit at banquet board.

Young Grimmer built and rigg'd a boat,
And launch'd it off the strand,
And swore to sail to the heathen king,
And win his daughter's hand.

So kindly blew the gentle breeze,
So well they plied the oar,
They reached the isle, and foremost there
Young Grimmer trod the shore.

Off to the heathen king he strode,
And, wrapp'd in scarlet cloak,
Up to the presence chamber went,
And thus the king bespoke.

"And heie you're sitting, heathen king,
"Over your festive board!
"I come to crave your daughter's hand,
"And wait your gracious word."

"My daughter think not thou to win,
"Nor woo the gentle may,
"Till first thou hast striven with Helmer Kamp,
"And fairly gain'd the day."

In kinder tone the Princess spoke,
A lovely maid and fair;
"None ever came from Bermer-eye
"Who went to combat there

"There never yet came champion back
"From fight on Bermer-eye;
"How small your chance my father knows,
"And means you there to die."

"Sweet maid," young Grimmer so replied
In scarlet cloak array'd,
"For coward loon I hold a swain,
"If he is of death afraid."

"Then I shall give you a sword of gold
"To gird upon your side,
"And with it freely take the field,
"Where listeth you to ride.

"The sword is of the ruddy gold,
"Of silver every pin,
"With this, young Grimmer, trust my word,
"The victory you shall win."

They wound aloft their silken sail,
They let their pennon fly,
And kindly breezes bare them on
Away to Berner-eye.

The bold young Grimmer, he it was,
Who steer'd his boat to land,
Where Helmer Kamp, the brawny chief,
Was waiting on the strand.

Said Helmer Kamp, for a scornful jest
Restrain he could no more,
"And who then is this little mouse,
"Comes shipwreck'd here ashore?"

"Thou callest me a little mouse,
"From thee I shall not run,
"And dear, I trow, thy joke shall cost,
"Ere yet the day is done."

Young Grimmer met his bulky foe,
And drew his lady's blade,
And Helmer Kamp he cut to shreds,
And well his vaunting paid.

His silver and gold they took away,
As much as they could pile,
And home, in wealth and glory rich,
They sail'd from Bermer isle.

The maiden stands in her lofty bower,
Stands looking far and wide;
"Dear father, make the wedding feast,
"His ship I've e'en descry'd."

The maiden stands in her lofty bower,
Stands looking o'er the strand;
"Dear father, make the wedding feast,
"My knight is come to land."

Young Grimmer left his boat ashore,
Drew on his scarlet cloak,
And up to the royal chamber went,
And thus the king bespoke.

"And here you're sitting, heathen king,
"Over your festive board!
"I come to crave your daughter's hand,
"And wait your gracious word."

And then arose the heathen king
In all his pomp and pride,
And gave his daughter, lovely maid,
To be young Grimmer's bride.

poems.title: Grimmer (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Childe Grimmer paces the chamber floor,
And deftly a sword can wield;
"Now give us the maiden Ingeborg,
"Before we take the field."

"Me thinks thou'rt much too small a man
"To strike a vigorous blow,
"Nor couldest, feeble as thou art,
"Withstand a full-grown foe."

"As small and feeble as I may be,
"My weapon I can wield,
"And meet me foes, whoever may,
"I'll make them quit the field."

"A champion dwells in Birtingsland,
"A swordsman stout and brave,
"Him meet and slay, and then for bride
"My daughter thou shalt have."

Childe Grimmer left the royal hall
Heaving with smother'd ire;
"And now" ask'd maiden Ingeborg,
"What said the king, my sire?"

"A champion dwells in Birtingsland,
"A swordsman stout and brave,
"That champion if I meet and slay,
"Your hand then I may have."

"Then," spake the maiden Ingeborg,
"The king would you betray;
"In such unequal fight as that
"He knew what danger lay.

"But I will lend you a coat of mail,
"Which sword will never bite;
"And helm, whereon the heaviest hand
"No dint shall ever smite.

"And with a sword I'll arm you too,
"A finely tempered glaive,
"That cuts as well through hardest steel,
"As through the liquid wave."

The champion stands on Birtingsborg,
Looks out to sea so wide;
"What patch'd and paltry boat is that,
"At anchor seems to ride?"

Childe Grimmer little wight it was,
Who steer'd his boat to land,
And he of Birtingsland the lord,
Who held him out his hand.

"Welcome, Childe Grimmer, little wight!
"Here thou shalt dwell in peace;
"The half my land I'll share with thee,
"And give thee too my niece."

"Nay! that to the maiden Ingeborg
"Shall ne'er be told or penn'd,
"That I have taken thy niece to wife,
"Or made of thee a friend.

"But go will we to Vimming's hill,
"And settle there our strife,
"Nor either from the ring return,
"Till one has lost his life."

Spake thus that haughty champion,
So prompt was he of hand,
"The first blow I may claim as mine
"In this my proper land/'

With scornful taunt he then advanced,
His heavy sword swung round,
And with one blow Childe Grimmer fell'd,
And stretch'd him on the ground.

But undismayed Childe Grimmer rose,
Eager his strength to test;
"Thou too shalt stand as hard a blow,
"Ere sinks the sun to rest."

His sword in turn Childe Grimmer heav'd,
And well it did its part;
It cut the champion's helmet through,
And clave him to the heart.

These last few words the champion spake,
As down he fell and died;
"Oh that my brother Rodengard,
"Were standing near my side!"

And well was little Grimmer pleas'd
Had ended so the fight;
And booty took to his lady's land,
Both gold and silver bright.

The champion now on battle field
Lies weltering deep in gore,
But hale and sound Childe Grimmer lives
To rob his treasur'd store.

He stay'd not long in Birtingsland,
But sail'd with victory crown'd;
And joyful sail'd his comrades too
To share the spoil they found.

The maiden stands in her bower aloft,
Is gazing o'er the strand;
"And there I see my trulove knight
"His vessel steer to land."

Childe Grimmer, like a gallant man,
He made no long delay,
But kept his troth, and that day month
Was held his wedding day.

poems.title: Childe Ranild
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The King he has a daughter fair,
And young and shrewd is she,
Knows all that in the world is wrought,
And all that e'er shall be.
"Were I as wise!" childe Ranild said.

The troopers joust in castle yard,
All clad in coat of mail;
Ranild strikes in, and hits them hard;
Not apt is he to quail.
"Not very apt," childe Ranild said.

Up to her bower Childe Ranild went,
And pray'd his mother dear;
"O mother, give me better clothes,
"At mine the troopers jeer.
"Which vexes me," childe Ranild said,,

She found a cloth of coarse blue yarn,
And gave hi in more or less;
"Take that, and beg the royal maid
"To cut thee out a dress."
"That will I do," childe Ranild said.

He took the piece of coarse blue yarn,
And threw it on her knee;
"Fair maid, will you such kindness show,
"And garments cut for me?
"And cut them well,' childe Ranild said.

Long silent sat the maid so sage,
Sat musing in her mind;
"Childe Ranild, little weenest thou,
"To what thou art design'd."
"Some good, I trust," childe Ranild said.

She took a piece of velvet cloth,
His clothes of it to make;
"Go, enter thou my father's court,
"And service in it take."
"That will I do," childe Ranild said.

With joy they bare to the ocean strand
Anchor and slender oars;
So glad was all the royal troop
To sail to foreign shores.
And joyous too childe Ranild was.

Childe Ranild, looking out afar,
Stood forward on the prow;
"Here comes a man in iron clad,
"And well his boat can row.
"Hither he comes," childe Ranild said.

"Thou sailest like a gallant man,"
He thus to the steersman spake,
"Here roars in faith a boisterous sea,
"Might make a coward quake;
"Quite at thine ease/' childe Ranild said.

Childe Ranild drew and swung his sword,
As on the prow he stood;
He struck down fifteen champions dead,
And toss'd them on the flood.
"And there you lie/' childe Ranild said.

Then up and spake the youthful kemp
In shirt of ringed mail;
"Childe Ranild, stay, that I the blood
"From out the hold may bale."
"So bale it out," childe Ranild said.

"And once an uncle too I had,
"King Saxe the name he bare,
"And gallant men were his three sons,
"Their fate I fain would hear."
"Thou 'st found them then," childe Ranild said.

"The eldest son was Adam hight,
"The second one was Korc,
"The third son he Childe Ranild hight,
"Like steel the heart he bore."
"And such have I," childe Ranild said.

"And art thou then my uncle's son?
"And true what thou hast told?
"Then come with me to yonder isle,
"To Thrude's robber hold."
"Come thou with me," childe Ranild said.

"He took my treasured gold from me,
"The horse from out my stall;
"He took my good and faithful sword,
"My greatest grief of all."
"Why hold not fast?" childe Ranild said.

"Took he thy treasur'd gold from thee,
"Thy horse from out the stall?
"Took he thy good and faithful sword,
"Thy greatest grief of all?
"Had I that sword!" childe Ranild said.

"And art thou then my uncle's son?
"I'll stand thee in good stead;
"Follow thou me to yonder land,
"Or else I strike thee dead."
"Then come with me," childe Ranild said.

Thrude he stands on Happy isle,
And looks around so wide,
And sees so many a ship of war
Over the billows stride.
"'Tis even he, childe Ranild, comes."

Thrude he stood on Happy isle,
And wroth of mood he grew;
Up by its roots an oak he tore,
And 'fore the vessel threw.
"How to get in?" childe Ranild said.

Childe Ranild he with anger fill'd
So fiercely steer'd his boat,
In pieces seven he burst the trunk,
And sent them all afloat.
"I'll get in yet," childe Ranild said.

Into the cavern Ranild went
On floor so brightly gilt,
And finding there that famous sword
With both hands grasp'd the hilt.
"I've got thee now/ I childe Ranild said.

Thrude, the king of Happy isle,
His bar of iron hent;
And fearful sight it was to see,
How he at Ranild went.
"I bide thy blow," childe Ranild said.

As Thrude smote, so Ranild hew'd,
Nor one from th' other shrunk;
He hack'd from Thrude hand and foot,
And then he fell'd the trunk.
"There liest thou," childe Ranild said.

He took the dripping gory head,
And cast it in the sound;
And, after it the body threw
To join it on the ground.
"They'll meet again," childe Ranild said.

Childe Ranild went, this battle done,
To walk along the strand,
But gone were all the ships of war,
That lay before at land.
"How to get off!" childe Ranild said.

His gilded horn childe Ranild took,
And blew a blast so loud,
A crack was heard from shore to shore,
For snapp'd was every shroud.
"Come ye not back?" childe Ranild said.

That good and faithful gilded ship,
So well his blast she knew,
Asunder sailed her cables nine,
And back to Ranild flew.
"Right welcome thou!" childe Ranild said.

The heap of treasured gold he seized,
And on his war-ship stored,
And thankful reach'd his port and home
With all he had on board.
"Here sails the wealthy Ranild in."

The King on castle turret stands,
The Queen upon the wall;
"These heaps of gold, that Ranild brings,
"Where shall we store them all?
"Touch not what's mine," child Ranild said.

poems.title: Olger the Dane
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
King Burman in Iceland camp'd his troops,
A glittering shield display'd,
Would know what daughters had Iceland's king,
And whether a handsome maid.

"Listen and ponder, Iceland's king,
"What now I would say to thee;
"Thy daughter give me, the one so fair,
"Thy kingdom divide with me.

"Either give me the maid to wife,
"And share with me all thy land,
"Or else a champion find, so bold,
"As dares me in fight withstand."

"No daughter have I but only one,
"Maid Gloriant she is bight;
"I've her to Carvel the king betroth'd,
"And will not his friendship slight.

"I Ve long to another pledged her baud,
"King Carvel her trulove's name;
"But if he cannot his bride defend,
"The maid thou art free to claim."

"O hark to me, dearest daughter mine,
"Here's sudden and baleful news;
"King Burman has all his troops afield,
"And e'en for thy favour sues.

"A dauntless foe King Burman is,
"No trifler in battle he;
"A champion to meet him find we must,
"Or hither he comes for thee."

No longer silence the maiden kept,
But thus to her father spake;
"In dungeon yonder a captive lies,
"A spear with him he might break."

She cloak'd her, the maiden Gloriant,
And thither she took her way,
To where in a dungeon deep and dark
The captives around her lay.

The maiden Gloriant cried aloud;
"O listen, ye captives all,
"Let Olger Dane, if he still is here,
"Come forward to meet my call.

"And art thou living, good Olger Dane?
"Mine errand is quickly told,
"King Burn) an is come, and me demands,
"King Burman, the swarthy Trold.

"My father to him my hand wilt give,
"And not to a Christian man;
"If thou wilt save me, and beat the Trold,
"I'll help thee in all I can."

"A whole long twelvemonth a captive here
"I've lingered in iron band;
"All blessings on you, fair Gloriant,
"To lend me a helping hand!

"A whole long twelvemonth a captive here
"In hunger and pain and thirst,
"Too weak am I now to face the Trold,
"And battle with him the -first."

"O lend me thine aid, good Olger Dane,
"My honour and life to save;
"For rather than take that lothely Trold
"I would I were in my grave.

"The man is so grim, his horse so fierce,
"I speak but a noted truth,
"Many have seen it, and all declare,
"He bites with a wolfish tooth.

"They naught for their daily food will eat,
"But flesh from a Christian rent,
"And nothing will drink to quench their thirst,
"But blood with a poison blent."

"Your father he gave you a gallant man,
"King Carvel your trulove's name,
"And if no match for the Trold is he,
"King Burman your hand will claim.

"But give me again my own good horse"
"And give me my coat of mail,
"For your sake, Lady, I'll do my best,
"At Burman I shall not quail.

"King Carvel was long my comrade dear,
"O would that the truth he knew,
"That rather I went to certain death,
"Than Burman should seize on you!"

"Then hark! I'll give thee thy own good horse,
"Thy coat of the steel so bright,
"And sword-blade, that urged by hero's hand
"Through hardest of mail can bite."

She led from the dungeon Olger Dane,
And had him so richly drest,
And set him at table in highest place,
And pour'd him of wine the best.

King Burman into the courtyard rode,
To seize on the maid he thought,
But mounted and arm'd met Olger Dane,
Who set his designs at naught.

They fought for an hour, they fought for twain,
A third too, — and fought their best,
And then on a stone they took their seat,
Their limbs for a while to rest.

And there as they sat, the heathen king
Thus Olger the Dane bespake;
"Believe my God, and I spare thy life,
"And thee as a captive take."

Him answer'd as proudly Olger Dane,
For mercy did he not care;
"Go tell them in Hell, thy next abode,
"'Twas Olger who sent thee there."

Again those champions rose to fight,
And neither his ground would yield,
Till swords, and helmets, and all was smashed
And scatter'd about the field.

They fought so manfully, fought so long,
Till bleeding were both and tired,
And sank King Burman at Olger's feet,
And there on the field expired.

Olger gave to the gentle maid
The horse and the rider both,
"And now, instead of yon heathen hound,
"King Carvel may claim your troth,"

The King her father so pleas'd was he,
He rose from his royal place,
And welcomed from battle Olger Dane
With honour and kindly grace.

"Now rise, my daughter, my Gloriant,
"Thy gratefullest thanks to show,
"Thyself go welcome good Olger Dane,
"Who saved thee from all thy woe."

Then rising, the maiden Gloriant,
As slender as any wand,
She stripped him of sword and coat of mail
And all with her own white hand.

She drew him kindly within her arm,
And warmly his lips she kiss'd;
"How sound and hale from the fight return'd!
"Our Father in Heaven be bless'd!"

Then spake to his daughter Iceland's king,
And just were his words and kind;
"But Olger now to the chamber take,
"And haste thee his wounds to bind."

poems.title: Swain Felding
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The gallant Swain Felding he mounted horse,
To Rome-ward his way He bent,
And thankful may Danish pilgrims be,
That thither he ever went.

The gallant Swain Felding he mounted horse,
From Denmark he rode away,
And lodged one night with a lady fair,
A kind and a gentle may.

It was with a lady he found his home,
And peerless she was, so fair;
And him she seated the first at board
"Above all the knights who were there.

Swain Felding she seated the first at board
"Bove knights of the highest fame,
And then she pray'd him himself to say
The country from which he came.

She look'd at hid fine-wrought linen shirt
All broider'd with gold so bright;
"No needy poor pilgrim man is this,
"We're sheltering here to-night.

"'Tis surely no needy pilgrim man,
"Is here for the night our guest;
"'Tis either the king of Denmark's self,
"Or His of his knights the best."

"No king of Denmark am I, fair maid,
"Nor make me so high a boast;
"I'm but a needy poor pilgrim man
From Denmark's sandy coast.

"And, gentle my lady, let me say,
"And take not my words amiss,
"In Denmark too there are children born
"To want, and to wealth and bliss."

"I've heard it said, and I've heard it sung,
"That Danish men are so brave,
"And now I thank God that one is come
"This harried poor realm to save.

"O list to my grief, my noble Sir,
"O list to a moving tale;
"There dwells in my land a lothely Trold
"Has brought on us death and bale.

"There's come to my land a lothely Trold
"This realm to harry and waste,
"And saving of maids' and ladies' flesh
"No food will he deign to taste."

"Had I but a horse and coat of mail,
"Right welcome were now the chance
"For maiden so fair and nobly born
"To break with the Trold a lance."

They led from the stall fine Spanish steeds
So white and so gaily drest;
Like dogs they crouch'd on the ground with fear,
So soon as their heads he press'd.

"I gladly would give a hundred marks,
'"And all of the gold so red,
"Could I but borrow a Danish horse
"On Danish island bred."

Just then was passing a miller man,
"And I have a horse," he cried,
"As stout and as gallant a Danish horse,
"As knight could desire to ride,

"My horse is sprung of the Danish race,
"And nurtur'd in Seaby wood,
"And every time that he goes to mill,
"Bears fifteen hundred good."

"Now hark thee, mine honest millerman,
"Bring hither thy horse to me;
"And if we arc Danes, — we two — my troth! — -
"We'll snatch of the Southrons three."

With haunches high and a broad strong chest,
And all as the miller said,
Came forward the horse, and Folding's self
The saddle upon him laid.

He saddled and rein'd him, as seem'd him good,
And tight did he draw the girth,
Till burst was the band, and down the horse
Fell knuckling upon the earth.

"These fifteen rings of the massive gold,
"That I have from Denmark brought,
"I'll give them to pay for a saddlegirth,
"Can one for the gold be bought."

In making a girth for Folding's horse
Both matrons and maidens strove;
An ell in breadth, and a quarter thick,
So stout was the girth they wove.

He drew from his hands the gauntlets small,
From hands as a lady's white,
And saddled himself that noble horse,
Nor trusted to menial wight.

He girded so hard the brave good horse,
It could not endure the strain,
But fell before him on bended knee,
As tho' it would tell its pain

"And now that I see, good gallant steed,
"That thou hast a human wit,
"I'll slacken thy girth a hole or two,
"Before upon thee I sit."

The first assault that the heroes rode,
Their charge was so fierce and hard,
Swain Felding' s lance was broken in two
And shield roll'd on the sward.

'Twas then so subtle an artifice
Came into Swain Felding's mind;
"Return to-morrow to meet me here,
"And me thou wilt surely find."

And off to the church Swain Felding went,
By priest was duly sped,
And craftily fast on his spear-pole bound
A wafer of holy bread.

"Away with that crown-hilt useless sword!
"No such will I longer wear,
"And fetch me hither a cutter mast
"To serve me to-day for spear. "

The second tilt that the heroes rode,
So boiling with wrath were they,
The neck of the Trold was broken in two,
His head roll'd far away;

In three were his legs, in five his head,
His back was in pieces nine; —
Swain Felding then to the lady rode,
Would drink her a bowl of wine.

Nine knights she had sent, who off his horse
Should help her champion down;
"If you will our lily fair maiden wed,
"Then your's is our land and crown."

"Ah no! a maiden I've long betroth'd,
"Her father a lord at Rome,
"And if I should break my plighted vows,
"Awaits me a painful doom.

"A maiden, my friends, I've long betroth'd
"Away o'er the Eastern shore,
"And would not for tons of the ruddy gold
"Be false to the vow I swore.

"But build and with every comfort fill
"A house beside the way,
"And shelter beneath its friendly roof
"The pilgrims that hither stray.

"And chiefly our Danish pilgrims lodge,
"Nor spare of the wine and bread,
"And bid them to pray for Felding's soul,
"When he shall himself be dead"

poems.title: Swain Felding and Queen Judith
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There swarm to visit Denmark's realm
So many men of fame;
Aye, thither come more German knights,
Than I have the power to name.

The stately Danish king it was,
Two swains was heard to call;
"Go, knaves, the Swain Sir Felding bid
"Come to the council hall."

And in the Swain, Sir Felding came,
And stood before the board;
"What will you with me, Danish king?
"And wherefore send me word?"

"Hark thee, Sir Felding, faithful Swain,
"Mine errand thou shalt do;
"Embark, and off to Germany,
"And fetch my bride so true."

"If I to Germany shall go
"To fetch you home the fair,
"Alone, you well know Danish king,
"I cannot journey there.

"A hundred knights in iron clad
"These you for me must find;
"And let my coat, as fits my rank,
"With martin fur be lined. "

Their silken sail with gold so bright
On gilded mast they spread,
In two months time the gallant ship
To Germany had sped,

They furl'd their sail, and anchor cast
Out on the glittering sand;
And there swain Felding's self it was,
Who first debark'd on land.

In passing through the royal court
They donn'd each man his cloak,
And up to the presence chamber went,
And thus the king bespoke.

"Hail, highborn king of Germany!
"Here at your festive board!
"The king who rules the Danish realm,
"By me has sent you word."

"At table set these gentlemen,
"And bowl and towel bring."
Long ere the hour of rest was come,
His answer made the king

But up Swain Felding rose and spake,
Soon as fair Judith came;
"Shame on the hands, should wash thine eyes!
"On both those hands be shame!

"Shame and disgrace befall the hands,
"That ought to wash thine eyes!
"And shame on her, should water bring,
"And at thy bidding plies!"

"Hark thee, Swain Felding, stay thy sneers,
"Nor me presume to slight;
"For thou art — that I've learnt for truth —
Thyself a baseborn wight/'

"Let me be ne'er so basely born,
"I've kinsmen firm and tried,
"And daily clothe in scarlet cloth,
"And own the horse I ride."

"The vilest rogue, can he but find
"A pair of crimson hose,
"Comes bragging here to Germany,
"And calls himself a rose."

"The vilest wench, if red and white
"She wears her mottled face,
"Will come to our honest Danish land,
"And claim a Lady's place. "

Swain Felding up in his brawny arms
The bride, fair Judith, took,
And down in his ship so roughly set,
That all the vessel shook.

Their sails of silk they hoisted up
High on the gilded mast,
In two weeks' time to Denmark's coast
The briny seas had pass'd.

Swain Felding he the rudder held,
And steer'd the ship to land,
As e'en his lord, the Danish king,
Was riding along the strand.

Swain Felding waved his hat on high
To greet the Danish king;
"Urge not your steed so fast, my lord;
Tis no great prize we bring.,I

So soon as maiden Judtelille
Her bridal chamber view'd;
"Shame, M said she, "on the carpenters,
"Who here the timber hew'd!

"Shame on the bungling carpenters,
"Who shared the meat and beer!
"And on the Swain Sir Felding shame,
"The slothful overseer!"

"The posts are all of poplar wood,
"Of oak is every pin;
"Nor ought with Denmark's king to sleep
"A Judtelille therein."

Then up Sir Peter Kempe spake,
A hero stout and stark;
"I'll stake in joust with thee to day
"A horse and a hundred mark."

"Not much have I of gold and coin,
"Or aught that gold will buy;
"Our ladies' honour be the stake,
"A fall with thee I'll try."

The first assault those heroes rode,
They both spurr'd on so bold,
Swain Felding's lance was snapp'd in two,
And far his buckler roll'd.

Beneath her cloak smiled Judtelille
Her champion's feat to see;
"And such as this are all the men,
"I've hither brought with me."

In haste away to the bridal house
The Swain Sir Felding ran;
"My liege, lend me your horse to-day
"To ride and meet my man."

"Out from his stall my Grayleg lead
"With eagle-plumage hide;
"Him to the Swain Sir Felding give,
"Such horses he can ride.

"Out from his stall my Grayleg lead,
"Gold saddle on him lay;
"More than eight winters will have past,
"Since last he saw the day."

The second bout those heroes rode,
They charged with might and main;
Sir Peter's horse fell on his knee,
His head roll'd on the plain.

She wrung her hands, fair Judtelille,
And sorely seem'd distrest;
"O! that to Denmark I should bring
"My bravest knights and best!"

But gaily laugh'd the Danish king
Beneath his mantle red;
"Such are the Danish troopers all,
"By me are clothed and fed."

Fair Judith ask'd her morning gift,
As day began to break;
"Give me thy Swain Sir Folding's head,
"There's nothing else I take."

"Castles and forts I freely give,
"And wealth in ruddy gold;
"But give thee not the gallant men,
"Through whom my land I hold."

Then up the Swain Sir Folding spake;
As there he stood alone;
"If I to Judith bent a knee,
"I' faith 'twould break the bone."

poems.title: Little Katey
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Among the lovely maidens
Who serv'd the Prince's hall,
Was shining little Katey
A star above them all.

She like a star was shining
Beyond them all so fair,
As thus to little Katey
The Prince began his prayer.

"But hear me, Little Katey,
"And say thou wilt be mine,
"Seven silk-embroider'd dresses
"I'll give thee to be thine."

"I'll take no broider'd dresses,
"None such on me bestow;
"Those dresses give your Princess,
"Let me with honour go."

"But hear me, little Katey,
"And say thou wilt be mine,
"A fort and moated castle
"I'll give thee to be thine."

"I'll take no fort or castle,
"None such on me bestow;
"Those castles give your Princess,
"Let me with honour go."

"But hear me, little Katey,
"And say thou wilt be mine,
"A crown of gold I'll give thee;
"The brightest shall be thine."

"I'll take no crown or jewels,
"None such on me bestow;
"But give them to your Princess,
"Let me with honour go."

Aloft went little Katey,
And 'fore her lady stood;
"So said my lord, your husband,
"And urged me all he cou'd."

"Should he repeat the offers
"He made to thee to-day,
"Think thou on God Almighty,
"And firmly say him nay."

"But hear me, little Katey,
"If mine thou wilt not be,
"I'll make the gloomiest dungeon
"A dwelling place for thee."

In dark and noisome dungeon
The gentle maid he cast;
Himself the door he bolted,
And lock'd her in it fast.

"But hear me, Little Katey,
"If mine thou wilt not be,
"There yawns a spikeset barrel,
"Is ready now for thee."

Within that spikeset barrel
The gentle maid was bound,
And came himself the tyrant,
And roll'd it round and round.

But tho' her tongue was voiceless,
At heart the prince she bless'd,
And pray'd her heavenly father
To give him peace and rest.

And then two snowy pigeons
Came down from out the sky;
With them the gentle Katey
To heaven was seen to fly.

And two black frightful ravens
Came up from out of hell,
And off to a place of torment
They took the prince to dwell.

poems.title: Saint Olave's Voyage
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Olave and Harald disagreed,
Which should to Norway's rocks succeed.
At Tronhiem so pleasant it is to rest.

"Which of us two the best can sail,
"Shall rule all Norway, hill and dale.

"Which of us first shall reach the strand,
"Shall king be crown'd of all the land."

'Twas Harald Hardrade answer made,
"Be it even so, as thou hast said.

"But, if I sail today with thee,
"Then thou shalt change thy ship with me;

"For with thy Dragon's rapid pace
"How is my drudging Ox to race?

"Like wind-borne cloud thy Dragon flies,
"My Ox his way as slowly plies."

"Harald, if so it pleases thee,
"I will to these thy terms agree.

"If mine is a better one than thine,
"I'll take thy ship, and give thee mine.

"The lively Dragon thou shalt take,
"And I with the Ox my voyage make.

"But first we both to church will go,
"Before we either sail or row.

As Olave through the churchyard strode,
Like golden thread his tresses glow'd.

A message came in haste to say,
"Thy brother Harald sails away."

"So let them sail, if sail they will,
"To God's word we will listen still.

"But while at Mass I hear His word,
"Go ye and water take on board."

"We go to table, eat our meal,
"And hasten then to launch our keel."

They took their meal, and sought the strand,
Where lay the tardy Ox at land;

And water, anchor, rope and oar
They quickly aboard their vessel bore.

Saint Olave sat on the ship's prow;
"Now, Ox, in name of Jesus go."

Saint Olave seized his long white horn;
"Now go, as if in fields of corn."

Such strides the Ox began to make,
That high with billows foam'd the wake.

"See, thou who sittest on the mast,
"If Harald's ship we are catching fast"

"For all the world naught else I see,
"Than just the top of a lofty tree.

"And now I see near Norway's land
"A silken sail with golden band.

"And now where Norway's shoals must lie,
"I see the Dragon's mainsail fly.

"I see just under Norway's side,
"With rapid leaps the Dragon stride."

A blow on the Ox's ribs he gave;
"Put out thy strength and dance the wave."

Olave struck him across the eye;
"Now faster still to harbour hie,"

The Ox began to plunge and leap,
Their legs the crew no more could keep.

He took him cords of flax and bast,
And bound his sailors to the mast.

"How shall we sail?" the steersman cried,
"And who shall now the vessel guide?"

Olave the saint unglov'd his hand,
Himself went at the helm to stand.

"We sail o'er hills and cliffs today,
"Just where we find the nearest way."

Forth forth they go, and hill and dale
Melt into waves as on they sail.

They scud through fell and mountain blue;
And scare the cavern'd Elfin crew.

"Who sails there through my treasur'd heap,
"To make my aged father weep?"

"Turn thee to stone, and stone remain,
"And wait till I come back again."

They sail'd across the hills of Scone,
And froze the swarthy Elves to stone.

There stood a hag with spinning wheel;
"And why should we thine anger feel?

"Saint Olave, thou, with ruddy beard,
"Thy ship has through my cellar steer'd."

The Saint look'd back, "Thou hag of Scone,
"Stand there and turn to granite stone."

Onward without mishap they sped,
Before them rock and forest fled.

So swift they left them all astern,
No eye could longer aught discern.

Saint Olave forward aim'd his how,
The shaft fell on the deck below.

Down from the prow he shot the shaft,
It reach'd the frothing sea abaft.

Saint Olave, who on God relied,
Three days the first his home descried.

Harald so fierce with anger burn'd,
He into a lothely dragon turn'd.

A pious zeal Saint Olave bore,
And so the crown of Norway wore.

And now to church Saint Olave went
Humbly his heartfelt thanks to vent:

And while he round the churchyard paced,
His streaming hair a glory graced.

Whom God assists will win their aim,
Their foes win naught but grief and shame.
At Tronkiem so pleasant it is to rest.

poems.title: Saint Olave at Hornelen
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Saint Olave, good king, o'er Norway's land
So well and so wisely reign'd,
God's word he made wife and man obey,
And justice and law maintain'd.

Saint Olave down on the ocean strand
Had built him a gallant Snake,
And now on the Trolds at Hornelen,
His vengeance resolved to take.

But answer'd the steersman, as at the stern
With rudder in hand he stood;
"So grim are the Trolds at Hornelen,
"That harbour was never good."

Up spake King Olave so free and bold,
And sprang on his Ox's prow;
"Take tackle on board, and now cast off,'
"In Jesus' name let go."

The Ox he puff'd, and loud he blew,
And over the billows strode;
So sail'd Saint Olave to Hornelen,
With woe to the Trold's abode.

The giant he stalk'd from out the hill,
Along the hoary rocks,
And saw there Olave the sainted king,
And breasting the wave his Ox.

His eyes were like two burning pyres,
And yawning his mouth to shout;
His finger nails were hooked and long,
Like goat's horns hanging out.

A beard he had like a horse's mane,
That hung to touch his knee;
His body was long, and skagg'd with hair,
And fearful his claws to see.

"There never in older times or since
"A snake-ship has come to land,
"That off to my cavern I could not drag,
"With only a single hand."

"Then" answer'd him Olave, the sainted king,
He fear'd not a Troldish foe,
"Throw over the Ox thy cords and chains,
"And see how that will go."

The Ox he seiz'd by his horn and stern,
And thought to have crush'd with ease,
Bat into a cliff he sank himself,
Till over both his knees.

"Though here I must stand a sunken rock,
"And further I cannot move,
"A strain of the back and tug of hand
"With thee I would gladly prove."

"Hold thou thy peace, thou baleful sprite,
"Aud there as a rock remain;
"For never till Doomsday hurt shalt thou
"A Christian man again."

Out ran from a cavern an aged hag,
And yeird with a voice so shrill,
And look'd so grim, as she hobbled along,
He bade the old crone be still.

Much wonder'd at this the smaller Trolds,
Who dwelt on the rocky shore;
"But what has befallen our aged crone,
"That now she cries no more?

"Then surely this is the Redbeard saint
"Who long has threatened our race;
"If we with our iron bars come out,
"We'll give him but little grace."

But turn'd were their trunks to shapeless blocks,
Their necks to their body press'd,
Their backs all broken to pieces small,
And heads crush'd into their breast.

Such wonder at Hornelen then was wrought,
As never was wrought before;
The cave with water was drown'd so deep,
That no one could find the door.

So thanks let all men give to God,
And thanks to Saint Olave too,
The sailor to Hornelen now may steer,
Nor care for what Trolds may do.

poems.title: The Buried Mother
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Swain Dyring he journey'd up the land,
And von a lovely maiden's hand;

Seven years she lived his home to share,
And seven the sweetest children bare;

But stalking through the land came death,
And stopp'd that gentle lady's breath.

Swain Dyring rode again up land,
And gain'd another maiden's hand.

He won his bride, and home she came,
A grim and harsh ill -favoured dame.

When from her gilded wain she stepp'd,
The seven poor children stood and wept.

They stood, those little things, and cried,
But kick'd them off th' unfeeling bride.

She gave them neither bread nor beer,
"Hunger and hate will be your cheer.

She took away their bolsters blue,
"Bare straw shall be the bed for you."

She took away their fire and light,
"In blind -house ye shall sleep all night."

They cried one evening, till the sound
Their mother heard beneath the ground.

She heard it, as in her grave she lay,
"But go I must their pain to stay."

At God's high throne she bent her knee,
"O let me, Lord, my children see."

And such her prayer, and tale of woe,
That God in mercy let her go.

"But there on earth no longer stay,
"When cock shall crow the dawn of day."

Hi Out from their chest she stretch'd her hones,
And rent her way through earth and stones.

As through the street she glided by,
Loud all the hounds howl'd to the sky.

She reach'd her husband's courtyard gate,
And there her eldest daughter sate.

"O daughter mine, why so in tears?
"How fare my other little dears?"

"No mother at all art thou of mine,
"Thou'rt not like her, though fair and fine;

"My mother's cheeks were white and red,
"But thine are pale, and like the dead."

"And how should I be fine or fair,
"When death has bleach'd the cheeks I bear?

"Or how should I be white and red,
"So long, my child, as I've been dead?"'

She found her children's sleeping place,
And wet with tears each little face.

She nurs'd them all with mother's care,
She comb'd and dress'd their silky hair.

The infant babe she took on lap,
And offer'd him the welcome pap.

Her eldest daughter then she sped,
To fetch Swain Dyring out of bed.

And when before her chair he stood,
She chid him thus in angry mood:

"I left' thee store of beer and bread,
I find my children all unfed.

"I left thee bolsters of softest down,
"And here on straw I find them thrown.

I left thee many a good waxlight,
"And here they lie in the dark all night

"This warning take, thy duty learn,
"'Tis ill for you, if I return.

"There's crowing now the rooster red,
"And back to the earth must go the dead;

"And now I hear the black cock crow,
"Heaven's gate is open, and I must go.

"Now crows the white return of day,
"A moment more I dare not stay."

Whenever, hound was heard to whine,
They gave the children bread and wine.

Whenever hound was heard to bark,
They thought the dead walk'd in the dark.

Whenever bound was heard to howl,
They thought they saw a corpse's cowl.

poems.title: Sabbath Breaking
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Jonas Hawk and Sir Nilus Mard
Two comrades dear were they,
And rode together in chase of game
The morning of Easter day.

They pass'd the cloister, they pass'd the church,
Nor had they a thought of mass;
But hasten'd away with hawks and hounds
Off into the wild morass.

By church and cloister alike they rode,
And scorn'd any mass to hear,
And came on the heath, and told their dreams,
The weary way to cheer.

"It seem'd, as over the bridge I rode,
"My horse with a sadden bound
"Had started and thrown me off his back,
"And trod on me on the ground."

"And didst thou seem, Sir Nilus Mard,
"Across a bridge to ride?
"This vision doth surely, trust my words,
"Some evil for us betide."

Thus all so friendly these comrades rode
And came to a wooded hill;
"True, true, Sir Jonas, the dream I have dream'd,
"Does certainly bode us ill.

"My horse so wildly rear'd and plunged,
"My boots were full of blood,
"And senseless he threw me upon the turf,
"And ran to the forest stud."

But onward they rode, nor gave their dreams
One further thought or care,
For near them a tiny creature ran,
They took it to be a hare.

The creature spake with a human voice,
And utter'd the words so plain;
"Sir Nilus, hark thee! recall thy dogs,
"For me thou wilt chase in vain.

"A steak of my body thou wilt not broil,
"Though hunting me all the day,
"But when thou art come on the open field,
"A different game wilt play.

"Aye tho' thou hunt est me all day long,
"I come not beneath thy knife;
"But sure as thou dost so, trust my words,
"Thy comrade will lose his life."

"Sir Nilus, aware!" Sir Jonas cried
With loud and derisive shout,
"The hare is making for yonder wood;
"Now what are your dogs about?

"Yourself will have train'd those precious hounds,
"May well of the pack be vain;
"They run as swiftly on salty sea,
"As over the grassy plain!"

"Ride on," replied Sir Nilus Mard,
While anger heav'd his breast,
"Ride whither thou wilt, thou basely born,
"But make not my hounds thy jest.

"Ride whither thou wilt, thou basely born,
"Nor stop to chide at a hound,
"Perhaps thou mayest thy father find,
"Go scour the country round."

"No bastard nor fatherless child am I,
"For father! — I do know mine,
"He left to me household stuff and land,
"That never did one of thine."

They drew their circle upon the ground
In midst of the wild black heath,
And there they closed in an angry fight,
And struggled for life and death.

They fought for a day, they fought for two,
Alone on the moory plain,
Nor would they either the circle quit
Till one had the other slain.

And there lay both those gentlemen,
And slowly they bled to death;
And off their horses, and hawks and hounds
Fled wildly across the heath.

And they fought too, those noble steeds,
As were they with fury fill'd;
And hound beside them was match'd with hound,
Till each had the other kill'd.

Ah! luckless the hounds they bred and train'd.
The cause of so deadly strife,
Two comrades for them in combat fell,
And bootlessly lost their life.

The gentle Mettelille, sorely wept,
Sir Nilus's youthful bride,
And Sidselille, she, fair lovely maid,
Sat sorrowing, till she died.

And so I counsel you each and all,
Ride not to the healthful chase,
Till, late or early, you've been to church,
And pray'd to your God for grace.

poems.title: The Cruel Sister (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There lived an honest man and true,
might I follow thee!
And daughters had but only two;
So dupes t thou not me!

The younger bright as is the sun,
But black as dirt the elder one.

The younger suitors came to woo,
With tli elder none would have to do.

The younger loom and shuttle plied,
The elder slept at chimney side.

The elder took her sister's hand,
"Come, let us go to yonder strand.

"To yonder strand let us repair,
"And wash ourselves so clean and fair."

As on the younger stepp'd so gay,
The wind would with her ringlets play.

The elder follow'd close behind,
And anger fill'd her sullen mind;

As on a stone the younger trod,
She thrust her into the rushing flood.

"O hear me, sister, let me live,
"And thee my best gold cup I give."

"I'll get thy best gold cup, and more,
"But thou shalt never come ashore."

"O hear me, sister, let me live,
"And thee my buckle of gold I give."

"Thy buckle of gold I'll have, and more,
"But thou shalt never come ashore."

"O hear me, sister, let me live,
"And thee my trulove I will give."

"Thy trulove I shall get, and more,
"But thou shalt never come ashore."

By God's high will a tempest blew,
And on the coast her body threw.

Two minstrels walked along the strand,
And saw the maiden float to land.

They took her golden hair so long,
And therewithal their fiddle strung.

"To yon great house we'll now repair,
"Their merry wedding-feast to share/'

The first string ding a doleful sound,
"The bride her younger sister drown'd/'

The second string, as that they tried,
"In terror sits the youthful bride/'

The third string sang beneath their bow,
"And surely now her tears will flow/'

The bride stripped off her golden band,
