And laid it on the minstrel's hand.

Tuesday began her heart to ache,
And Thursday night smoked at the stake.

poems.title: The Cruel Sister (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There came a wooing suitors two,
And both the younger maid to woo.
Tis merry at summer tide.

To her alone their court they paid,
And much it vex'd the elder maid.

"Dear little sister, take my hand,
"And go with me to yonder strand."

"But why then go to the water-side,
"When all our clothes are wash'd and dried?"

"We'll wash ourselves as white as snow,
"And be more like two sisters so/'

With flowing hair the younger went,
On ill designs the elder bent.

The younger maid stepp'd on a stone,
And by the elder down was thrown.

"O dearest sister, let me live,
"And thee my gilded shrine I'll give."

"What profits me thy gilded shrine,
"Unless thy trulove too is mine?"

"Him give I not my life to save,
"Nay, rather sink beneath the wave."

"Float on then, float away to sea;
"Thy trulove safely falls to me."

A storm from th' east began to blow,
And drive the body to and fro.

The sea roll'd in, so hard it blew,
And on the coast the maiden threw.

It chanced two minstrels paced the strand,
And saw the body float to land.

They took her locks of yellow hair,
With them they strung their bows so fair.

They then cut off her fingers small,
And made their fiddle-screws withal.

So to the nearest town they went,
To share the feast and merriment.

A lively tune they fain would play,
The fiddle sang a piteous lay;

And ever, when they drew their bow,
Counted its wrongs, and told its woe.

It said "My sister sits as bride,
"And he is my trulove at her side/'

poems.title: Sir Morten of Fogelsong
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Morten, lord of Fogelsong,
Rode over the greenwood lawn,
And there he breath'd a poison blast,
About the morning dawn.
Dead rides Sir Marten of Fogelsong.

He gave the cloister his good grey horse,
The church a sum of gold,
And died, and with a solemn dirge
Was laid beneath the mould.

All heap'd with earth, as best they could,
They left his buried corse,
But ere the toll of midnight bell
He rose and mounted horse.

A knight there was, Sir Folmer Skot,
Rode over hill and dale,
And after him Sir Morten rode,
And pray'd him hear his tale.

"O stay, thou good Sir Folmer Skot,
"And kindly lend a ear,
"And by my holy Christian faith
"No harm hast thou to fear."

"But first, Sir Morten, tell me how
"Thou ridest here to day,
"And only yesternight a corse
"We laid thee in the clay?"

"It's not for doom I am riding here,
"It's not at court to sue,
"But only for a plot of ground
"To two small orphans due.

It's not because of buried gold,
It's not to venge a wrong;
But for those orphans' little field
Forsworn to Fogelsong.

"Now haste to Lady Mettelille,
And tell her my request,
"She give those orphans back the field,
"And let my soul have rest.

"And tell the Lady Mettelille,
"If doubt should cross her mind,
"That close beside my chamber door
"My slippers she may find.

"Those two nightslippers, where they stand
"Beside the chamber door,
"Tonight ere toll of midnight bell
"Shall both be full of gore."

"Go then, go rest thy weary bones, "
Sir Morten, noble knight,
"For on my Christian faith I swear,
"Those orphans get their right."

And all in black Sir Morten went
Down to his dark abode,
And black were both his hawk and hound,
And troop that with him rode.

The noble Lady Mettelille
Obey'd her lord's request,
And gave the children back their field,
And so his soul had rest.

poems.title: Maribo Well
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Algrave loud on his cornet blew,
The long and weary night
The Queen in her bower his signal knew.
Of love I feel the might.

She call'd to her page "Run, boy, with speed,
And hither to me the Algrave lead."

The Algrave he stood before her board;
"What wish you, my Queen? why send me word?"

"Dear Algrave, if once the king were dead,
I'd make thee lord of my gold so red.

"O softly! my Queen, hush! say not so;
"There may be listeners; who can know?"

They thought full surely none else was near,
The King had listened with heedful ear.

The king two servants was heard to call;
"Go bid the Queen to the audience hall."

"Now tell me, my fair and graceful Queen,
"What was it you told the Count yestre'en?"

"I told him no other than this, I vow,
"Than just how great and how good wert thou"

The King two servants was heard to call;
"Go bid the Count to the audience hall."

"Now tell me, Sir Count, and tell me right,
"What told you the Queen of me last night?"

"I told her, and nothing else, I vow,
"How good and noble a king wast thou."

He bade his page boy "The cooks go call,
"And bid them come to the audience hall.

"Go, chop yon Algrave to pieces fine,
"And serve him up to the Queen to dine.

"Go, chop him to pieces as small as fish,
"And serve him up on the Queen's own dish."

The Queen saw what on the table came,
"Now that is surely no kind of game."

She look'd again, and she rightly guess'd,
"The count it must be, the cooks have dress'd."

To save him she knew was not too late,
And cuird each morsel, the small and great.

She wrapp'd them up in an ermine fine,
And laid them all in a gilded shrine.

Those morsels she took, so chopp'd and rent,
And straight to the Maribo fountain went.

She dipp'd them where clearest the water ran,
"Stand up, stand up, thou Christian man!"

And up on his feet did the Algrave stand,
Thank God for his mercy, and leave the land.

poems.title: Saint Stephen and Herod
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A virgin pure was risen on earth,
The rose of womankind,
The fairest maid in all this world,
For Queen of heaven designed.

Her cheeks were like the roses red,
Her neck as ermine fair;
Because so sweet a maid she was,
Our Lord was she to bear.

In glory th' angel Gabriel came,
To Mary sent was he;
"Tis from the Lord of hosts I come,
"Christ's mother you shall be."

Answer the pious Mary -made,
As God put in her mind;
"His holy will be done: in me
"His handmaid he shall find."

For two score weeks with child she went
Without or pain or care;
On Yule-night, by His own high will,
Her blessed Lord she bare.

Saint Stephen saw the star's bright shine,
As he his horses drave;
"Of truth is now the Prophet born,
"Who all the world shall save."

"On Stephen's tale," King Herod said,
"No faith will I bestow,
"Unless this roasted cock stand up,
"And clap his wings and crow."

Straight clapp'd his wings the cock, and crow'd,
"Our Lord is born to-night"
From off his throne King Herod fell,
And swoon'd away for fright.

Uprose the King and mounted horse,
To Bethlehem town to ride;
He fain that little child would kill,
Which all his power defied.

But Mary took in arms her babe,
Joseph his ass's rein,
And so through Jewish land they rode
To Egypt's sandy plain.

Full fourteen thousand babies small
The tyrant caused to slay;
Jesus, ere sank the sun to rest,
Was thirty miles away.

poems.title: Saint Gertrude
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Gertrude was e'en the fairest may
Of all the isles in Charles's sway.
Help us thou virgin Saint Gertrude!

Gertrude's godfather, newly dead.
Had left the maid his towers so red.

Then came a count with ruthless band
To spoil and waste the maiden's land.

Gertrude went out with staff and book.
Her silent way to the churchyard took,

She read a chapter, two she read.
And chaunted prayers to wake the dead.

She read so loud, she sang so long,
Until the dead man heard her song.

With hollow moan he rais'd his head,
"Who dares upon my grave to tread?"

"'Tis I Gertrude, god-daughter thine,
"O help me, dear god-father mine!

"There's come a count with ruthless hand
"To waste and ravage all my land.'

The dead man stretched his long leg hone,
And rent the walls and marble stone.

'Twas far to go, the pathway strait,
And slow and shamhling the dead man's gait.

In through the door the dead man stepp'd;
The living all to comers crept.

All but the guilty count had fled.
But he stood up and fought the dead.

In two the dead man broke his back.
In three he made his leg-hones crack.

"Gertrude, Gertrude, enjoy thy land,
"SAnd save me from the deadman's hand."

Back to his grave, a weary track,
She bare the dead man on her back.

"And what, if now I let thee live,
"Wilt thou thy dear Godfather give?"

"Over thy grave a church I'll build,
"With glittering gold its roof I'll gild.

"Beneath a cross shall rest thy bones,
"In marble shrined, and precious stones.
Help us thou virgin Saint, Gertrude!

poems.title: The Victory of Patience
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The lovely maiden Ellensborg,
An orphan she was left;
Of parents, — father and mother both, —
In tender years bereft.

Her father and mother both had died,
Her brothers and sisters too,
When Lave Stisen, a wealthy knight,
The maiden came to woo.

He gained the slender Ellensborg,,
To her he pledged his hand,
And trusted her to his mother's care,
And left his native land. I

Off started Lave Stisen, he.
And went to the wars away;
Right glad was Esbern Anderson,
That he at home could stay.

As Lave Stisen vent on board,
And pushed his boat from land;
Off galloped Esbern Anderson
Across the yellow sand.

He mounted, Esbern Anderson,
Wrapt in his purple cloak,
Up to the ladies upper room,
And thus to the maiden spoke.

"My greeting little Ellensborg!
"This kindness show to me,
"Make me a shirt all richly wrought
"With gold embroidery."

"Should I make up a shirt for you,
"And broider it with gold,
"My trothplight man would hear of it,
"And all his love grow cold."

They knew not, they, while so they talked.
That any else were near;
There stood outside the waiting maid.
And every word could hear.

That little treacherous waiting maid.
She sat her down and wrote,
And off afar to a foreign land
To Stisen sent the note.

"A stag is in our garden ground,
"He nibbles off the leaf,
"And if you come not quickly home,
"Will bring the root to grief."

With sorrow Lave Stisen read
What she, the maid, had penn'd;
"Now help me God in heaven above!
"How will this story end?"

As Lave Stisen towards his home
Came riding up the street,
His mother and eke his trothplight maid
Went out the knight to meet.

They led him both so joyously
Into the banquet room;
So little knew fair Ellensborg,
What soon should be her doom.

"Welcome, my dearest trulove, home
"From all the toils of war!
"Where have you stay'd this long long time
"In foreign lands afar?"

"What time I march'd from home away,
"A modest maid wast thou;
"I hear that Esbern Andersen
"Is much too friendly now."

"So help me God, who dwells on high,
"And thou Our Virgin Queen!
"I treated him, as I had done,
"Had he my brother been."

He shut her up in a room of stone.
Where three whole years she stay'd;
And in her stead for leman took
The little waiting maid.

None to the maiden dared to speak,
Or e'en to her prison go;
Sir Lave's mother, and no one else,
Went thither to and fro.

And in Sir Lave's mother came
With step of stately grace;
"God's mercy! little Ellensborg,
"How pallid grows thy face!"

"Aye!" answered maiden Ellensborg,
So meek and gently bred;
"A poor lone orphan girl am I,
"My parents both are dead."

Sir Lave's mother heard her tale
Drew on her scarlet cloak,
And mounted up to the upper -room,
And thus her son bespoke.

"Good day. Sir Lave, greet thee well,
"My dearest son and heir!
"Now wilt thou not thy trulove wed,
"So good she is and fair?"

Sir Lave rose and spake in haste,
A wrathful man to view;
"O no, my dearest mother, no,
"That will I never do.

"No, mother, that I'll never do,
"I'd rather far be dead:
"Next Sunday make my marriage feast,
"My leman I shall wed."

"And if the marriage day is fix'd,
"And she to be thy wife,
"Grant heaven she make thee soon repent,
"And plague thee all thy life!"

Sir Lave took his scarlet cloak.
And -went to the room of stone,
Where still was pent little Ellensborg
And sorrowed all alone.

"Now list to me, little Ellensborg
"So gentle and so fair;
"Go to my bridal chamber thou,
"My bridal bed prepare.

"The silken counterpane above,
"The fur beneath it spread,
"My leman sleeps between the two,
"For her prepare the bed.

"To her, my leman, I shall give
"A gown of velvet pile;
"To thee I mean to give one too,
"But woollen that, and vile.

"A precious belt I'll give to her
"With gold to hold it fast.
"A girdle too I'll give to thee,
"But that shall be of bast."

And thus the maiden Ellensborg
With modest gentle air;
"Whatever clothes you give to me,
"Contented I shall wear."

It was that very Sunday next,
So holy was the tide.
Sir Lave Stisen off to church
Would with his leman ride.

The leman stood in the upper room
In velvet robe so gay,
And outside maiden Ellensborg
In gown of wadmal gray.

The leman girded on her belt,
With gold she made it fast;
Her's too the maiden Ellensborg,
And that was made of bast.

Then out the good kind mother spake,
Nor longer could forbear;
"God's mercy, child, and daughter mine!
"What wedding clothes to wear!"

As joyously as off to church
The leman drove away,
As sorely did his trulove grieve.
That she at home must stay.

When mass the priest had duly sung,
And lesson read beside,
He with his leman mounted horse
Home to his house to ride.

In came to the hall the little page.
In kirtle red was drest;
"And here Sir Lave's leman comes
"Under the mountain crest.

"Her wain is all so brightly gilt,
"Her horses dapple gray;
"I never yet, sweet Ellensborg,
"Saw any thing so gay."

The leman on the bridal chair
They placed to head the board,
And Esbern Andersen it was
The bridal goblet pour'd.

The guests they ate, and quaff'd the wine,
Nor stayed to drink too deep.
For soon Sir Lave Stisen rose,
Would fain retire to sleep.

They left the leman all in state
Reclin'd on silver bed;
Nor long did Lave Stisen wait,
But up to the chamber sped.

It chanced Sir Lave Stisen's cloak
From off his shoulders fell;
Fair Ellensborg she picked it up,
For still she loved him well.

She hasted so, little Ellensborg,
To pick him up his cloak.
That, as she stoop'd, her belt gave way,
And all asunder broke.

And thus spake maiden Ellensborg,
Her secret thoughts she told;
"Too fast holds that which ought to break,
"And broken is what should hold."

"Now what is that?" Sir Lave said,
In eager haste he spake,
"Say what is that which ought to hold,
"And what was that which brake?"

"What burst in two and ought to e held,
"That was my belt of bast;
"My heart it is that ought to break,
"And yet it holds so fast/'

Sir Lave's leman up and spake,
And laugh'd to see her pain;
"Twere very little loss, I deem,
"Should thy heart burst in twain/'

Sir Lave spake in other tone,
For no bad man was he
"To hear thy words little Ellensborg,
"I truly pity thee.

"Hark thee, my leman, take thee hence!
"Quick! leave the bridal bed,
"And hither thou, my trulove, come,
"For none bat thee I'll wed."

There to their bedside came the priest
And join'd them man and wife;
"Ood grant," said maiden Ellensborg,
"Our friendship last for life!"

And now the gentle Ellensborg
No longer grieves or weeps,
Bat nightly on Sir Lave's arm
In wedded comfort sleeps.

His mother to the bridal house
At early morning went,
To ask how with his youthful bride
The wedding night he spent.

"So pleas'd with her, my gentle bride,
"The livelong night I've lain,
"That deep and sorely do I rue,
"I ever gave her pain/'

"Now then. Sir Lave, list to me,
"And do the thing that's right;
"Thy leman give young Anderson
"To wed this very night."

Loud rose the joy of all the house,
And voice of song and lute;
To him he did his leman give
And granges two to boot.

poems.title: Jesus and the Virgin Mary (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
On Yule night Christ to man was given,
Praised be Jesu's name!
A star that night was set in heaven,
From the Holy Spirit came.

In cradle Mary laid him down
Clad in his little linen gown.

A slumber over Mary crept,
And gone was Jesus, while she slept.

Mary, in tears and full of woe,
She sought him long through frost and snow.

She took a pilgrim's staff in hand,
And wandered forth to IsraeVs land.

Where first she trod on Israel's ground,
Joseph her own goodman she found.

"My goodman Joseph, answer me,
"Hast thou my Jesus chanced to see?"

"Aye! sooth, I've seen thy dearest son;
"He's not long since to his garden gone.

Ont to the garden Mary hied,
And Jesus mid the flowers espied.

"O tell me, thou, my son so dear,
"Why cause thy mother grief and fear?"

"Mother,' he said, "have I not need
"My flowers to tend, my beds to weed?

"I weed them all from first to last,
"And what bear thorns, away I cast.

"The thorns they go to a place of dole,
"I cast them into a murky hole."

poems.title: Jesus and the Virgin Mary (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Here we come to sing our lay.
Welcome, welcome, month of May!
Little pretty girls so fair.
Far and wide
At summer-tide
Are rosebuds springing every where.

The Virgin and her blessed Son
Up to Jerusalem were gone;

She went to church, but while she pray'd,
In slumber sank the Holy Maid:

And when she woke from sleep' again,
Gone was He from where he had lain.

Mary looked among the chairs,
Where the maidens sat at prayers.

She look'd behind the holy tree,
Where many a sinner bent the knee.

At last, as to the stile she came,
There Hallelujah met the dame.

"Hark Hallelujah! dear old friend,
"Hast thou seen Jesus hither wend?'

"Up at Jerusalem yestre'en
"Thy dear son, Jesus, I have seen.

"I heard him there, I saw him there,
"A gory crown of thorns he bare.

"With whips his little back they flay'd,
"Of leather straps new scourges made."

This song we yet must sing again,
Little pretty girls so fair.
Before we think of all his pain.
Far and wide
At summer -tide
Are rosebuds springing every where.

poems.title: Jesus and the Virgin Mary (C)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
I've heard a sung, I've learnt the same,
How God will sinners spare,
A song about Lord Jesus Christ,

The Son he sits and tells his dream
On his sweet mother's knee:
"I've dream'd tonight that wicked Jews
"Will doom and martyr me."

They led him up and down the streets
In sight of all the town,
And thorns and thistles gathered up.
And plaited him a crown.

Out to the cross they led him then,
And nail'd him on the wood:
"Now must I bear the pangs of death
"Alike for bad and good!'

Out to the cross they led him forth,
And hammered in the spike:
"Now must I bear the pangs of death
"For poor and rich alike!"

And then they brought a blind man up
To take a lancets hilt;
He drove it into Jesus side,
And holy blood he spilt.

That pure and holy blood they took,
And smear'd it on his eye;
The blind man gain'd his sight anew.
And saw Lord Jesus die.

"Have mercy. Lord, on me poor man,
"And pardon me my crime,
"And father and mother I will leave,
"And seek some distant clime.

"Have mercy. Lord, on me poor man,
"And pardon me my sin,
"I'll make my pilgrimage afar,
"And leave my kith and kin."

poems.title: Mary Magdalene
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Beside a fountain stood a dame.
And thither too Lord Jesus came.

"Hark, dame! a draught from this clear spring!
"And in thy hand the water bring."

"Welcome thou art to quench thy thirst,
"I'll fetch my silver goblet first."

"Didst thou but pure before me stand,
"I would have drunk it off thy hand."

Pure as a newborn babe, she sware,
She free from sin was standing there.

"Swear thou not so, for in the earth
"Lie three to whom thou gavest birth;

"The first one is thy father's son,
Thy brother's is the second one.

"The third begot the parish priest;
"That of thy sins was not the least."

The woman fell at Jesus' knee;
"O dearest Jesu, shrive thou me."

"I thee none other shriving give,
"Than seven whole years afield to live;

"No other meal whereon to feed,
"Than groweth on the grassy mead;

"No other draught to cool thy lips,
"Than dew that from the herbage drips."

When seven long years she thus had spent.
To seek this sinful dame He went.

"Hark thee, my daughter, answer me,
"If well thy fasting liketh thee?"

"So liketh me this fasting mine,
"As tho' I ate of bread and wine."

"So then shalt thou partake of heaven,
"And 'fore my mother stand forgiven."

poems.title: Saint James and the Vision of Hell
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Saint James had taken a stone for seat,
Help us, Lord, and save!
And fain would rest his weary feet;
Send us, great Christ, thy grace.

And Jesus came, and bade him, hail!
"Thou now to a foreign land shalt sail/'

"To foreign lands how shall I steer,
"And neither ship nor cutter here?"

The stone with staff Lord Jesus smote,
And set the mighty mass afloat.

Gently the same began to glide,
And then a hundred miles it hied.

From window look'd the heathen king;
"I never saw a stranger thing.

"Such wonder never met mine eyes;
"Yon rock with a man upon it flies.

"What dost thou in my land design?
"My God is better far than thine."

"If better thou thy God hast found,
"Bring me the son yestre'en was drown'd."

"No son of mine was drowned yestre'en,
"My son was lost years now fifteen."

Saint James the Holy Bible took,
And sang by turns and read the book.

A chapter read, a chapter sang,
Till on his feet the deadman sprang.

He floated up so white and red,
As though he never had been dead.

"Tell me, my child, where hast thou been,
"So many years since thee I've seen?"

Father, I've stood at heaven's high door,
"Where all are glad, and grieve no more;

"And down to the gates of hell I've gone,
"Where those must sit, who ill have done;

"Seen her, who once her mother slew,
"On red-hot stool the murder rue;

"Seen him, by whom his father died,
"In hell on red-hot saddle ride;

"The hostess, she who mix'd her wine,
"In hell I've seen her sit and pine;

"The trader, he who falsely weight,
"In hell I've seen his theft repaid;

"The bailiff too, with hat so high,
"In hell I've heard for taxes cry;

"And seen the spoilt unruly chit
"In hell on glowing iron sit.

"Over them hangs a cloak of lead,
"And melts, as burns the fire so red."

poems.title: The Angel's Errand
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Virgin Mary paced a wood,
And plucked the flowers that round her stood.

The brown she pluck'd, and blue so sweet,
She wished the Master she could meet.

Our Lord sat on his heavenly throne.
And th' angel bade in kindly tone:

"Down to the earth thy journey wing,
"And up to me the Virgin bring."

A bird sat on a linden-spray.
And trill'd a sweet and heavenly lay.

He sat him on a peartree rod,
And sang of Christ, and sang of God.

One day he sang, he sang for three,
Before she chanced the bird to see.

But when she heard the notes he sung.
How much she joy'd in heart and tongue!

"Lord Jesus, grant this bird were mine,
"I'd seat him on a gilded shrine.

"Lord Jesus, would the bird were tame!
"I'd seat him on a golden frame."

The Virgin open'd windows three,
But into none of them would he.

She open'd five, she opened all,
Yet came not in that bird so small.

She went, bright as the streamlet clear.
To lure the little songster near.

He greeted her in tones of love,
"Tomorrow thou'rt in heaven above."

"In heaven shall I tomorrow be?
"Then I my Saviour there shall see."

The maid went out so sound and hale.
But breathed a blast of deadly bale.

"Sister, a coverlet o'er me spread,.
"Stand thou, dear mother, near my bed.

"Oh! brother, were a priest at hand!
"My dearest father near me stand.

"My parents, weep not ye for me,
"In heaven we soon each other see.

"And now my spirit I commend
"Into my blessed Saviour's hand."

Between the hours of four and five
They laid her down in bed alive.

Between the hours of eight and nine
Her breath in peace did she resign.

To clothe her corpse stood Mary there,
Her soul to heaven good angels bare.

And now with God is her abode,
Because a stedfast faith she show'd.

The maid had plighted Christ her love,
And now she dwells in heaven above.

poems.title: The Rich Man's Soul (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Death to the rich man's mansion went,
Was purpos'd the rich man's self to hent.
The tongue may talk, but the soul shall answer at
Judgement day.

"O death, o death, prithee, let me live,
"And thee I will all my goldheaps give."

"It is not thy ruddy gold I crave;
"Thyself thou art due to fill thy grave.

"Bring hither the coin, the great and small,
"So sinfully gained, so loved withal."

Tho' many were willing his coin to share.
Was no one his guilty soul would hear.

The rich man he cross'd his children all,
And little he thought on Adam's fall.

That day in revel and feast he kept,
The night in his sinful mansion slept:

But burst his heart, and his soul slipped out,
And left his body a cast off clout.

So many bad spirits crowded round,
The soul no longer a refuge found.

It sat itself down on the rich man's breast;
"God help me! where find I refuge best?"

But thither an angel wing'd his flight,
And rescued the soul from Satan's might.

Loud shouted the devil a fearful wail;
"That soul shoot dead and on cross tree nail."

mortals, repent, while yet ye may,
Nor think on the world your trust to lay;

Ere sun and moon shall have ceas'd to rise.
And fallen the stars from out the skies.

poems.title: The Rich Man's Soul (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A golden cross the rich man wears,
And little for Jesus Christ he cares.
The tongue may talk, but the Soul shall answer at judgement day,

But into the rich man's house came death,
And 'ere the sunrise stopped his breath.

Down on his mouth they laid his soul,
It cursed his body, part and whole.

They laid the soul on the rich man's breast,
"God show, where comfort it finds, and rest!"

They led the soul through murky woods,
To land and money and household goods.

They laid the soul on scales to weigh,
"If sin thou hast done, thou'rt now my prey."

But down on the scale three blood-drops fell,
And shudder'd with fear the sprites of hell.

So soon as account of its life was given,
The soul slipp'd into the gate of heaven.

poems.title: The Miraculous Cure
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Biorn to foreign service went.
Far far away seven winters spent;

And first when all those years were past,
He came to his long left home at last.

Sir Biorn rode up to his courtyard gate,
And near it he saw a pilgrim wait.

"Good Pilgrim, plodding thy way from Rome,
"Hast thou pass'd lately my trulove's home?"

"Aye! yesterday morning I was there,
"And saw and spoke to your trothplight fair.

"And truly were none so fair as she,
"But just for a secret injury.

"The loveliest maid beneath the sun
"Has but one leg to stand upon."

Sir Biorn he call'd his varlets twain,
"Go ye, my palfrey to girth and rein.

"Haste, bring me my good grey palfrey round;
"And get, ye others, that pilgrim bound.

"Down into the tower the slanderer throw,
"While I to the lady's dwelling go."

He halted where lived his trothplight maid,
And met him Christine in furs array M.

"Here standing, Christine, so lovely still!
"How fares my trothplight Ingelille?"

"Fair Ingelille sits in her lonely room,
"To spin her gold and to ply the loom:

"But while the silk with the gold she weaves,
"Her heart with a secret sorrow heaves."

Sir Biorn in a mantle wrapp'd his head,
And up to Ingelille's chamber sped.

She saw at the door her trulove stand,
And kindly she held him forth her hand.

The soft blue cushioned couch she pressed,
"Here seat you with me, Sir Biorn, and rest/'

Fair Ingelille call'd - "Go maiden mine,
"And bring me hither the horn of wine."

"I taste not of wine or other thing,
"Unless my trulove the goblet bring."

Fair Ingelille then her tale began.
While streaming tears from her eyelids ran.

"Now hark, Sir Biorn, sit at my side,
"My troubles from you I will not hide.

"In th' evening at twilight I was born;
"My mother had died ere dawn of mom:

"And while they laid her in Christian mould,
The passing bell for my father toll'd.

"Of all but a brother was I bereft,
"And me in a cloister that brother left.

"The foster-mother he found for me,
"A good and a gentle dame was she.

"Her maidens they nursed me one by one,
"And round the gallery let me run.

"As, tired, to bed I wish'd to go,
"A boiling cauldron stood below

"I tripp'd, and fell within its brim,
"And so was scalded off a limb.

"For when they drew me from out its wave,
"My foot there could no master save.

"And now take back this clasp so red,
"For wrong it were for me to wed."

With crutch beneath her mantle blue
And tearful eyes the maid withdrew.

Out to the garden alone she went
With grief in her gentle bosom pent

She knelt and pray'd on her bare knee;
"Jesus, Lord, show grace on me.

"Lord Jesus, help me, hear my cry,
"And I will a virgin live and die."

'Twas on a crutch she thither crept,
But back on both her feet she stepp'd.

"Take back, Sir Biorn, your clasp of gold;
"Tho' now you may wish your bride to hold.

"Take back again your golden band;
"Tho' now you may wish to gain my hand."

He offer'd her all the gold again,
"Fair maiden, my trulove still remain.'

"O keep it yourself, the gold so bright,
"My love to you I shall never plight.

"The clasp and the band yourself retain;
"I'll nevermore trust a knight again. '

"I now retire to a cloister cell,
"Will there to Oar Lady's service dwell."

And into the cloister she withdrew,
And with her went all her maidens too.

poems.title: Saint George and the Dragon
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
"Saint George, mine errand thou shalt ride,
"My true and loyal knight,
"At Tahiam, that mighty town,
"Against the Dragon fight.

Outside the gate there lies a pool,
"And well 'tis wall'd with stone;
"Therein a lothely dragon dwells,
"The bane of all the town.

"Each day some wretch doth he devour,
"Or puffs his poisonous breath,
"And who inhales its baleful stench,
"Is doom'd to a speedy death."

The King and Emperor counsel took,
The rich and eke the poor.
Who to the Dragon next must go.
And whom he should devour.

The lots were cast, and doom'd to death
The Princess too must go;
And much the king her fate bewail'd.
And wrung his hands for woe.

"Rise then, my daughter, dress thyself
"All in thy best array:
"I thought to see thee a Prince's bride,
"And not a Dragon's prey."

Up rose the maiden, dress'd herself
In richest robe of state,
Took in her arms a little lamb,
And left the castle gate.

As tearful out of town she went,
And much and deeply sigh'd,
No child was there in all the place,
But for the maiden cried.

She stood before the mountain cave,
And peered around so wide;
And there the knight Saint George she saw
In gallop towards her ride.

His horse was white, his banner red,
By that the knight was known;
"Speak, noble maiden, speak, and say,
"Why here you stand alone?

"And tell me, noble maiden, why
"You drop the frequent tear;
"If robb'd you've been, or foully used,
"Your grief I fain would hear."

"I weep that to a lothely worm
"My parents me must give;
"Ride, gallant youth, ride hence away,
"If longer you would live."

"Fly will not I, nor leave your side
"In this your hour of grief;
"I've to the holy Virgin vow'd
"To haste to your relief."

While there they stood in sweet discourse
That gentle saintly pair,
Out flew the Dragon against the knight
Forth from his mountain lair.

Into his gorge the lance he drove,
And splintered it in three,
But, swift as any hird could fly,
Unsheathe his sword did he.

As swift as any hird could fly,
He drew and dealt his blows;
"I charge thee by the Holy Ghost
"Thy fetid maw to close.

"Come now, fair maiden, loose your belt,
"And bind his head withal,
"And let your friends and townsmen see
"The monster led in thrall."

In to the city then they went,
That saintly pair so brave;
"King, take on the Christian faith,
"Your realm from peril save/'

"Thy faith we take, myself and realm
"Of all and each degree:
"My daughter, her to thee I give,
"Thine equal she will be."

"Nay, though she be of equal rank,
"My troth I dare not plight,
"I've to the Virgin made a vow
"To live her loyal knight."

poems.title: Ordeal by Fire
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sorrow lies wait at all men's door,
Grant God it come not in!
And so may little Kirstin say
Anent her kith and kin;
This sorrow, friends, I owe to you,
To whom I've ever been so true,

Sir Peter home from council came,
Was riding up the street;
And out she stepp'd, his daughter dear.
With greetings him to meet.

"Welcome, Sir Peter, home again,
"Welcome, my father dear;
"Now what was at the council said?
"What tidings met your ear?"

"This is the news I learned today,
"And little else beside;
"Thy trothplight man has thee forsworn,
"And chosen another bride.

"Thy trothplight man has thee forsworn,
"And says, report is rife,
"That thou hast led these eight years past
"A wicked wanton life."

"Believe not thou, my father dear,
"That I have wrought that sin;
"These falsehoods told some other maid,
"Would fain my trulove win."

"Ah! list to me, my daughter dear,
"And what thy sentence, learn;
"E'en now the peasants cart the logs,
"And thee tomorrow bum."

Kirstin with calm and cheerful breast
Drew on her purple pall:
But they, who raised her on her horse
Wept, maids and matrons all.

Forward they rode across the mead,
And through the flowery ling;
And all who pass'd her, far or near.
Might hear the maiden sing.

So cheerful little Kirstin rode.
As she to town drew nigh,
And saw from far the mighty pile,
And flames sport in the sky.

When on the grassy mead she came,
Fair Kirstin smiled and said;
"And here then has my trulove knight
"Prepared my bridal bed!

"And all so scarlet are my sheets,
"My bolsters are so blue;
"Knights, who shall so their daughters wed,
"Grant God there be but few!"

The little Kirstin then they seiz'd,
Her golden locks untied,
And all that stood around the pile,
In bitterest sorrow cried.

"Sir Olave, forward! you're the knight,
"Betroth'd with me to wed;
"Yourself lift up and lay your bride
"Upon her bridal bed."

And up that knight Sir Olave rose,
So ruthless he of mood,
And lifted little Kirstin up,
Upon the blazing wood.

His trulove rais'd that cruel knight.
And on the faggots laid;
The flame shrunk back, and left unscathed
The good and gentle maid.

There, as amid the fire she stood.
Aloud fair Kirstin cried;
"Believe you now, my father dear,
"How much on me they lied?

"All praise and thanks to God in heaven,
"Who heard my anxious cry!
"I'll now within the cloister's pale
"A virgin live and die."

Then came in tears her trothplight man,
And fell down on his knee;
"I pray you now in God's great name
"Forego your wrath with me."

"Henceforth to Mary, holy maid,
"My life I vow to give,
"And pledge me never, while on earth,
"With any man to live."

Into the cloister Kirstin went
With all her gold so red;
Sir Olave rode in shame away,
And soon with grief was dead.

poems.title: The Maid on the Pyre
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
His sister Ivar ask'd one night,
Roses my counsel keep
"Thy troth wilt thou thy brother plight?"
While others round us sleep.

"Nay that forbids the God above,
"That sister plight a brother love."

"If it thou wilt not plight to me,
"A lying charge I'll make on thee."

"Lie, as thou wilt, so foully lie,
"That from thy head thine eyes may fly.

"Lie as thou wilt, on thee the shame,
"For Christ will prove me free from blame."

His head wrapt in his scarlet hood,
Ivar before his father stood

"Hail, father, o'er thy cheerful cup!
"How breddest thou thy daughter up?"

"So well I've taught my dear Eline,
"That day by day her worth is seen."

"I state but what beheld mine eyes,
"Th' archbishop with thy daughter lies.

"Nor in that sin alone is he,
"But with him all his followers three."

The count up from his table stood,
His face with anger red as blood.

"Now, Ivar, say, my dearest son,
"What with thy sister shall be done?"

"Fit doom methinks, for crime so vile
"Were death on blazing faggot pile."

Ivar call'd out his servants two,
"Go ye to the wood and billets hew."

They builded up both asp and oak,
And bright the flame rose through the smoke.

With willow and asp they heap'd the pyre,
And fearful glared the bickering fire.

His four and thirty swains were there,
And in the labour all must share.

Out came Eline so fair and fine,
And saw the fire in green -wood shine.

"But tell me,' ask'd that maid so fair,
"What fire doth in the green -wood glare?"

"The fire that yonder gleams so red,
"That is to be thy bridal bed."

"'Fore God no reason do I know,
"Why thus my bridal bed should glow.

"'Fore God I've wrought no sin nor ill,
"That bed so bright I'm doom'd to fill."

Her brother took her lily hands.
And laid her on the blazing brands.

She cried amidst the scalding flame,
"Give me to drink in Jesus' name".

"Here in the forest flows no rill,
"No drop thy burning thirst to still."

Her mother ran, poor sorrowing wretch,
A stoup of wine from home to fetch.

The grateful draught she brought from town.
But Ivar knock'd the pitcher down.

Then soar'd two doves from out the sky,
And towards the pile were seen to fly.

Amid the brands their course they stay'd,
Eline to follow them they bade.

"If I to heaven shall go with you,
"Must go my father and mother too."

"Freed shall thy mother be from pain,
"Bat here thy father must remain."

Twas two flew down, and home flew three.
The fairest of all of them was she.

There came two ravens from out of hell,
And Ivar took with them to dwell.

"Twas two flew up, and back flew three;
The foulest of all of them was he.

In heaven there stands a golden stool.
And there Eline shall drink her Yule.

Below a coffin stands in hell,
His Yule keeps Ivar in its cell.
Roses my counsel keep
While others round us sleep.

poems.title: The Murdered Wife
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Christine to Sir Peter bent her low,
"Oh say, may I home to my father's go?"

"To go to thy father's thou art free,
"But what is thy grievance to tell of me?"

"I've naught to my father of thee to tell,
"But that thou art handsome and bred so well."

Christine has the open highway ta'en.
Sir Peter a nearer narrow lane.

As home she was riding up the street,
Came out her father his child to meet.

"Now tell me, Christine, true answer give,
"How dost thou at home with thy husband live?"

"Tis well that my lord and I agree, —
"But better his leman he treats than me.

"For when with his leman he goes to meat,
"Alone with my servants I mast eat.

"While they are at wine and dainty cheer,
"Must I with my servants drink of beer.

"While they together in bed are laid,
"Must I go sleep with my serving maid.

"By day I must work the quern-stone round,
"By night my neck is with iron bound."

"O cease, my daughter, thy tale of woe,
"And both thy brothers with thee shall go."

"And follow me home, who follow will,
"My death is but all too certain still.

"Aye let them follow, and all who can,
"My life is the prize of a ruthless man."

As back she came to her home once more,
There stood Sir Peter before his door.

"Now tell me, Christine, and nought withhold
"What grievance hast thou to thy father told?"

"Naught else to my father had I to tell,
"But that thou art handsome and bred so well."

A pace or two backward Sir Peter stepp'd,
And off with a blow her head he swept.

Her two bold brothers rode up the street,
"Why comes not our sister her guests to meet?"

"Christine she sits in her room of stone,
"And drinks her mead and her wine alone."

They searched each crevice and comer round,
And cut in pieces Christine they found.

Sir Peter a little aside they drew,
And chopped at a blow his neck in two.

They clad their sister in ermine fine,
But tossed Sir Peter to dogs and swine.

Straight soaring from heaven two doves were seen,
And back to heaven they took Christine.

Twas two came down, and home flew three,
The fairest of all of them was she.

There came two ravens from out of hell.
And took Sir Peter with them to dwell.

"Twas two flew up, and back flew three,
The foulest of all of them was he.

poems.title: Henry of Brunswick
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Duke of Brunswick, a knight so bold,
His like shall we ever again behold?

So ready in tourney and battle strife
To grapple his foe, to risk his life!

The Duke at night from his sleep awoke,
So vivid his dreams, and thus he spoke.

"Allow me to go to a distant clime,
"I live not else to the morning's prime."

"If such be your will, I'll not say no;
"But whither then means my lord to go?

"And when the wine shall I mix and brew?
"And when again shall I look for you?"

"O stay for me years but only eight,
"And after that time no longer wait.

"If then I am come not back again,
"Wed thou with thy best and dearest swain.

"But list to my words, choose not a hare
"To lie in the bed where lay a bear,"

There follow the Duke to the ocean strand
His knights all thirty, and steered from land;

And sobbing there was, and tears not few,
As knights and their ladies bade adieu.

Afar to the East he led his band,
And came to the heathen soldan's land.

His bravest he fought, and battles won.
He battled his way to Babylon.

Bat there did the heathens gain the day,
And captive they led the Duke away.

He dragg'd the harrow, he dragg'd the plough,
So little avail'd his dukedom now.

The Duke for eight years his thraldom bore
With wounds unheard, and many a sore.

He toil'd as a horse from day to day,
But never forgot to our Lord to pray.

And He inclined him his wrath to tame,
And truly to serve the heathen dame.

One day that her husband was gone from home.
She bade him from out his dungeon come;

And sent him loaded with store of food
A seven weeks' journey through the wood.

All under his old and tattered plaid
He belted a well-tried sabre blade;

And while through forests and wilds he went,
He met with many a strange event.

A lion, fighting a grisly pard,
Was well nigh faint, they fought so hard.

"Welcome, Duke Henry! o help thou me,
"And then I will serve and follow thee.'

"Would God that I had the strength and skill,
"This grisly pard I would gladly kill.

The lion, he hit, and the Duke hit hard,
And soon they fear'd the grisly pard.

As threaded the Duke that tangled ground,
Went with him his lion like faithful hound;

And journeying onward, it so befell.
They found a hermit before his cell.

"Duke Henry, welcome! With morning's light
"Thy wife will wed with another knight.

"Thou needest no pain or grief to feel,
"But seat thee and share my frugal meal;

"Refresh thee, and sleep thy toil away,
"And I to my God will go to pray."

The Duke on a stone he slept so sweet;
The faithful lion was at his feet;

But ere he scarcely an hour had slept.
That stone five hundred miles had leapt.

The Duke awoke, as a shepherd sung, —
And heard a lay in his German tongue.

"Now hark, good shepherd, and answer me,
"Whose flock thou art driving across the lea."

"This flock it belongs of Brunswick's dame,
"And once Duke Henry own'd the same.

"fiut far in the East the Duke is dead,
"And she will tomorrow another wed."

"Good shepherd, and may a pilgrim share
"The mirthful feast and the dainty fare?"

"They grudge thee neither the meat nor wine,
"But welcome the pilgrim to sit and dine."

The Duke to the Court walk'd up the street,
The lion as lackey was at his feet.

Much wonder'd the citizens all to see
That lion attend him so faithfully.

The Duke at the kitchen threshold stood,
"O give me a bit of the steaming food."

He saw and call'd to the waiting maid,
And her to carry his message pray'd.

"Go thou to the bride my prayer to make,
"I fain to her health a glass would take."

Up into the hall the damsel hied,
The pilgrim's message she told the bride.

"He bade me his prayer to you to make,
"He fain to your health a glass would take."

"And where has he known me, and who is he
"To send so bold a request to me?

"Go, damsel, that holy pilgrim call,
"And bring him up to the banquet hall."

She saw, in drinking the glass of wine,
The half a ring at the bottom shine.

The bride sprang up from the festive board,
"And now Duke Henry has kept his word."

"Ah nay!" said the bridegroom, "for vouch I can,
'Tis not Duke Henry, that pilgrim man."

"My friend, we yonder each other knew,
"Where once together the plough we drew.

"And shave me my beard, and wash my hair,
"My scars will plainly the truth declare.

"My daughter so lovely to thee I give,
"But I with my wife myself will live."

And all was joyous again and gay,
And deeply they drank their wedding day.

poems.title: Erik Emun and Swarthy Plog
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The lark at dawn of the morning sang,
Beneath the brow of the greenwood hill
Sir Carl from his bed as gaily sprang.
Avenge it the king of Denmark will,

He first put on him a shirt so new,
His green silk jacket on that he threw.

His buckskin boots he drew on his feet,
And over them gilded spurs so neat.

He buckled his spurs and his horse bestrode.
Alone to the court of Assizes rode.

Unguarded and fearless he went his way,
Though many an omen he met that day.

In walked Sir Carl to the hall of doom
The people retired to make him room.

But summon'd the king his nine stout swains,
And bade them to lay Sir Carl in chains.

Uprose nine stout and active swains,
And bound, as he bade, Sir Carl in chains.

Sir Carl outside of the town they took,
And there on a new made wheel they broke.

To swarthy Sir Plog the news came back,
"The king has thy brother upon the rack."

Up sprang Sir Plog and across the board,
Nor tarried to waste one single word.

He drew on his leg his buckskin boot,
And gilded spurs upon either foot.

He buckled his spurs and his horse bestrode,
And off to the Court of Assizes rode.

He urged his horse to his utmost speed,
And gallantly sprang that noble steed.

As entered Sir Plog the justice hall,
Uprose the king in his scarlet pall.

"Had I not come to the hall so late,
"Things would not have been in such a state."

"If so thou talkest with tongue so free,
"Thou gettest the self-same doom as he."

He call'd nine servants and each a knight;
"Up! bind ye Sir Plog before my sight."

"If there be a manly heart in thee,
Thyself thou wilt lay the bonds on me."

King Erick he toss'd his gloves aside.
Sir Plog with his spear the court defied.

He first slew four, and he then slew five.
He left nor trooper nor king alive.

Aye eight at a blow and nine he slew,
The king and his bravest troopers too.

He slaughtered them all and cleared the room,
And drove with his brother's body home.

poems.title: Ebbe Galt
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
In Holding sit the King's men all,
And drink till dawn of day.
Among them sits young Ebb Gait,
And dearly his freak will pay.

He rose from wine, young Ebbd Gait,
And rode through Rosenshaw,
And there in a luckless hour for both
A farmer's wife he saw.

"List now! Thou pretty farmer's wife,
"Show me the way to town,
"I'll give thee gold, and a handsome gift,
"A gay new Lundish gown."

Aye, Sir, you seem so gently bred
The way I'll gladly show.
"How much I fear these drunken men!
"God help me, while we go!")

But when he reached the farmer's house,
From bad he grew to worse,
He beat them all, and outraged heaven,
So foully did he curse.

The farmer's wife went to and fro,
For best of meat and drink,
But what for her he had in view,
Was bad as one can think.

With spurs he tore her trembling limbs,
He dragg'd her by the hair;
Had not the ale his master been,
Such deeds did he not dare.

"And now you've had your will of me,
"To both our loss and shame,
"I pray by all that's good above
"You tell me what's your name."

"The horse I ride is dapple-gray,
"My cloak is striped with blue,
"My men have call'd me Ebb. Gait
"Since service first I knew."

Back to his home from Sessions house
The honest farmer came.
And met in tears and bitter grief
Poor Gundelille, his dame.

"On me there's fall'n a foul disgrace,
"While you were still away;
"And never, come what luck there will,
"Shall I forget the day.

"I went across to Rosenshaw
"Our pretty foals to house,
"And there on horseback met a knight
"All heated from carouse.

"My hair he seized, and dragged me down,
"And wrought me greater shame;
"No more may I your wife be call'd,
"No longer bear your name."

He clasp'd her in his arms again.
And tapp'd her pallid face;
"My own dear wife you still shall be,
"To you 'tis no disgrace."

The honest farmer went to court
To tell his sad distress;
"My wife has been most foully used
"And here I seek redress."

Wroth was the Danish king thereat,
And grasp'd his glittering knife;
"If here he serves who did thee wrong,
"This deed shall cost his life.

"Good farmer, hear me, honest man,
"All in thy coat of gray;
"The youth who did thy wife this wrong,
"His name I bid thee say.

"His name then I will not conceal,
"One all too widely known;
"He bears the name of Ebb Gait,
"Is serving near thy throne."

Full sad was then the Danish king,
And black as earth his face;
"Ebbe, the grief that fills my heart
"No time will ever chase.

"And is it thou, my sister's son,
"Has done this lawless deed?
"I rather had lost the half my realm,
"Than death for it decreed."

Then summoned up the Danish King
His nephew, Ebb Gait;
"Come forward thou, my sister's son,
"Disprove or own thy fault."

And forward stepp'd young Ebbe Gait,
So bold of speech was he;
"Bring thou thy housewife here to court,
"She'll not complain of me."

The honest farmer turn'd his head,
And look'd along the hill;
"Here comes astride her dapple gray
"My housewife Gundelille."

"You know that when, Sir Ebb Gait,
"You came with us to dine,
"I pour'd you with unsparing hand
"The best of mead and wine.

"The sparkling ale, the luscious mead
"I gave your men and you;
"To treat our guests with hearty cheer
"My husband's wish I knew.

"I spread for you a bed of silk,
"As suits a noble knight,
"And show'd you in to sleep thereon
"With tapers burning bright.

"I with my children went to rest,
"As I was wont to do,
"And well you know, Sir Ebbe Gait,
"You broke the door in two.

"My five poor faithful waiting maids
"Are ill from blows you gave,
"And three my best and bravest swains,
"Are dead and in their grave."

Uprose Sir Peter, Ebbe's sire,
A hero strong and bold;
"I bid my horse for Ebb's life,
"And a thousand marks of gold"

But answered him the Danish king,
"For judgement here he stood;
"I'd give myself thee thousand marks,
"Release him if I cou'd.

"iVe sworn to pass a righteous doom,
"To heaven I dare not lie;
"The woman he has foully used,
"This instant he shall die."

"Ha!" said the young Sir Ebb, Gait,
The while he passed the Queen;
"I should not so regret my life,
"Had she but fairer been."

"What?" answer she with royal grace,
"What was the wife to thee?
"And had her face been black or white,
"Thou should'st have let her be."

They led the handsome Ebb Gait
Away to the bushy field.
And off his shoulders chopped his head,
And laid it on his shield.

poems.title: The Wake
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There's Wake tonight, and off they throng,
They revel there all that revel will
They take their part in the dance and song.
But wakes at her home fair Signelille.

She went to her mother, and so she spake;
They revel there all that revel will
"And, mother, may I not see the Wake?"
She wakes at her home fair Signelille.

"But what at a Wake art thou to do?
"No brother hast thou, nor sister true.

"No brother or friend thy part to take,
"Thou shalt not go to a noisy wake.

"The King and his gay young men will come;
"No — listen to me, child, stay at home."

"The Queen is coming and all her train,
"To chatter with them I were so fain."

So long and so hard her suit she drave,
Her grudging consent the mother gave.

"Go then, my daughter, if such thy bent,
"Thy mother to wake rooms never went."

Fair Signelille up to her chamber hied,
And dress'd her in all her maiden pride.

She set on her head a golden crown,
Her hair left floating in tresses down.

And over the grassy mead she sped,
As went the queen and her maids to bed.

But when she came to the courtyard gate,
Was going the dance of stag at bait.

She saw young knights so gaily fling,
And dance with the rest himself the king.

The king held forward his hand so free;
"Come, lovely maiden, and dance with me."

"I'm come to the Wake across the dale
"To see and to tell the Queen my tale."

"Then trip it with us to a lively strain,
"Till she comes back to the dance again."

She stepp'd to the front as a graceful wand.
And danced away on his royal hand.

"Now, Signelille, listen to what I say,
"And sing me of love some tender lay."

"Of lays or love-ditties know I none;
"I'll try in their stead some other one."

She sang her song with a voice so clear,
Its notes the queen in her bed could hear.

She ask'd, as up in her bower she lay,
"Now which of my maidens dared to stay?

"Who, tell me, can this sweet songstress be?
"Why came she not hither to bed with me?"

"That," answer d the page in his red array'd,
"Is not any royal bower-maid.

"None other a song like that could trill,
"Bat th' upland maiden, Signelille/'

"Haste! hither my purple mantle bring;
"I'll go there and hear the maiden sing."

And when she came to the courtyard gate,
Was going the dance of stag at bait.

Three times they had danced it, and danced it still;
The queen stood gazing on Signelille.

That, thought Sophie, is a monstrous thing,
That Signelille dance with Denmark's king.

She call'd to her maid, "Up, maiden mine,
"And fetch me hither a horn of wine.

"Fetch hither the richly moulded horn,
"But drop in it first an Adder-corn."

Up stepped the king to his queen, Sophie;
"Wilt thou not enter the dance with me?"

"Before a place in the dance I fill,
"Must drink to my health fair Signelille."

She drank but a sip to quench her thirst,
Her guiltless heart in her bosom burst.

The king was a while with horror mute;
The maid lay lifeless before his foot.

"A fairer than she has ne'er drawn breath,
"Or guiltless come to a fouler death."

Both maids and matrons wept full sore,
As into the church her corpse they bore.

"O! had she but heard her mother's rede,
"Such would not have been her cruel meed."

poems.title: Sir Buris and Christine
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
King Waldmar and Sophie his queen
Spake in their hall of fair Christine.

"My lord, be not my wish denied,
"Let fair Christine be Buris' bride.

"Thy sister she, my brother he,
"These two a noble match might be."

"Never, while me is granted life,
"Shall horse-thief take Christine to wife.

"She stands adorn'd with every grace,
"But stamped the groom' on his low face."

Pale grew as corpse the queen Sophie;
"And why this disrespect to me?"

"With angry hand she struck the board;
"I'll get revenge that churlish word."

King Waldmar marched to a foreign land,
And left his realm in Buris' hand.

With him went many a gallant knight
Sworn in his country's cause to fight.

To one amid this noble band
He gave Christine his sister's hand.

A mighty prince and gently bred
Was he who should his sister wed.

Sophie and Buris sat at board.
And much she thought of Waldmar's word.

"Now, Buris, hark, dear brother mine,
"Try to decoy this maid so fine."

Sir Buris stared, as spake the queen,
"But what can this, my sister, mean?

"A deed so foul I'll never do,
"As her for aught but bride to woo."

"To woo or wed her thou wert free,
"Had not my lord so jeer'd at thee."

With that she struck the board in ire;
"I rede thee do as I desire/'

Sir Buris cloak'd and left the queen,
And went to see the fair Christine.

Early and late he sued in vain,
The maiden's love he could not gain.

"Sir Buris, would you me mislead?
"Would Waldmar pardon such a deed?"

He turn'd with pallid cheeks away,
For much he loved that gentle may.

Sir Buris took his scarlet cloak,
And went to queen Sophie and spoke.

"To win a maid so good and chaste
"The bravest knight his breath would waste."

"A lover's part thou playest well,
"And knowest not a Runic spell!"

"I'll serve my lord till he return,
"Thy spells I'll never stoop to learn.

"Me, whom he left his realm to sway,
"Me his own sister lead astray!"

"Take in thy hands the Runes I write,
"Use them thyself this very night."

Those fatal Runes he duly spread,
Where the fair maid Christine must tread.

And all o'erwhelm'd with shame and woe
That night to Buris she must go.

She came and tapped with gentle knock;
"Sir Buris, rise, the door unlock!"

He rose in scarlet robe array'd,
And led within the lovely maid.

That night in Buris arms she passed,
Of health and happiness the last.

As month by month stole on, was seen
A change of shape in fair Christine.

She bade her maid in saddest tone
Come with her to the room of stone.

"Bring the five women in to me,
"And bring with them the queen Sophie.

"Run thou, my page, to yonder hall,
"Sir Buris seek, and hither call."

There on the threshold met the twain,
And told their mutual tale of pain.

Linked arm in arm and faint with woe,
They paced the chamber to and fro.

Now closed the king his yearns campaign,
And came with glory home again.

As at the door she saw him stand,
Gave him the queen her open hand.

The king looked round, "But tell me where,
"And why not here my sister fair?"

Beneath her mantle smiled the queen;
"Her for three months I've never seen."

"Were I the queen, I'd pains bestow
"To make my maids good manners know."

"Me she no longer will obey;
"She little cares for what I say."

"What of my sister dost thou tell,
"Who all her life behaved so well?

"That in the ston room she was laid,
"And bare a child, an infant maid."

"Hash!" said the king, and angry grew,
"Thy tale, Sophie, is all untrue."

"'Tis naught but sober truth I've said,
"Myself I saw her laid in bed."

Five gallant knights then call'd the king;
"Ride, and my sister hither bring."

The knights on Waldmar's errand sped,
But wished they rather had been dead.

They came and tapped with gentle knock;
"'Tis we, Christine; the door unlock."

Her maid got up and drew the pin;
"We pray you, may we enter in?"

"Enter you may this room of stone,
"But borne an infant here has none."

Full sad of heart Sir Peter grew;
"Would that thy words were only true!

"Rise, fair Christine, and dress," he cried,
"This night to your brother you must ride.

"Dress with all haste, make no delay,
"For home your brother came today."

"Then swathe my child in linen fold;
"Me she will never more behold.

"Rear her, my maids, in Christian lore;
"Sad is the fate for her in store.

"Call her the little 'Ingelille,'"
"My luck is like to play me ill.

"And thou, dear bower-woman mine,
"Bring to me here my gilded shrine."

The coins that stored in it were found,
She dealt to her faithful servants round.

To her she gave the largest share
Who should the little infant rear.

A goodly heap for her she piled
Kindly to treat her little child.

"Too well does every woman know,
"If I this ride can undergo;

"Will know, how ill in such a plight
"I'm fit to take a ride by night."

They rais'd her up so woebegone;
Like threads of gold her tresses shone.

The long rough ride so ill she bare.
She fainted on the chamber stair.

Up at the window laughed Sophie;
"Come hither now, your sister see."

She dandled little Knud and smiled;
"Rejoice, in Jesus' name, my child."

They lent her help to mount the stair;
"Lady, repose in Jesus' care."

She pass'd the door, she crossed her breast;
"Christ, on thy grace alone I rest."

When at the door he saw her stand,
King Waldmar held her forth his hand.

She gave him her's "And glad' said she,
"Am I that you at home I see."

Such grace to fair Christine he show'd,
That queen Sophie with anger glow'd.

King Waldmar fill'd a glass with wine,
"Now drink to me, dear sister mine.

"And hear, Christine, nor say me nay,
"Sing me of love some tender lay."

"Lovelays, my brother, know I none,
"I'll try to sing some other one."

"I'll have thee dance and sing thy lay,
"And make my guests a festive day."

The fair Christine began her song.
Behind her tripp'd a gallant throng.

While she so gaily danced and sang,
The king amid the dancers sprang.

He danced her in, he danced her round,
With all his trials nothing found.

He proved her much, he proved her long,
But nothing found in dance or song.

"Sophie my queen, rest on thee shame
"With lies to soil my sister's fame!"

"Now by God's holy word I swear,
"That she indeed a daughter bare/'

With that she seiz'd her, bared her breast,
And out a milky streamlet pressed.

The king with grief turn'd pale as clay,
And swoon'd Christine, and senseless lay.

"Thy wedding feast I thought was nigh,
"But thou this very night shalt die.

"Thou should'st have been a Prince's wife,
"This very night shalt end thy life.

"A death, as hard as death can be
"This very night shall light on thee."

Down on her knees she humbly pray'd;
"O brother, be thine anger stay'd."

"To such can I no mercy show;
"On earth thou shalt no longer go.

"For crime so insolent and great
"Naught less than death shall be thy fate.

"Unweeting all I promised thee
"To the King's son across the sea."

His little pageboy call'd the king;
"Hither five heavy scourges bring."

"Thou needest not four whips or five;
"One will not leave me more alive."

She knelt and pray'd on naked knee,
"Lord God, in mercy look on me."

As in his hand the whip he took,
With deepest sorrow Waldmar shook.

"O rise and help me, Queen Sophie;
"You and your brother ruin'd me."

"Dishonoured were my name and race,
"If I should plead for one so base.

"Nay let her death be so severe,
"It fill with terror every ear."

He scourg'd her, till upon the floor
Were trickling round her streams of gore.

She turn'd her to the queen and wept,
And fain beneath her robe had crept.

"O let me hide beneath your pall,
"For His sake, His, who died for all!"

In tears and anguish prayed Christine,
But spurn'd her back the cruel queen.

"So long, my brother, let me live,
"That I my last bequests can give.

"Take you my forts and all my lands,
"For life and death are in your hands.

"My child I give my gold so red;
"She'll yet avenge me, when I'm dead.

"The queen I give my silver'd knife,
"For she betrayed my tender life.

"Thee, Boris, too may God reward,
"That here I've had a fate so hard.

"So then my testament I've made;
"My brother, be thine anger stay'd.

"To Christ I yield my soul and die;
"None other friend on earth have I."

As "Fare ye well" she bade them all,
Wept every guest that sat in hall.

In tears both dame and maid were seen,
All save Sophie, the wicked queen.

So gently sank that rose to death,
In God's hand yielded up her breath.

'Twas then King Waldmar sorely griev'd.
And deep remorse his bosom heav'd.

"Sophie, a vicious wife thou art,
"That pity could not touch thy heart.

"On thee, Sophie, rest lasting shame!
"For what is done 'tis thou to blame.

"And now is dead this gentle rose,
"And where shall her poor corpse repose?"

"Toss her upon the Riber street,
"Where daily tramp my horses feet/'

"That triumph thou shalt never have,
"To prance thy horses o'er her grave.

"At Westerwick in cloister gloom
I'll leave her corpse and raise a tomb"

He buried her in solemn state,
And all his days be mourned her fate.

"rn now to a gloomy cell retire,
"And live debarred of light and fire.

"On me shall shine no beam of sun,
"Till penance for my sins I've done."

His page he then was heard to call;
"Sir Buris bring to the audience hall.

"Hark, Buris, what I say to thee;
"How hast thou kept thy faith with me?

"A vineyard gave I thee to keep,
"And bitter now the fruit I reap.

"Its fairest vine hast thou laid waste,
"And lifelong sorrow thou shalt taste."

Humbly Sir Buris bent him low;
"My lord, thy mercy on me show."

"Nay, but on thee shall be repaid
"The death that died th' unhappy maid."

"The direst vengeance, thou canst take,
"I'll gladly bear for her dear sake."

"His horse-thief eyes tear from his head,
"For he that lovely wife misled."

Tom from his head were both his eyes
Despite the queen his sister's cries.

They lopp'd him off the stirrup foot,
They lopp'd the dexter hand to hoot;

Then brought him on the castle green
To taunt and mock Sophie the queen.

With feign'd respect in courtly guise
They served her up her brother's eyes.

"This mighty lord, thy brother, see,
"Him who so princely great would be."

To forge a chain then bade the king.
And him to Westerwick to bring.

Eleven long years he there was kept,
But day by day to her tombstone crept;

And all his lands to Waldmar gave
Only with her to share her grave.

He died, was laid beside Christine;
But Waldmar ne'er forgave the queen.

poems.title: Ingerlille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
With Queen Sophie King Waldmar sat,
Of times gone by ran on their chat;
While lightly tripped the dancers.

"My lord, since fair Christine's decease
"Say, where lives Ingerlille, thy niece?"

"I've given her yonder moated tower,
"And mean to give her greater power:

"And all the days I live will prove,
"How dearly I the maiden love.

"A father she shall find in me,
"And she in turn my daughter be."

"'Twere well," that wicked queen replied,
"Could Ingerlille at court reside.

"In you a father she might find,
"In me a mother quite as kind."

Her the king answer'd plain and flat;
"Not from thy heart hast thou said that.

"Such as thy treatment yet has heen,
"In thee no mother she has seen.

"And well is Ingerlille aware,
"That thou no love for her dost bear.

"How canst thou love the very maid,
"Whose mother's life thou hast betray'd?"

"Why not the pretty maiden love,
"If faithful she and trusty prove?

"Consent, my lord, that Ingerlille
"Enter my service, if she will."

"Aye, if she will, my leave I give,
"That Ingerlille with thee may live.

"Get ready, knaves, the gilded wain,
"And fetch my niece to court again."

Up to the maid the pageboy went;
"This wain for you your uncle sent."

"And gladly" said that maid so sweet,
"I drive with thee the king to meet."

She toss'd her shears and broidery down,
And dress'd herself in silken gown.

And all in scarlet robe array'd
They seated her, the lovely maid.

As Ingerlille drove up the street.
Went out the king his niece to meet.

And in his arms the royal Dane
Lifted her down from out the wain.

"Welcome, my niece, thou budding bloom!
"Right welcome thou to an uncle's home!"

The maid he robed in scarlet red,
And then to the upper chamber led.

As at the threshold she was seen,
To meet her rose Sophie, the Queen.

"Would that I knew," thought Ingerlille,
"What means this grace, and what her will!"

The King the maiden drew aside,
"Here at my court wilt thou reside?

"And is it, toll me, Ingerlille,
"To serve us hero thine own free will?"

"Hear," said the Queen, "what now I say,
"Thou stayest here till Easter day:

"In nothing else hast thou to serve,
"But what I say to thee, observe.

"Attend me, bring the clothes I wear,
"And day by day my bath prepare.

"With hand and foot good service do,
"And follow me, where'er I go."

"My king, and uncle, say, may I
"With open heart make my reply?"

"To speak thine inmost mind be free,
"And talk to her, as she to thee."

"Ill should I care for name or fame,
"If I your waiting maid became:

"Little respect should I deserve,
"Did I a Bishop's leman serve.

"For what I say, mine eyes have seen,
"The Bishop dallying with the Queen."

"Stay, Ingerlille, my dearest niece,
"From such unworthy slander cease."

"Help me the Virgin Queen on high,
"As truth I speak and do not lie!"

"If the court service thou dost spurn,
"Where wilt thou else thy living earn?"

"In some calm cloister I will live,
"To God alone my service give."

"And there within thy cloister wall
"To all thy mother's vices fall."

"On her has long since closed the tomb,
"And thy deed was her cruel doom.

"While my poor mother sleeps below,
"Thy shameless face thou darest show."

King Waldmar's cheek grew red as blood,
And wan as clay the guilty stood.

"If true is all that thou hast said,
"Sophie no longer shares my bed.''.

"Do not, dear maid, such language hold,
"For true is not what thou hast told."

"True are the crimes I've charged on thee,
"Murder and foul unchastity."

"Hark, my sweet niece, do thou reply,
"What death my guilty queen shall die."

"That best may say herself the queen,
"For well she knows what scourges mean.

"The same death die this worthless wife,
"By which she took my mother's life."

His little pageboy bade the king
At once five leather scourges bring.

"Fetch the five hither; haste, boy, baste;
"And all the five Sophie shall taste."

They lash'd her, till upon the floor
Were trickling round her streams of gore.

She crept beneath the maiden's cloak.
But back she spurn'd the wretch, and spoke:

"Dishonoured were my name for life,
"Could I protect thee, worthless wife."

The lash so long and hard they plied,
Till on the floor she sank and died.

"Dead is the Queen, her crimes repaid;
"Now where shall be her carcase laid?"

"Where she my mother's grave had plann'd,
"Under the street beside the strand."

"So be it. — Bear her off with haste,
"Under the pavement be she placed."

There in the street now lies Sophie,
And Ingerlille rules house and fee.

There lies Sophie beneath the mould,
And Ingerlille enjoys her gold.

Herself at last, with glory crown'd.
As Queen ruled long on English ground.

poems.title: King Waldemar's Suit to Dagmar
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Strang with Waldmar, Denmark's King,
Sat over the festive board:
Between them there passed in friendly chat
Full many a mirthful word.

"Get ready, Sir Strang, thy ship and crew
"To launch on the rising tide;
"For off to Bohemia thou shalt sail
"To fetch me my youthful bride."

"Good;" answered Sir Strange Ebbe's son,
"And warily spake he so,
"But if to Bohemia I shall sail,
"Who is there with me to go?"

"Sir Limbeck of Aggerliouse take with thee
"The first of thy gallant crow,
"And take the wealthy Sir Peter Glob,
"Knights both of them good and true.

"The bishop of Seeland also take
"So pious and deeply read;
"And take Sir Albert of Eskilsey
"So clever and courtly bred."

Sir Strange to go on board his ship
Went down to the river bank;
And walk'd beside him the king himself
And many a man of rank.

They loos'd their hawser, and tossed about
For se'nnights more then three,
But saw the Bohemian coast at last,
And glad were his men and he.

They furl'd their sail and their anchor dropped,
And hasted to leap on land;
Sir Strang( of all the gallant crew
Was first on the foreign strand.

Their herald they then before them sent
The news to the court to bring,
That they who had landed, the envoys were
Of Waldmar, the Danish king.

The King made answer that come they might
To make him their message known;
And where they passed to the audience hall.
Was silk on the pavement strown.

"My greeting,' great and glorious prince,
"The king of the Boiers' land!
"The king of Denmark has sent to you
"To sue for your daughter's hand."

The servants water and napkins brought,
And seated them all at board,
And rose from his chair the noble lord,
To answer. in kindly word.

He rose to meet them, the good old King,
He rose from his seat with grace,
And kindness was in his words and tone.
And beam'd in his worthy face.

Sir Strang told him in courtly phrase
The wish of the Danish king;
"And may we back to our Danish homo
"A gracious answer bring?"

"A gracious answer V surely give,
"Ye gallant good men and true;
"Sit down to the table, my knights, sit down,
"I'll give you the answer due."

The King he went to the ladies bower.
Would rede of the queen demand;
"Now here there are come the Danish lords
"To sue for our daughter's hand."

"If Waldmar, the Danish king, indeed
"Our daughter will have for bride,
"We'll give her to him the mighty man,
"And many a gift beside,"

They dress'd her with jewels of brightest gold.
And into the hall she came;
Sir Strang and she, this gentle maid,
Should seat them and play a game.

And into the hall a board they brought
With purest of gold bestrown,
That he Sir Strange might play with her,
And talk with her all alone.

And all on a chequer board of gold
Three times their game they tried;
Sir Strang he won the lovely maid,
And claim'd her for Waldmar's bride.

They brought her array'd in robe of silk
Again to the festive board;
"Behold the gentle and lovely maid
"We give to your Danish lord."

They brought her before the stranger knight
So courtly and brave and good.
And, rising, Sir Strange with due respect
Before the maiden stood.

And now as the hour of night drew on,
And twilight and darkness spread,
Sir Strang must rise and leave the board,
And follow the bride to bed.

"Now tell me, Sir Strang, and truly say,
"While here we are only two,
"Is he — is Waldmar, the Danish king,
"As handsome a man as you?"

Sir Strange he turned him towards the sun,
And solemnly made reply;
"Indeed, sweet Dagmar, the Danish king
"Is handsomer far than I."

They spread on the ground their silken robes,
And led her aboard the ship;
She wished her parents a long farewell,
And bade them the hawser slip.

And thus had the good Bohemian king
His daughter her duty taught;
"When thou to thy Danish realm art come,
"Be honour thy constant thought.

"In piety virtue and fear of God
"Let all thy life be spent,
"And ever thy subjects be in thy thoughts,
"Their hopes on thy care be bent."

They steer'd their vessel away from land.
They merrily plied their oars,
And sighted in less than two months time
Their native Danish shores.

They anchored, and Dagmar, the lovely maid.
So happily came to land,
As Waldmar himself, the Danish king.
Was riding along the strand.

"But tell me, Sir Strang Ebbeson,
"Ere yet to the quay we reach
"What one-eyed and squinting youth is that
"Is riding along the beach?"

"O softly, Dagmar, gracious maid,
"No ill of the rider say,
"For he is king of our Danish isles,
"And him do they all obey."

"Now light, Sir Strange, shame on thee,
"So speciously thou canst lie;
"Methinks yon rider, your Danish king, "
"Has only a single eye."

"O trust me, my fair and lovely maid,
"You ought to he glad and gay;
"Your lifelong never shall you regret
"The voyage we end today.

"For me, as long as I live and breathe,
"My faithfulness I will prove,
"And all the nobles of Denmark too
"Will serve you with equal love."

They drank the wedding in joy and peace.
And gaily they passed the day.
King Waldmar and Dagmar, the lovely queen,
As happy and blithe as they.

Aye, merry and glad were great and small,
The wealthy and eke the poor.
But chiefly with all their heart rejoiced
The burgher and honest boor.

All, all that in Denmark dwelt were glad,
Wherever the news was told,
And gave to Sir Strang precious gifts,
And treasure of ruddy gold.

poems.title: Queen Dagmar in Denmark
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Queen Dagmar's Bridal".
poems.text:
The queen so good of Beyerland
She gave her daughter rede;
"And now to Denmark thou shalt come,
"And honour be thy meed.

"To Denmark thou shalt come anon,
"And win thee rank and fame;
"Tax not the honest humble boor,
"And he shall bless thy name.

"The gift thou first shalt ask thy lord,
"Ask him with smiling cheer,
"He let the bishop oat of jail,
"Waldmar, thine uncle dear."

Anon were costly robes of silk
Over the highway spread,
And down to the Ocean's shelly beach
The maiden Dagmar led.

They hoisted high the silken sail,
They gaily plied the oar,
And scarcely two short months at sea
They reached the Danish shore.

They came, and forth their anchor cast
Out on the glittering sand.
And lifted maiden Dagmar up,
And set her first on land.

They lifted maiden Dagmar up.
And set her first on land.
The king of Denmark's self was there,
And gave the maid his hand.

Anon were costly robes of silk
Over the highway spread.
And to the castle all in pomp
The maiden Dagmar led.

The morrow, ere a sunbeam yet
Had cleared the mirky lift.
The maiden Dagmar woke from sleep,
And craved her morning gift.

"With joy I make my first request,
"O let my prayers avail!
"That bishop Waldmar you forgive,
"Aud set him free from jail,

"The second boon I ask of you,
"And ask with equal glee,
"Forgive the boors their plough-pence all
"And set your captives free."

"Hush! hush! my queen, and say not so,
"That never will I do,
"Or, ere a single year were out,
"A widow'd queen were you."

She took the crown from off her head,
And gave it back the king;
"Why should I then in Denmark stay,
"And gain here not a thing?"

"Haste ye, and fetch Sir Strang in,
"And fetch me Knud my swain,
"And let them ride to Attingborg,
"And loose the captives' chain."

The bishop, when from jail he came,
Could hardly walk upright;
"I've sat here eighteen tedious years,
"And counted day and night."

Queen Dagmar took a golden comb,
And comb'd his yellow hair;
For every single lock she. dress'd,
She dropp'd a scalding tear.

"O weep not, gentle queen, for me,
"Nor sorrow for me more,
"For I shall fully venge my wrongs,
"Ere yet a year is o'er."

"Hash! bishop Waldmar, say not so,
"From all such words refrain;
"If back you come to Attingborg,
"I loose you not again."

poems.title: The Queen and the Mermaid
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The King he has got him a Mermaid caught,
She trips on the floor so gay,
And had her into the dungeon brought,
His will she would not obey.

The Queen two servants was heard to call,
"The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"Go, bring her to me to the castle hall,
"I'll make her my will obey."

In came the Mermaid before the board,
She trips on the floor so gay,
"What will you, my Queen? why send me word?
"I cannot your will obey."

The Queen with her hand the cushion press'd,
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"Come hither, and seat thee with me to rest,
"I'll have thee my will obey."

"What! is it your wish to take my life?"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"For under the cushion is hidden a knife,
"How should I your will obey?"

"If that thou knowest, thou knowest more,"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"So tell me the fate for me in store,
"And prithee my will obey."

"Your fate, my Queen, if I knew and said,"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"On blazing pile you would have me laid,
"Your will I fear to obey.

"You bear three children, three lovely boys,"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"And you, their mother, your child destroys,
"And so your will I obey."

"If such is to be my own sad fate,"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"Then tell me, what luck doth them await?
"And prithee my will obey."

"The sceptre of Denmark the one shall hold,"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"The other shall wear a crown of gold,
"And so thy will I obey.

"The third shall be widely famed as wise,"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"For him it is fated his mother dies,
"And so thy will I obey."

The Queen she veil'd her in purple cloak,
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
And went to the King in his room, and spoke;
Her will she had made her obey.

"My lord, my dearest, oh hear my prayer,
"The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"Now give her to me, so line and fair,
"I've made her my will obey."

"The Mermaid I give not up to thee,"
She trips on the floor so gay,
"Seven ships of mine she has drown'd at sea,
"And would not my will obey."

The Queen grew pale, she griev'd so sore.
The Mermaid is tripping so gay.
And fainting she fell on the chamber floor.
Her will she had made her obey.

"Oh think no more on the words I spake,"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"But her to the sea with your ladies take,
