"You've made her your will obey."

She dress'd the Mermaid in red and gold,
She trips on the floor so gay,
Although she had even her death foretold,
She made her her will obey.

And thus the Queen to her ladies spake,
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"The Mermaid down to the sea-shore take,
"I've made her my will obey."

They left her to sport on the billows blue,
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
The Queen she wept, and her ladies too.
She made her her will obey.

"Ah! cease your sorrow, and weep no more,"
She trips on the waves so" gay,
"For heaven has opened to you its door,
"And now your will I obey.

"Above is your dwelling among the blest,"
The Mermaid is tripping so gay,
"And comfort awaits you there, and rest,
"And so your will I obey."

poems.title: Queen Dagmar's Death
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Queen Dagmar's Death".
poems.text:
Queen Dagmar is lying at Rib sick.
In Ringsted is made her grave,
And midwives, as many as Denmark has,
She summons her life to save.

"O fetch me one of them, fetch me two,
"Fetch all that are known as wise,
"But fetch little Kirstin first of all,
"For her do I chiefly prize."

As into the chamber Kirstin came
With modest and cheerful air.
Queen Dagmar, to welcome her, rose from bed,
So pleased that the maid was there.

"If thou to give me relief from pain
"Canst any thing write or read,
"Then robe shalt thou in a scarlet pall,
"And ride on my own gray steed."

"If I could any thing read or write,
"That would I so gladly do,
"But tight you are bound as in iron band,
"'Tis fearful, my queen, but true."

She took in her hand Saint Mary's book
To read of some goodly spell.
But blinding tears soon filled her eyes.
And streams on her bosom fell.

They carried her out, they carried her in,
But little did matters mend;
"Then since it is going from bad to worse,
"Up, after my husband send."

Her own little page had heard her words.
And hasted away with speed;
The saddle he took from off the beam.
And laid on a milk-white steed.

The king is standing on chamber stair,
And looking around so wide;
"Methinks it is some small page I see
"So sorrowful hither ride.

"Aye hither he wends, that same small page,
"To bring us a tale of woe;
"Oh heavenly Father, 'tis in thy hand,
"How matters with Dagmar go/'

In stepped to the hall the tiny page,
And stood him before the board;
"Queen Dagmar has sent me to fetch you home,
"Would fain with you speak a word."

The King his chequer board shut in haste,
The dice they rattled and rung;
"Forbid it our Father who dwells in heaven,
"That Dagmar should die so young!"

They bitted with gold their steeds so white,
And richly they had them dress'd,
And rode at a stretch to Roskildby,
Before they would stop to rest.

The king has ridden from Gullandsborg
With fully a hundred swains.
But ere he is come to Ringsted bridge.
Queen Dagmar's alone remains.

He enter'd the town and voices heard
Of wailing and loud alarm;
Queen Dagmar, as e'en he rode up street.
Had died upon Kirstin's arm.

He open'd her chamber door, and saw
The bearers and eke the bier,
But came little Kirstin and gave her hand,
And fain would his sorrow cheer.

"Oh still your sorrow, my lord and king,
"For her who has even died;
"We've saved an infant, a lovely boy,
"We cut from your Dagmar's side."

"I beg of you, ladies and maidens all,
"To kneel with me round her bier,
"And offer a prayer for Dagmar's soul
"To let me her wishes hear."

Queen Dagmar she wakes and rises up.
All bloody her eyes and red;
"Alas and alas, my noble lord!
"Why trouble the peaceful dead?

"My prayer and the first request I make
"I trust, my lord, to gain;
"All outlawed men to their homes restore,
"And loosen the captive's chain.

"My next, the second request I make,
"I urge for your own dear sake;
"That Berngerd, ray lord, that base bad dame
"You never to wife will take.

"And this, my third and my chiefest prayer,
"I trust you will grant me too;
"That Knud, my youngest and dearest son,
"Be ruler here after you.

"O leave him to be in Denmark king,
"My youngest and dearest boy,
"Tho' Berngerd will bear you another son
"Will him if he can destroy.

"Had I on a Sunday not laced my sleeves,
"Or border upon them sewn,
"No pangs had I felt by day or night,
"Or torture of hell-fire known.

"No more I may answer, my noble lord,
"No more I may stop to say;
"God's angels are sitting on thrones in heaven,
"And beckon me hence away"

Her eyes grew dim with death again,
And black as the earth her cheek;
"The bells of heaven are chimed for me,
"No more may I stay to speak/'

poems.title: Niels Ebbeson
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Niels Ebbeson".
poems.text:
Count Gherrit summoned all his men,
From Sleswick marched away;
There never was seen a finer band
Before or since that day.

With banners flying twenty-eight
The border land he crossed,
And pitch'd his camp on Danish soil;
Who dared withstand his host?

Count Gherrit would to Randers ride,
That course he came to choose,
Though long had been his fate foretold,
He there his life should loose.

He cared not, he, for spaewife's tale,
His fate would even test.
Would visit burgher, knight and boor,
An all-unwelcome guest.

He came with eighteen thousand bows,
Yeomen and knights beside.
Had forty thousand men in all;
Who could their force abide?

He sent to bid Niels Ebbeson
To come without delay;
A sure safe-conduct offered him,
And escort on the way.

Count Gherrit met Niels Ebbeson
North-side of Randers strand;
"Bight welcome here, Niels Ebbeson,
"How fares your native land?"

The Count embraced Niels Ebbeson,
And courteously they spoke;
But mirth was none in their discourse,
And even less of joke.

"Welcome, my dear Niels Ebbeson,
"Welcome, right welcome here!
"How is North Jutland now disposed,
"What tidings meet your ear?

"And tell me how your kinsmen fare,
"And how your gentle wife;
"And whether you will fight with me,
"Or ask a truce to strife."

"North Jutland, that is well disposed,
"All well and cheerful there;
"Come you, my lord, for war or peace?
"Your motive, pray, declare.

"Up in North Jutland I have friends,
"And wealthy kinsmen too,
"And ready all to meet your Grace,
"If they your wishes knew."

"No fool, Niels Ebbeson, art thou,
"Nor man of boorish mind,
"But sure, if thou the road hast lost,
"Another path to find.

"So hark thee now, Niels Ebbeson,
"Wilt thou mine errand ride?
"How many troopers serve with thee,
"On whom may be relied?"

"Among the Jutes both faithful friends
"And kinsmen I can show,
"Who gladly all will follow me
"To meet their country's foe.

"And now with me are thirty men
"Like these who're standing here,
"And be they more, or be they less,
"Alike to me are dear."

"Thirty such troopers dost thou lead?
"It shows thy ready zeal;
"Tomorrow bring to Bugge's yard
"A hundred clad in steel."

Back stepp'd a pace Niels Ebbeson,
And warmly made reply;
"There's neither belted knight nor swain
"Has dared give me the lie.

"Nor is there man or wife alive,
"Shall ever give it me,
"That I will move a foot for him,
"Till I've replied as free."

"Nay hark, my dear Niels Ebbeson,
"No words thereon to spill, —
"Off to thy friend Sir Bugge, and learn
"If he is loyal still."

"If I shall now your errand ride,
"And to Sir Bugge's go,
"Then what on your part I shall say,
"I first would gladly know."

"Sir Bugge has long defied my power,
"And young Paul Gloh as well,
"And Andrew Frost, who first of all
"Came in your troop to swell.

"And thou thyself, Niels Ebbeson,
"Hast riding at thy side
"Men, who till lately shared my bread,
"And me have now defied.

"First I will name young Eske Frost,
"And then his brothers too,
"Who all, without my yea or will,
"From serving me withdrew,

"Many to whom I've kindness shown,
"No more on me depend;
"Ride thou and learn Sir Bugge's plans,
"And see to what they tend."

"I know not what Sir Bugge plans
"To do or let alone;
"But Andrew Frost, while serving you,
"His loyalty has shown.

"A gallant man. Sir Andrew Frost,
"His honour stands so high,
"When he his furlough wished to have,
"His furlough why deny?

"There's still in force from days of old
"A rule in Danish land,
"That troopers, who will serve no more,
"Their furlough may demand.

"None here is consecrate for life
"But monks in cloister pent;
"The trooper rides, the trooper bides,
"E'en where he is most content."

Count Gherrit shortly answered him,
Nor more would stay to know;
"No man his master may desert,
"Just when he likes to go.

"And do not thou, Niels Ebbeson,
"Stop talking here too long;
"But quit at once this Danish realm,
"Or I shall have thee hung.

"With passport thou art hither come,
"With passport thou may'st go;
"I'd make thee, but for breach of faith,
"A thing or two to know."

"You plighted me your princely word,
"Let, what there might, ensue;
"If now you harbour ill designs,
"Your treachery you may rue.

"Robbers you may on gallows hang,
"To hawks and crows a prey;
"So lightly fly from home not I
"From wife and child away.

"If quit I must my native land,
"My children, friends and wife,
"You'll call the day you saw me here
"The worst of all your life."

"I'll hear no more, Niels Ebbeson,
"Off to thy home! begone!
"Or I shall crush thy mail on thee,
"And that I'll do anon."

"No man has yet seen me alarm'd,
"No eye has seen me quake;
"Count Gherrit, look to your affairs,
"A good defence to make."

"Talk on and vent thy rage and spite,
"As ever seems thee best;
"Thou'rt till tomorrow safe for me,
"Till sinks the sun to rest.

"Till evening hour tomorrow night
"Thou goest 'safe and free,
"And then, as true as I'm a Count,
"I'll come and visit thee."

Off rode to his home Niels Ebbeson,
"And raised his hand on high;
"Count Gherrit, I shall soon be back,
"On that you may rely."

Niels Ebbeson the highway took.
And hotly spurr'd his hors";
The count he dared not follow him
With all his mighty force.

On, till he reached his homestead gate,
He rode at utmost speed;
He told his lovely wife the news,
And pray'd her give him rede.

"Good day, my own, my dearest wife,
"What rede you give me, say:
"The Count will banish me the land,
"And warn'd me yesterday.

"He laid before me there his terms
"To choose me one of three,
"To swear him troth, to quit the land,
"Or hang on gallows tree."

"Methinks the harshest course, my lord,
"Were best to serve our turn,
"To slay the Count, or o'er his head
"The house and all to burn."

"Go eat and drink, my gallant swains,
"And gaily pass the cup;
"We meet in town our work to do,
"Ere yet the sun is up.

"This night, while all in darkness lies,
"The news will come to hand,
"And every good and faithful swain
"Will by his master stand."

Those troopers sware a solemn oath
And on it staked their life,
To ride with him, where he should ride,
And back him well in strife.

They rode by night to Lady-wood,
Their horses there they tied,
And off to find the bald-head Count
To Randers town they hied.

But when to Randers-bridge they came,
'Twas thus their leader spake;
"The swain who will not go with us,
"At once his furlough take."

Then forward stepped the youthful Trost,
The one he thought so true;
"My lord, that furlough give to me,
"And horse and saddle too"

The boon he ask'd was granted him,
His horse and saddle too;
Before the set of sun that day
He proved to his master true.

Niels Ebbeson he found the horse,
Where slept the Count within,
And with his spear-point beat the door.
And rais'd a mighty din.

"O rise, my lord, Count Gherrit, rise,"
"Up from your sleep awake,
"The Duke, your brother, sent us here;
"His letter come and take/'

"Hast thou been by my brother sent?
"Thou shalt not tarry long:
"Meet me tomorrow in Cloister church
"'Tween mass and matin song."

"O let your page the letter take,
"The latch a moment raise,
"For Rib town is hard beset,
"And Colding all ablaze.

"I've e'en left Ribe hard besieged,
"Colding and Vedel burnt;
"And hark! Niels Ebbeson is hung,
"I've that for certain learnt."

"If what thou say est is the truth,
"Good news hast thou to tell,
"And high shalt stand in my esteem,
"While I'm alive and well."

"O let him in. Count, let him in,
"No longer now delay,
"The victory's won, the land subdued,
"Hear what he's come to say."

Count Gherrit out of his window look'd.
And saw the threatening foe;
"Wretch that I am to've hither come!
"'Tis Ebbeson below."

They beat the door with spear and shield,
They brake the bolts in three;
"If thou art there, thou bald-head Count,
"We'll drink a health to thee."

"Wait there below, Niels Ebbeson,
"I'll make thee full amends;
"We'll send to fetch Duke Henry here,
"And other mutual friends."

"Not so thou spakest yesterday
"Oat there on Randers strand;
"Thou wouldest either hang me up,
"Or I should quit the land."

Then thus the Count's small pageboy cried,
Of Niels's kindred born,
"If you are duped with crafty words,
"You'll bring yourself to scorn."

Then up and spake the swarthy swain,
Because he was not white
"'Tis time we cease this idle talk,
"And let the sword-blade bite."

"I've neither fort nor massy tower
"So rich a prize to guard,
"So spare ye not of thrust or blow,
"But deal them quick and hard."

They seiz'd and held his yellow locks
Nor let his prayers avail,
But from his shoulders chopped his head
Over the bedstead rail.

They made it known by beat of drum.
Soon as the Count was slain,
And gladly then would Ebbeson
Move out of town again.

He call'd his men and hasted off,
He dared no longer stay.
But cross'd his march Sir Ove Hals,
And thought to hem his way.

"Now hark thee, good Sir Ove Hals,
"This hindrance prythee cease;
"For brother in-law to me art thou,
"So let us pass in peace/'

"How nearly we are both allied,
"All that full well I know,
"But thou hast foully slain my lord,
"Nor will I let thee go."

Sir Ove soon was forced for aid
His Holster men to call,
But slain, before the day' was closed,
Were he and his troopers all.

In wrath they drew their glittering blades,
For Niels would not retreat;
And fought till lay Sir Ove's head
Low at his kinsman's feet.

Randers bridge went Ebbeson,
Behind him stormed the foe,
But little Trost his swain was there,
And heav'd the bridge below.

True to his uncle proved that day
Young Trost his sister's son,
For, when the Holster men came up,
Bridge o'er the stream was none.

Niels with a poor old woman lodged,
She had two loaves of bread,
And one she gave Niels Ebbeson,
Who struck the bald-pate dead.

God bless thy soul, Niels Ebbeson,
Thou wast a worthy Dane,
And in thy native land's behalf
Its foreign foes hast slain.

And Jesus bless each Danish man
As well with mouth as hand.
If he with all his heart and soul
Defends his native land.

poems.title: The Robbers at Nordenshaw
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Robbers lurking at Nordenshaw
From out the green-wood creep,
And march by night to the farmer's house,
Their Yule with him to keep.

They've marched away to the farmer's house
With each in hand a spear;
"Come, cousin, see, we are kith and kin,
"Tap us thy Christmas beer.

"And, farmer, lodge us all tonight,
"And well with liquor ply,
"And with us leave thy pretty wife,
"Or, farmer, thou shalt die/'

"I'll freely pour my mead and ale,
"And well I'll serve you too;
"But, Sirs, by all that's good above,
"No outrage on us do.

"Now if upon my house ye seize,
"And lord it at your will,
"And if ye put my wife to shame,
"That were outrageous ill."

Some on the table threw their swords.
Some cloaks of fur so fine,
Some bade the honest farmer's wife
Bring in the beer and wine.

A cloth of woven silk she took,
And over the table spread;
And there her ale and wine they drank.
And ate her meat and bread.

A cautious wife was Oaselille,
And used her words with care;
She rose and told the robber guests
She would their beds prepare.

No thought had she, good Oaselille,
With them to share her bed;
But left them feasting, and for help
Through the dark forest sped.

With harried step through bush and field
Ran on the lusty dame,
And after four long weary miles
To Drost Sir Peter's came.

She reached Sir Peter's courtyard gate,
Drew on her mantle blue,
And boldly up to the upper room,
Sir Peter's chamber, flew.

"Wake up, Drost Peter Hoseale, wake,
"No moment longer sleep;
"The thieves, that lurk'd at Nordenshaw,
"With us their Christmas keep.

"What! still, Sir Peter, slumbering en
"Nor yet but half awake?
"Those robbers twelve are at the Grange,
"All twelve are now to take."

Then rose the Drost and call'd his men,
And bade them all to arm;
"Wake up, my men, there's come tonight
"Good news from yonder farm.

"Wake up, no moment more delay,
"And d'on your trusty mail;
"For Nilus Ufridson is there,
"And not the man to quail."

"Where," ask'd those sturdy robbers twelve,
They'd drunk of ale so deep,
"Where's now the farmer's pretty wife?
"We'll have her here to sleep."

"Chide not, good Sirs, a short delay
The grey-coat farmer said;
"She is even now to the chamber gone
"To make her guests their bed."

The farmer out of his window looked,
And saw the Drost's array;
"There stop here thirty men at arms,
"Are dress'd like cushats gray."

Then answered Nilus Ufridson,
"Of such I'm not afraid,
"If but my comrades stand as firm,
"And faithful prove my blade."

"No," answered Lave Rimordson,
"And scanned the troop afield,
"For such men care we not a bean,
"To them we'll never yield."

They beat the door with sword and spear
And raised a fearful shout;
"Up up, Sir Nilus Ufridson I
"Thy gang and thou come out"

"Seven tons of gold I'll give thee, Drost,
"And silver other five,
"To let us hence in peace depart,
"My men and me alive."

"Thy silver, Nilus, heed I not,
"As little heed thy gold;
"Through thee weeps many an orphan child
"For friends beneath the mould."

Hard fought Sir Nilus Ufridson;
And well he kept his ground,
And heavy were from bar and beam
The blows he dealt around.

Nor less did Lav Rimordson,
But fought with might and main,
Till at the hilt by dint of blows
He broke his sword in twain.

He dash'd the hilt against a stone,
The blade stuck in the mould;
"And now, my only chance of life,
"I'll try good words and gold.

"Drost Peter Hoseale, spare my life,
"And do me no disgrace;
"I'm near of kin to the Danish Queen,
"And of an Emperor's race."

"If near of kin to the Queen thou art,
"And all so nobly born,
"Why to the Farmer's didst thou go,
"And treat his rights with scorn?"

So seized Sir Peter all the twelve,
And townward march'd them off;
And set them side by side on poles,
The people's jest and scoff.

And there they lie on rack and wheel
To bear the heat and cold;
But to the King the Drost has brought
Twelve heavy chests of gold.

poems.title: Folker Lowmanson
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Young Folker serves in Waldmar's court,
With honour grace and fame;
And dear to both the knight and squire,
And maid and courtly dame.

How well these ladies loved him all,
They show'd in words and mien,
But mostly she whom best he served,
Helwig the Danish Queen.

King Waldmar over his table sat,
"Now would," said he "I knew,
"Why to the ladies Lowmanson
"So faithful is and true."

Then up and answer'd him the page,
And show'd but little skill,
For 'twas the counsel he gave the king,
That wrought such grievous ill.

"Let Folker Lowmanson be seiz'd,
"And laid in iron bond,
"And soon you'll see, which lady fair
"Of Folker is so fond."

He came to court, as he was wont,
So gay and void of fear.
He little thought, what gloomy news
Was there to meet his ear.

Matrons and maids he greeted, all.
And one by one address'd,
But Helwig most the good kind queen,
For her he loved the best.

In came to the bower the little page,
And stood before the board.
And cunning was that wight of speech
To choose the fittest word.

"My greeting, Folker Lowmanson,
"In dainty robes array'd,
"To Nyborg you must ride today,
"For so my master bade."

"To Nyborg must I ride today?
"And is thy message true?
"Farewell then, Helwig, dearest Queen,
"For ever I part from you."

Up rose young Folker Lowmanson,
"Farewell he bade them all,
And went to stand before the king,
Up in the lofty hall.

Queen Helwig sat, and wrung her hands,
With many a bitter tear;
"God! let me never live the day
"Of Folker's death to hear."

And in went Folker Lowmanson
Before the King to stand;
And thus it was King Waldmar spake,
And this his stern demand.

"Now hark thee, Folker Lowmanson,
"A handsome knight thou art;
"Hast thou been sitting in lady's bower
"To win some maiden's heart?"

"So help me thou, great God of heaven,
"In pressing hour of need!
"For no one's hurt have I been there,
"Or any evil deed."

Bat seiz'd was Folker Lowmanson,
And off to Nyborg sent,
And there with chains on hand and foot
In dungeon closely pent.

They locked a collar round his neck,
And fetters on his feet;
"But what have I then done amiss,
"That me so ill ye treat?"

Up answered him the little page,
And he was standing near;
"What crime was thine, Queen Helwig ask,
"The dame to thee so dear."

"So help me, God, who on the cross
"Hast suffered death and scorn!
"Helwig the Queen's no whit the worse,
"That I've been ever born."

With look so calm — for his guiltless life
In naught had been to blame —
He sent the kind good Queen 'farewell,'
"Fare weir to maid and dame.

"Bid them 'farewell', and let the Queen
"Hear this my latest breath,
"I gladly, now that die I must,
"For her sake suffer death."

They set a barrel full of spikes,
For so King Waldmar bade;
And poor young Folker Lowmanson
Was in it to be laid.

Folker, when doom was on him passed,
Into the barrel sprang;
As many as saw his cruel doom,
They keenly felt the pang.

The queen stood on the chamber steps,
And all too well could hear,
How toll'd the bells in Nyborg church.
As passed poor Folker's bier.

She heard his deathbell, Denmark's Queen,
And call'd her groomboys twain;
"Quick, lads! my palfrey! bring him round
"With saddle on and rein.

"Bring me my saddled palfrey round
"And wait for me below;
"For I will ride to Nyborg town,
"Poor Folker's fate to know."

With anxious heart did Denmark's Queen
To Nyborg urge her horse,
And at the gate his bier she met.
And on it Folker's corse.

Such honour shown to son of knight
I never yet could hear;
The Queen of Denmark walk'd on foot
Herself before his bier.

Queen Helwig sat awhile, and wept
Beside young Folker's grave;
And then a thousand marks of gold
For masses for him gave.

In tears Queen Elelwig mounted horse
And silent homeward rode,
For in her heart a, lifelong grief
Had taken its abode.

And up to the castle wall she came,
And reached the outer gate,
Where waiting her in scarlet robe
The Danish monarch sate.

"Welcome my Queen! but, tell me, why
"These tears, this mournful mien?
"Have you to Nyborg gone today,
"And there your Folker seen?

"Now tell me on your Christian faith,
"And on your conscience swear,
"Was Folker not of all on earth
"The man to you most dear?"

"No more than with your other swains
"Had I with him to do;
"For your sake those I love the most
"Who truest are to you.

"Yourself I love with all my heart,
"As God will witness bear;
"And knights and squires, who serve you well,
"To me are always dear.

"But tell me now, my noble lord,
"All in your robe of state;
"Was it alone on my account
"That Folker met his fate?"

Silent she bosom'd up her grief,
She smiled no more, nor wept,
But died beside him the first night,
That with the king she slept.

poems.title: Tove-lille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The dancers are tripping on castle green,
With hair all flowing there trips the Queen.
And Waldmar to both has plighted troth.

A group of young maids Queen Helwig leads,
And next in the dance to her Tov treads.

Queen Helwig she turns and looks behind,
And griev'd is she Tov there to find.

"But listen, ray Tov, maid so neat,
"'Tis silk thou art tossing before thy feet!"

"And silk I have every right to wear,
"Who hope to be queen within the year."

"While I am alive the crown is mine,
"And thou but a mistress, a concubine."

King Waldmar behind a sheltering screen
Is chatting with Tov about the queen.

"Now would to heaven that she were dead!
"And then with the crown I'd grace thy head.

"Were once Queen Helwig upon her bier,
"The glittering bliant thou shouldst wear."

"O hush! my king, hush! and speak not so;
"There may be listeners: who can know?"

"And let them listen who listen will;
"If matters were so they were not ill.

"For fairer wouldst thou be turn'd to clay,
"Than she in her gold and best array."

They thought they were chatting there all alone,
But Helwig had heard their every tone.

So gave he to Tove a juwell'd band,
A richer one graced not Helwig's hand.

He gave her a casket of rare device,
With that did he pay her honour's price.

Queen Helwig she hade her pages twain;
"Go summon me Tov hack again."

In came fair Tov before the hoard;
"What will you, my queen? you sent me word."

"Fair Tovelille, say, what could it he
"Was passing between the king and thee?"

"There nothing was said by us, not a word,
"Tou might not as freely yourself have heard.

"A knight very lately ask'd my hand,
"I did but the king's advice demand/'

"Such lying and craft will not avail;
"Too well do I know how false thy tale.

"If thou art to be this country's queen,
"Thy hair should first in the snood have been."

King Waldmar to war must march away.
Queen Helwig to guard the kingdom stay.

"Queen Helwig, as I from home must go,
"Guard thou my kingdom from every foe.

"But chiefly I charge thee, hap what will,
"To care for the lovely Tovelille."

"I'll watch her and guard her, have no fear,
"As safely as wert thou ruling here."

The queen got heated a bathing room,
And cruel and hard was Tove's doom.

She made her enter, she barr'd the door,
And urged the furnaces more and more.

Fair Tovelille felt the stifling heat;
Her shrieks in the bathroom reach'd the street.

Queen Helwig was standing in castle-yard,
And heard her dying a death so hard.

Ere came King Waldmar again ashore,
Was Tovelille, gentle maid, no more.

But never again, when she was dead,
Put Waldmar the crown on Helwig's head:

Nor even again was Waldmar seen
To smile on his guilty cruel queen.

poems.title: Sir Ebbe's Daughters
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Ebbe he built a lofty bower
That still his name has kept;
Where starlings sang and nightingales,
And where his daughters slept.

Sir Ebb to do his lord's behest
To Iceland needs must sail,
And gave those maidens the bower in charge,
And thence a dismal tale.

For with their mother a foul design
Sirs Scammel and Bonde planned.
How Ebbe's daughters they might win,
And how with scandal brand.

The younger brother was sore afraid
To do the maidens wrong;
"Sir Ebb a bitter revenge will take,
"And tarries not so long."

His mother jested at all his fears,
Her cheek with anger pale;
"There's not thy father's mood in thee,
"At danger so to quail.

"With none but little serving hoys
"The lonely hower is manned,
"And were they all in iron clad,
"'Gainst you they could not stand."

The morrow, soon as dawn'd the day,
They made their weapons bright,
And after sunset mounted horse,
And reach'd the bower at night.

And there those two discourteous knights
Broke through the chamber floor,
And all against the maidens' will
Came up within their bower.

They, starting from their tranquil sleep,
Look'd round in wild dismay,
For at their snowy sides reclined
Scammel and Bond lay.

In vain those maidens tried by turns
To melt their heart with tears;
By turns would threat their father's wrath.
And seek to move their fears.

The knights, ere shone abroad the sun.
Arose and went their way;
They thank'd the ladies for what they took.
But dared no longer stay.

Sorely the younger sister griev'd
Such insults on them shown;
"We'll leap into the lake at once,
"And sink us with a stone"

"Not so, the elder daughter spake
"Nay, my dear sister, nay!
"We'll wait till comes our father home,
"He'll venge it, if he may."

And now from Iceland home again
Sir Ebbe rows ashore,
And both his daughters come in tears
To meet him at his door.

"Welcome, dear gentle father home!
"But hear a dismal tale;
"Sirs Scammel and Bond have used us so,
"Our hair we now must veil."

As heard Sir Ebbe the mournful news,
There heav'd his breast a sigh;
"Bootless my journey, if blood of man
"Again my sword shall dye!"

"Our game they are, nor need hast thou
"Of whetted sword or mail;
"To wreak full vengeance for our wrongs
"Our own two hands avail."

As folk were going all to mass
On Yule tide's holy night.
Sir Ebbe's daughters started off
With daggers polish'd bright.

"What ails Sir Ebbe's daughters twain,
"That they attire them so?
"And why without these naked blades
"To church can they not go?"

Scornful the Lady Mettelille
Smiled, as she saw them pass;
"Rise, ladies, rise, my sons' two wives
"Would in to hear a mass."

Sirs Bonde and Scammel forward went
At th' altar step to kneel;
Signild and Trunde came behind
Close following them at heel.

On northside in the weapon house
Trunde her dagger drew,
And south in front of the altar light
The base Sir Bonded slew.

On northside near the altar stop
Fair Signild drew her knife,
And at the church-door down below
Sir Scammel lost his life.

"Now see two widows here we stand,
"At least they shared our bed;
"Take up your sons, a dainty meal
"To eat with salt and bread."

Stain'd with that blood stood Hoiby church
For seven long years in ban.
Nor sermon all that time was preach'd.
Nor buried there a man.

They built a chapel on Helen's hill,
And there folk went to pray,
Until their sorrow moved the Pope
To take his ban away.

poems.title: Ellen Ove's Daughter
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
'Twas Ellen, Ove's daughter fair,
Was theme of every tale.
Nor that for all her heaps of gold,
Or fields of hill and dale.

'Twas not for all her heaps of gold,
Or grassy meads so fair.
But that at court so much was praised
The beauty of Ellen's hair.

Sir Magnus call'd his men, and bade,
His horse be duly drest;
"I'll ride across to Verslevsgard,
"And be fair Ellen's guest."

To learn with truth how matters stood
He ask'd at Sailing sound;
"Say, is Sir Ove now at home,
"Or on some foreign ground?"

Then answer'd him the ferryman,
And so began his say;
"Sir Ove is now no more at home,
"He left it yesterday."

Sir Magnus rode to the churchyard stile;
And there his horse he bound.
And hasted off on foot to church,
As best the way he found.

There stood the fair young maidens all,
Each at her mother's side;
But Ove's daughter stood alone.
And dropp'd a tear and sigh'd.

Sir Magnus stepp'd across a bench,
Stepp'd over two and three;
"Ellen, Ove's daughter, rise,
"And plight your troth to me."

"Nay!" answer'd him the maiden fair,
While tears bedew'd her face;
"I'm only Ellen's waiting maid,
"Of very humble race.

"These hose my mistress lent to me,
"And eke this pair of shoes;
"She lent me too my crown of gold;
"Her trust I'll not abuse."

She stripped a ring from off her hand,
And the aged parson fee/d;
"Now do, by all that's good above,
"Your longest lesson read."

While at the altar step she stood,
Her crown of gold she wore,
But in a coarse grey woollen hood
She pass'd the outer door.

Soon as she reached the churchyard gate,
She loos'd her lover's steed,
And rode him off to Sallingsound,
And, sooth, at fullest speed.

Amaz'd Sir Magnus stared about.
As he from church withdrew;
For off was Ove's daughter fair.
And what was he to do?

"While I delay'd so long at Mass
"To hear that droning priest,
"Has Ove's daughter, Ellen, flown,
"And stolen my trusty beast."

When Ellen came to Sallingsound,
"Up ferryman!" she cried,
"This money take, and good round gift,
"And off to the other side."

When half the Sound they had rowed across
She loosed her flowing hair;
"Sir Magnus, hark! this twelvemonth yet
"Thy hed I shall not share."

But when on the other bank she stood,
Her hat she gaily waved;
"Farewell, Sir Magnus, fare thee well,
"I've now my honour saved."

poems.title: Sir Asbiorn Snare
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The King and Sir Asbiorn Snare sat,
All under the greenwood tree
Were drinking their wine with friendly chat;
And summer smiled over the lea.

With mead and with wine they fill their glass,
All under etc.
And hours in chatting of Christel pass.
And summer etc,

"Now, King of the Danes, my asking hear;
"Give me little Christel, your daughter dear."

"The maid is but ten years old or less,
"And cannot yet make your gala dress."

"Fair Christel is young, may learn to sew,
"Do you but her hand on me bestow."

Sir Asbiorn Snare to Rib hies,
And silk for a habit and sindal buys.

On silk and sindal his gold he spends.
And all to the youthful maiden sends.

So soon as Christel had seen her task,
She ran to her nurse her rede to ask.

"O hear me, my nurse, your counsel say;
"This cloth has been sent me homo today."

"To render it back methinks were best,
"For, Christel, be sure 'twas sent in jest."

Fair Christel alone to her chamber paced.
And cut the cloth to her own good taste.

She seated herself on a working chair,
And broider'd it all with skill and care.

Fair Christel she worked the jacket's side
With fishes, that in the streamlet glide.

She worked on the shoulder fifteen knights,
With swords in their hands all hack'd in fights.

She work'd the sleeve with a flowery ring,
And maidens therein, who dance and sing.

She sew'd on his breast a scene of bliss,
A knight to his lady gives a kiss.

"And now that at last my task is done,
"Who is there that home with this will run?"

Then up little Christers page and spake;
"'Tis I your work to the knight will take/'

Sir Asbiorn gazed at the work he brought,
"God bless the fingers that this have wrought."

"But how," said the page, "Sir Asbiorn, say,
"Will you the maiden, who worked it, pay?"

"What other reward should be her right,
"Than me for her husband, so brave a knight."

The page he home to his mistress flew;
"The knight now makes his demand for you."

"Go bid him across the brook to sail,
"He catches not me with an idle tale.

"Go bid him the stream himself to cross,
All under the greenwood tree
"He'll make me not mourn ray honour's loss."
The summer smiles over the lea.

poems.title: King Swerker the Younger
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Young Swerker rose before his lord,
In solemn council rose,
And told his lord a piteous tale.
The sum of all his woes.

"My brother has driven roe from home
"Out from the land of Swede,
"But lend me you, my lord, the men,
"I'll well repay his deed."

"Aye, Swerker, men I'll lend to thee,
"Both Seelander and Jute;
"Better than they are none on earth
"To slash a blade or shoot."

A great and solemn mass was sung
One holy Sabbath day,
And Swerker march'd to Oresund,
And sail'd his troops away.

Young Swerker stands on his ship's prow.
And gazes o'er the Sound;
"God, let me either win today,
"Or in these waves be drown'd!"

Together rush'd those highborn lords.
And hard they battled too;
A piteous game, a guilty strife
Where son the father slew!

And forward.rode the Danish men
With words of haughty scorn,
And fear'd the Wester Gylling men.
As peasants mow their corn.

The Danes they won the day indeed
With grievous toil and pain;
The field was all a bath of blood,
And heap'd with maim'd and slain.

A host of eighteen thousand men
Had left the Danish shore,
But saving three and three times five
Came hack again no more.

The owl and eagle hoot and yell
On every hill and dale,
And widows weeping leave their hearth,
And orphan children wail.

The lady sits in bower aloft
Waiting her husband home,
And blood-stain'd comes the horse he rode,
But brings his saddle toom.

poems.title: Thule Vognson and Gray Swain
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
In church at Lund, a council sat,
And many the knights and squires thereat;

The maid and the dame, the knight and squire,
And Danish queen in her red attire.

Dame Mett got made a golden chair.
That into the church her servants bare.

In secret her chair of gold was wrought,
With pride to the church at Lund brought.

As into the church dame Mette went,
His eyes on the lady Sir Gray Swain bent.

As down on her chair dame Mette sat,
Sir Gray Swain began to mock thereat.

As she at the Altar bent her knee,
To sit on her gilded chair went he.

Dame Mette she turn'd from th' Altar round,
And tears from her eyes dropp'd on the ground.

"Sir Gray Swain, Sir Gray Swain, up, quit my chair,
"For never together shall we sit there."

Sir Gray Swain he seized her topknot fast.
And down on the floor Dame Mett cast.

As home to her dwelling rode the dame
Her sons all seven to meet her came.

The youngest a costly mantle spread,
That on it his mother's foot might tread.

"O welcome. Dame Mette, my mother dear,
"But why on thy cheek the briny tear?"

"And would ye then know why tears are there?
"Sir Gray Swain has driven me off my chair.

"They put on me, since your father died,
"Such violence and wrong and scorn beside/'

Her cloak she toss'd on the board again;
"Sir Thul, remember thy father slain"

"Dear mother, no longer shed a tear,
"You soon shall the best of tidings hear.

"Now lend me, mother, your scarlet gown,
"And set on me, sister, your golden crown:

"And lend me your ermined mantle red,
"And so will I go and venge the dead/'

A pageboy was at Sir Thule's side,
A friend of Sir Gray Swain good and tried.

He proved him his faithful friend that day,
He sent a message to warn Sir Gray.

"Go home, Sir Gray Swain, and leave the crowd;
"The sons of Sir Vogn your death have vow'd."

"Why should I so hastily home again?
"There's coming so gay a bridal train."

"Haste! haste! the delay you will surely rue;
"Those maidens are plotting no good to you."

Sir Thul the foremost led the band;
Sir Gray Swain he held him out his hand.

"Nay take to thee back thy hand again;
"hou know est it has my father slain."

"Whatever the wrong I did to thee,
"I paid it with gold in ready fee.

"In silver and gold I paid thee down
"Three thousand marks to the utmost crown."

"Tor him thou "hast paid me what was fair,
"But push'd my mother from off her chair."

"So God and his angels by me stand!
"I touch'd her not either with foot or hand."

Sir Thule a sword from his mantle drew,
Away to the church Sir Gray Swain flew.

Sir Thul pursued him with deadly hits,
And cut Sir Gray to a thousand bits.

The blood at Saint Mary's shrine was shed,
And both at Saint Stephen's now lie dead.

poems.title: Mar Stig
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Mar Stig wakes up at midnight hour,
And tells his wife so dear;
"I've dreamt to night a wondrous dream,
"God knows what danger's near.

"I seemed to see my gallant ship,
"Shrunk to a little boat,
"And wild it drifted, all its oars
"Gone overboard afloat.

"I dreamt we rode across a bridge
"Over the boiling flood,
"And me my horse threw off his back,
"And ran to a forest stud.'

"O list, my lord, calm all your fears,
"And cast your cares away;
"It means, the boors and tenantry
"Their taxes come to pay."

In came Mar Stig's small chamber swain,
And stood before the board;
"There's hither come King Brick's page,
"And waits to see my lord."

Uprose the youthful knight, Mar Stig,
And dress'd before his bed,
And down to the courtyard went to hear
What Brick's envoy said.

"O list to me, young knight, Mar Stig,
"List to the words I bring;
"Mount now, and come at once to Court
"To see the Danish king."

"But hark thee, tiny chamber swain,
"What I will say to thee;
"If thou dost know the king's design,
"Conceal it not from me."

"The king's design I cannot tell,
"But that you'll quickly hear;
"Only that you shall take the field,
"And the king's banner bear."

The young Mar Stig these tidings heard,
In mantle wrapp'd his head,
And, mounting up to the bower aloft,
Approached his lady's bed.

In stepp'd Mar Stig, and closed the door,
And sorrowful he grew;
"So then, fair lady Ingeborg,
"My dream is proving true,

"What of my gallant horse I dreamt,
"That off to the stud he fled,
"Means that on battlefield I'm slain,
"And left there lying dead."

"Be calm, my dear, ray noble lord,
"Be calm, and say not so;
"There dwells our Saviour Christ above,
"Wards off the deadly blow."

The young Mar Stig he mounted horse,
And rode to the royal gate,
And, waiting found the Danish king
Wrapt in a dress of state.

"List now the words, young knight Mar Stig,
"That I would say to thee;
"This season thou shalt take the field,
"The banner bear for me."

"If I this season take the field,
"And march and risk my life,
"Will you, king Erick, guard from harm
"My fair and gentle wife?"

King Erick smiled beneath his cloak,
And spake in crafty tone;
"Safe she shall be, as though she were
"A sister of mine own.

"So well will I thy lady watch,
"And keep her free from harm,
"As though thou wert thyself at home,
"And she were on thine arm.'

The young Mar Stig with all his men
Rode off for war and fame,
And left his lovely Ingeborg
A prey to grief and shame.

The young King Erick call'd his swains.
And bade his horse be drest;
"We'll up the country ride anon,
"And be the lady's guest."

"He rode within the courtyard gate,
His head wrapped in his hood,
And mounting up to the bower aloft
Before the lady stood.

"Greet you, fair lady, Ingeborg!
"This kindness to me show;
"Make me a shirt, and eke the same
"With gold embroidery sew."

"If I should cut a shirt for you,
"Or broider one with gold,
"Mar Stig would wrathful be with me,
"And all his love grow cold."

"O list, sweet lady, Ingeborg,
"Be you but kind and true,
"I'll ever, while I live and breathe,
"Both love and honour you."

"Mar Stig has given me a ring of gold,
"Hung on my neck a chain,
"And true to only him, my king,
"I lifelong will remain.

"You fairly vow'd, when young Mar Stig
"Rode off to take the field,
"Me as your sister you would watch,
"From every danger shield."

They lit the festive tapers all.
And bitter tears she shed.
As with the king they took her off
With him to share her bed.

The lovely Ingeborg she pined
With grief and care and shame,
That day and night to claim her love
This lewd King Erick came.

Mar Stig, his battles bravely fought,
March'd home again from war,
Such baleful tidings met his ear
In foreign lands afar.

Mar Stig he near'd his dwelling place,
Came riding up the street,
But went not out fair Ingeborg
Her gallant lord to meet.

Mar Stig he leaped from off his horse,
And stepped within his door,
But rose the fair dame Ingeborg
To welcome him no more.

Mar Stig awhile in silence stood,
"And why then," reasoned he,
"Will rise the lady Ingeborg
"No more to welcome me?"

"What time you march'd away from home,
"I bare an honoured name,
"But now alas I'm Denmark's queen,
"And lead a life of shame.

"What time you march'd away from home,
"A knight could call me wife,
"But now alas I'm Denmark's queen,
"And care no more for life.

"I'll never sleep another sleep
"Within your arms again,
"Until the king who outraged me,
"King Erick you have slain.

"I'll never sleep another sleep
"Pressed to your fair white side,
"Till Erick, he who wrought my fall,
"That villain King has died."

Mar Stig he clad himself and men
In mail of steely ring,
And off to a general council rode,
And there defied the King.

Forth came the knight, the brave Mar Stig,
Before King Erick stood,
And greeted all his Aldermen
And thanes of noble blood.

And thus Mar Stig in open court
Spake out devoid of fear;
"My wife by force has been abused,
"For that I'm standing here.

"While in my country's cause I fought,
"And daily risk'd my life,
"You, you, King Erick, stay'd at home,
"And forced my gentle wife."

King Erick smiled beneath his cloak
His crafty part to play;
"Her will was quite as good as mine,
"She never said me nay."

"There's an old saw/' Mar Stig replied,
And sorrowful he spake,
"That Injury goes on before
"And Insult in it's wake.

"You've done me great and grievous wrong,
"Have foully used my wife;
"This deed, King Erick, hear my words,
"Shall surely cost your life."

So left the court the knight Mar Stig,
And raised his hat on high;
"Aldermen, hear me witness all,
"That I the King defy."

"Hark thee a word, young knight Mar Stig,
"Cease from thy tone of pride;
"I'll give thee town and moated fort
"And grassy land beside."

"I care not, I, for tower or fort,
"Not such the amend I claim;
"Would that the deed were yet undone
"That brought my wife to shame!"

"Mar Stig, my man, ride not so fast,
"I cannot hold thee pace;
"If thou wilt be my friend no more,
"So let our friendship cease."

"It is not I who ride so hard
"To make you feel my might;
"There's an old saw, you've heard the same,
"That might, my lord, makes right

"It is not I who fide so bard,
"Or play the tyrant's part,
"But many a hound can hold at bay
"The fleeting hind and hart.

"Mark well, I've here disclaimed the faith
"That once to you I owed,
"And that at times a little tump
"Upsets a mighty load."

Dame Ingeborg for Ranild sent,
A youth, her sister's son.
Him made the king his table swain,
And so was he undone.

These two, dame Ingeborg and he.
Their plans began to lay,
How the king Erick they might snare.
And how might seize and slay.

This page, as sat the king at meat.
Before his table stood,
And told the king of hart and hind.
That played in the green wood.

"I know where play the hart and hind,
"And thicket where they hide;
"If seems you good, my noble lord,
"We'll thither take a ride."

King Erick rose and call'd his swains
To saddle his good gray steed;
"We'll to the council ride across,
"And see how matters speed.

"Ride ye, my men, and find a place
"Where we may lodge tonight,
"While I with Ranild ride to see
"If what he says is right."

So off to Wyborg rode his men
To find him lodging there,
For least of all things did he dream
Of Ranild's crafty snare.

Ranild he took a lonely road
That Erick little knew,
And truly all the plans he laid
With craft he carried through.

They hunted stag, they hunted hind
They, chased the fleeting roe,
They stay'd so long, that at the last
They saw the daylight go.

In gloomy mood King Erick spake,
As sank its parting ray,
"Thou, heavenly father, be our guide,
"For here I'm all astray."

The King into the thicket peer'd.
As closed the darkling night,
And soon was ware of a small house,
Where burnt a fire and light.

He stepped within the woodland but,
And sad at heart was he.
But found a lovely maiden there
As eye could wish to see.

Her he clasped fondly round her waist,
And straight began to woo:
"Hear me, fair maid, nor say me nay,
"To night I sleep with you."

"Answer me first" the maid replied
In laughing merry tone,
"Answer me first, King Erick, you,
"What deed you last have done?"

"Sweet lovely maid, if that you know,
"More tidings you can give;
"So tell me, lovely maid, but this,
"How long I've yet to live?"

With hearty glee laugh'd the fair maid,
And this her dubious word;
"That question ask the little hook
"Whereon is hung your sword."

King Erick fain had held the maid.
But this he tried in vain,
She slipped away between his hands.
He saw her not again.

So long as with the King she stood,
Blazed there a cheerful fire.
But soon as she had fled away.
Was naught but tangled briar.

"My lord," said Ranild, so began
That crafty traitor's say;
"My lord, while still there shines the moon,
"'Twere best to haste away.

"There lies hard by a little town
"Outside this tangled wood,
"And thither we may ride, my lord,
"If seems your lordship good.

"So far at least we well may ride,
"While still the moon is clear;
"And hereabouts, trust me, my lord,
"From foes we've naught to fear."

They rode and came to Finderup,
And sought to lodge the night,
Bat at that late untimely hour
Was out both fire and light.

In Finderup barn they stall'd their steeds,
And there, they made their bed:
How little had ever thought the King
To lodge in such a shed!

"Ranild," the young King Erick spake,
An anxious man was he,
"Ranild, my page, lock thou the door,
"I trust my life to thee.

"Make fast this barn's poor crazy door,
"In thee must I confide;
"Think on that bold young knight, Mar Stig,
"And how he me defied."

"Mar Stig my kinsman will at times
"Blurt out an angry word,
"But none the greater harm from that
"Threatens my noble lord.

"The lapwing guards the smallest spot
"She rests upon afield,
"The one she builds her dwelling on
Trom danger cannot shield."

No other sword or spear was that
He placed beside the door,
Than, truth to say, two barley straws
That lay upon the floor.

No sooner in the barn were they.
And the frail door had barr'd,
Than those came, Ingeborg had sent,
Into the farmer's yard.

With sword and spear they beat the door
And rais'd a fearful shout
"'Up, up. King Erick! up, my lord!
"And leave your lair and out!"

"Hark ye," young Ranild call'd aloud.
And made them quick reply;
"There's no King Erick lodges here,
"On this ye may rely."

He threw upon him heaps of straw,
He threw upon him hay;
To say the truth, he did it all
To show them where he lay.

He then with well-feign'd zeal began
The beams to hack and hew,
A traitor scoundrel proved himself,
His lord the King he slew.

"Now who to Wyborg town will ride
"Behind the murder'd king?
"And who to the queen at Scanderborg
"The dismal news will bring?"

Not one will ride to Wyborg town
Behind the murdered king;
The news to the queen at Scanderborg
They sent a boy to bring.

In came the little messenger,
And stood before the board;
A cunning child of speech was he
To find the fittest word.

"Hail, Queen of Denmark, hail, my queen
"Array'd in scarlet red!
"Erick is slain, our youthful king,
"And lies in Finderup dead.'

"This for thy tidings thou shalt have,
"As sad as is thy tale
"Long as I live thy place at board,
"Thy meat and cup of ale."

"From his right side they drove a sword
"Through to his other arm;
"O guard the child whom Denmark loves,
"And shield him well from harm.

"From left arm too they drove the sword
"Through to the other side;
"O guard from harm that little child,
"Our Denmark's hope and pride."

At Findenip kill'd Mar Stig his king,
And little rued his deed,
But rode across to Skanderborg,
And urged his horse to speed.

From window peer'd the Danish queen
In chamber, where she sate;
"And hither comes the selfroade King,
"Is riding through the gate."

"No self-made king at all am I,
"Whatever thou may'st say:
"The sheriff Lowman, was it not,
"Last in thy bosom lay?

"What carest thou for Erick's death,
"What needest thou to wail,
"With sheriff Lowman near thy side
"And all alive and hale?'

Up then and spake Duke Christopher
Array'd in scarlet red;
"Sad news it is that dead he lies,
"My dearest father dead."

And further said Duke Christopher,
And spake the words with grace;
"I'll thee, sure as I bear the crown,
"From home and country chase."

"And if from home I must away
"Out on the chilly flood,
"I'll many a wife a widow make
"Of best and noblest blood.

"If I from Denmark must away
"Trom wife and infants small,
"I'll out of Denmark fetch my food
"In winter spring and fall."

He spake and off from Skanderborg,
At fullest speed he rode,
And took his course to Molderup,
His Ingeborg's abode.

Back to his own dear home and wife
Mar Stig rode up the street,
And she, the fair dame, Ingeborg,
Went out her lord to meet.

His news he told, the young Mar Stig,
And clasped her round the waist;
"I've slain the King, left dead the wretch
"Who thee has so disgraced.

"Wilt thou go penniless with me?
"An exile's lot to share,
"Or live some rich man's concubine,
"And the foul title bear?"

"Far rather will I forth with thee
"To share an exile's lot,
"Than, as a rich man's concubine,
"My fame so foully blot"

Mar Stig withdrew his men to Helm,
And there he made abode,
And pale grew many a manly cheek
That pass'd along the road.

This house and all its battlements
So quickly did he raise,
He took to finish all this work
Only two nights and days.

So strong he built his house at Helm,
Its walls he made so fast,
He little cared for shot or stone,
Or what thereat were cast.

The peasant drives his team afield,
And tearful sows his corn;
"Help us, thou gracious God in heaven,
"The Helm has got a horn."

And there Mar Stig builds up his Helm
With battlement and wall.
And vain the might of king and men
To make that fortress fall.

poems.title: Mar Stig's Daughters
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Mar Stig left orphan daughters two,
Sad fate had they to undergo.
The elder took the younger's hand.
And wide they round the world must roam.

The elder took the younger's hand,
And so they went to Sweden's land.
King Byrge home from Sessions came,
So wide they round the world must roam.

King Byrge home from Sessions came.
And there they stood his alms to claim.

"What girls are these before my gate?
"What do ye waiting here so late?"

"Mar Swig's two orphan daughters we,
"We sue to you for charity/'

"Out of my yard then both the two!
"Your father Stig my uncle slew."

"We're not for Erick's death to blame,
"'Twas but to earn our bread we came."

The elder took the younger's hand,
And so they went to Norway's land.

King Erick home from Sessions came,
And there they stood his alms to claim.

"What two poor women then are you?
"What are you hither come to do?"

"Mar Stig's two orphan daughters we,
"And sue to you for charity."

"Now tell me, can ye bake and brew,
"Or other useful service do?"

"Nay, we can neither bake nor brew,
"Such menial work we cannot do;

"But from our mother, who is dead,
"We've learnt to spin the golden thread.

"Brocade too we can weave, as fine
"As could the Queen's own maids design;

"But spinning gold and weaving wool,
"Have hearts with sorrow always full;

"And since we both our parents mourn,
"Wear cloaks so threadbare, old, and torn.

"Were still Mar Stig alive at home,
"To such distress we had not come.

"Were not our poor dear mother dead,
"We needed not to beg our bread."

King Erick spake in kindest tone,
"I've long and well your father known;

"A ready man of tongue and hand,
"As one might find in Danish land."

He clad them both in scarlet pall,
And led them up to the ladies' hall.

Their grief he bade them now restrain,
In him their father find again.

With broider'd work the younger strove
To fill the web her sister wove.

Her skilful hand the task begun
With th' Holy Virgin and her Son;

But on the second piece was seen
With ladies round her Norway's queen;

And next the antler'd stag and doe,
And then herself so pale with woe.

With equal grace and skill she wove
The angels in the skies above.

She took the work from off the frame,
And knelt before the royal dame.

"Would that you stood in mother's stead!"
And bitter were the tears she shed;

"Did we a mother find in you,
"Tay we might earn and honour too.

"One single piece still leaves us poor,
"And long must we our lot endure."

The elder one on sickbed lay,
The younger nurs'd her night and day.

The elder died and found relief.
The younger lived in pain and grief;

Till on the maid so fair and good
The king his youngest son bestow'd;

With him she found a rank and home,
Nor needed more the world to roam.

poems.title: Mar Stig (No. 6)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Tis gaily danced in Riber Street,
The castle now is won
There dance the knights with nimble feet,
'Tis held for Erick's son.

On Riber bridge they are dancing too,
The castle now is won
There dance the knights with hollow'd shoe
'Tis held for Erich's son,

'Tis Riber Ulf begins the fling,
With all his heart he serves the king.

And dancing there is Tage Mouse,
A captain he in Riber House.

There's dancing there Sir Saltensee,
And all his wealthy kinsmen three.

And there the noble Limbecks fling,
Who scarcely rank below the king.

Behind them dances Byrge Green,
And many a knight of noble mien.

And there there's dancing Johnie Kan,
And wife behind, the Lady Ann.

Next dances Rank, a gallant knight,
And wife, fair Berngerd, all in white.

Volrayen next, and eke his dame,
The gentle Lady — what's her name?

And there there's dancing Iver Helt,
Came with the king across the Belt.

Awhile stood Ronald Lang in doubt,
To go or not and join the rout.

"But for this soft and flaxen hair,
"By all that's good, I'd soon be there.

"Aye! but for this yet rosy cheek,
"I'd soon take part in yonder freak"

He joined, and, as he danced away,
Struck up the while a merry lay.

He led the song, he lightly sprang.
And all the knights in chorus sang.

Uprose the maiden Buckleshoe,
And vow'd to be to Ronald true.

With silk was braided up her hair,
And all so lightly danced the fair.

She led the knights within the wall
With swords beneath then: mantles all.

By crafty plan and lucky chance
The castle now is won,
With song and laugh and merry dance

poems.title: Mar Stig (No. 7)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Ranild bade saddle his charger gray,
'Twas told me oft before,
"I'll be the Algrave's guest today,
"Tho' friends I have no more.

Ranild rode up to his castle gate,
'Twas told him oft before
Where ermine-clad the Algrave sate,
Tho' friends he had no more.

"Hail noble Algrave, here I come,
'Twas told thee oft before,
"To fetch my trothplight Kirstin home,
"Tho' friends I have no more."

Then up and spake her mother dear,
"'Twas told thee oft before,
"For thee is bride no longer here,
"For friends thou hast no more."

"I'll either with the maid return,
"'Twas told you oft before
"Or else your house and chattels burn,
"Tho' friends I have no more."

"Nay set not thou the house on flame,
"'Twas told thee oft before,
"E'en take the bride thou'rt come to claim,
"Tho' friends thou hast no more."

In mantle wrapt the gentle maid,
'Twas told her oft before,
On Ranild's good gray horse was laid,
Tho' friends he had no more.

No other bridal bed had they,
'Twas told her oft before,
Than bush, and field, and new made hay.
For friends he had no more.

"The wood has ears, the mead can see,
"Twas told thee oft before,
"A wretched outlawed pair are we,
"For friends I have no more."

"And had you not King Erick slain,
"'Twas told you oft before,
"We still might in the land remain,
"But friends we have no more."

"Stay, Kirstin, stay, such words forbear:,
"'Twas told thee oft before,
"Where strangers are, take greater care,
"For friends we have no more."

With that he slapped her cheek so red,
"'Twas told thee oft before,
"It was not I, smote Erick dead,
"Tho' friends I have no more."

poems.title: Mar Stig (No. 8)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Report is rife in all the land
Ranild at last is caught;
He surely had never gone from Hieira,
His doom had he bethought;
A death of torture he must die,
As he has long been taught.

Ranild he stepped within the door,
Good evening' bade the king,
And all the guard of gentlemen,
Who round him stood in ring;
"Christ! may no son of loyal Dane
"Such trouble on him bring!

"But, King Erick, noble liege,
"Remember you no more;
"The best was I of all the swains
"Your father's livery wore;
"And you through wood and flowery mead
"In arms so often bore?"

"Full well I know thou servedst here
"For clothes and food and pay;
"And, like a vile and treacherous knave,
"My father didst betray;
"For which the stake thy carcase bears,
"If I but reign a day."

"My hands and feet hack from my limbs,
"Tear from my head these eyes;
"With racking tortures martyr me,
"The worst you can devise;
"So much the wrong I've done your house
"For vengeance on me cries."

"Thine eyes put out, that will we not,
"Nor lop thy hands or feet;
"But with a traitor's hardest death
"The worst of traitors treat;
"And on our father's murderer take
"Such vengeance as is meet."

As forth from Roskilde he was led,
He wrung his hands anew,
And tears to see him go to die
Wept ladies not a few;
He turn'd him round, and bade them all
A thousand times Adieu.

They led him forth to where the rack
Stood ghastly on the plain;
"Christ, from such a martyring death
"Protect each honest Dane!
"Had I but stay'd at Hielra this year,
"And there in safety lain!

"Now were there here one faithful friend,
"Who home for me would go,
"And would my sorrowing wife Christine,
"Her path of duty show!
"Christ, look on my children dear!
"O comfort thou their woe!

"And you, I pray, good Christian folk,
"Who here are standing round,
"A Pater noster read for me,
"That grace for me be found;
"And that this night I reach the land,
"Where heavenly, joys abound."

poems.title: Sir John Rimord's Son's Shrift
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The grass is green beneath the ship,
She is rotting on the shore:
A captain, brave as was Sir John,
Shall never steer her more.

In Ribe sits the Danish King,
And writes a stern decree,
To summon out his liegemen all,
And bid them put to sea.

"Now" said Sir John, as o'er his neck
His linked mail he threw,
"Who sails not out with us today,
"Nor loyal is, nor true.

"Aye" said Sir John, said Rimord's son,
And girded on his sword,
"Who sails not out with ns today,
"A traitor is to his lord."

"Tonight we'll drink a full carouse,
"Can we but get the ale;
"Tomorrow, if the breeze is fair,
"We'll put to sea and sail."

"Such words'' said Rimord's son, Sir John,
"Let none to our lord convey;
"His will and written brief we've heard,
"And needs must all obey."

The skipper Hogen, pious man.
The scowling heavens he scann'd;
"Who ventures out to sea today,
"Alive no more shall land."

But up spake Rimord's son, Sir John,
And loud he made it ring;
"And who goes not on board today,
"Is traitor to his King."

Again from his window gazed abroad
That skipper old and sage;
"No man can put to sea today,
"While storm like this shall rage."

But undismayed did Rimord's son
His sturdy comrades hail;
"In God's name off with me, my Danes,
"And spread aloft the sail."

Scarce out from land, they saw the waves
With fury rage and roar;
Th' old skipper Hogen through the mist
Could see the lea no more.

In fearful sport on the wild sea
They saw the billows rise,
And mute and sad the old skipper sat,
The teardrops in his eyes.

"Fore wind and wave drove on the ship
Amid the tempest din,
And still and gloomy sat Sir John,
His hand beneath his chin.

While every squall across the deck
The salty billows drove,
Still, as though ladies cut his hair,
Was he not seen to move.

"But where are now the troopers bold,
"Yestreen such speeches made?
"Let them now take the helm in hand,
"The anchor's fairly weighed.

"Aye! where are all the braggarts now,
"Who lately made such boast?
"Let them go stand beside the helm,
"The sail is fairly loos'd/'

'Twas so that ancient skipper spake.
His face with terror pale;
"There's here some murderous wretch on board,
"Hinders the ship to sail.

"Up, men, we'll cast the lot about,
"On whom it falls we'll see;
"And if there sails a villain here,
"Go overboard shall he."

And it was Rimord's son, Sir John,
With manly voice he cried;
"Go, fetch me, boy, the chequer board,
"The dice shall that decide."

They cast them out, the dice so small,
They tried them throw by throw,
And so it fell, 'twas e'en Sir John,
That overboard should go.

"We've sail'd away so far from land,
"No holy priest is near;
"But ne'er the-less my shrift I'll make,
"Our Lord in mercy hear."

And so did Rimord's son, Sir John,
Fall on his naked knee.
And make his shrift before the mast
Out on the roaring sea.

"Beguil'd full many a widow fair
"And many a maid have I,
"But never dream'd, that out at sea
"'Twas fated I should die.

"Widows and maids beguil'd have I,
"And many a virtuous wife,
"But never dream'd in happier days
"I here should lose my life.

"I landed once at Helsingborg
"For murder, waste; and spoil,
"And many an honest peasant boy
"Buried in heathen soil.

"Cloisters I've burnt, and churches too,
"Or robb'd of all their worth;
"And many a pious nun deflour'd
"Of high and noble birth.

"Thanks be to thee, thou great good Christ,
"For grace thou now hast given!
"For lost had surely been my soul,
"Had I been drown'd unshriven.

"If one of you should come to land,
"And chance to meet my bride,
"Tell her she is free to pledge her hand,
"For in the sea I've died.

"But if, when you shall be on land,
"My mother ask for me,
"Tell her I serve the king at court,
"And live in health and glee."

Three money-pouches took Sir John,
And firmly about him bound:
"A boon for him who lays my corse
"Beneath some holy ground."

Loud rose their cry, as crosswise spread
He sank to rise no more.
And took a wild untravell'd path
Down to the Ocean's floor.

Of all the seven and seventy men,
That forth from court had gone,
There came no more than five to land,
Sir John's small page was one.

"Now let us out to the churchyard go
"For Rimord's son to pray;
"For never again will Danish King
"His equal have in pay."

There's lying dry at Borringholm
The riven and useless boat,
And tossing on the ruthless stream
Their wretched corpses float.

poems.title: Axel and Walborg
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There play'd at dice on golden board
Two dames of high degree,
And watch'd their shifting course of luck
With mutual hearty glee.

There round and round and upside down
The dice so nimbly ran;
And round and round goes fortune's wheel
With course as hard to scan.

The Lady July and Denmark's Queen
At table sat and play'd,
While on the floor with crabs and pears
I'll ere play'd an infant maid.

With fruit and flowers the pretty child
Was carrying on her game.
As thither on his road to Rome
Sir Axel Tordsen came.

He greeted dames and maidens all,
That graceful virtuous knight,
In secret was the gentle child
His hope and his delight.

He tapp'd.the baby's fair white cheek,
And took her on his knee;
"Would heaven thou wert a woman grown,
"My sweetheart thou shouldst be."

"Ah! no!" in gold embroider'd dress
His sister thus replied;
"Tho' she this very night were such,
"She could not be thy bride."

Up spake that maiden's mother too,
And true her words and frank;
"Too nearly are you both of kin,
"Tho' equal be your rank."

His ring of gold the knight took off
And gave her for a toy:
That ring, long ere she came of age,
Had robb'd her heart of joy.

"My little bride mark thou my words,
"Betroth'd are we today;
"And now I "go to serve a king
"In countries far away."

Sir Axel, good and gallant knight.
Must on his journey ride,
And off to a neighbouring nunnery
Was sent his little bride.

She learnt to read, and ply her hand
On broidery work and lace,
And daily grew in good repute,
And modesty and grace.

Her manners, noble as her birth,
Won praises more and more;
Her sound good sense, and sparkling wit,
And all her varied lore.

In cloister eleven years she pass'd.
Until her mother died.
And then the queen took her to court
And kept her near her side.

Sir Axel serv'd in th' Emperor's house
With golden spurs at heel;
And at his side with knightly grace
He bare the trusty steel.

There, as he in his chamber slept
Reclined on silken bed,
Scar'd with a frightful dream he woke.
And toss'd his weary head.

Walborg his bride he seem'd to see
Robed in her velvet dress.
And at her side Prince Hagen stand
Some eager suit to press.

Soon as the lark at morning dawn
Trill'd forth his lively song,
In haste up starting from his bed
His clothes he round him slung.

He saddled him his trusty gray,
And off to the forest sped;
Would hear the bird's sweet song, and drive
Sad thoughts from out his head.

But e'en while musing on his dream
He sauntered through the wood,
Right in his path with scrip and staff
A wayworn pilgrim stood.

"Good day, God greet thee, holy man!
"And whither bent to go?
"That thou art from my native land,
"Thy dress doth plainly show."

"In truth I'm sprung from Gildish race,
"In Norway have my home,
"And e'en fulfil a vow I've made
"Of pilgrimage to Rome."

"If thou of Gildish race art sprung,
"Thou'rt kin then of mine own:
"Say, has my bride forgotten me?
"My Walborg hast thou known?"

"Aye, Sir, I know thy Walborg well,
"A lovely maid is she,
"And many a son of gallant knight
"Would fain her suitor be.

"Full oft that graceful maid I've seen
"In robe of sable drest,
"'Mong all the maids, who serve at court,
"The fairest and the best.

"She's grown like a bright lily flower
"Borne on its stem so green;
"Mong all the maids in all the land
"No fairer may be seen.

"Since in her tomb beside her lord
"The Lady July sleeps,
"Most loved and honoured near her side
"The Queen fair Walborg keeps.

"Gold rings her fair white hands adorn,
"With pearls her hair is tied;
"And wheresoever the maid is seen,
"She is call'd Sir Axel's bride.

"Yet nevertheless her nearest kin,
"Against the general voice,
"Will give Prince Hagen thy betroth'd,
"And much thereat rejoice."

Sir Axel heard the pilgrim's tale.
And round him wrapped his cloak,
And went and stood before the throne,
And th' Emperor thus bespoke.

"Hail, Henry, sovereign great and good!
"Here at your feet I stand
"To beg a furlough hence to ride
"To see my native land.

"My patrimony is at stake,
"My parents being dead,
"And still more for my bride I fear,
"Lest her another wed,"

"Furlough, Sir Axel, grant I thee
"To see thy home again,
"And will, until thou comest back,
"Thy place for thee retain."

As with a glittering troop in arms
From court Sir Axel rode;
A happy journey wish'd him all
That in the court-yard stood.

So hard he spurr'd, with thirty men
Had he begun his ride,
But when he reached his mother's house,
Was no one at his side.

And now Sir Axel Tordsen came
Up to the court-yard gate,
And there he saw in rich attire
His sister Helfred wait.

"Here waiting, Helfred, sister mine I
"Nor thinking me to see!
"How fares that Rose of flowers, my bride?
"My Walborg, how is she?"

"Thy pretty Walborg is in health,
"No fairer can be seen,
"Of all the maids, who serve at court,
"Most favoured by the queen."

"Thy counsel, prithee, give me now,
"Helfred, my sister dear,
"How with my bride I may converse
"Unheard by other ear."

"Then wrap thee well in robe of silk,
"Dress thee in costly fur,
"And say that I've a message sent,
"To tell to none but her.'"

Sir Axel crossed the chamber bridge
Up to the ladies hall,
As e'en from vesper they returned,
The Queen's fair maidens all.

He grasp'd his lovely Walborg's hand,
And softly thus he spake;
"I'm Lady Helfred's messenger,
"This letter, prithee, take."

She broke the seal, and spread it ont,
And saw what in it lay;
Therein were tender words of love.
That only one could say.

She found enchased in five gold rings
Roses and lilies bright;
"Sir Axel Tordsen gives you these,
"Your long betrothed knight.

"You've vow'd to me to be my bride,
"And will to me be true;
"And I, while in the world I breathe,
"Will be as true to you."

There, while they cross'd the balcony,
They plighted them their troth;
And each the other firmly bound
By solemn mutual oath.

By holy Dorothy they sware,
And Virgin Queen on high,
They would with honour spend their lives,
And would with honour die.

Sir Axel rode in th' Emperor's court.
And blithe and gay was he;
And in her chamber sat his bride,
And fairly laugh'd for glee.

While so they passed nine months away
Apart in distant land,
Eleven counts' sons had bent the knee,
And sued for Walborg's hand.

Eleven so brave and gallant knights.
The gentle maiden wooed,
And twelfth, the King's son Hagen came,
And late and early sued.

"O hear me, Walborg, gentle maid,
"If me you'll love and wed,
"I'll make you Queen and Norway's crown
"I'll set upon your head."

"And you, Prince Hagen, list to me,
"Your crown I'll not receive;
"I've sworn Sir Axel secret troth,
"Nor basely will deceive."

In grief and wrath went Hagen forth,
And round him wrapp'd his cloak;
Before the Queen, his mother, stood,
And these the words he spoke.

"Hear me, dear Lady mother mine,
"Your help I would obtain;
"My suit fair Walborg has repulsed
"With jest and proud disdain.

"Aye! though I offer wealth and rank,
"My royal crown and land
"Sir Axel has her plighted troth,
"And him she gives her hand."

"And bound in honour is the maid
"To keep the oath she sware;
"But others in my court thou'lt find
"As noble and as fair/'

"There may be others highly born
"And rich and fair of face,
"But rival Walborg cannot one
"In goodness or in grace."

"If thou shouldst seize the maid by force,
"All tongues would cry thee shame;
"Nor were it long, ere arm'd for fight
"Sir Axel hither came."

Forth from her bower Prince Hagen went,
And wrath was he of mood;
As met him robed in swarthy gown
The Blackfriar brother Knud.

"What means, my son, this woeful look?
"Say, what may be thy care?
"If aught has happ'd to mar thy peace,
"Thy griefs to me declare."

"Good father, sad is my mischance,
"And great my secret pain;
"Sir Axel's bride I dearly love,
"But cannot hope to gain."

"Nay! though fair Walborg be his bride,
"His wife she cannot be;
"Tor in the Blackfriar cloister here
"We keep their pedigree.

"Two sisters' children are they both,
"The lover and eke the bride;
"And both one nurse held at the font
"At Highborg, where she died.

"Dipp'd at one font, by cloister law
"Two brethren they must be;
"And, as our books will duly show,
"Akin in third degree.

"To chapter summon all thy clerks,
"This point let them decide;
"And sentenced shall Sir Axel be
"To quit his lily bride."

Prince Hagen heard and bade his swains
"Go Walborg's uncles call;
"Beg them in secret all the three
"Come to. my council hall."

These Counts, so gallant all and brave.
They stood before the board;
"What may our gracious lord desire?
"We wait his royal word."

"The boon I ask, is that your niece
"With me in honour live,
"And be my queen and share my realm;
"Will ye the maiden give?"

Then answered him her uncles three,
And blithe were they of mood;
"In lucky hour was born the maid,
"For whom our Prince has sued."

They rose and sought the royal bower,
Wrapt each in ample cloak;
And greeted first the stately Queen,
And Walborg next, and spoke.

"God speed thee, Walborg, dearest niece,
"And happy mayst thou live!
"For thee our lord, Prince Hagen, sues,
"And thee to him we give."

"And have my uncles so agreed?
"The truth then I will say;
"Sir Axel, he is my trothplight man,
"Nor him will I betray."

"Nay!" answered her those uncles three,
So wealthy all and bold;
"Nay, niece, thee cannot we allow
"With him thy vows to hold."

Prince Hagen then his summons wrote
To all the clergy round,
And bade th' Archbishop come himself
With seventy clerks renowned.

"Now shame!" the Archdeacon Erland said,
As he the letter view'd;
"Foul shame on all who this devised,
"And most on Brother Knud!"

The Archbishop stood before the board,
And thus the Prince addressed;
"I'm at my Prince's bidding come;
"Would know what his request."

"I've to a maiden plighted troth,
"Whom ye shall wed to me;
"For tho' Sir Axel has her heart,
"His wife she shall not be."

A summons then those clergy wrote,
And publish'd far and near,
That 'fore the Archbishop at th' Assize
These lovers both appear.

The matin song was duly sung
At early morning tide;
And with his trulove off to church
Sir Axel now must ride.

But, as he climb'd his tall war-horse,
Sighs heav'd his manly breast;
And Walborg in her carriage sat
With pain as ill repressed.

While through the greenwood glade they rode,
"But seldom," Walborg cried, '
"Doth happy bosom sigh with grief,
"Tho' sorrow smiles may hide."

Before the gate they lighted down,
St. Mary's churchyard gate,
And with their kin and gallant knights
Walked into church in state.

But, while they waited in the aisle,
The clergy there to meet.
Their pallid faces told of woe.
And hearts with grief replete.

And now with silver-mounted staff
The grave Archbishop came,
And all the Blackfriar Brotherhood
To prove their blood the same.

With ponderous register in band
Stepp'd forward Brother Knud,
And show'd that Axel and his bride
Were near akin by blood.

Alike of ancient Gildish race
Were both so highly bred.
And kinsmen in the fourth degree.
And therefore could not wed.

One dame had held them at the font,
The knight and eke the maid;
Sir Asbiorn sponsor was to both,
Such match the church forbade.

Akin alike by birth and blood,
An J that in fourth degree,
Akin too at baptismal font,
Wedded they could not be.

Up to the Altar led they then
The lady and the swain,
And placed a kerchief in their hands,
And cut the same in twain.

The kerchief into halves was cut,
To each an equal share;
The stoutest man must yield to fate,
And what is doom'd him, hear.

"Ye've cut in twain this handkerchief,
"Ye've given us each a piece,
"But so will not our love be rent,
"Or lifelong ever cease."

The ring they off her finger stripped,
The bracelet off her hand,
And gave the knight his gifts again,
And brake the nuptial band.

Upon Saint Olave's altar stone
Sir Axel cast the gold,
And sware that lifelong for the maid
His friendship he should hold.

The heaving silk on Hagen's breast
His ill-pent wrath betrayed;
"If Walborg thou canst not forget,
"Then she is no more a maid."

But up the wisest clerk of all
Archdeacon Erland rose;
"Who has not learnt the power of love,
"Of man but little knows.

"Water may slake the glowing brand,
"May quench the hottest flame,
"But fiercer far the rage of love,
"No mortal that can tame.

"Aye, great as is the midday's heat,
"Where broils a southern sun,
"Is greater still the force of love,
"And vanquish that may none."

Array'd in silken robe so red
Prince Hagen made reply;
"This matter I'm resolv'd to clear,
"Though on the morn I die."

With anger boiling in his breast
The broad stone then he trod;
"Here shalt thou swear without reserve
"Before Almighty God:

"Tomorrow morning thou shalt swear
"On His most holy Word,
"If'Walborg is for thee a maid,
"And swear it on thy sword."

"Such evidence if I shall give,
"My oath I'll freely make;
"And ready stand in combat too
"My life thereon to stake."

Sir Hogen's wife, fair Eskelin,
From sleep awoke in fright;
"Saint Brigit, tell me what shall mean
"The dream I've dream'd tonight?

"The lovely July seemed to come
Trom slumbering in her grave,
"And pray me all so piteously
"Her daughter dear to save.

"My Lord, seven gallant sons have I,
"And thirty men each one;
"And they shall arm, and stake their lives,
"That her no harm be done.

"My Lord, let saddle chargers ten,
"And like a noble ride,
"And lend her countenance, and see
"That her no ill betide.

"Seven sons have we, seven youthful dukes,
"All brave and doughty wights,
"And fain would see them quit themselves
"Like gentlemen and knights.

"The Lady July and myself
"Were of two sisters born,
"And lost for aye were our good name,
"If Walborg came to scorn."

The morning dawn'd, and o'er the heath
The sun had flung his glare.
As towards the castle rode the knights
The solemn oath to swear.

There clad in arms Sir Axel stood;
And stretched them forth his hand;
"Welcome, ye counts of Gildish house,
"Come here with me to stand."

Eleven the knights who forward strode,
In sables drest were they;
"We with Sir Axel make our oath,
"God rule it as He may."

As fast as raindrops fall, the tears
Ran down the maiden's face;
"Where now am I kind friends to find?
"How wretched is my case!"

Cold answer made her uncles three;
And these the words they spake;
"Thyself, since rede thou hast ask'd of none,
"Alone the oath must take/'

The"good Archdeacon Erland rose.
And what he said was true;
"Find kinsmen wilt thou many a one,
"Though friends, I fear, but few.

"Aye! kinsmen hast thou still, enough,
"But friends wilt hardly find;
"God help thee from thy danger, maid,
"And calm thy troubled mind."

"My parents both are dead and gone,
"Bitter and great my woe;
"But that I free from guilt have liv'd,
