"Will God in mercy show.

"My mother is under a marble stone,
"My father Immer too;
"Were they alive and here with me,
"Were then my kinsmen true!"

But while in deepest woe she sat,
And sobb'd aloud and wept,
Sir Hogen up to the castle rode,
And towards the maiden stepped.

Forward he came with hasty stride,
And these the words he spake:
"Fair Walborg, I will stand by thee
"This oath, with thee to take.

"My wife is Lady Eskeline,
"To whom thou'rt very dear;
"She and thy mother were of kin,
"And therefore I am here.

"Now forward, all ye seven my sons,
"Your oaths together make;
"Sir Carl's seven sons from Sonderland
"Their part with us shall take."

Eleven young Duke's sons forward stepp'd
In sable robes so fair;
In richest raiment they were clad.
And curl'd eir yellow hair.

Eleven young counts, they form'd a group,
All gallant men and bold:
And hair they wore in graceful curls,
And swords that gleam'd with gold.

"Here next the maiden we will stand
"With her the oath to swear;
"Ye noble pair, come forward both,
"That every one may hear

His sword-hilt then Sir Axel grasp'd,
On massbook laid his hand,
While round him all his kinsmen stood,
A bravo and wealthy band.

And there with sword-hilt in his hand,
Its blade laid on a stone,
He sware a clear unquibbled oath,
And made her virtue known.

"My Walborg, though my early love,
"And all my worldly bliss,
"I never yet too near approached,
"Or once enjoy'd a kiss"

Then by Our Lady sware the maid
With hand on holy book;
"My eyes were never yet so bold
"As once on him to look."

With canopy raised o'er her head,
And royal pomp and pride;
They bare her weeping to her bower.
And call'd her "Prince's bride."

In to the hall Prince Hagen came.
And these the words he spake;
"This evening neither knight nor squire
"His journey home shall take.

"Witness, that Walborg I betroth,
"My heart and realm to share;
"Witness, that she is now ray Queen,
"And crown of gold shall wear."

The cloth was spread, and table fill'd,
And quaff'd the mead and ale;
Bat with his bride Sir Axel stayed,
And sad their mutual tale.

"Now prithee, dearest Walborg, say,
"While here we sit alone,
"To still our painful longings, both,
"What now may best be done?"

"If wed the Prince I really must,
"Tis much against my will,
"For though I live a thousand years,
"To you I am faithful still.

"Up in my chamber I shall sit,
"And gold-embroidery weave;
"Live all my days in solitude,
"And like the turtle grieve.

"She slumbers not on. leafy bough
"Retired from noonday heat;
"Nor ever sips the limpid stream,
"Till muddied with her feet.

"But you will in the greenwood ride,
"And chase the hare and roe;
"Aud banish every thought of me,
"And all your grief and woe."

"Nay, though to chase the forest deer
"So gaily I may ride,
"What shall I do at midnight hour,
"When sleep's to me denied?

"I'll straight for silver coin and gold
"My patrimony sell,
"And, till I grieve myself to death,
"In some far country dwell."

"Ah no, my lord, leave not your home,
"Nor sell your pleasant land,
"But send to good Sir Asbiorn word,
"And ask his daughter's hand.

"Sue for his daughter Adelaide,
"That gentle maiden wed;
"And further cares I'll take on me,
"And stand in mother's stead."

"I'll take no other maid to wife,
"No other will I woo;
"The Emperor's daughter could I have,
"To thee I'd still be true."

And here the good Archdeacon came,
And gently tapp'd the pair;
"Bid ye each other now Good night,
"And try your fate to bear."

Then rose the Archbishop, bold of speech,
And loud he shouted out;
"On Blackfriar Knud a lasting shame,
"Who brought this thing about!"

Sir Axel bade the maid Good night,
His voice betray'd his pain;
For laden was his heart with grief
As captive wretch with chain.

Fair Walborg now with all her maids
Must to her bower retire,
But felt her heart burning with grief,
"As glows a smouldering fire.

So soon as dawned the ruddy morn,
And sun was seen to shine,
Began the queen to call her maids.
And each her task assign.

She bade them round about her sit,
To work the gold so red;
But Walborg stood apart from all, —
Her heart with sorrow bled.

"List, Walborg, tell me, dearest maid,
"Why sittest thou aside?
"And why it gladdens not thy heart
"To be the Prince's bride?"

"Much rather I'd Sir Axel have,
"And share his less renown,
"Than in a royal palace dwell,
"And wear all Norway's crown.

"Tet, little as it profits me,
"My kinsmen may be glad;
"Tho' daily tears my face bedew,
"And heart be ne'er so sad."

They pass'd their time in sullen grief,
Two weary months went o'er,
That neither smiled, or pastime found,
She or Sir Axel more.

Now reached the land a fearful war,
A foe untaught to yield,
Hagen, the Prince, to stem their force
Himself must take the field.

He summoned all his men to arms.
The clergy and eke the lay;
Such as had strength to wield a sword,
To war must all away.

As captain-general o'er his host
He bade Sir Axel go.
And, like a highborn gallant knight,
To arm he was not slow.

By its two colours white and blue
Was known o'er all the field,
And by the bleeding hearts thereon
Sir Axel Tordsen's shield.

They reach'd the plain, and saw the foe
In burnish'd armour glance;
Their manhood soon was put to proof;
'Twas not a ladies' dance.

Sir Axel fought with hero mood,
To guard his native land;
And, sooth, made many a saddle void
His sharp and weighty brand

He dealt them round his deadly blows,
And o'er their corpses rode;
His anger spared not of them all
The best and noblest blood.

He struck the lords of Oppeland
From off their steeds so tall.
And slew King Amund's sons to boot;
Brave dukes and margraves all.

As thick the jostling arrows flew,
As peasants toss their hay;
And, pierced with wounds, among the slain
Himself Prince Hagen lay.

Sir Axel, when he saw the Prince
Had fallen from off his steed.
Through banded foemen clove his way
To aid him in his need.

"Sir Axel Tordsen, hear my prayer,
"Do thou avenge my fall,
"And then take Norway's crown and land,
"The bride therewith and all."

"Aye! well will I avenge thy death,
"As every tongue shall tell;
"No force of blow shall make me swerve,
"No numbers me repel."

Sir Axel sought the thickest fight,
So fierce was he of mood,
Whoever dared to meet his gaze,
Sank weltering in his blood.

He fell'd around him mailclad men,
As peasants reap their corn,
And bore him as became a knight
Of noblest lineage born.

They beat the helmet off his head,
They clove in twain his shield,
But till his sword brake in his hand.
Was he not made to yield.

Eight were the deep and ghastly wounds.
That gored his manly breast,
As in his tent with aching hearts
They laid him down to rest

His life's blood spouted out in streams.
The price for victory paid:
The latest word Sir Axel spake
Was of the lovely maid.

"To Walborg bear my last farewell,
"May God to her be kind;
"In heaven we soon shall meet again
"Unhinder'd joy to find."

In came Sir Axel's little page,
And stood before the board:
A quick and skilful child was he
To choose the fittest word.

"O take ye robes of linen white,
"And leave your silk so red,
"For know that Hagen, royal prince,
"And Axel, both are dead.

"Prince Hagen on his bier is stretched,
"They're tolling now his knell;
"Sir Axel well aveng'd his death,
"But bravely fighting felL

"Through Norway's land the voice of fame
"Our victory shall record,
"But many a boor has lost his life,
"And many a noble lord."

How bitterly Queen Malfred wept,
Will every mother know;
Fair Walborg too in secret moan'd,
And wrung her hands for woe.

She call'd her Page, and bade him run,
And nimble he should be;
"Go, thou, my gilded casket fetch,
"And bring it in to me.

"And ye put to my good grey steeds;
"My life to God I'll give,
"Nor e'er forget Sir Axel's death,
"So long as still I live."

Before Saint Mary's churchyard gate
She lighted from her wain.
And once for all went into church
Weeping with grief and pain.

She there took off her crown of gold,
And laid it on a stone;
"henceforth no other man I'll wed,
"But live for Heaven alone.

"Already twice I've been betrothed,
"But never was a wife;
"Will now apart from worldly cares
"In cloister pass my life."

They brought her in the treasured gold
Stored in her gilded chest,
And this she gave to those she had found
The kindest and the best.

A neckband, all of finest gold
With precious jewels hung,
She gave the lady Eskelin,
For having lov'd her long.

Two bracelets in the casket lay,
And weighty clasps to both,
And these she to Sir Hogen gave,
Who sware with her the oath.

And gold and silver all so bright,
A hundred rings or more,
She dealt among the gallant dukes,
Who witness for her swore.

To priests in cloister cell and church
A goodly sum she paid,
That for her own and Axel's soul
Might daily Mass be pray'd.

She gave to widow and orphan child,
And pilgrim on the road;
And on the image of Saint Ann
Her crown of gold bestowed.

"Come forward, Bishop, reverend man,
"The mould upon me cast;
"And let me swear the cloister vows;
"This boon I ask the last.

"Dear good Archbishop Ogey, come
' "Devote me now to God;
"I never leave this cloister more,
"But for the churchyard sod."

On face of many a gallant knight
The teardrops trickled fast,
While on the gentle Walborg's arm
The clods of earth they cast.

So into cloister Walborg went.
And much restraint she bore.
And mass or matins never miss'd.
Nor broke a rale she swore.

To cloister many a lady comes
For beauty far renown'd,
But none so fair as Walborg was,
Whose equal ne'er was found.

'Twere better far to be unborn
Than live in constant woe.
In trouble cat one's daily bread,
Nor taste of pleasure know.

May God forsake the wicked wretch,
Who two like these would part,
Where glows a warm and mutual love
In young and virtuous heart.

poems.title: The Power of the Harp
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Peter took from home his bride.
But while she rode, she deeply sighed.
Say, why my love these tones of grief?

"Does you your horse or saddle fret?
"Or marrying me do you regret?"

"Me does not horse nor saddle fret,
"Nor marrying you do I regret."

"Or that because my wealth is small,
"You may not me your equal call?"

"I sigh not that with wealth so small
"I cannot you my equal call."

"For father lost grieve you so sore?
"Or that you're now a maid no more?"

"For father grieve I not so sore,
"Nor that I am now a maid no more.

"I grieve and sigh, because I know,
"What death I am doomed to undergo.

"It is the long frail bridge I fear,
"Where lost were both my sisters dear;

"The roaring stream, the treacherous bank,
"Where my poor sisters slipp'd and sank."

"Sigh then no more, my dearest bride,
"My twelve brave swains shall with you ride.

"With you shall ride my faithful swains,
"And I myself will hold your reins."

But when they came to Rosenshaw,
A golden-antler'd stag they saw.

They mark'd him all, and off they hied,
And all forgot the gentle bride.

With gold her horse's feet were shod.
On fifteen nails of gold he trod;

But on the bridge his foot he lost,
And her in the roaring torrent toss'd.

Sir Peter came and turn'd him round,
But no where could the bride be found.

His swains Sir Peter call'd, and told,
"Haste! fetch me, swains, my harp of gold."

So sweet Sir Peter's music rang,
The birds aloft in answer sang.

And up the Merman heav'd his head,
And in his hand the maiden led.

"Dear knight Sir Peter, cease your spell,
"And take the bride you love so well,"

"'Tis good thou dost my bride restore;
"But render up two sisters more."

Sir Peter touch'd the string again.
The birds flew down to hear his strain.

The Merman rose and came to land,
And held a maid in either hand.

"O cease. Sir Peter, cease thy strain,
"For I no sisters more retain."

And now the bride no longer weeps,
But nightly with Sir Peter sleeps.

poems.title: German Gladenswain
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Danish king and his youthful queen,
They sat at their festive board.
And many a tale they told by turns
Anent the salty Fiord.

The Danish king and his youthful queen
Were sailing through the foam;
And better that day for both their sakes
The queen had stayed at home.

The ship roird on the heaving deep.
The wind no longer blew.
And over them, greedy to sink them all,
The fierce wild raven flew.

"If any there are beneath the waves,
"That hinder the ship to sail,
"I'll give you silver and ruddy gold,
"To send us a favouring gale.

"And thou, wild carnage raven, hark!
"Forbear our vessel to drown,
"And pounds by weight of silver and gold
"Fifteen I'll pay thee down."

"Of gold or silver no need have I,
"A different gift I claim;
"Whatever thou bearest beneath thy belt,
"To me thou givest the same/'

"Naught else beneath my belt do I bear
"Than this my bundle of keys,
"If God shall bring me alive to land,
"rii others have made for these."

She took the bundle of keys so small,
Those over the board she threw;
The fierce wild raven her words had heard.
And joyous away he flew.

The queen stepped out on the glittering sand,
And bitter the grief she felt;
She noted, that German Gladenswain
Had quickened beneath her belt.

And when in the onward flight of time
Five months were past and gone,
She went aloft to her bower, the queen,
And bare a lovely son.

'Twas eventide, as the babe was born,
They took him to church by night.
They christened him German Gladenswain,
And hid him the best they might.

They nurs'd that infant the winter through.
They nursed him for winters nine,
Till he the gallantest youth was grown.
That ever met mortal eyne.

So well he throve, and so well he grew.
So well too his horse could ride;
Yet oft as his mother beheld the boy.
From bitterest grief she cried.

"O tell me then, dearest mother mine,
"Nor answer to me deny,
"Why weep you, and why so dolefully moan,
"So often as I go by?"

"O listen then, German Gladenswain,
"I've reason enough to grieve,
"For thee as a babe to the Trold I gave,
"And he will his gift receive."

"Nay, listen to me, my mother dear,
"And lay your sorrow aside;
"Whatever the fate that God decrees,
"The same I must e'en abide."

One Thursday it was, an autumn day,
At th' early morning hoar,
A loud shrill voice the ladies heard,
As open stood their bower.

And in that lothesomest raven came,
And sat by the queen, did he;
"Now call to your mind, my gracious Queen,
"The gift that you made to me."

She swore by God, and she swore by men.
By heaven and earth and all,
That she nor daughter nor son had borne,
Nor any her own could call.

Away that lothesomest raven flew,
And yeird a scream of joy;
"Wherever I find young Gladenswain,
"I claim for my own the boy."

When German was fifteen winters old,
He fain his betroth'd would see;
A daughter she was of England's king.
And none was so fair as she.

And more and more he daily long'd
To go to his lovely bride;
"But how shall I come to the seagirt isle
Across the salty tide?"

So rose young German Gladenswain,
And round him his mantle threw.
And up to the ladies' lofty bower.
To speak to his mother flew.

In came young German Gladenswain,
In scarlet array'd was he;
"O lend me, mother, your feather-dress
"To cross the salty sea."

"My feather-dress on a hook is hung,
"Its plumes drop on the floor;
"If thou to a foreign land dost go,
"I see thee again no more.

"The wings for thee are much too long,
"They spread so wide in the air;
"If I till midsummer live, my son,
"I'll make me another pair."

He d'on'd the dress, and across the sea
He flew for many a mile,
And met the raven so wild and fierce,
That dwelt on a lonely isle.

So boldly he flew, and skimmed the wave,
Or rose to the clouds on high.
Till, distant afar from either shore,
He heard a frightful cry.

"Well met, young German Gladenswain,
"So long where hast thou been?
"A little and tender babe thou wast,
"As gave thee to me the Queen/'

"O leave me, raven, and let me fly
"My lovely young bride to see,
"And soon as I hither return again,
"I'll render myself to thee."

"I'll set on thy body a special mark
"To bear with thee hence ashore;
"WhereVer thou sittest with knights and squires,
"Forgettest thou me no more."

His right eye out of his head he peck'd,
Drank half of his heart's best blood;
Yet flew the youth to his trulove's bower
Across the briny flood.

And there so blood-besprent and pale
He stayed his airy flight;
The maidens, who sat within the bower,
Shrank trembling aback with fright.

Their laugh and frolic the maidens ceased.
Their games no longer play'd;
But rose and clasped her fair white hands
His ladylove Adelaide.

"Right welcome, dear German Gladenswain,
"But where have you been in fight?
"And why are your clothes so stain'd with blood?
"And why is your cheek so white?"

"Farewell, for ever, dear Adelaide,
"Away from you I must fly;
"My life the ravenous monster claims,
"Who tore from my head an eye."

She took in her hand a silver comb,
Herself she dressed his hair.
And dropp'd on every lock she comb'd,
A bitter and scalding tear.

On every tangled lock she dress'd
The bitterest tear would flow,
And much his mother she cursed the while,
The cause of all his woe.

She clasp'd him fondly within her arms
In loving and long caress;
"Oh! cursed be she, the wicked queen,
"Who brought on us such distress."

"Nay cease, I prithee, dear Adelaide,
"My mother so to ban,
"She could not avert, what fate decreed;
"Avert it what mortal can?"

He drew on his limbs a feather dress,
And rose to the sky so blue;
His bride drew on her another dress,
And, whirring, behind him flew.

"O turn to your home, dear Adelaide,
"Turn back from your flight so high,
"For open is standing your chamber door,
"Your keys on the pavement lie."

"Though open be standing my chamber door,
"And keys on the pavement lie,
"I'll follow you, wheresoever you go,
"Be near to you, when you die.

Whatever the birds, in the air she met,
She clipp'd them at once in twain;
The raven alone she could not reach,
To leave him among the slain.

Then turn'd her, the lady Adelaide,
And lighted upon the strand;
But left there of German Gladenswain
Was nothing beside his hand.

In wrath she flew to the clouds so high.
That ravenous bird to seek;
And eastward she flew, and to west she flew,
Her vengeance sworn to wreak.

Whatever the birds, in the air she met,
She clipp'd them in pieces three,
She met the raven, and into ten
She clipped him with dismal glee.

She hover'd about that dreary heath,
Till wasted with grief, she died;
For love of her German Gladenswain
So mournfully sank his bride.

poems.title: Sir Olave (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "The Elfin Shaft".
poems.text:
Sir Olave a journey at nightfall rode,
It seem'd as if round him daylight glow'd.
But what avails bewailing?

The hill he had trodden, where all by night
The dwarfs were tripping their dance so light.

And oat of the group a maiden flew,
Her fair white arm on his shoulder threw.

"Oh sweet Sir Olave, a moment bide,
"And tell me whither so fast you ride."

"So fast I am speeding across the lea
"My dearest, my own betrothed to see.

But smiling she held him forth her hand;
"Tou first with me in the dance must stand.

"And if with me you list to live,
"Oh! rich are the gifts I have to give.

"I'll give you a horse to ride, a dun,
"To Rome and back in an hour will run.

"I'll give you that steed so fleet and bold,
"And with him his saddle of finest gold.

"I'll give you such harness of steely mail,
There's not a man living should make you quail. uri

"I'll give you so finely wrought a brand,
"As never was waved in hero's hand.

"The benches and chairs, whereon you sit,
"You'll see them of golden chain-work knit.

"And wrought of the gold each drawbridge stands,
"As pure as the rings that grace your hands."

"O keep to yourself your gold so red,
"For I must home to the maid I wed."

She struck the knight on his cheek a stroke
That splash'd the blood on his scarlet cloak.

She struck him a blow on his back as well,
And fainting down to the earth he fell.

"Up now, Sir Olave, and speed away,
"Thou livest but only a single day."

Sir Olave he guided round the rein.
And sick and sorry rode home again.

He rode till he reached the courtyard gate,
Where waiting him still his mother sate.

"Sir Olave, tell me, my son so dear,
"Why comest thou home so sad of cheer?"

"Hold thou, dear mother, this faithful beast,
"Haste thou, dear brother, to fetch a priest."

"From words so gloomy, my son, refrain;
"The sick will often get well again.

"But tell me, so be thy wish obey'd,
"To whom thou leavest thy trothplight maid?"

"All ye, my seven brave brothers, ride,
"With due respect meet ye my bride.

"And you, my mother so dear, I pray,
"Kindly to greet that lovely may."

They heard as nearer the town they drew,
The bells all ringing, as were they new.

Then spake in faltering voice the bride,
Her sorrow she could no longer hide:

"But why has this ringing now begun?
"For sick here or dying know I none."

"Because it was ever our country's mode
"To ring the bride to her new abode.

"'Tis mode all over this island's side
"To ring to her home a chosen bride."

As into Sir Olave's house she stepped,
There silent the ladies sat and wept.

With anxious doubt and fear she spake,
Her heart with sorrow was like to break:

"And why then do all these ladies grieve,
"And not with rejoicing a bride receive?"

There was not a lady, of all were there.
To answer the bride a word would dare.

She enter'd the lofty banquet room.
But sorrow had paled her roses bloom.

They led her to sit in the bridal chair,
And knights to her hand the goblet bare.

She ask'd them, the while she sat at board,
In tone of sadness she spake the word:

"I see so many both come and go,
"But still my bridegroom Sir Olave no."

Sir Olave's mother, she then replied,
But ill her grief could a mother hide:

"Sir Olave went out with his hawk and hound
"To beat the heath and the forest round.'

"And are then his hawk and his hound more dear
"Than I, the young bride who waits him here?

"With greyhounds in leash will he rather ride,
"Than sit in a room beside his bride?"

At th' evening hour, as 'fell the dew,
The bride from the banquet hall withdrew.

They kindled the bridal torch so bright,
The maid to her bridal room to light.

But, as she was standing beside the bed,
Behind her the little page-boy said;

"O list to the truth, Sir Olave's bride,
"This very morning my lord has died.

"Stretch'd out on his bier he lies above;
"His brother demands your hand and love/'

"That day, be assured, shalt thou not live,
"That I my troth to two brothers give."

She begg'd the ladies so earnestly,
She might but her bridegroom's body see;

They threw her open the chamber door,
And there was the stage upon the floor.

Fair Ingelille press'd before the crowd.
And back from his face drew off the shroud.

But one farewell to the dead she spake,
So much did her heart within her quake:

A single kiss on his mouth she pressed.
And burst was her heart within her breast.

Sad sight as ever has met the eye,
To see the maiden for sorrow die.
But what avails bewailing?

poems.title: Sir Olave (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "The Elfin Shaft".
poems.text:
Sir Olave he speeds his lonely way
To bid his friends to his wedding day.
The Elves in chorus with mirth and glee
Are dancing beneath the greenwood tree.

And four he saw dance, and five saw dance,
The Elf-king's daughter herself advance.
The Elves etc.

She tripp'd from out of the Elfin band,
And smiling she held him forth her hand.

"O welcome, Sir Olave, but why such speed?
"Come hither with me the dance to lead."

"Nay dance, that neither I will nor may,
"Tomorrow is e'en my wedding day."

"But listen. Sir Olave, come dance with me,
"I've boots of buckskin to give to thee.

"Two boots of buckskin that fit so neat,
"And golden spurs for thy knightly feet."

"Nay dance, that neither I will nor may,
"Tomorrow is e'en my wedding day."

"Yet listen, Sir Olave, come dance with me,
"A shirt of the silk I'll give to thee;

"A shirt of the silk so white and fine,
"My mother has bleach'd in the moonbeam's shine."

"Nay dance, that neither I will nor may,
"Tomorrow is e'en my wedding day."

"Yet list, Sir Olave, come dance with me,
"A helmet of gold I'll give to thee."

"Thy helmet of gold I'll freely take,
"But join will I not in thine Elfin wake."

"And dost thou refuse to dance with me?
"Then sickness of death shall follow thee."

Between his shoulders a blow she dealt;
Such blow till then he had never felt.

She set him again on his horse astride,
"Go home and comfort thy pensive bride/'

He rode till he came to the castle gate,
The place where his anxious mother salt.

"O hear me, what is it, Sir Olave, speak,
"Has blanched so pallid thy manly cheek?

"No wonder, dear mother, my cheek is white,
"I've been at the Elfin dance tonight."

"But O Sir Olave, my son, my pride,
"Say what shall I answer thy gen,the bride?"

"O tell her I ride the green wood round
"To prove the speed of my horse and hound/'

There came at the early dawn of day
The bride and her suite in full array.

They quaff'd the mead, and they quaff'd the wine;
"But where is Sir Olave, dear bridegroom mine?"

"Sir Olave, he rides the green-wood round
"To prove the speed of his horse and hound."

She rais'd the mantle of scarlet red; —
There lay Sir Olave, and he was dead.

The morrow, as dawn'd the early morn.
Three corpses from out the gate were borne.

The one was his mother, and one his bride;
For sorrow they both had sunk and died.
The Elves in Chorus with mirth and glee
Are dancing beneath the Linden tree.

poems.title: Malfred and Mogens
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Yarl march'd forth to battle field,
And there he lost his life,
And many a brave and honest man
Fell in that deadly strife.

The King of Norse his summons sent
To arm and take the field,
And would that lyar, gallant Yarl,
Should bear the royal shield.

Sir Ivar rose and bade his squire
To saddle and bring his horse;
"To Bergen I will ride today,
"And see the king of Norse."

With purple cloak around him slung
He passed the castle gate,
And mounted to the council hall,
Where sat the king in state.

In to the hall Sir Ivar came,
"A yarl so brave and good.
And rose with grace the King of Norse,
As he before him stood.

Uprose that noble King of Norse,
The royal cushion press'd;
"Come hither, Ivar Ulfson, Yarl,
"And here beside me rest.

"The King of Swede has challenged me
"For honour and for life,
"My kingdom at my hand demands,
"My daughter too to wife.

"But hark. Sir Ivar Ulfson, Yarl,
"My trust I place in you;
"I'll furnish you with coat of mail,
"And steed and saddle too.

"To you my banner I shall trust
"To bear it like a knight;
"Let not the crown of Norway fall
"A prize to Swedish might."

"So help me Friga, help me Thor, "
"And never me forsake,
"Thy banner I shall well defend,
"My life thereon I stake.'

So spake Sir Ivar Ulfson, Yarl,
And round him wrapp'd his cloak.
And up to the ladies' chamber went.
And thus the Queen bespoke.

"Hail, Queen of Norse, so nobly born
"Of England's royal race;
"I trust to you my daughters small,
"And pray you show them grace.

"The one can link a chain of gold,
"The second, she can sew,
"The third is still a baby child,
"Alone can hardly go.

"A little baby child the third
"With apples still at play,
"And pale their cheeks — Their mother's dead,
"Dead and beneath the clay."

"Go then, Sir Ivar, go in peace,
"Thy mind from care be free;
"As though they were the King's and mine,
"I'll. cherish all the three."

With all his bright gold trappings on
Came out Sir Ivar's horse,
And bare to court his daughters three
Before the Queen of Norse.

Sir Ivar forth to Sweden marched,
His troops to victory led;
He saved his crown for Norway's king.
But fell in battle dead.

Thereon the Scalds a poem sang
His glorious deeds to tell,
And, long as Norway stands, will sing,
How brave Sir Ivar fell.

The Queen of Norse in chamber lay,
And grievous sick was she,
And to and fro, to nurse her, went
The Yarl's fair daughters three.

The Queen of Norse her servants call'd,
And on her errand sped;
"Go, fetch the fortune-telling wife,
"To stand before my bed."

In came the fortune-telling wife,
And stood before the board;
"What will you, Queen of Norse, with me?
"Why have you sent me word?"

"Now hear, good fortune -telling wife,
"What I would ask of thee;
"If thou dost know these maidens' fate,
"Conceal it not from me."

"I freely tell at your behest
"What none but you may hear,
"There's for the third, the fairest maid,
"The hardest lot to bear.

"Fair Ulvilde off to Scotland sent
"Will be a noble's wife,
"But, ere have pass'd a year and day,
"Is doom'd to lose her life.

"Fair Rngnfred here, in Norway's land,
"Both rank and fame shall reach,
"And own abundant land and gold,
"And wise shall be of speech.

"For Malfred, fairest of the three,
"For her are all my fears;
"Her Mogens, royal prince, betrothed
"In childhood's early years."

Long did her troubled anxious thoughts,
Through the Queen's bosom whirl:
"My son a royal maid shall wed,
"And not this needy girl."

Up spake the haughty Queen of Norse,
"My knights to council call,
"And ye, bid Mogens, royal prince,
"Attend me in the hall."

Into the hall Prince Mogens came,
And stood before the board;
"What will you, mother dear, with me?
"Why have you sent me word?"

"Now tell me, Mogens, royal prince,
"Tell me on word of knight,
"Is any maid in Norway's land
"Thy" love and heart's delight?"

"I love no maid in all this world,
"Or any living dame,
"Except Sir Ivar's youngest child,
"Whom, prithee, let me claim."

"But what with Malfred shouldst thou do?
"She works not golden thread;
"Nay! Mogens, hark thee, royal prince,
"A richer thou shalt wed.

"O what with Malfred shouldst thou do,
"A young and friendless maid?
"Nay, my son, cause me not this grief,
"Be from thy purpose stay'd."

"If I fair Malfred may not have,
"Nor make the maid my wife,
"I vow that I'll no other wed,
"Or maid or dame, for life."

The Queen of Norse bade build a boat,
Of rotten plank so frail,
And gave that young and faithful pair
Full bitter cause to wail.

She placed the maid on board the boat.
And drove it off from land;
"God grant that thou may'st drown at sea,
"And never reach a strand!"

When daylight waned, and o'er the deck
The waves dash'd to and fro,
Trembling the Yarl's fair daughter sat.
Nor ceased her tears to flow.

The vessel drifted off to Spain,
And drove upon the sand,
And soon on horseback came a prince,
A chief in Spanish land.

The weeping maid he gently rais'd,
And on his horse bestowed,
And back to his mother's.house with her
By th' easiest path-way rode.

And there a month fair Malfred stay'd,
And there she stayed for three;
And grew to be the loveliest maid,
That man with eyes might see.

Queen Judith sicker grew, and sank,
And in her bower lay dead,
As Mogens saddled his good grey steed,
And forth one evening sped.

Bat while he through the green-wood pass'd,
And not a house was nigh.
Twelve robbers met, and stopp'd his horse,
Nor power had he to fly.

They bound the Prince both hand and foot,
And dragg'd him down to shore,
And sail'd with him to a foreign land
And great the woes he bore.

Fair Malfred on the balcony,
Was gazing down below,
And there the prince, her trulove, saw
Sit in a boat and row.

Fair Malfred sought the royal bower
Wrapp'd in her purple cloak,
And stood before the queen of Spain,
And thus the Queen bespoke.

"Hail! gracious lady. Queen of Spain,
"O kindly give me rede,
"How from a cruel robber band
"My brother may be freed."

"I'll give thee rede, dear daughter mine,
"The safest rede I may;
"A purse of gold and silver coin,
"Thy brother's price to pay."

She ransom'd him, the royal prince,
Unbound his fair white hand;
A horse and saddle too she gave,
And welcomed him to land.

The Spanish lord his servants bade
The meats and wine prepare,
And many a knight to his castle bade
His marriage feast to share.

"A maid from a distant foreign land
"Is she, I mean to wed;
"For, though with gold I bought the maid,
"She's good and gently bred."

The bride they placed on bridal bench.
They pour'd the mead and wine;
But still, while all around was gay.
Her cheeks were wet with brine.

When on the steps at th' evening hour
The dew began to fall,
The gentle bride to bed retired,
And left the banquet halL

All on her costly bridal bed
They laid the lovely may,
Nor long did he, the Spanish lord,
To follow her delay.

The Prince had donn'd his coat of mail,
And crept beneath the bed,
And waited long in silence there
To hear the bridegroom's tread.

And then unsheath'd the royal prince
His silver-mounted knife,
And ruthless stabb'd the Spanish lord,
And took his guiltless life.

He slew that lord, and left his corpse
All bleeding on the floor;
"Rise, Malfred, rise, and haste with me
"To flee the Spanish shore/'

Out to the stable-yard they went,
They took the Spaniard's steed,
And down to the shore, the bride and he,
They rode at utmost speed.

They found a boat and stepped on board,
And steer'd before the gale,
And late one night beneath a grove
They moor'd and furl'd their sail.

He took ashore his lady love
So gently on his arm,
And placed her on the grassy sward
So far, he thought, from harm.

But where they laid them down to sleep
Under a linden tree,
A mountain Elf the lovers saw.
And full of rage was he.

The vengeful Elf crept from his cell,
And, all to wreak his spite,
The lady from her lover's arm
He stole away by night.

Three days Prince Mogens search'd the land,
But found his bride no more,
And wound aloft his silken sail,
And steer'd for Norway's shore.

The Prince bade ask both far and near,
If aught of her were seen;
He spared not of his niddj gold,
And less the silver sheen.

With all his search he nothing heard,
He nothing of her found,
For in the cavern Malfred lay
With Elf-wives under ground.

Prince Mogens on his trusty steed
To th' Upland rode away,
And maiden Thorelille betrothed,
A fair and lovely may.

As week by week five months or more
Were pass'd away and gone,
His bride, that in the cavern dwelt,
Brought forth an infant son.

There year by year nine winters through
Must, she with Elves reside,
And there her son so strong was grown,
On horseback he could ride.

She waited till on Christmas eve.
The Elves their dance begun.
And then from out that dismal cave
She carried off her son.

She led him over the mountain wold;
She reached the yellow sand.
And found a vessel at anchor there.
And push'd it off from land

Her fair white hand the rudder steer'd,
And stoutly tugg'd the oar,
Till with her son she reached a bay,
And there debark'd on shore.

To Mogens house fair Malfred went,
Up to his courtyard gate.
And there stood Mogens, royal prince,
In sable robe of state.

"O hear me, Mogens, royal prince,
"What now I say to thee;
"Think of the past and call to mind
"The troth thou gavest me."

"Plighted to Thor is the troth,
"That once to thee I gave;
"Nor knew I, but that thou wast dead,
"And sleeping in thy grave."

"And must I," Malfred so replied
In tone of grief so mild,
"Must I then bear a leman's name?
"Unfathered go my child?"

"Silver and gold I'll give thee both,
"And moated forts so fair;
"To manhood rear this gallant boy,
"And live devoid of care."

"I cannot live from trouble free,
"Nor lay my grief aside,
"While Thorelille's thy wedded wife,
"And me thy bed denied."

Fair Malfred, still thy grief and care,
"In peace let Thor dwell,
"And I will sometimes ride across,
"And comfort thee as well."

"Thy leman I will never be,
"Nor bear a leman's name;
"Thou 'st vow'd in Spain to marry me,
"That promise now I claim."

Uprose then Mogens, royal prince.
And round him wrapped his cloak,
And, mounting to the ladies bower,
He thus to Thord spoke.

"O hear me, Thord, dearest wife,
"And thou my course decide;
"Here's Lady Malfred come to land,
"My first affianced bride."

"Then saddle for me my good grey steed,
"I'll here no longer stay;
"If Lady Malfred's come to land,
"Let her not go away."

Up to the ladies' bower aloft
The lovely Malfred came,
And rose the gentle Thorelille,
And met the stranger dame.

"Welcome, fair Malfred, welcome home
"To these your lordly towers!
"I to my mother's house will go,
"Your husband shall be your's."

"O Stay, dear Lady Thorelille,
"To this my plan agree;
"Prince Mogens shall with my good will
"Retain both you and me."

In Norway's land this came to pass,
And still their fame survives;
For eighteen winters dwelt the Prince
With both his noble wives

In mutual love and peace they lived
Each to the other true,
Nor e'er exchanged one angry word
Those eighteen winters through.

poems.title: The Dalby Bear
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There roar'd a bear on Dalby wold,
And strong and fat was he and bold.
But peace let us in Denmark hold,

Both Ox and Horse that bear had slain;
And wrought the. farmers grief and pain.

They planned and plotted night and day,
How best the bear to seize and slay;

So to the wood their swine they drove,
And let them near his covert rove.

"Now," said the bear, as there he lay,
"What guests are these come here to day?"

Fierce he rushed down from out his lair,
And found a Christian standing there.

One hour he with the farmer fought,
And down to the ground his victim brought;

He crunch'd his heart with greedy bite.
As e'en rode up a gallant knight.

"Come on" said Bear, and foam'd with rage,
"With thee I'll gladly now engage.

"Threat as thou wilt, and do thy best,
"I'll put thy bragging to the test.

"Thou'rt arm'd, 'tis true, with martial gear,
"But teeth and claws are worth thy spear."

One day they fought, aye did they twain,
And all the third they fought again.

The fourth day, e'en as night began,
The bear at last had fell'd the man.

"Ne'er shalt thou boast, my gallant knight,
"That thou hast beaten me in fight.

"My sire, a king of high renown,
"And queenly mother wore a crown;

"But through a base stepmother's spell
"A woeful change my form befell.

"Forced to these forest wilds to go
"I wrought the farmers grievous woe;

"No season did my robberies cease,
"I left them not a moment's peace.

"That base stepmother was to blame,
"Whose magic spell bewitch'd my fame.

"'Twas her foul art and treacherous hand,
"That bound my neck with iron band;

"This band if thou hast strength to break,
"Thy life, now forfeit, I'll not take."

"I'll gladly help thee in thy need,
"And shall through Mary's son succeed.

"For break the spell, and burst the band,
"That can alone His mighty hand."

A cross the knight made o'er the beast,
And burst the band and him released.

The bear arose a graceful knight,
And gain'd his father's crown and right.

And nobly was his friend repaid
With the king's sister, lovely maid.

How well together lived the three,
The base stepmother griev'd to see;

Till, mad with spite and baffled pride,
She leap'd a beetling cliff and died.

poems.title: Young Swennendal
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Young Svejdal".
poems.text:
And it was he, young Swennendal,
Would play with golden ball,
And drove it into the maiden's bower,
And paled her cheeks withal.

"Hark thee! throw not, young Swennendal,
"Thy golden ball at me;
"There dwells a maid in Hovensland,
"Is longing after thee.

"No rest shall ease thy weary limbs,
"No slumber close thine eyes,
"Till thou hast freed that lovely maid
"From trance, wherein she lies."

Young Swennendal could rest no more,
But round him wrapped his cloak,
And mounting up to the upper room
His troopers thus bespoke.

"Sit here, my men, and quaff at board
"The wine and luscious mead;
"But I to Goliat cave must go,
"To ask my mother rede."

Alone he went, young Swennendal,
And wrapped him in his gear.
And took his way to Goliat cave
His mother's rede to hear.

And there did he, young Swennendal,
Beat on his mother's mound,
Till walls and stones and beams and grave
Were crumbling all around.

"Who is it here disturbs my sleep?
"Who deals these heavy blows?
"And may I not in peaceful sleep
"E'en in my grave repose?

"Who is it here? who beats so hard
"And seeks to give me pain?
"What not beneath the marble tomb
"In peace may I remain?'

"Young Swennendal, thy youngest son,
"'Tis I, my mother dear;
"And I have come to Goliat cave
"Counsel of thee to hear.

"he maid in a spell has bound me fast,
"And this her cruel vow;
"That rest no more shall ease my limbs,
"Nor slumber cool my brow."

"And spell-bound has the maiden thee?
"Made she this vow indeed?
"Three gifts then I'll on thee bestow,
"Shall serve thee in thy need.

"I'll give thee first a stout grey horse,
"And faithful he'll be found;
"He tramps as well on ocean wave
"As on the 'solid ground.

"I'll give thee too a sword of gold,
"Gird it upon thy side,
"And, where thou journey est in the world,
"In safety thou shalt ride.

"I'll give thee too a golden key,
"Its name is Adelring,
"Use but that key, and every lock
"Shall open to thee spring.

"I'll give thee too a table-cloth
"Spun of the moorgrass wool;
"Desire whatever meat thou wilt,
"With that it shall be full."

Young Swennendal he journey M forth,
And found a little lane;
A herdsman there his cattle drove
To pasture on the plain.

"O tell me. Herdsman, honest man,
"What now I ask of thee;
"To whom belongs the mighty herd,
"Thou drivest o'er the lea?"

"These cattle," said that aged man,
"That on the pasture run,
"Are all the maid's at Hovensland,
"Whom knight has never won."

"And tell me, Herdsman, honest man,
"What now I ask of thee;,
"If thou dost know that lady's fetch,
"Conceal it not from me."

"The lady's fetch right well I know,
"But never will reveal,
"For if her secret I betray,
"Her anger I shall feel."

"If thou the lady's fetch dost know,
"Conceal it not from me;
"If I become this country's king,
"I'll make a count of thee."

"Eight lions watch her night and day,
"Nine grisly bears beside;
"And only on an Elfin horse
"May any near them ride."

"If Elfin horse can help me hero,
"For that I do not lack;
"I've brought with me an Elfin horse,
"I'm sitting on his back/'

"The portals are of marble stone,
"The locks of steely plate,
"And only with an Elfin key
"Can any through the gate."

"If Elfin key is all I want,
"Then through the gate can I,
"For this is e'en an Elfin key,
"Is hanging on my thigh."

As through the gate young Swennendal
And up the courtyard went,
Lowly the bears and lions crouch'd.
And linden humbly bent.

From window loop the lady peered
To see the novel sight;
"Eat whence then is he hither come?
"And who, this handsome knight?"

Her little page the lady call'd,
The truth she longed to know;
"Ask, whence is come the handsome knight,
"And why he halts below."

But answered thus young Swennendal;
"The Lady of Hovensland
"Must hither come to hear the truth,
"Herself before me stand/'

So came the lady of Hovensland,
Herself before him stood;
"And whence has come this handsome knight?
"Why cross'd the briny flood?"

"It is from Denmark's isle I'm come
"To this your foreign clime,.
"To see the lady of Hovensland,
"And how she spends her time."

"And art thou come from Denmarks isle?
"Then prithee let me hear,
"How fares the brave young Swennendal,
"The youth to me so dear?"

"And is it then young Swennendal,
"Who is to you so dear?
"None else than he, young Swennendal,
"Is with you halting here."

And there was costly velvet cloth
And silk and sindal spread,
When Swennendal the gentle maid
To bridal banquet led.

Five days they held the marriage feast,
And wine they gladly pour'd,
And there was he the aged man
The uppermost at board.

poems.title: Knight Stig's Wedding
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Knight Stig was sprung of noble birth,
A finer man was not on earth.

Knight Stig at court an office bare,
And maids and ladies brush'd his hair.

He stood to serve the royal board,
But Kirstin deign'd him not a word.

"I'll try tonight a Runic spell,
"Tis now seven years I've learnt it well."

With right hand mead and wine he drew,
With left hand potent Love Runes threw.

But what he had to Kirstin thrown
Roll'd on beneath Rigissa's gown.

Knight Stig as pale as ashes stood,
Rigissa blush'd as red as blood.

Knight Stig in mantle wrapp'd his head.
And up to his nurse's chamber sped.

"O nurse, dear nurse, your counsel give,
"How to escape the court, and live.

"I would on Kirstin cast a spell,
"But it beneath Rigissa fell.

"I'll saddle me my trusty gray,
"And up, and gallop far away."

"And ride thou mayst round Funen's land,
"At night the maid will near thee stand.

"Around the world thou mayst have sped,
"At night thou 'It find her near thy bed.

"Thy wofated cheer I rede thee keep,
"Go home to bed, and go to sleep.

"The maid will come, and tirl the pin,
"But rise not up, nor let her in.

"Perhaps her tiny hands avail
"From chamber door to' pick the nail.

"Up to thy bedstead she will creep,
"But hush, and feign thee fast asleep.

"She then will tap thy chin so fair,
"And gently smooth thy golden hair;

"And then she'll kiss thy lips so red,
"But lie as still, as wert thou dead."

He heard and thought her counsel best.
And went and laid him down to rest.

As soon as fell the evening dew,
Rigissa took her mantle blue;

She tapp'd his door with gentle knock;
"Rise up, sweet knight, your door unlock."

Appointment I have none to keep,
"Unlock to no one, while I sleep."

With fingers small the nails she drew.
Aye fifteen nails, beside a screw!

She sat her down, that maid so fair,
And fondled with his yellow hair;

She kiss'd his cheek and lips so red,
Bat still he lay as he were dead.

She claps'd him to her snowy breast.
But still the knight his voice repressed.

He woke at last and round him gazed;
"Now who has all this turmoil rais'd?

"I'll in your brother's court disclose,
"That you it is break my repose."

"Go then, and make what plaint you will,
"I'll follow you and love you still."

To court as soon as broke the day, —
To make his plaint he took his way.

"My liege, I've here a charge to make,
"Your sister comes my rest to break."

The King to his page was heard to call;
"My sister bid to the audience hall."

Rigissa stood before the board;
"Why has my brother sent me word?"

"This knight stands here a charge to make,
"That thou hast come his rest to break."

"The truth it is. — To him I went,
"And coldly welcome back was sent.

"I'll bear in hand the glowing steel,
"And prove him pure by God's ordeal."

The King the matter turn'd in mind;
"A better match she could not find."

And soon the court was glad and gay;
The King his sister gave away.

Great too the joy throughout the land,
That Stig it was had gain'd her hand.

Stig bade them brew and mix the wine,
And ask'd the king himself to dine.

The king he ask'd with knight and swain.
And eke the queen and all her train.

Said the good queen, as there she rode,
"So be on virtue rank bestow'd.

"Last year must Stig as trooper ride,
"And now the Princess is his bride.

"Last year he serv'd in stallboy's stead,
"Now shares the king's own sister's bed.

"But said the Queen, and check'd the rein,
"Can this indeed be Stig's demesne?"

"Stig's house it is," a page-boy cried,
"And famed for beauty far and wide.

"I aside with ruddy gold 'tis dight,
"And outside all with silver bright/'

As up to the house they ride in state,
Stand five white bears ' before the gate.

As through the court they take their way,
Both stag and doe about them play;

And round a pond is grouped a herd,
With many a curious beast and bird:

Where lind and poplar throw their shade,
The graceful hart and hind are laid;

And skipping through the pleasant grove,
Whatever beasts in forest rove.

The dames, she meets in banquet hall,
Are courtly highbred ladies all:

Inlaid with amber glows the floor,
The cieling gilt with lettered lore:

With golden plate the board is full,
The cloth of finest moor-grass wool:

The walls are built of marbles rare.
And ivory posts the cieling bear.

As o'er the floor the dancers sped,
The graceful knight the revellers led.

Graceful he tripp'd before the band,
Two silver cups in either hand.

He then to his bride a goblet drain'd,
That aye was best, that God ordain'd." isn

While to his dearest bride he drank,
Bloomed wood and field and flowery bank;

With leaves and blossoms every tree;
The paragon of maids was she.

So soon as fell the evening dew,
"He and his bride to bed withdrew;

And great is now Sir Stig's delight,
With royal bride to pass the night;

And she no further trouble knows,
But may with knight Sir Stig repose.

poems.title: Knight Stig's Death
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Uprose the Danish King and spake;
"Knight Stig, my banner thou shalt take/'

"Too young am I, too weak my hand
"To bear your flag to foreign land."

"Young as thou art, yet do thy best,
"And front the foe with dauntless breast."

"If then your banner I must take,
"A new and bright one let me make.

"Behind it's yellow blue and red
"Falls battling many a warrior dead."

They march'd away to a foreign land;
The banner never left his hand.

Like hay the pelting arrows sped,
And lighted on his sleeve so red.

They glared bright as a burning brand,
They lighted on his very hand.

Then spake the king; "Stig, quit the strife;
"Throw down the banner; save thy life."

"Never shall hear my bride in town,
"That the king's banner I threw down.

"Never shall hear my bride on land,
That the king's banner left my hand."

"Ha!" cries the king in grief and pain,
"Stig lies beneath the banner slain."

The king with glory won the fight,
But lost his life the gallant knight.

The king rais'd high his royal hand;
"Our Danish men have gain'd the land:

"How gladly rode I home again,
"Were but Knight Stig amid the train!"

The King came back, rode up the street,
And him his sister went to meet.

"Welcome, my brother, home from war!
"O say how fared ye all afar?"

"All to my wishes; all went well;
"But that afield thy bridegroom fell."

The maid her hands so wildly wrung.
Her rings across the benches sprung.

"My sister, hark! thy grief control,
"And thine shall be the rich Sir Cole."

"Nay," said the lady, "nay," said she,
"Never shall he have claim on me.

"The rich Sir Cole he may be hight,
"He's not like Stig my gallant knight.

"He in my arms shall never sleep,
"For Stig, Knight Stig, I'll daily weep.

"He at my side shall never lie,
"For Stig, Knight Stig, I'll daily sigh/'

poems.title: Sir Peter and Mettelille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
O Lord, our sorrows deign to hear,
And calm the troubled breast;
Sad lot is his who bears a heart
With secret grief oppressed.

Sir Peter wooed fair Mettelille,
A long and weary while;
Five years in vain he press'd his suit.
He never won a smile.

"Now listen, gentle Mettelille,
"No longer spurn my love,
"And all the days, I yet may live,
"My kindness you shall prove."

"My brother serves the King in court,
"A gallant knight is he;
"Go, ask that brother his consent,
"'Tis he should judge for me."

"To ask your brother his consent
"My time will not allow;
"But meet me, dearest Mettelille,
"Beneath the greenwood bough."

"If you not one short hour can spare
"For my sake him to see,
"Me will you never live to meet,
"Beneath a greenwood tree."

"If you to this will not comply,
"So strong a Rune I'll write,
"That both your honour and your love
"I'll win in your despite."

"And if you throw that Rune on me,
"And vilely work my fall,
"To God my lifelong night and day
"For vengeance I will call.

So strong a Rune Sir Peter wrote,
And under her mantle threw.
It made her very fingers bleed,
And tears of anguish drew.

Beneath tli unwary maiden's cloak
He threw that fatal Rune,
And stepped at once aboard his ship,
And sail'd that very noon.

The seasons slowly pass'd away,
Till gone were winters three;
And sad was she, so much she long'd,
The knight again to see.

She rose, the gentle Mettelille,
Drew on her scarlet cloak,
And mounted to the ladies bower,
And greeted them and spoke.

"Hail all ye dames of high degree!
"And hail, ye maidens fair!
"Is here one who will go Avith me,
"My weal or woe to share?"

Then little Christel up and spake;
"It's I, dear Mettelille,
"It's I will be your faithful friend
"In good luck or in ill."

Silent and sorrowful of mood
She left her father's town.
Bare-foot, bare-headed, unarray'd.
In but a silken gown.

Fearless alike of toil and storm
She reach'd the sandy shore;
And while herself she steer'd the boat,
Fair Christel pull'd the oar.

She sail'd across the briny sea
With sorrow, pain and toil,
And came where in a foreign land
Sir Peter owned the soil.

The watchman on his turret stood,
And looked around so wide,
And saw the gentle Mettelille,
And boat beneath her glide.

The watchman donned his mantle blue,
And duly sped his way,
To where asleep in lofty bower
The knight Sir Peter lay.

"Two maids of rank from o'er the sea
"Are come this morn to town,
"Barefoot, bareheaded, unarray'd,
"In but their silken gown."

"And are there really landed here
"Two maids from o'er the sea?
"Then one will be fair Mettelille,
"Quick! bring her in to me."

Sir Peter rose from downy bed,
And round him wrapped his cloak.
And up to his mother's chamber went.
And thus the dame bespoke.

"Hail! dearest mother, prithee rise,
"In robe so rich array'd,
"And meet and welcome Mettelille,
"My long-sought lovely maid."

Those ladies in his court he met,
And stretched thorn forth his hand;
"Right welcome, gentle Mettelille,
"To this our foreign land."

"Hark ye, Sir Peter, what ye' ve done,
Is grievous wrong and shame;
To lure me from my father's house,
"And sully thus my fame."

"Nay listen, gentle Mettelille,
"No harm shall you betide,
Tor scarlet you shall daily wear,
"And slumber at my side."

"And though I wore your ruddy gold,
"And dress'd in silk so red,
"If I should your mere leman be,
"With grief I soon were dead."

"Nay listen, gentle Mettelille,
"No griefs have you to fear;
"In wedlock you shall live with me,
"And richest scarlet wear."

He warmly press'd her fair white hand,
Her tears he kindly dried.
And up to his mother's bower aloft
"He led his trembling bride.

Sir Peter's mother tapp'd her cheek,
And gently drew her near;
"Welcome, my dearest Mettelille,
"Welcome, my daughter here!

"And let thy bosom, Mettelille,
"From sorrow now be free,
"For I will, all the days I live,
"A mother be to thee."

Sir Peter, he too, kindly spake,
Press'd on her lips a kiss.
And sware that all the wealth he own'd,
Should aid their mutual bliss.

She on his bosom laid her head,
And deeply did she sigh;
"I'm come from home to a foreign land,
"On you alone rely."

Sir Peter, like a gallant knight,
His troth did not betray.
But when the month was duly past,
He held his wedding day.

poems.title: The Twelve Wizards
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of George Borrow (1826), titled "The Heroes of Dovrefeld".
poems.text:
At Dovrefield over on Norway's reef
Were heroes who never knew pain or grief.

There dwelt there many a warrior keen,
The twelve bold brothers of Ingeborg queen.

The first with his hand the storm could hush,
The second could stop the torrent's rush.

The third could dive in the sea as a fish,
The fourth never wanted meat on dish.

The fifth he would strike the golden lyre.
And old and young to the dancing fire.

The sixth on his horn would blow a blast,
Who heard it would shudder and stand aghast.

The seventh go under the earth could he,
The eighth he could dance on the rolling sea.

The ninth tamed all that in greenwood crept,
The tenth not a nap had ever slept.

The eleventh the grisly lindworm bound,
And will what he would, the means he found.

The twelfth he could all things understand,
The done in a nook of the farthest land.

Their equals were never seen there in the North,
Nor any where else on the face of the earth.

poems.title: The Raven
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Raven he flew at eventide,
By day he did not dare;
Ill luck must they be fain to meet.
Who better cannot fare.

Over the walls the Raven flew.
And round the dwelling swept.
And saw, where in her lonely bower
Sat Ermeline and wept.

He flew to South, he flew to North,
He flew to the clouds so high,
And still he saw fair Ermeline
With grief her needle ply.

"Now tell me, Lady Ermeline,
"Why sheddest thou the tear?
"Is mother, father, brother dead,
"Or any friend as dear?"

Fair Ermeline to her window stepped,
Look'd up and looked below;
"Now who is here will comfort me,
"And hear my tale of woe?

"O thou, Wild raven, stay thy flight, i
"And hither come to me,
"My tale of sorrow thou shalt hear,
"I'll tell it all to thee.

"To one, my equal, and a Prince,
"My father gave my hand,
"But him my harsh stepmother drove
"Afar to an eastern land.

"And much as each the other loved,
"And would together live,
"She me to a foul mis-shapen imp,
"Her sister's son, would give.

"A brother too that once I had,
"Sir Verner, knight so brave,
"Him too my stepmother transformed,
And from his country drave."

"Now tell me, Lady Ermeline,
"What wilt thou me repay,
"If to thy trulove on my wing
"I bear thee hence away?"

"I'll give thee silver, give thee gold,
"And jewels bright and rare,
"If thou wilt carry me to my Prince,
"And still my grief and care/'

"Thy silver need I not, nor gold,
"Nor jewels' costly shine,
"But let for my reward thy son,
"Thine eldest son, be mine."

She stretch'd him forth her lily hand,
She grasp'd his foot with joy,
And on her Christian faith she sware
To give her eldest boy.

He took the Lady Ermeline,
And set her on his back.
And flew above the stormy sea
A high and giddy track.

He rested on a castle tower.
And closed his swarthy wing;
"Now hero, dear Lady, dwells the Prince,
"To whom I thee should bring."

And there the brave Sir Nilus stood
With silver cup in hand;
"Welcome, dear Lady Ermeline,
"To this our foreign land.

"How, Raven, shall I thee repay
"For bringing me my bride?
"I've, since I loft my Danish home,
"Heard no good news beside."

The good Sir Nilus, gallant knight,
He made no long delay,
Bat held his troth, and that day month
Was kept his wedding day,

With joy and peace they quaff'd the wine,
Forgot their grief and care,
And, soon as forty weeks were past,
A son that lady bare.

That very night the raven came,
And Hat upon the roof.
And claim'd, what Lady Ermeline
Had vow'd in his behoof

She wrung her hands, and wept and griev'd,
She had not borne a maid;
"And, tho' it cost thy tender life,
"The bird must be repaid."

Around the house the raven flew,
A foul and fearful bird,
And maids and matrons wrung their hands.
And doleful cries were heard.

Sir Nilus proffered gold and towers.
So massive every one;
Would give the Raven half his land,
Could he but keep his son.

"Unless I get that little babe,
"Mine anger thou shalt taste;
"I'll slay thyself, devour thy flesh,
"And all thy realm lay waste."

Her child then took fair Ermeline,
Wrapt him in linen fine;
"Farewell my son! Of this thy death
"The guilt alas is mine."

They carried out the infant babe,
That on her bosom slept;
And loud were then the cries of woe,
And many those that wept

Fast in his claw he seized the child,
And croak'd a dismal joy;
Sir Nilus stood, and deeply groan'd
To see him clutch the boy.

The right eye out of his head he peeked
And half his hearths blood drank,
And straight became the ravenous bird
A knight of princely rank.

And in that knight, as brave a one
As ever brake a spear,
Beheld the Lady Ermeline
Her long-lost brother dear.

The people all, who throng'd the yard,
Knelt bare-kneed on the ground,
And pray'd to God his grace to show.
And heal the infants wound.

Full happy now is Ermeline,
Nor longer moans and weeps;
Has son and brother both restored,
And with Sir Nilus sleeps.

poems.title: The Wicked Mother-in-Law
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Ov has daughter but only one,
All under the mountain side
And she to Elling as bride is gone,
So warily there they ride.

Sir Styg Kob was her husband bight,
A gentleman he, and a gallant knight.

Twelve months, twelve wearisome months so slow
With twins did the lady Thor go.

They brought her here, and they took her there,
But worse was her state with all their care.

Sir Styg, wrapt in his purple cloak,
Went up to his mother's bower and spoke.

"Dear mother, your counsel! for great my grief;
"Say, when shall my Thor find relief?"

"None finds she, till she in. childbirth pain
"A twelvemonth and forty weeks has lain."

"Ah, no! that cannot indeed be so,
For forty only did Mary go."

Thor: "Since here my anguish is still the same,
"Pray carry me back to whence I came."

"The steeds have been to their pasture led,
"he groomboys are all asleep in bed."

"If neither coachman is here nor swain,
"I'll venture on foot across the plain."

These words had Thorelille scarcely said,
Before to the gate the steeds were led.

Sir Styg he lifted her up with pain,
And laid her down on the gilded wain.

He gently laid her on cushions blue.
And drove her safely the courtyard through.

But when to the wood of rose they came,
Brake down with the weight the carriage frame.

"I must a most wondrous woman he,
"That thus my carriage should break with me"

"Fear not, my Thorelille,' he replied,
"I'll walk and you shall on horseback ride.'

'Twas so they came to the outer gate,
Where Mett, Sir Styg's sister, sate.

"O sister, prithee, good counsel give,
"Say how my Thor we may relieve."

Fair Mettelille followed the wild heath tracks.
And two little babies made of wax;

Then wrapp'd her head in a scarlet cloak,
And thus to her mother went, and spoke.

"O mother, forego your grief and fear,
"And take on your arm your grandsons here."

"What? did I not then with key and ring
"Reverse and spell-bind every thing?

"I surely the room with spells possessed,
"Save under Thorelille's bridal chest."

Full quickly they made the chest give place,
And laid her down on the vacant space.

She scarcely a moment was seated there.
Before she two healthy children bare.

"O grant me, heaven, for mercy's sake,
"But time my dying bequests to make.

"My gown of the silk with pain and woe,
"Let that to Sir Styge's mother go.

"My silver'd shoes to his sister hear,
"With gladness and comfort long to wear.

"To dear Sir Styg a rose I give,
"Grant God that it soon with him may live!"

poems.title: The Coward Bridegroom
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Tyge Hermandsson".
poems.text:
It was upon a Saturday
The rain began to fall;
Sir Tyg, 'twas his wedding day,
In silence paced his hall.

Sir Tyg out of his window gazed
With frequent anxious look;
"My bride too dearly I should buy
"In crossing yonder brook.

"Now hark thee, Nilus Benditson,
"Thou hast so tall a steed;
"I pray thee ride and fetch her home,
And help a friend in need."

"Gladly," said Nilus Benditson,
And archly spake aside;
"I'll play my friend a pretty prank,
"If I shall fetch the bride."

Off rode Sir Nilus Benditson,
And went the bride to meet;
There hung both silk and velvet green
Before his horse's feet.

All clad in silk and golden lace
Did friends and kinsmen ride,
And slowly took their way to church
Beside the gentle bride.

Awhile before the door she stood,
Like blushing rose her hue,
And bade them towards the water look,
If Tyg were in view.

"Nay" answer'd Nilus Benditson,
And prompt the words he spake;
"He dared not cross yon angry stream,
"E'en for his trulove's sake."

They placed her on the bridal seat
In all her costly gear,
And often out of the window look'd,
If came Sir Tyg near.

From silver cup both wine and mead
They pour'd for every guest,
And waited on till eventide
And th' hour to go to rest.

On bridal bed they left the bride
Sir Tyg there to wait,
And all in anxious hope and doubt
Three weary hours she sate.

The priests they stood around the bed,
And sang with all their might,
"No bridegroom comes to claim his bride,
"Who sleeps with her tonight?"

Then forward brave Sir Nilus stepp'd,
And cast his silver'd shoe;
"Tis I will sleep with her tonight,
"And faithful be and true."

They quaffed in turn the wedding cup,
And hearty draughts they took,
The while Sir Tyg Hermanson,
Still fear'd to cross the brook.

'Twas not until the Wednesday mom
The stream began to fall,
And then came Tyg Hermanson,
And brought his bridesmen all.

Sir Tyg came to the wedding house,
And saw the pomp and state;
But answer'd him the youthful bride,
"Ride back, 'tis now too late."

"But listen, gentle Sidselille,
"A word I have with thee;
"Thou 'st wedded with another man,
"And foully cheated me."

"And hear, Sir Tyg Hermanson,
"A thing I'd have you know,
"I will not such for husband take,
"As fears the rain and snow.

"Now had'st thou been a gallant man,
"And had my love at heart,
"Thou wouldest with thy naked sword
"Have dash'd the waves apart"

"In cloister then I'll go and live
"A friar of orders gray,
"And trust me, gentle Sidselille,
"I come no more this way."

"Yet if the stream should be so low,
"And I should see thee back,
"If I have cheeses more than two,
"I'll put one in thy sack."

poems.title: The Ready Reply
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
"But sister dear," a brother said,
"Do you then never mean to wed?

"Oh wait! At this my tender age
"I would not yet my hand engage."

"Yet might I trust the public voice,
"You have already made the choice."

"So people talk, and talk they may,
"Believe not all that gossips say."

"And who was then the handsome knight
"Rode from your door with morning's light?"

"No knight — no high-born cavalier:
"My stable-boy and his horse were here."

"Then near your bed two pair of shoes!
"Now whose were they? pray, tell me whose."

"No man's shoe, brother, think not so,
"'Twas but my slippers lay below."

"And then that little cherub head,
"Was lately sleeping upon your bed?"

"No cherub that, or baby small;
"What lay there sleeping was my doll."

"How heard I then in passing by
"Within your door an infant cry?"

"So cry not infants; 'twas my maid
"Because of a wardrobe key mislaid."

"And pray, what might the cradle mean
"So slily hid behind the screen?

"No cradle; be not rash to blame,
"You've seen perhaps my broidery frame.

"And if you, brother, more will know,
"With answers I shall not be slow,"

When women fail to make reply,
Then look to see the ocean dry.

poems.title: Ebbe Skammelson
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Ebbe Skammelson".
poems.text:
Northward in Thy Sir Skammel dwelt.
For wealth and goodness known;
Five sons had he, so courtly bred,
And two to manhood grown.

The one bight Ebbd Skammelson,
And Peter one, — the young;
A doleful story it is to hear,
The fate that o'er them hung.

Ebb laid saddle upon his horse,
And rode to an isle away,
And there betroth'd fair Adelaide,
A sweet and lovely may.

He won the gentle Adelaide,
A lily flower was she,
And brought her home to his mother's house,
And went himself to sea.

But first in the ladies lofty bower
He wish'd his bride adieu;
"While in the royal court I serve,
"Remain to your promise true.

"Wait for me, gentle Adelaide,
"Your honour keep in mind;
"Meanwhile I go to a distant land,
"A livelihood to find."

But while young Ebb serves at court.
And rank and fame pursues,
His brother Peter stays at home,
And her, his trulove, woos.

Ebbe he serves the king at court
To earn him gold and fee;
His brother Peter builds a ship
And rigs it out for sea.

His brother Peter builds a ship.
And ploughs the salty tide,
And steers across to North Jutland
To court his brother's bride.

And there young Peter Skammelson,
In scarlet cloak array'd,
Mounts to the ladies bower aloft.
Where sits that lovely maid.

"My greeting, gentle Adelaide!
"Your troth if me you'll plight,
"With love and honour all my days,
"Your favours I'll requite."

"How should I plight my love to you?
"Or share your house and land?
"Your brother Ebb, he it is,
"To whom I've pledged my hand.

"My vow to wait for eight whole years
"With all my kin I made;
"I will not marry another man,
"And that the King too bade."

"But," answer'd Peter Skammelson
In scarlet mantle dress'd;
"Ebb is in the royal court,
"And makes your love his jest."

Then up his cruel mother spake,
And evil rede she gave;
"Accept then Peter Skammelson,
"For Ebb he is a knave.

"Ebb is in the royal court,
"And glory wins and fame;
"And there's in the Queen's bower the maid,
"Is Ebb's latest flame.

"So take thou Peter, my younger son,
"With all his towers so red;
"For Ebb Skammelson, be sure,
"Another maid will wed."

"Nay hark thee, Peter Skammelson,
"Choose thee some other wife;
"I give no other man my troth,
"So long as he has life.'

"Hear then the truth in earnest tone
The mother so replied;
"Hear but the truth, fair Adelaide,
"Ebb last autumn died."

Then rose the maiden Adelaide,
As lily stalk so slim,
And Peter Skammelson betroth'd,
And gave her hand to him.

They hastened for the marriage feast
The luscious mead to brew.
While Ebb serv'd the king at court,
And nothing of it knew.

Ebb, when two months now were past,
At dead of night awoke,
And of the vivid reams he had dream'd,
He thus to his comrade spoke.

"It seemed that through my room of stone
"A glowing fire did glide,
"And there my brother Peter burn,
"And burn my lovely bride."

"Then surely, Ebbd Skammelson,
"Some trouble is near at hand,
"For when one dreams of blazing fire,
"It bodes a naked brand.

"Bat that it was thy room of stone
"All in a blaze of fire;
"That bodes that Peter Skammelson
"Betrothes thy heart's desire."

Up started Ebb Skammelson,
And braced his sword to side,
And sought the king, and furlough gain'd,
Home to his friends to ride.

In eager haste he mounted horse,
And he so swiftly flew,
A seven day's journey home from court,
The same he rode in two.

So well did Ebb time his speed,
As not to come too late.
The day they held their wedding feast
He reached his father's gate.

"Hark thee, and tell me, little page,
"What now I ask of thee;
"What means this joyous festival,
"And whence the company?"

"Here are the ladies met, Who dwell
"Along the North-sea shore,
"And their's are all these gilded wains,
"That halt at Skammel's door.

"They've dress'd and deck'd thy brother's bride,
"And therefore are they gay;
"Thy brother and gentle Adelaide
"Keep here their wedding day."

Outside stood Ebb's sisters two
With gold cups each in band:
"O welcome, Ebbe, brother dear,
"Back to your native land!"

Welcome so kind his sisters gave,
And rich rewards they won.
While e'en his parents stood aloof,
And welcome showed him none.

Buckle or brooch he gave them each
Of gold all richly wrought;
Gifts he had bravely earn'd at court,
And home to his trulove brought.

The one begg'd him at home to stay;
The other forth to go;
"If but one night thou stayest here,
"'Twill bring us bitter woe."

His parents pray'd him enter in
And take his seat at board;
But mute was Ebb Skammelson,
And answered not a word.

He turned his horse to leave the yard.
And fain would ride away;
His mother caught and held the rein,
And begg'd him there to stay.

She brought him forth a cushioned stool,
Would have him sit to dine,
"Nay'' answer'd Ebb Skammelson,
"Leave me to pour the wine."

With pearls and gold so gaily deck'd
There sat the lovely bride;
As oft as Ebb upon her gazed,
With grief at heart he sigh'd.

When daylight leaned, and o'er the field
Was shed the glistering dew,
Kissing with grace the fair young bride
From banquet hall withdrew.

With joyous hearts to the bridal house
They led the gentle fair,
And Ebb begged to head the train
The bridal torch to bear.

"And how!" said Ebb, when they came
Before the chamber door,
"The troth you plighted me the first,
"Remember you no more?"

"I've since to your brother plighted troth,
"Given all I had to give,
"But will a mother be to you,
"As long as I may live."

"Not for a mother wooed I you,
"I wooed you for my wife;
"And therefore Peter Skammelson
"Has now to end his life.

"Consent, fair maiden Adelaide,
"With me to go away;
"And be my fate, e'en what it will,
"My brother I will slay."

"And though your brother you should kill,
"You would not gain my love,
"For I should grieve myself to death,
"As on her bough the dove/'

To hear her Ebbe Skammelson
With anger fiercely frown'd,
And muttering vengeance on them both
Stamped wildly on the ground.

With that into the bridal house
They led the gentle bride,
But Ebb bare beneath his cloak
A drawn sword at his side.

He entered in and slew the maid,
Where near her bed she stood,
And left her lofty crown of gold
All swimming in her blood.

He took the gory dripping sword
Slily beneath his cloak,
And turning back to the banquet hall
He thus to his brother spoke:

"Hark thee, young Peter Skammelson,
" Tis time to leave the wine;
"Thy bride sits in her bridal bed,
"And seems for thee to pine."

Up rose young Peter Skammelson,
But sad at heart was he;
For well his brother Ebbe's rage
Was in his face to see.

"Now listen, Ebb, Skammelson,
"And lay thy wrath aside,
"Sleep thou with gentle Adelaide,
"To thee I yield the bride."

"Go, Peter, thou, nor longer leave
"The maid to pine alone;
"The bridal house and bridal bed
"With roses are bestrown."

But as young Peter Skaramelson
From banquet hall withdrew,
His brother cleft his head in twain.
And him so foully slew.

Great was the grief in bridal house.
And great the hall's dismay,
For dead were bride and bridegroom both,
E'en on their wedding day.

His father got a grievous wound,
His mother miss'd a hand;
And Ebbe Skammelson must forth
A vagrant from the land.

His brother, murderously slain.
And gentle bride lay dead.
And far and wide must Ebb roam.
And beg his daily bread.

From such a wedding. Gracious God,
Hinder both young and old!
Sour is the wine, and harsh the mead.
Where such sad news is told.

poems.title: The Raven Rune-Bearer
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
'Tis little May walks on the strand,
And wrings with grief her lily hand.

It's summer tide, and all so fair;
Oh! had she but her trulove there!

A swarthy raven came in sight,
Winging to north his rapid flight.

"Hark thee, wild raven, what I say,
"Canst thou for me a rune convey?"

"Thy rune with equal speed I'll take,
"As can thine hand the letters make."

Straight at her feet the hird she saw.
And wrote the runes within his claw.

He flew that day, he flew for three,
Ere he her trulove's sail could see.

He lighted down upon the prow,
The runes in the knight's hand to throw.

The knight his archer call'd, and said,
"Shoot me that fierce wild raven dead."

"Knight, gallant knight, shoot not at me,
"And breeze so fair I'll give to thee."

The ship sped on, the raven flew,
They reached the island both the two.

The ship below, the bird above,
They came to the knight's ladylove.

poems.title: Ribolt and Guldborg (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Ribolt, an heir of noble name.
For Guldborg glow'd with secret flame.

His court to the infant child he paid.
And more he loved the full grown maid.

"Thy troth to me, dear Guldborg, give,
"And come to a fairer land to live.

"Away to a blessed land we'll go,
"Where you shall never taste of woe;

"We'll off to a distant island fly,
"Where you shall live, and never die."

'You take me not to a land so fair,
"But I shall sorrow find and care;,

"Nor to an isle with me could fly,
"But where to God it's due to die/'

"Sweet leeks for grass each season brings,
"And all the year the cuckoo sings.

"For water run the brooks with wine,
"O trust me, Guldborg, and be mine."

"But how with you get through the gate,
"So closely watch me small and great?

"My parents watch me night and day,
"Brothers and sisters every way;

"And then my bridegroom always near,
The very one I chiefly fear."

"Tho' watch your kinsmen young and old,
"Your plighted word you still must hold.

"Put on my polish coat of mail,
"My helmet d'on in place of veil:

"Gird to your side my trusty blade,
"And none will know you then for maid.

"With golden spurs strapp'd on your feet
"Shy not or kith ")r kin to meet/'

In mantle blue he robed his bride,
And set her on his horse to ride.

They journey'd forth, till on the wold
They met a certain Baron bold.

"But say, Ribolt, dear comrade mine,
"Where bast thou found a page so fine?"

"My youngest brother he; — he is come
"On his first ride with me from home."

"Thou canst not hide the truth from me;
"Nay, Guldborg, nay, His thou I see.

"For tho' thy dress a man bespeak,
"I know too well thy rosy cheek;

"I know thy fair soft hair withal;
"I serv'd once in thy father's hall.

"And thu I know not shoe nor cloth,
"I know to whom thou 'st plighted troth."

A brooch of gold from off her waist
Upon the Baron's hand she placed:

"Now wheresoe'er you come today,
"Of me, dear Baron, nothing say."

To Kiillo house the Baron rode,
Where knights were met and goblets flowed.

In Truid's house he found thom all,
And Truel in his banquet hall.

"Sir Truid, what, man, here carouse?
"Ribolt is bearing off thy spouse."

Sir Truid bade to sound alarm,
"Up, gallant troopers, up and arm!"

An hour they rode at rapid pace,
When Guldborg look'd, if friends gave chase.

"My father's horses there I see,
"And my betrothed in chase of me."

"Guldborg to such a service deign,
"Light down and hold our horses' rein. "

"Now if in fight you see me fall,
"My name I pray you not to call.

"And if you see the blood run red,
"Be silent, lest you name me dead."

Ribolt in mail was soon array'd.
For Guldborg lent her willing aid.

On the first group he dealt a blow,
Laid Truid and her father low.

He met the next, and did not spare
Her brothers with the golden hair.

"Stop, stop, Ribolt, o stay thy hand,
"And sheathe I pray thy murderous brand.

"At least my youngest brother spare,
"The news let him to his mother bear;

"The mournful news that all are dead;
"Alas that she a daughter bred!"

The moment Guldborg named his name,
A fatal blow, the deathblow came.

Ribolt his weapon slung to his side,
"Come, Guldborg, come, now further ride."

Through Roseholt both in silence went.
Nor gave to joy or sorrow vent.

"Ribolt, but tell me, I implore,
"Why art thou cheerful now no more?"

"Because I am faint from loss of blood,
"And then I am tired, and sad of mood;

"I know full well, from failing breath,
"My heart is in the grasp of death."

"Wait but till I my stay-lace find,
"It well may serve thy wound to bind."

"There's naught to do, God give thee grace,
"Of little help is now thy lace."

At last they reach'd the castle gate,
Where in the court his mother sate.

"Welcome, Ribolt, from weary ride,
"And is that lady then thy bride?

"I ne'er saw one with face so white,
"Or less with gold and jewels dight."

"No wonder she should look so pale,
"She has been where stouter hearts would quail.

"O God, that I one hour might live
"For time my last bequests to give!

"My father, take this faithful beast;
"O dearest mother, fetch a priest.

"Brother, for love thou bearest me,
"My dearest bride I give to thee."

"The maid I were full fain to win,
"If free I could remain from sin."

"Fear not; I once, I do confess,
"Enjoy'd, but only once, a kiss."

"Nay troth to both two brothers give,
"That will I never, while I live. "

Ribolt ere crow of cock was dead,
Guldborg, ere morning sun was red.

Three corpses from that house they bare,
In one day three, and all so fair;

Ribolt himself, his gentle bride,
And mother, who from sorrow died.
