poems.title: Rederbrand and Guldborg (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Rederbrand heard, as he lay on shore,
Fair Guldborg sing in her maiden bower.

"Now, Guldborg, listen to what I say,
"Wilt thou on a journey with me away?

"O gladly with theo would I leave the land,
"Were it not for the spies that round me stand.

"Horo watch me my parents by night and day,
"And sisters and brothers, so hard are they.

"My uncle, a traitor, is always near,
"And he is the one, whom most I fear."

"Do thou thy gold in a casket stow,
"While I to saddle my charger go."

Sir Rederbrand went to her father's stall.
And look'd at the horses, one and all.

He view'd the chesnut, he viewed the gray,
The saddle upon the best to lay.

The maid he caught by her slender waist.
And wrapt in his mantle on horseback placed.

They rode, with mantle around her thrown,
Away from the yard, unseen, unknown.

But when from the town they reach'd the plain,
There met them Sir Peter, the traitor swain.

"Sir Rederbrand! ah! well met! good day!
"And where have you stolen that gentle may?"

"Not stolen is she, but my own dear niece,
"One whom I from cloister thrall release."

"Sir Rederbrand, tell not a tale untrue,
"Ere thee I had seen, I Guldborg knew.

"For tho' in a mantle so blue she rides,
"Her golden tresses no mantle hides.

"Her scarlet kirtle she may not show,
"But well her rosy fresh cheek I know.

"Guldborg, Guldborg, deceive not me,
"For surely, too surely 'tis thou I see.

"I know thee well by the silver'd shoes,
"And more by the knight I see thee choose."

Sir Peter he d'onn'd his scarlet cloak,
And went to Erick the king, and spoke.

"Hail, Erick, my liege, so great and grand,
"Your daughter is off with Sir Rederbrand."

The King to his troopers was heard to call;
"Up! bind on your heads your helmets all.

"Your helmets d'on, and your coats of mail,
"Sir Rederbrand he is not wont to quail."

Fair Guldborg turned, and behind her spied
Her father and eighteen men beside.

"O Rederbrand see, my trulove dear,
"My father and eighteen men draw near."

He seated her down on linden leaf;
"Betray not, I pray thee, or joy or grief."

He seated her under the linden tree;
"Be silent, whatever thou chance to see."

He left his clothes on a mossy stone,
And met his foes in his shirt alone.

He slew her father and eighteen more,
And still was unscathed of wound or sore.

"Rederbrand, Rederbrand, now forbear,
"For my sake my younger brother spare."

He shook at the maiden the gory blade;
"Thy due t were, should it on thee be laid/'

He seated his bride on his horse again,
And painfully guided himself the rein.

As through the forest their way they broke,
No sound they utter'd, no word they spoke.

"Rederbrand, tell me, my knight so dear,
"What now is become of thy wonted cheer?"

"God help thee for aid, that thou canst give,
"I doubt if I most am dead, or live/'

They rode for many a weary mile,
And fain would the knight repose awhile.

He down on the grass his mantle spread.
And struggled a moment, and there lay dead.

Fair Guldborg wept, and her fingers wrung;
"God help a poor friendless girl so young!"

She seated herself on his horse, and rode.
And came alone to the Queen's abode.

"O hail. Queen Ellen, and God you speed!
"And say have you not of a handmaid need?

"In gold I can work, dress ladies' hair,
"And sheeting of moorgrass wool prepare."

"If thou art so able to braid and sew,
"Then into my maidens' chamber go."

They all on brocade their needles plied.
Except fair Guldborg, who sat and cried.

They all were working with gold on knee,
Except fair Guldborg, so sad was she.

Queen Ellen came in, and slapp'd her face,
"And why not working thy golden lace?"

"Queen, from chiding and blows forbear,
"My task I'll finish with greater care."

But ere on the morrow had dawn'd the day,
A corpse in her bed fair Guldborg lay.

poems.title: Hildebrand and Hille (C)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Hylle, lost in dreaming thought.
Her seam is broidering all distraught.

She broiders that with silken thread,
She ought to work in gold so red;

And where with silk she ought to sew.
Is seen the ruddy gold to glow.

The good queen hears, how lost in dream
Sits Hillelille, and spoils her seam.

And she has veird her royal head,
And up to her maidens' bower is sped.

As o'er the threshold steps the queen,
Hylle stands up with reverent mien.

"Now hark thee, Hillelille, my child,
"Why sewest thou thy seam so wild?

"Thou sittest lost in thought, like one,
"Whose joy and peace of mind are gone."

Fair Hillelille the cushion pressed,
"Seat you, my gracious Queen, and rest.

"Seat you, my Queen, nor say me no,
"And hear me tell my tale of woe;

"For tired were you to stand so long,
"As I were telling all my wrong.

"A kingly crown my father wore,
"And rank of queen my mother bore.

"My father rear'd me up in state,
"And chose twelve knights on me to wait.

"One knight there was amid the train;
"Alas! my heart I let him gain.

"My lover hight Duke Hildebrand,
"A royal prince of English land.

"On horses two our gold we stow'd,
"And on a third ourselves we rode.

"We reached a house as waned the light,
"Where we had wish'd to pass the night

"We heard a knock at midnight hour,
"My brothers seven were at the door.

"He tapp'd my cheek, O cease thy fears,
"And dry, my love, these useless tears.

"Now if thou shouldest see me bleed,
"Then, lest thou name me dead, take heed.

Forbear, if thou should'st see me fall,
"My name in any case to call.

"Forward he rushed to hew and slay,
"Till fifteen knights before him lay.

"Hildebrand, sheathe now thy blade,
"For my sake be thine anger stay'd;

"My youngest brother's life forego,
"At least to him some mercy show.

"But hardly had I call'd the name,
"To Hildebrand his deathblow came.

"My brother seiz'd my trembling hand,
"And tied it up to his saddle band.

"My locks he loosed from off my brow,
"To bind me to his saddle-bow.

"And on he rode through thickest wood,
"Till all my body streamed with blood;

"Onward, nor once for pity stay'd,
"Though thorn and briar my bosom flay'd;

"Nor crossed the road so small a root,
"But wrench'd or tore my tender foot.

"At last we reached the castle gate,
"And there my sorrowing mother sate.

"My father built a tower so high,
"Where closely prison'd I should lie.

"With iron spikes he fenced it round,
"Inside with brambles fill'd the ground.

"Turn, where I would, by some sharp thorn,
"My hand or foot was rudely torn.

"My mother fain would see me sold,
"My father dead beneath the mould.

"They bartered me against the bell
"In Maryby is heard to knell.

"It gave, that bell, one single stroke,
"With one my mother's heart it broke."

In tenderest tone then spake the Queen,
And on her cheek the tears wore seen.

"And now that thy sad tale is done,
"The Duke, thy lover, was my son."

Hylle her tale could scarcely tell,
Ere swooning to the earth she fell;

And great the good kind Queen's dismay,
For on her bosom dead she lay.

poems.title: Hillelille and Hildebrand (D)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Hillelille in her bower sits,
Her fine-wrought seam no moment quits.
"To God alone is known my care,
"I tell it not to mortal ear."

But broiders that with silken thread,
She ought to work in gold so red;

And where with silk she ought to sew,
Is seen the ruddy gold to glow.

A message soon to the Queen is brought,
"Fair Hillelille sews all distraught."

The Queen has veil'd her royal head,
And up to Hillelille has sped.

"Why daily toiling on, my child,
"And yet thy needle ply so wild?

"Because my happiness is fled,
"I weep and wildly draw the thread.

"My father was a king so great,
"Twelve knights must at his table wait.

"My tender age from harm to guard
"These knights he bade hold watch and ward.

"Eleven were brave and ne'er deceived,
"The twelfth of honour me bereav'd.

"A king's son he from English land,
"Who won my heart, named Hildebrand.

"But scarce within each other's arm,
"We heard below a dire alarm;

"My father o'er his castle call,
"Up! up! my men, and arm ye all;

"Your mail put on, your courage show;
"Sir Hildebrand's a stubborn foe.'

"They beat the door with sword and spear;
"Get up, Sir Hildebrand, come here.'

"He gently tapp'd my pallid cheek,
"My name I pray thee not to speak;

"Nor, if some drops of blood should fall,
"To death thy bleeding lover call.'

"From out my door he boldly flung,
"And hard and fast his sword he swung.

"Upon their foremost rank he flew,
"Seven of my fair-hair'd brothers slew;

"And would have slaughtered with the rest
"The youngest, whom I loved the best.

"Then cried I, 'Stay, Sir Hildebrand,
"For my sake stay thy murderous hand;

"At least my youngest brother spare,
"The news let him to his mother bear.'

"Alas! the name was scarcely said,
"Ere eight deep wounds had laid him dead.

"My brother then with knotted band
"Bound to his girth my aching hand.

"And there was not so small a root,
"But wrench'd or tore my tender foot;

No straggling briar that cross'd the road,
"But me its share of torture owed;

"No stream so swift, or deep a dam,
"But in it dash'd his horse, and swam.

"At last we reach'd the castle gate,
"And there in tears my mother sate.

"A prison tower he bade them build,
"With thorns and brambles had it fill'd;

"And dressed in silk from out my bower
"He threw me into the dismal tower.

"Where'er I turn'd, by same sharp thorn
"My foot or arm was rudely torn.

"My mother fain would sell me, she,
"My brother hang me on gallows tree

"They sold me, brought with me a bell,
"In Maryby is heard its knell.

"It gave a first, a fatal stroke,
"Enough, my mother's heart it broke/'

Before her story all was said,
The maid in the Queen's arms lay dead.

poems.title: Hillelille in Her Chamber (E)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Hillelille up in her bower
Her seam is stitching hour by hour;

On seam so white her needle plies.
And sewing weeps the while and sighs;

"To none save God is known my care,
"I tell it not to mortal ear."

A little page her grief has seen,
And Ellen told of it, the queen.

"Fair Hillelille sits in her bower,
"But weeps and sighs from hour to hour."

The queen has veil'd her royal head,
And up to the maidens bower is sped.

"My child, why toil thus day and night,
"Yet nothing work but seam so white?"

"Because my peace of mind is fled,
"On seam so white I ply the thread.

"As I was twelve years old or so,
"My father march'd against the foe.

"But ere from home he went away,
"Twelve knights he chose with me to stay.

"Eleven were brave and ne'er deceived,
"The twelfth of honour me bereav'd.

"My father storm'd with rage so sore,
"Would never hear or see me more;

"Would sell me into slavery he,
"My mother drown me in the sea.

"They sold me and bought a new church bell,
"In Mary by is heard it's knell:

"It gave, that bell, one single stroke,
"With that my mother's heart it broke:

"It gave one more, that fatal bell,
"And dead my noble father fell."

"Now tell me how the traitor knight,
"The same who won thy heart, was hight."

"A king's son he who wrought my shame,
"Aud Hildebrand the traitor's name"

"What! Hildebrand! has he so done?
"My son it surely was, my son.

"No mother has that knight but me,
"And, trust me, he shall marry thee."

Fair Hillelille at words so sweet
For joy sinks fainting at her feet.

The poor pale girl Queen Ellen rears,
And comforts her and kindly cheers.

poems.title: Hyldebrand and Hyldestlil (F)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Hyldestlil sits in her bower,
And stitches caps from hour to hour.

But what should glow with gold so red,
All white she sews with silken thread.

"O listen, Hyldestlil, my dear,
"And let me all thy sorrow hear."

"My father was a King so great,
"That fifteen knights must on him wait.

"The fifteen serv'd his board for fee,
"The youngest one dishonour'd me.

"My tale one day, when none were near,
"I trusted to my sister's ear.

"But she a secret could not hold,
"And mine to both our parents told.

"My father, a stern harsh man was he,
"Would hang me high on gallows tree.

"My mother, stung with grief as sore,
"Would sell me, she, to a foreign shore.

"And so they sold me for the bell
"Is in St. Mary's heard to knell.

"As struck that bell its one first stroke,
"My wretched mother's heart it broke.

"They sold me into a distant land,
"And so I came to your Grace's hand-"

"But tell me, Hyldestlil, my child,
"How he, that knight so fine, was styled?"

"Sir Hyldebrand that gallant's name,
"Who won my heart and wrought my shame."

"What! Hyldebrand? has he so done?
"And that is e'en my youngest son.

"If Hyldebrand has caused thy pain,
"Then he shall make thee glad again."

"Queen, o Queen, this rending ache!
"It cannot be — My heart will break."

She lay on the Queen's lap and wept.
Until with tears her kirtle dripp'd.

Sobbing on the Queen's breast she lay,
Until her bursting heart gave way.

In rode Sir Hyldebrand, and saw,
As e'en they laid her out on straw.

"Hark, Hyldebrand, my dearest son,
"There lies thy dearest, dead and gone."

"And dead is she to me so dear?
"Then longer tarry I not here."

Against a rock he stayed his sword.
And through his heart the weapon bored.

poems.title: Sir Peter and Dame Margaret
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Peter it was, a wealthy knight.
On pilgrimage went to Rome,
And Margaret left, his graceful wife,
To tarry the while at home.

But when he returned from Rome again,
That gallant and wealthy knight,
His wife Dame Margaret went not oat
To bid him, her lord, alight

He mounted the stair to the ladies' bower,
Mid matrons and maidens stood;
Dame Margaret only rose not up,
So gloomy she was of mood.

They fain, those matrons and maids, would know,
How fared Sir Peter at Rome,
And he. Sir Peter, about his wife.
How she too had fared at home.

"Tis well that I fared in foreign lands
"Through wintery frost and rain,
"But tell me why Margaret came not out
"To welcome me home again/'

Sir Peter, as over his board he sat,
Thus darkly began to rime;
"Now here in my house there serves a swain
"Was born at a luckless time.

"I planted and nurs'd in my garden ground
"The lily and blushing rose;
"But spite of my care amidst my flowers
"A weed in my border grows.

"I planted and nursed in my garden ground
"Each pleasant and lovely bloom,
"But sprung has there up a noxious weed,
"While I was delayed at Rome.

"A stag has housed in my fenced yard,
"He treads on my flowers so bright;
"He thinks to destroy the only plant,
"That once was my heart's delight"

Sir Peter he sits at his table's head,
Sits riming a bitter strain;
Dame Margaret paces the chamber floor,
So racked is her heart with pain.

The Dame retires to her bower aloft,
And deeply she feels her crime;
In sobbing and sighs she vents her grief,
So keen is Sir Peter's rime.

She quits her work, and in gilded chest
Lays scissors and broider'd lace,
And goes to the room, where sits her lord.
And stands before the deis.

"O grant me a favour, my noble lord,
"Nor be my request denied;
"I fain would go to my father's house,
"Tonight thither I would ride.

"For news is told me that he is sick,
"And lies at the point of death,
"Nor would I for all the gold I own
"Not list to his latest breath."

"If 'tis to thy father that thou wilt go,
"That boon I will not deny;
"And if thou stayest a whole year round,
"As happy alone live I.

"Aye, if thou stayest a whole year round,
"And if thou shalt stay there two,
"And if thy lifelong, I grant thee leave
"As pleases thyself to do."

"My father he gave me, my wedding day,
"Five carriages bright with gold,
"I prythee, Sir Peter, my gracious lord,
"That one of them I may hold."

"The day thou camest from home to me,
"He carriages gave thee five,
"But forth, Dame Margaret, forth on foot,
"Not one of them thou shalt drive."

Dame Margaret left her lord, and went
In safety to place her store;
In casket and chest she lock'd her gold.
But friend she had now no more.

Dame Margaret down to the drawbridge went,
And gazed on the towers so red,
"Lord God, look down on a poor lone wife,
"With grief I shall soon be dead."

Her bundle of keys Sir Peter took,
And laid in his daughter's hand;
"Thy mother thou never shalt see again,
"Or listen to her command."

His daughter with maidenly grace replied.
For well she her duty knew;
"Indeed, my father, the truth I tell,
"Full loth were I that to do."

Dame Margaret came to her father's house
As red as a rose in bloom,
And all that were there, came gaily forth
To bid her a welcome home.

Her father went to the courtyard gate
So hearty and gay of cheer;
"My daughter Margaret, welcome home!
"How gladly I see thee here!

"Right welcome to me, my graceful child!
"My daughter, and none but she!
"And how does thy lord and husband fare,
"The gallant Sir Peter, he?"

"'Tis well that the Knight Sir Peter fares,
"He's newly return'd from Home;
"A sad and a luckless day was that,
"He took me to share his home/'

"I gave thee for husband as brave a man,
"As over on earth was seen,
"And thine is the fault, and thine alone,
"If any thing's come between,"

"You gave me for husband as brave a man
"As walks in the light of day,
"But what has happened to mar our peace
"Too well do my cheeks betray.

"You gave me for dowry both fertile land
"And castles with moated wall,
"But now whatever has marr'd our peace,
"'Tis he is the cause of all.

"Sir Peter has tarried so long at Rome,
"And there he has learnt to rime,
"And when he entered his house again,
"For both was a dismal time."

"Now list to my voice, my daughter dear,
"And this is the rede I give;
"We'll build thee a cloister, where all thy days
"In happiness thou shalt live/'

"And though a cloister you build for me
"Henceforth to the end of time
"I never shall find my peace therein,
"Till pardons me God my crime."

"Then off with thee, Margaret, daughter mine
"And out of my sight away!
"Nor ever again to rest thy head
"Come hither at close of day."

"Yet" answer'd her mother with tearful eyes,
For pity had touch'd her heart,
"Here let her remain this single night,
"Tomorrow again depart."

"Twas late, and the cheerful day had closed,
And fallen the misty dew,
As up from her seat Dame Margaret rose
And off to her bed withdrew. "

As soon as had risen the morning sun,
And daylight abroad had shed,
Dame Ingerlille mounted the chamber stair,
And went to her daughter's bed.

She came to the room, Dame Ingerlille,
Where Margaret's body lay.
For stretched on her bed she found her there
As cold and as pale as clay.

With sorrow her heart had burst in twain,
And so had the guilty died;
Sir Peter courted a wealthy maid,
And won her to be his bride.

poems.title: John Rand's Courtship
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Ride once across to Dovre Fell,
There heroes drain the goblet well.

'Twas there had drunk his fill John Hand,
Nor less the wealthy Rosenvand.

They sat at chess, and, While they play'd.
They pass'd their jokes on many a maid.

"But hark! there's one, my Rosenvand,
"The chastest maid in all the land.

"She's heavenly fair, a peerless wife,
"But wooing her may cost thy life.

"Now, Rosenvand, dear comrade mine,
"Let's ride and see this maid so fine."

They up and saddled each his steed,
And off to the maid's abode with speed.

They reach'd the mill-stream, cross'd its flood,
'Twas eddying waves of crimson blood.

"But hark, John Rand, my comrade dear,
"What means this wondrous business here?"

"'Tis blood of knights shed all to waste,
"Who came to woo this maid so chaste."

"Then hark, John Rand, let's draw the rein,
"And ride in safety home again."

"I fear not, I, to risk my life,
"And hap what may, I'll see the wife."

They rode and reach'd the palisade.
Of bloody swords they found it made;

And stuck on every stake therein
They saw the head of a deadman grin.

"But hark, John Hand, my comrade dear,
"What means this wondrous business here?"

"Tis heads of knights, so brave and true,
"Who came the gentle maid to woo."

"Then hark, John Rand, let's draw the rein,
"And ride in safety home again."

"I fear not, I, to risk my life,
"And hap what may, I'll see the wife."

They rode and reach'd the castle gate.
Where at her ease the maiden sate.

"But how so madly bold are ye,
"As dare to come and visit me?"

"The cause, fair maid, that here we came,
"Is your great worth and beauty's fame.

"We would but on a lady gaze,
"Whom far and wide all vie to praise."

"Welcome, my stout, my brave John Rand!
"None else than you shall have my hand.

"There pleasures me one thing alone,
"Such daring mood as you have shown.

"The rest that here besieged my gate,
"Were cowards all, and met their fate."

And in that knight and lady went,
And many an hour in revel spent.

poems.title: Little Christel and Her Captive Bridegroom
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Upstood fair Christel, left her bower
Her bead wrapt in her cloak,
And went to her troopers' banquet ball,
And greeted them and spoke.

'Hail, gallant troopers! here ye sit
"And gaily drain the can,
"For Holsterland we march at dawn
"To fetch my trothplight man."

" Before the king of Holsterland
Fell Christel on her knee;
"I'll for my bridegroom give my gold,
"And all my ready fee."

"Thou shalt not get for gold or coin
"Thy bridegroom from my hands,
"Until I have thy father's house,
"And forest, where it stands.'

"Thou shalt not get my father's house,
"Nor yet the forest round;
"Nor ever get one stake thereof,
"While I am alive and sound.

"And if my bridegroom I get not
"For gold and ready fee,
"I'll set your Holster house on fire,
"Nor leave you time to flee."

"But, little Christel, hark, ray maid,
"Thou'rt strangely bold of tone!
"Where stand then all thy gallant men?
"Thou'rt surely nut alone?"

"So small and young as still I am,
"I lead my troops afield;
"Twelve thousand maidens march with me,
"And bear a spear and shield."

Up stood the King of Holsterland,
And out of window gazed;
Twelve thousand troopers, stout and tall,
In burnish'd armour blazed.

Then call'd his page the Holster King,
And thus was heard to say;
"Let little Christel's bridegroom free,
"And that without delay."

Bravo, fair Christel! thus in arms
Her faith did she maintain,
And brought to her kingdom bravely won
Her bridegroom back again.

poems.title: Sir Olave and Fair Mettelille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
As home Sir Lave rode from town,
To welcome him ran his daughter down.

"O welcome, my father, home from Ting!
"Now enter and tell me the news you bring."

"In every month the news is rife,
"That thou art to be Sir Olave's wife/'

"If pledged me the knight his hand indeed,
"God bless him, and well his purpose speed."

But soon Sir Olave on sickbed lay.
And sent his page for his trothplight may.

"Go bid her her virtue and love to show,
"And visit me now that I lie so low."

Fair Mett in mantle wrapped her head,
And up to her mother's chamber sped.

"O tell me, mother, if dare a maid
"Go visit a lover on sickbed laid?"

"No shame but honour deserves the maid,
"Who visits a lover on sickbed laid."

Fair Mett in tears led out her steed,
And mounted and rode to the knight's with speed.

And soon she came to his courtyard gate,
Where wrapped in her robes his mother sate.

"Dame Sidselille, hail! and kindly say,
"How fares my trulove, your son, today?"

"III fares your trulove and knight so dear, —
"Sir Olave is dead and on his bier/'

She trusted her not, nor heard her more,
But rode and stopp'd at Sir Olave's door.

So soon as he saw her before him stand,
The Knight to welcome her gave his hand:

Then beckoned a nimble pageboy near;
"Go fetch me the gilded casket here."

The casket upon his knee he placed,
And her with its precious treasure graced.

Gold rings and bracelets he gave her nine,
That glitter'd with jewels' costly shine.

He gave her his broadest brooches too;
To see it his mother angry grew.

"But gently, my son, and give not all,
"But think on my brothers and sisters small."

"My brothers have homesteads and land beside,
"But ne'er at my table has sat my bride.

"My sisters have cornfields and grassy lea,
"My dearest came never to bed with me."

Then round to the wall he turn'd his head.
And sank,' and at midnight hour was dead.

Sir Olave was laid in his silent grave,
And Mett her hand to his brother gave.

poems.title: Sir Lowman and Sir Thor
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Lowman rode to a distant land,
Aye! though ye dance so fair and fast
Wooed Ingerlille, and won her hand.
She must and shall be mine at last.

"But, Ingerlille, my dearest, say,
"How long you'll wait, while I am away."

"Faithful to you for winters eight,
"If needs I must. I'll gladly wait."

When past were all these eight long years,
Sad was the maid with doubt and fears.

Her friends and brothers all agree
That she this year shall wedded be.

"To rich Sir Thor we'll give her hand,
"More gold has he than Lowman laud.

"More gold Sir Thor wears on his breast,
"Than Lowman keeps in treasure chest.

"More gold he wears on arm and hand,
"Than worth is all Sir Lowman's land."

Five days in banqueting they spent,
Nor yet to bed the lady went.

Nine days they drank from morn till eve,
Yet still her seat she would not leave.

But when there closed another day,
They took her then by force away.

"If to my bed I needs must go,
"First let me mount and look below."

Up on the balcony went all,
And ships they saw both great and small.

"Those fluttering sails of blue and brown,
"Those very sails my hands have sewn.

"Those varied colours tell their tale,
"That yonder floats Sir Lowman's sail.

"Ride, brother Peter, to the sea!
"Haste thee, and show thy love for me."

Sir Peter rode and reached the strand.
As came Sir Lowman's ship to land.

"Peter, my friend, my dearest still,
"How fares my trulove Ingerlille?"

"Well doth she fare, thy trothplight may,
"And drinks her marriage feast today/'

"Seven years did I on sickbed lie,
"And pity 'twas I could not die.

"Curse on the sea and billows blue,
"They did not break my ship in two!"

"Sir Lowman, hush! curse not thy life;
"This evening she shall be thy wife.

"Haste now, but keep thee calm and still;
"For true thou 'It find thine Ingerlille."

"Hark thee! let me thy palfrey take,
"And thee I'll lend my gilded snake."

Sir Lowman quick the horse bestrode.
And fleet as any bird he rode.

The bridal torch, e'en as he came.
Blazed at her door its ruddy flame.

With joyous haste Sir Lowman sped,
And sat him on the bridal bed.

"Off with ye, bid Sir Thor good night',
"Say, I'll sleep with his bride so bright.

"Tell him, my sister he may keep,
"But leave his bride with me to sleep.

"Seven tuns of mead and eight of beer
"I'll give him towards his wedding cheer."

"Up now, Sir Thor!" the pageboy cried,
"Sir Lowman sleeps beside thy bride."

"And that be may, I'll not repine,
"For his she was, ere she was mine."

"With thy fair bride he means to sleep,
"But says, his sister thou may'st keep.

"Seven tuns of mead and eight of beer
"He gives thee towards thy wedding cheer."

"My hand to his sister here I plight;
"My bride may sleep with him tonight."

Their wedding feast with jokes and fun
They kept together both in one:

And changed their griefs to mirth and jest,
For each had her he loved the best.

poems.title: Torkild Trundeson
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Young Torkild as brave a swain is he,
As sword ever girt on side,
And every day, that dawns in th' east.
He mounts on his horse to ride.

He rides as early to greenwood glade,
As twitter the birds on tree,
And Adelaide, gentle maid, betrothes,
And daintily fair is she.

He rides to Sir Lave's to hunt the deer
That over his forest roam.
And eke to Adelaide plights his vow
To wed her and bring her home.

And there with her Torkild stay'd a night,
And there he stay'd for two.
And nobody ask'd, why there he came,
And what he did nobody knew.

None ask'd Sir Torkild why there he came,
And what he did nobody knew.
Except fair Adelaide/s waiting maid.
And Torkild's servants two.

His bride to his heart he warmly press'd,
And talked to her long with glee:
Sad pity it is, when those must part,
Who fain together would be.

"But, Torkild," up spake the waiting maid.
In duty and honour taught;
"Take care that upon my lady's fame
"No stain of disgrace be brought."

"Nay," answered young Torkild Trundeson,
With solemnest tone and face;
"Nay, trust me, Eline, thou faithful maid,
"I bring her to no disgrace."

Young Torkild has bidden them cut her clothes,
As e'en she would have them made;
And every seam in his lady's dress
With tissue of gold belaid.

So rich with gold and so tastefully wrought
Her robes to the bride were shown;
"God's blessing" said she," on the tailors all,
"Whose fingers the dress have sewn!

"God bless them, the tailors, all and each,
"Who hand on the dress did lay!
"God bless above all my Trundeson,
The cost of it he must pay!"

The king at his court a diet held,
Bade every knight attend,
Yet came not Torkild Trundeson,
Till just at the diet's end.

It was on a Sunday, after mass,
That solemnest holy tide.
Young Torkild Trundeson mounted horse,
Away to the king to ride.

Young Torkild he rode within the court.
The foremost his swains among;
The king from his lips would hear the truth;
"Where tarried hast thou so long?"

"I rode to the wood with hawk and hound,
"The game for a while I chased,
"And every sportsman, who hunts the deer,
"Is tempted the time to waste."

"Thou ridest so long in greenwood sLaw
"A chasing Sir Lave's game,
"The deer, thou lovest so well to chase,
"The hunter himself will maim.

"Some better pastime I'll find for thee
"Than chasing Sir Lave's deer;
"Sir Esbern Snar and thou shalt hence,
"And over to Iceland steer."

Then answered young Torkild Trundeson,
With courteous humble mien;
"I gladly would now at home remain,
"As oft as I there have been."

The king of the Danes his answer heard,
And struck with his hand the board,
And moody and silent he stood awhile
To think upon Torkild's word.

"I ween there are those will pity feel,
"And often will think on thee;
"Make ready, young Torkild Trundeson,
"To Iceland to sail for me."

Right deftly could Torkild Trundeson
His words to the purpose bend;
"'Tis you are my lord, and I your swain,
"I go whither you may send."

It was on a Sunday, the hour of prayer,
A holy and solemn fete,
He sent his swain to the village priest
To beg him for him to wait.

Uprose young Torkild Trundeson,
Bade saddle his trusty gray,
And rode across to the selfsame church,
Where Adelaide went to pray.

He entered the church, young Trundeson,
And up to the altar drew.
And greeted the ladies and gentle maids
With honour to ladies due.

He talk'd to the matrons and eke the maids,
As each in her turn came near,
He talk'd to Adelaide first and last.
For she was the one most dear.

"Now who for the king to Iceland sails?
"Say, mother, who that shall be."
"None other than Torkild Trundeson,
"The gallant so dear to thee."

"I care for Torkild no more nor less
"Than just any other swain:
"God grant that I live the happy day
To see him at home again!")

The holy mass to the end they sung,
The rest of the people went,
But still some moments in sweet discourse
Those lovers so gladly spent.

"Now, Adelaide, listen, my gentle bride,
"No reason hast thou to wail,
"I leave thee for but a few short months,
"And only to Iceland sail.

"So short a voyage is quickly sped,
"To Iceland the time is brief."
"Yet seemeth the shortest time too long,
"To those who are left in grief."

And only when Torkild mounted horse
Did Adelaide leave his side,
And turned her back to her home again,
And bitterly wept and sigh'd.

With sorrowing hearts that youthful pair
Had bidden each other adieu,
And soon unmoor'd was the gallant ship,
And kindly the breeze that blew.

No more than four of his faithful swains
Took Torkild across the main;
"Ye others will stay to guard my bride,
"Till hither I come again."

They hoisted on high the silken sail
To float from the gilded mast;
From Denmark to Iceland's distant shore
In only two months they pass'd.

The wind blew steady, the ship sped on,
The waves were sporting around.
But moody sat Torkild Trundeson,
Nor utter'd his lips a sound.

Then up Sir Esbern Snar spake,
And slily he framed his speech;
"One would not have thought the sea so rough,
"As Trundeson's cheek to bleach."

"I'm ready to sail a sea with thee,
"And a thousand guilders stake;
"And ready with thee to break a spear
"For all good lasses sake/'

They came to the port, and anchor threw
Ont into the glittering sand;
Sir Esbern Snar and Trundeson
Were foremost to leap on land.

They stopp'd as they crossed the castle yard,
Around them their cloaks to fling,
And up to the lofty chamber went,
And bow'd them before the king.

"Hail King of Iceland, in royal state
"Here sitting at banquet board!
"The king of the Danes a brief has sent,
"And in it his royal word."

The king of Iceland the letter brake,
And when he had read it all,
Took out from his pouch a little knife,
And cut it to morsels small.

And wrathful the king of Iceland spake.
The more he the matter weighed;
"Has ever been known a swain so poor
"To wed with so rich a maid?

"Now listen, young Torkild Trundeson,
"I'm well acquainted with thee;
"Seven barrels of silver it was so bright,
"Thy father assess on me.

"Seven barrels of silver it was so bright,
"Thy father assessed on me,
"And eight as full of the purest gold
"I take not to pay for thee."

"But," answer'd young Torkild Trundeson,
As boldly as he might dare,
"The guilt of wrongs that a father wrought,
"Tis hard that a son should bear"

"Nay, hark thee, young Torkild Trundeson,
"B'or how does the proverb run?
"The little pigs pay, and make amends,
"For what th' old sow has done."

"But," answered young Torkild Trundeson,
"There is also an ancient saw,
"That smallest puppies in time grow up
"With sharpset teeth in their jaw."

The troopers they all their furlough gain'd
Off homeward to wend their way.
Save only young Torkild Trundeson,
And he must in Iceland stay.

The troopers they all might go on board.
And each to his trulove hie.
But he young Torkild should stay behind.
And down in the dungeon die.

Young Torkild Trundeson him they seized.
And into a dungeon threw;
His thoughts were on ladies and maidens fair.
But most on his bride so true.

The king's men all stood looking on
In anger and grief around,
As Torkild, their comrade, so was seiz'd,
And left in a dungeon bound.

Then up spake Torkild's own small page,
Array'd in a kirtle red,
"I'll either with Torkild home return,
"Or stay with him here till dead."

"Now listen, Sir Esbern, and kindly do
"The favour I ask of thee;
"To Adelaide give a thousand adieus,
"And pray her to think on me.

"And tell her to dance as she used, and sing,
"And bid her be blithe and gay;
"I trust to wed her, and bring her home
"In less than a year and day."

Their silken sail on a gilded yard.
They out to the breezes spread.
And thence in less than two short months
They over to Denmark sped.

The gallant Sir Esbern, he it was
The foremost debark'd on land.
And Adelaide, she the gentle maid.
Who gave him her snowy hand.

"Oh welcome, Sir Esbern, welcome home!
"Now tell me, but tell me true;
"How fares young Torkild Trundeson,
"Who sail'd from the land with you?"

"Young Torkild is serving the Iceland king,
"Is serving for rank and fee;
"He sends you, his dearest, a thousand adieus,
"And true to his vows will be.

"He bids you will neither lament nor wail,
"But still be as blithe and gay,
"And trusts to fetch you to share his home
"In less than a year and day."

The gentle Adelaide made reply,
With weeping and downcast eyne;
"Our heavenly father guide our fate,
"That Torkild may yet be mine."

Up answer'd Trundeson's own small page
In kirtle so red array'd;
"He's still upon Iceland's frosty shore
"In dungeon and darkness laid."

"And is then Torkild on Iceland's isle,
"And sitting in dungeon cell?
"For my sake it was, too well I know,
"That him this fate befell.

"In durance is Torkild Trundeson?
"In fetters of iron set?
"I'll venture my own for Torkild's life,
"Him never will I forget."

Sir Stephen Jonson, out near the Sound,
Bade saddle on horse to lay,
"I'll ride to Sir Lave's across the land
"A visit to him to pay.

"My greeting, Sir Lave, noble knight,
"In raiment of sable drest!
"Fair Adelaide give me to be my wife,
"The daughter you love the best."

Then answered Sir Lave, and thus replied.
His thoughts in his bosom pent,
"I first will ask in the ladies' bower,
"If she will herself consent/'

"My greeting, Adelaide, daughter dear!
"In comfort I'd see thee live:
"Sir Stephen has ask'd thee, and e'en to him
"Thy hand I am fain to give."

The gentle Adelaide thus replied,
To God and to man she sware;
"I never had thought upon wedded life,
"Or wish'd for its pains and care."

"The youth," said her mother, "in Iceland lies,
"On whom thy heart is set;
"But him, though home he return again,
"For husband thou shalt not get."

"I care for Torkild no more nor less,
"Than just any other swain:
"(May God in his mercy rule our fate,
"That home he return again!)"

Then answer'd fair Adelaide's waiting maid,
And thus she spake and said;
"Give ye to my lady no other swain,
"Than whom she herself would wed."

"What!" answered Sir Lave, and spake in baste.
So ready of word and deed,
"I give my daughter to whom I will,
"Nor ask of my handmaid rede."

The lady's consent they ask'd no more,
Nor ever had she said yea,
But that day month was a banquet held.
And drunk was her wedding day.

As evening closed, and all in state
The bride to her bed was brought,
Fair Adelaide then and her faithful maid
A crafty device bethought.

"Now listen, Eline, my faithful maid,
"Be bride for the night for me,
"And great the kindness from this day forth
"I lifelong will show to thee."

"Aye," answered the good little maid, Eline,
So faithful she was and true;
"Whatever, my mistress, may be your will,
"I gladly will do for you."

When even had come and th' hour of rest.
Their crafty device they play'd;
The lady she stole from the bridal house,
And left in the bed her maid.

Soon after Sir Stephen Jonson came,
And tapping her lily cheek;
"Say is it on me your heart is bent?
"Be truthful, my dear, and speak."

"Aye/' answer the sly little maid, Eline,
Well feigning her lady's voice,
"Indeed it is you, whom best I love,
"And Torkild is not my choice."

So soon as the early morning dawn'd,
They shifted the parts they play'd;
The lady, she went to the bridal house.
And out of it crept the maid.

When now with its light the rising sun
Had brighten'd the morning hour,
Arose from his couch the Danish king.
And went to the bridal bower.

"Sir Stephen, with silver coin shalt thou
"And ruddiest gold be paid,
"To shroud it in silence, if doubt thou hast,
"Thy lady was not a maid.

"I'll give thee. Sir Stephen, the silver coin,
"I'll give thee a band of gold;
"If any the smallest doubt thou hast,
"Let nothing thereof be told."

"O keep it yourself, the silver coin,
"Keep also your gold so red,
"For she was indeed a loyal maid,
"You gave me yestreen to wed."

"If true is all that thou tellest me,
"And she was a maid indeed,
"The captive, young Torkild Trundeson,
"ShU straight from his bonds be freed."

They drank her marriage in mead and wine,
And gaily they held carouse,
And when in the feast eight days had pass'd,
They led to her home the spouse.

In five month's time came Torkild home,
From Iceland's frosty side,
And learnt that Adelaide, once his own.
Was now Sir Stephen's bride.

It was on a Sunday's early morn,
So holy and good the day.
Young Trundeson forward sent his swains
To beg of the priest to stay.

As Torkild enter'd the church's aisle,
All golden his tresses shone;
How sorry his heart, his face betray'd,
So pallid and woe-begone.

Then asked young Torkild Trundeson,
With reverence due he spake,
"The crown that Adelaide used to wear,
"Who dared from her head to take?"

Then up and answer'd the little page,
To Torkild he thus replied;
"Sir Stephen Jonson he took her crown,
"He dwells on the south-sea side."

The holy mass to the end was sung.
The people had gone their way.
But Torkild to greet his friends and kin
Was fain in the church to stay.

He talk'd with ladies a"d maidens fair,
As each in her turn came near,
He talk'd to Adelaide first and last,
For she was the one most dear.

"And now, my Adelaide, truly say,
"What here I demand of thee,
"If thou of thy choice didst break the troth,
"That once was plighted to me?"

"Ah no!" fair Adelaide thus replied
With truth in her look and tone;
"For that must answer, and not myself,
"My kinsmen and friends alone."

"Now hark thee, Adelaide! hear my words,
"If such be thy wish and will,
"I'll thee and thy husband soon dispart,
"Sir Stephen I'll out and kill."

"Nay, list to me, Torkild Trundeson,
"Though married I was with pain,
"The God who has linked our hands in one,
"He only can part again.

"And list to me, Torkild Trundeson,
"A favour I'll ask of you,
"Mount horse, and up to Sir Peter's ride,
"His daughter so fair to woo.

"Let not your choice on the youngest maid,
"Nor yet on the eldest fall,
"But sue for the gentle Sidselille,
"For she is the best of all.

"Sue you for the.gentle Sidselille,
"For graceful and fair is she,
"And those who have seen her, have often said,
"How much she resembles me."

"For thy sake, Adelaide, so I'll do,
"I will to Sir Peter's go,
"But that I never shall love the maid,
"Too well do I feel and know."

So bade young Torkild Trundeson
To saddle his trusty gray;
"I'll up and off to Sir Peter's ride,
"A visit to him to pay."

"My greeting, Sir Peter, noble knight
"In mantle so richly drest!
"O give me the gentle Sidselille,
"The daughter you love the best."

'Twas thus that the good Sir Peter spake;
He spake as a cautious man;
"I'll first go up to the ladies' bower
"My Sidselille's will to scan.

"God greet thee, my daughter Sidselille,
"In every comfort live!
"Young Torkild has ask'd thee, and e'en to him
"Thy hand I am fain to give."

"Nay" answer'd the gentle Sidselille,
In honour and virtue bred,
"It is not right to betrothe a swain,
"Another would wish to wed."

They let her follow her own desire,
And gladly she answer'd, yea
And soon as a month was fully past,
Th drank their wedding day.

But first went Torkild Trundeson
To ask of his mother rede;
"Who, tell me, should be the chosen dame,
"The one who my bride should lead?"

The mother beneath her mantle smiled,
And thus to her son replied;
"Beg Adelaide once so dear to thee
"Herself to escort thy bride."

He mounted his horse, young Trundeson,
And up to Sir Stephen's rode,
And there at his door in martin pall
Sir Stephen Jonson stood.

"My greeting, Adelaide, lady fair,
"Array'd in so rich a weed,
"O say, wilt thou be the chosen dame,
"The one who my bride shall lead?"

Awhile fair Adelaide silent stood,
Nor what she should answer knew;
Sir Stephen Jonson it was, said 'yea',
"And that thou art free to do."

Two robes of the richest silk she cut,
Of sindal two more beside,
Not one of the guests had brought such gifts
To honour the gentle bride.

Not one of so many wedding guests
So handsome a gift would give:
She gave to the bride the very swain,
With whom she herself would liv.

She mounted, the gentle Adelaide,
And rode to meet the bride.
And crimson sindal and costly silk
Was hung on her horse's side.

They rode across the grassy fields,
And through the green-wood glade;
And on her saddlebow all the while.
Young Trundeson's hand was laid.

When evening came, and the hour of rest,
To bed they led the bride.
But still with Adelaide Torkild stood
In tender discourse aside.

"But all the longer we tarry here,
"The worse will matters be,
"And thee will reproach thy fair young bride,
"My lord be as wroth with me."

"So God protect me and all my days
"From sorrow and anguish keep!
"I rather would still with thee discourse,
"Than go with my bride to sleep."

Fair Adelaide she the curtains closed,
But griev'd at her heart and sigh'd;
A silken coverlet o'er them threw;
"Would Heaven I were the bride!"

Fair Adelaide left them there to rest,
And bolted the chamber door;
And him and his bride she wish'd Good night
A thousand times o'er and o'er.

Sir Stephen Jonson was deadly sick,
And lay on his bed so low,
And spake, as his gentle Adelaide
Went anxiously to and fro.

"Unkindly with us the Lord has dealt,
"That children were none at all."
"That profits, said she, thine own rich kin;
"On me will the damage fall."

Sir Stephen sicker and sicker grew,
And turn'd to the chamber side,
And ere there another hour had struck,
He sank on his bed and died.

In came to the hall a little page
Was clad in a kirtle red;
A Pater noster he pray'd for him.
And told them the knight was dead

Young Torkild Trundeson shut with joy
His chequer board all so bright,
And pray'd to Heaven might rest in peace
The soul of the buried knight.

Three months had pass'd, and Sidselille
The loveliest infant bare;
But sad is the tale, in childbed died
The mother herself so fair.

The gentle Adelaide benches spread,
And warmly to God she pray'd;
"O grant me in less than a year and day
"Nor widow to be, nor maid."

Then ordered young Torkild Trundeson
To saddle without delay;
"To gentle Adelaide's house I'll ride,
"A visit to her to pay."

He mounted his horse and reached her house,
And thus to the lady spake;
"Permit me, Adelaide, this one night
"My lodging with you to take."

"Right welcome. Sir Torkild Trundeson,
"Dismount from your horse, and rest
"Henceforward you here shall find your home,
"And need not to be my guest,"

And so were at last those lovers met
With mutual great delight;
Their only sorrow to find so short
So pleasant a summer night.

The gentle Adelaide, while alone
She still in her chamber stayed.
Had given to one of Torkild's swains
Eline her waiting maid.

Then order'd young Torkild Trundeson
To saddle without delay;
"I'll up the land to Sir Lave's ride,
"A visit to him to pay."

As came young Torkild Trundeson,
And enter'd within the gate,
There stood Sir Lave before the door
All clad in his dress of state.

"Now hail. Sir Lave, good noble knight,
"In raiment of sable drest!
"Fair Adelaide give me to be my wife,
"The daughter you love the best."

Sir Lave with caution his answer gave.
His thoughts in his bosom pent;
"I first will ask in the ladies' bower
"If she will herself consent."

"My greeting Adelaide, daughter dear,
"In every comfort live,
"Young Torkild has ask'd thee, and e'en to him
"Thy hand I would gladly give."

"With needle and scissars and broider'd work
"My living I meant to gain;
"The trouble and care of wedded life
"I wish not to bear again."

"With needle and scissars and broider'd work
"The living to earn is small;
"Nay thou shalt again a husband wed,
"Like other good women all."

Fair Adelaide round to her mother turn'd,
"And smiling so archly said,
"And yet is Torkild the selfsame swain,
"You said' should never wed."

They gain'd fair Adelaide's own consent,
And gladly she answer'd yea
And after a month bad duly pass'd,
They drank her wedding day.

They drank right gaily the wedding feast,
And joyous and glad they were,
And seven, as fair as their hearts could wish,
The children the lady bare.

poems.title: Medelwold and Sidselille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
All in their lofty bower so still
Sat with her mother Sidselille.

Gold web they wove, till on her gown
The drops of milk ran trickling down.

"Dear Sidselille, I'd gladly know,
"How from thy bosom milk should flow?"

"No milk, tho' so you seem to think,
"But mead I had yestre'en to drink."

"But those are things unlike indeed,
"So white is milk, so brown the mead."

"Then, since the truth I cannot hide,
"I'm Medelwold's affianced bride."

"And true is what thou hast even told?
"The armnced thou of Medelwold?

"Then high on gallows hang shall he,
"And blaze below the pile for thee/'

Fair Sidselille in her mantle wrapt
Sped to the chamber where he slept.

She waked him up with gentle knock,
"Rise, Medelwold, the door unlock."

"Appointment I have none to keep,
"Unlock to no one, while I sleep."

"O draw the bar, dear Medelwold,
"My mother has the truth been told;

"And thou, she swears, shalt hang on high,
"And bum on blazing faggots I."

"Nay, hang, that will I not for thee,
"Nor burn below shalt thou for me.

"In casket store thy gold away,
"While I go saddle me my grey."

He wrapp'd her well in purple weed.
And laid her gently upon his steed.

But when they reach'd the grove of rose,
She pray'd she might awhile repose.

"Of length of road dost thou complain?
"Or does the saddle give thee pain?"

"Not of the road do I complain,
"It is the saddle gives me pain."

His mantle blue he soon has spread,
"Fair Sidselille, make that thy bed."

"O that my waiting maid were here!
"Without some help my death is near."

"Thy maids are far away from thee,
"Nor other servant here but me."

"I'd rather lay me down and die,
"Than now let any man be nigh."

"Nay, bind thy kerchief round my head,
"And I will serve in nurse's stead."

"O for a draught of water clear,
"My sad and aching heart to cheer!"

Young Medelwold, so good and true,
For water took her silver'd shoe;

And through the thicket broke his way,
To where a distant streamlet lay.

Deep in the dale he reached the spring.
And there two nightingales heard sing:

"With two small infants by her side
"Your lady in the grove has died."

He heard, but heeded not their lay.
And hastened back his weary way;

But when he found the grove again,
Too true had been their doleful strain.

He dug a grave, was broad and deep,
And laid all three therein to sleep;

But seem'd, while still he lingered near,
Beneath his foot their cries to hear.

So on a rock he stay'd his sword,
And through his heart the weapon bored:

And there with her, his bride so true.
Now buried lies her lover too.

poems.title: Sir Tonne
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Tonn forth from Alsey rode,
His sword slung at his side,
Alike on tented field and sea
A hero stout and tried.

Sir Tonn off to the green-wood rode
To chase the hind and hare,
And there the Dwarf-King's daughter met
With other maidens fair.

She sat with golden harp in hand
Beneath a linden tree;
"See hither the knight Sir Tonn rides;
"I'll make him come to me.

"Sit down, sit down, my maidens all,
"And thou, my page, be still;
"I'll play a rune that shall with flowers
"The field and meadow till."

She play'd a rune on golden harp,
And, when she touch'd the string.
The wild bird sitting on the bough
His song forgot to sing.

The wild bird sitting on the bough
His song forgot to sing;
The hart that in the green-wood skipped
With joy forgot to spring.

Charm'd with her runes the meadow bloom'd,
And greener grew the wood;
In vain Sir Tonn spurr'd his steed,
Move he no longer cou'd.

Sir Tonne sprang from off his horse,
No farther wish'd to ride,
And to the Dwarfs fair daughter went,
And sate him at her side.

"All hail, Dwarfs daughter, lovely maid!
"Of flowers the peerless rose!
"No mortal man thy beauty sees,
"But straight with passion glows.

"Hear me. Dwarfs daughter, beauteous maid!
"Plight thou thy love to me,
"And all the days, I have to live,
"I'll faithful be to thee."

"Ah stay. Sir Tonn, gallant knight,
"Nor me thy homage bring;
"My hand another lover claims,
"Our own Dwarf-people's king.

"My father dwells in mountain cave
"His courtiers round him stand;
"My mother dwells there too and plays
"With gold in lily hand.

"Myself I've stolen from out the cave
"My golden harp to play;
"But in a month my bridegroom comes
"To fetch me hence away."

"Before the Dwarf enjoy the luck
"Thee for his bride to take,
"I'll risk in fight my life for thee,
"My sword in shivers break."

"Ah! nay'' the dwarfs fair daughter said,
"From idle hopes refrain;
"A fairer maid thou well may'st find,
"Me thou shalt never gain.

"Now haste, Sir Tonn, gallant knight,
"And prithee speed thy pace;
"For both my father and bridegroom come
"Within a little space."

Then peer'd her mother from out the cave,
Would know who there might be;
And saw Sir Tonn, where he stood
Beneath the linden tree.

Out from the cave her mother came
With fierce and angry mien;
"But how then, Ulfhild, daughter mine,
"Here in the wood so green?

"'Twere better in thy mountain cave
"To work thy bride-Attire,
"Than here to sit beneath a tree,
"And strike the golden lyre.

"The King of Dwarfs didst thou betrothe,
"To him thine honour plight,
"Nor oughtest thus with runic strain
"To've bound yon gallant knight."

The Dwarf-wife went with all her train
Within the cavern door;
And with her went Sir Tonn too,
But saw and heard no more.

For o'er a chair she spread for him
A costly silken cloak
And on it sat the knight in trance,
At cockcrow first awoke.

The Dwarfs wife call'd her little page,
And hade him bring the hook,
And therewithal from off the knight
Her daughter's spell she took.

"Awake! I've thee for honour's sake
"Unbound from Runic spell;
"And full securely may'st thou now
"My daughter's art repel.

"And further still, Sir Knight, to prove
"What love for thee I bear,
"I'll wis a gentle bride for thee,
"A rose of beauty rare.

"For I was born of Christian folk,,
"Tho' dwarfs took me to wean;
"My sister, lady Adeline,
"Of Iceland is the queen.

"Her daughter once was stolen away,
"And vain her mother's search,
"For she no more to dance may go,
"No longer drive to church.

"E'en from her window's loop to look
"That maiden may not dare,
"Nor with the King may play at chess,
"Unless the Queen is there.

"No man, except that aged king,
"She ever yet has seen;
"And nightly locks her chamber door
"Herself the cautious Queen.

"In Upsal sits this captive maid,
"And Ermeline is hight;
"With iron bolt and massy chain
"Her door is fastened tight.

"The aged king to a brother's son,
"Designs to leave his land;
"And he, young Allevod, when king,
"Will claim the maiden's hand.

"Now horse and saddle give I thee,
"And spurs of gold beside;
"Thy way thou 'It find, tho' ne'er so wild
"The track, thou hast to ride.

"I'll give thee too a dress to wear
"With seams of golden braid;
"And on thine arm a broad red shield
"With jewels all inlaid.

"I'll give thee a precious golden band,
"And runes therein are bound,
"That when thou speakest, every word
"As from a book shall sound."

Then out her daughter Ulfhild came,
"Such love she bare the knight;
"And I'll give thee a trusty sword,
"And hence all burnish'd bright.

"And never shalt thou miss thy way,
"As wild as it may be,
"Or ever any foe engage,
"But gain the victory.

"Whatever track thy ship shall sail,
"Safe thou shalt come to land,
"Nor e'er receive in battle-fray
"A wound from mortal hand."

Now came her mother Thorelille,
And sparkling wine she pour'd;
"Haste from our cavern, haste away,
"Ere home returns my lord."

Sir Tonn through the green-wood rode,
And brightly gleam'd his spear,
" As riding towards his mountain cave
The Dwarf himself drew near.

"Well met. Sir Tonn, gallant knight,
"Right nobly steps thy horse;
"Now, tell me, is thy journey long?
"And whither bent thy course?"

"It is a courting I will ride,
"To win a blooming rose,
"And dare to couch the spear I bear
"Against the doughtiest foes."

"Ride on, Sir Tonn, noble knight,
"' "Ride on in peace, good bye;
"In Upsal lives a champion bold,
"Thy strength will gladly try."'

Sir Tonne rode to essay his luck
And came to Swedish land.
And saw beneath a spreading tree
Nine knights in armour stand.

Each bare a helmet on his head,
A shield before his breast,
And at his side a trusty sword.
And glittering lance in rest.

"There stand ye nine stout Swedish knights,
"Will ye your valour prove?
"For ruddy gold, or glory fight,
"Or for your lady love?"

Up spake the first. Prince Allevod,
So proud was he and bold:
"Enough have we and crave no more
"Of glory or of gold.

"A noble maid at Upsal sits,
"And Ermeline her name;
"For her sake let us break a spear,
"See which her hand shall claim."

Their first charge rode with all their force
Those gallant heroes twain,
And spears fell shiver'd on the grass,
And shields were rent in twain.

Again a second charge they rode,
And that with greater force,
And Allevod with broken neck
Was thrown from off his horse.

Much vex'd were they, the Swedish knights,
And tried to venge his fall,
But fortune did not prove their friend.
Sir Tonn beat them all.

Fain o'er their shoulders did the knights
Their purple mantles fling,
And mounted up to the lofty hall,
And stood before the king.

"A Jutish knight is come to land
"With raiment pied and striped,
"Eight knights he has wounded on the field,
"So ill for them he piped.

"Eight knights he has wounded on the field,
"And left them halt and lame;
"And Allevod, thy nephew, kill'd,
"Curse on his Jutish name!"

Then answered them the aged king,
All with his long gray hair;
"Avenge me on the plaided Jute,
"And sable ye shall wear."

Out rode those Swedish warriors all,
And thought a prize to gain,
But soon their laughter turn'd to woe.
And all their joy to pain,

Their calf-ekin dress they still must wear,
Nor sable earn'd that day,
And daily still must wrap their limbs
In cloth of wadmal gray.

Much were those Swedish warriors vex'd,
And mournful plaint began;
"There dares none in the world to strive
"Against this Jutish man."

Sir Tonne he to Upsal rode
With glory clad and grace;
The Swedish warriors dared no more
That doughty knight to face.

He kill'd the bear, that watched the door,
He broke the bar in twain;
And her released, the lovely maid.
So long in thrall had lain.

The Swedish courtiers all were still,
No word escaped their tongue;
A grudging grim consent the Jute
"From all of them had wrung.

He worsted all those Swedish knights,
The Lion and eke the Bear,
And enter'd into the lofty bower,
To see that peerless fair. -

"Welcome, Sir Tonn', gallant knight!
"Right welcome thou to me I
"For, if I should the truth avow,
"I've sorely long'd for thee.

"'Twas told me while a little child,
"A foreign knight should come,
"And Allevod my gaoler slay,
"And take me with him home.

"And now, Sir Tonne, gallant knight,
"Be true and good to me;
"For in the world is other none
"I rather wed than thee."

Then spake Sir Tonne, gallant knight,
And clasp'd the lovely fair;
"Forsake thee nevermore will I,
"By th' Highest name I swear."

He carried off the willing maid,
And all her treasure top.
And sail'd with her to Denmark home,
Each still to the other true.

He took her back to his Jutland home,
And led her to her bower,
And Alsey people all with joy
Embraced that blooming flower.

The knight Sir Tonne's love for her
From day to day increased,
And soon as thirty days were past.
He made his marriage feast.

In Iceland, when the news was brought.
That Ermeline was found.
Were greatly joy'd the King and Queen,
And all their people round.

The King he sent from Iceland word
To pray Sir Tonn come,
And share with him his northern realm,
And there to make his home.

Sir Tonn launch his gallant ship,
Spread sail on gilded mast,
And with his bride reached Iceland's shore,
Ere two whole months were past.

It was Sir Tonn gallant knight.
Who steer'd his ship to land,
And Iceland's aged King and Queen,
Who waited on the strand.

"Welcome, Sir Tonne, gallant knight,
"To this our foreign shore!
"My island kingdom far and wide
"Shall all be thine, and more."

The aged King resigned his realm.
And had Sir Tonne crown'd.
And soon was all the island his.
And all the lands around.

Now is Sir Tonn gallant knight
A happy man, I ween;
He rules in Iceland far and wide.
And sleeps with Ermeline.

He's now become a mighty king.
Whom towns and forts obey,
And never wish the Swedish knights
To see him come their way.

poems.title: Fair Ingeborg's Disguise
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Ingeborg let clothes be made,
"I'll try," said she, "a courtier's trade."
Such secret sorrow she feels for him.

She mounted horse in livery drest,
"I'll ride and be the Prince's guest."
Such secret sorrow &c.

"O Prince, give ear to what I say,
"And deign to take me into pay/'

"A clever horseboy much I need,
"Had I but room to stall his steed.

"Yet well may his with mine agree,
"And he shall share my bed with me."

Three years to serve the Prince she stay'd,
And no one knew she was a maid.

Three years she serv'd in horseboy's stead,
The foals to grass and water led;

She drove them back again to stall,
A boy they thought her, one and all.

She pleas'd the Ladies old and young.
So tender were the lays she sung.

Like threads of gold her ringlets shone,
'Twas that the Prince's favour won.

But while she plied about the court,
Her hair grew pale, and breathing short.

And strange to see such change in her,
She could not buckle on a spur.

And what was stranger still, they saw.
Her sword she could no longer draw.

The Prince he bade five maidens call.
None lovelier found among them all.

With purple mantle round her thrown
They took her into the house of stone.

And soon, reclined on bolsters blue,
She sat there nursing infants two.

In came the Prince, and great his joy
To see with twins his stable-boy.

He gently stroked her pallid face;
"This crown upon thy temples place,

"Henceforth art thou my wedded wife,
And true to thee I'll be for life."

poems.title: Ingefred, Torluf's Daughter
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Lav and good Sir Iver Blay,
So blithe and so kind of heart,
Two comrades were they, whose mutual love
No force could ever part.

'Twas once at the royal board they sat,
As I have the story heard,
And chatted about the pretty girls
With many a pleasant word.

And boldly the young Sir Lave rose,
On table struck hi? hand;
"There's not a maiden in all the world,
"My tongue could long withstand."

"Well done! but," answered Sir Iver Blay,
And much at his boasting smiled,
"I think that I know one pretty girl,
' "Were not so soon beguiled.

"Sir Torlufs daughter so well I know,
"I bet she is not cajoled;
"Try all your wheedling power of words,
"Or all your glittering gold."

"I'll wager my house, I'll wager farm,
"I'll wager — aye! my neck,
"I'll have the maid, if I go tonight,
"Tomorrow at my beck.

"Aye! wager will I both wealth and life,
"My farms and my ready fee,
"That Torlufs daughter, fair Ingefred,
"A leman shall be for me."

"O talk not wildly, my hearty friend,
"Nor risk your estate and gold:
"If you but knew her so well as I,
"Your bragging were not so bold."

Uprose Sir Lave, and thus he spake,
And lifted his hand on high;
"Tomorrow, if I should live so long,
"That maiden win will?

Sir Lav he bade his ready knaves.
His horse be duly drest;
"Tomorrow I'll up the country ride,
"And be Sir Torlufs guest.

"I'll mount me, and up the country ride,
"A visit to him to pay;
"I fain would his handsome daughter see,
"And win that lovely may."

So rode Sir Lav and came so bold,
In through Sir Torlufs gate.
And there stood his daughter, fair Ingefred,
Attired in her robe of state.

"Hail, Ingefred, Torlufs daughter fair,
"Incline you to be my love,
"And all the days that I have to live,
"My kindness you shall prove."

"Nay! nay! Sir Lav, go on your way,
"This year it is not to be;
"You cheated the lovely Silverlille,
"Whose like you will never see.

"And then the virtuous Blidelille,
"You plighted her your troth,
"And soon as your wishes you had gain'd,
"You broke your knightly oath.

"And next you have wronged fair Mettelille,
"And caused her bitter woe;
"God grant to my father length of life,
"To me you will not do so.

"Or I should sit in my lonely bower,
"And sorrowing heave my breast,
"While you afar off were drinking wine,
"And making my love your jest."

"But hear me, Ingefred, gentle maid,
"And be not, I pray, so cold,
"And I will give you a store of wealth
"In silver and eke in gold."

"Twelve marks of the best and purest gold,
"And twelve of silver too
"My father keeps in his treasure chest,
"And so. Sir Knight, adieu."

"But hear me, Ingefred, gentle maid,
"My wife if you will be,
"I'll give you at Bearsholm a lofty fort
"And one upon the sea."

"My father, Sir Knight, has castles too,
"And massive forts as well,
"If I should marry the youth I love,
"He'll find us where to dwell."

"O gentle Ingefred, change your mind,
"And kindly hear my prayer,
"On every finger of your fair hands
"Rich jewels you shall wear."

"Five rings my father Sir Torluf has,
"And jewels as pure and fine,
"If either of them I wish'd to wear
"All five, I am sure, were mine."

"But hear me, Ingefred, gentle maid,
"An ear to my pleading bend,
"And followers, proper men and tall,
"Shall daily your steps attend."

"Sir Lav, I'm neither halt nor blind,
"Nor fear I to walk alone;
"If footmen I wanted, my father's men
"Would follow me every one."

"But Ingefred dear, for mercy's sake
"Incline you to be my wife,
"For if your hand I should fail to gain,
"I've forfeited land and life."

"Sir Lav, my friend, I'd quite as soon
"That you in your grave lay dead,
"As stand myself in the Maiden-court
"For your sake pale and red.

"My mother is now in heaven above,
"And daily my loss I weep;
"She bade me with e'en her latest breath
"My honour safe to keep."

"If your good will then I cannot gain,
"Of all my farms I am shorn,
"And soon on my bier, a lifeless corpse,
"Shall into my grave be borne."

"This -night, and this very hour comes home
"My father from closed Assize,
"So haste. Sir Lav, and off, begone,
"You never will gain your prize.

"Beside, there is serving the king at court
"A gallant, Sir Iver bight,
"If he your errand should come to know,
"You'll be in a doleful plight.

"And then I have nine bold brothers too,
"Your match. Sir Lav, they;
"And all have sworn me a solemn oath
"They never will me betray. "

Sir Lav guided his horse about,
Ride homeward he dared no more;
For lost were his house and his fifteen farms,
And peril beside in store.

Well done, fair Ingefred, noble maid,
Who proved herself so true!
She rules in her dear Sir Iver's house.
And wears a silver'd shoe.

poems.title: Fair Mettelille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sirs Peter and Olave at table sat,
Beneath a linden tree
And joked in a long and pleasant chat.
My sweetheart waits for me.

"My friend Sir Olave, you've long delay'd,
"Now choose you and marry some pretty maid."

"Nay marry! What need I for wife to care,
"While this my good little horn I wear?

"I've only to sound my gilded horn
"To fool the soberest girl that's born.

"There's none in the town or country round,
"But jumps as she hears it's merry sound."

"I know a maiden, lives at the mill,
"You never will gain, try what you will.

"I'll bet you the finest horse I rifle,
"You win not Mett, my own fair bride."

"And I'll bet mine, my favourite white,
"She comes to my chamber this very night.

"Your pretty young bride — I'll stake my neck,
"I'll teach her to trip at Sir Olave's beck."

So soon as the dew was on the ground,
Began Sir Olave his strains to sound.

He tuned his harp, he touched the string,
Aid over the fields she heard it ring.

And then on his horn he blew so shrill,
That list to it must fair Mettelille.

She rose — and she knew not what to do —
"And must I then go? — at nightfall too?"

She stood in doubt — she still delay M —
"But thither I dare not take my maid."

At last with only her little hound
She started to thread the forest ground.

All closely wrapt in her mantle blue,
She near to Sir Olave's dwelling drew.

She gently tapped at his door, did she —
"Sir Olave, oh let me in — His me."

"Who's there? I've given my bail for none;
"I'll open to no one by night: — Begone."

"O rise, and let me not beg in vain;
"Nor banter and jest to give me pain."

"As bad as it is to bear the slight,
"You'll not come into my room tonight.

"Right welcome you were to share my bed,
"But that Sir Peter you're sworn to wed.

"And tho' to you I may be so dear,
"Sir Peter is living and much too near."

"O rise, Sir Olave, and let me in,
"The dew will ruin my costly skin."

"Well, if your ermines are wet with dew,
"Turn outside inside, and so adieu!"

"But if to my prayer you still say no,
"Let one of your pages with me go."

"The evening so clear, and the moon so bright,
"You'll find the way to your home aright.

"While over the field her beams are shed;
"Go home to your chamber, and go to bed."

Fair Mettelille went, and her little hound,
Alone they must thread the forest ground.,

But when they came to the garden gate,
There waiting his bride Sir Peter sate.

"And welcome, fair Mett, but how so gay!
"Where stayed then hast thou so late today?" '

"My dear, I had only stolen out
"To gather some flowers and sundry krout:

"And such have I cull'd both red and white,
"As just at their prime were found tonight.

"I stopp'd by the way and slay'd so long
"To list to the nightingale's tuneful song."

"'Twas not to list to a bird, that sang,
"But how that horn of Sir Olave's rang.

"Such furtive visits, and such like game
"Are certain to bring us both to shame.

Trom night-walks and visits like these refrain,
"I trust that it happens not again.

"And hark ye, my sweetheart Mettelille,
"Go back to your bed, and there lie still:

"Go back to your chamber, and go to sleep,
"If me you would wish my vows to keep.

"I've lost a horse, that was all my pride,
"By thy being such a faithless bride."

She went, but whither, — that no one knew,
Or where the night-wind her ashes blew:

For soon was glowing her room with flame;
So bitter she felt her grief and shame.

Sir Peter he mourn'd her long and sore;
Nor dared Sir Olave to meet him more.

So prove not your brides, — my counsel take —
Nor yet on their truth your honour stake.

poems.title: Sir Sallemand
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A brave young knight, Sir Sallemand,
And Mett, such her name,
They dearly each the other loved,
The knight and eke the dame.

His passion could Sir Sallemand
Nor check, conceal, nor guide,
Tho' both were of two brothers born,
By blood so near allied.

An aunt had he, Sir Sallemand,
Dame Ingeborg by name,
And of(en he to her house would ride
To tell and wail his flame.

"Right welcome here, Sir Sallemand!
"Welcome, dear nephew mine!
"Up in my chamber take your seat,
"And drink of mead and wine."

But rather chose the pensive knight
Out in the cool to stand.
And there the goblet brought his aunt,
And placed it in his hand.

"I cannot eat, I cannot drink,
"For me no goblet fill;
"My thoughts are on my lady-love,
"My dearest Mettelille."

"But listen, good Sir Sallemand,
"Such hopeless passion quell;
"So near akin as you and she
"Together may not dwell."

"If Mettelille I may not have
"To soothe my cankering pain,
"Shall never any, dame or maid,
"Sleep in my arms again."

"If you Have plighted her your troth,
"Send off at once to Rome,
"And pray the Pope to pardon you,
"Before you bring her home."

"Ye Ladies know each in and out
"Like market-going wain;
"I've none in all the world beside
"To whom to tell my pain."

And as that kind good lady bade.
The knight sat down and wrote.
And sent his page to Mettelille
To carry her the note.

To ask the Lady Mettelille,
The knight that letter sent,'
If she with him would go to Rome
To beg the Pope's assent

She wrote and gave her maid the note.
And in it thus replied;
"Where in the world so e'er he went,
"Would she be at his side."

Then bade the knight Sir Sallemand
His trusty steed to shoe,
And she, Dame Mettelille, her wain
Got furnish'd all anew.

And so the knight and lady fair
From Denmark rode away,
But in their tearful eyes was seen
How sorrowful were they.

As into Paris town he rode,
His lady near his side,
Came out the good kind burgers all
To meet the knight and bride.

They spared not costly silken cloth
To spread beneath her feet.
But all their kindness could not cheer
A heart with grief replete.

The lily up to her room they led,
But worse and worse she grew;
Sir Sallemand went to and fro,
He show'd himself so true.

"Cheer up, dear Lady Mettelille!
"Cheer up! no longer grieve,
"Tomorrow comes the brief from Rome,
"That wedded we may live."

"Nay, hear me, dear Sir Sallemand,
"All further trouble spare,
"Go fetch a priest to give me shrift,
"My pain I cannot bear."

Up in her chamber soon was heard
A cry of loud alarm;
Fair Mettelille had sunk and died
All in her lover's arm.

And in the church, while sang the priests
The dirge's dismal note.
Sir Sallemand's heart burst in twain,
And blood pour'd from his throat.

South of the church they buried her,
And north of it the knight,
But from their breasts two roses sprang
That brought their love to light:

For kindly those two roses twined
Their flowers of crimson hue;
Since Tristram's and his Isold's death
Was never love so true.

poems.title: The Retorted Rune
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Prince he paces up and down.
And deftly swings his blade;
"Fair Margaret, grant me Heaven but this, —
"You for my trothplight maid!

"Fair Margaret, grant me Heaven but this, -
"That you were even mine,
"And never but in my fond arms
"Should you again recline.

"You never but in my fond arms
"Should lay you down to rest;
"And faithful swains I'd choose for you
"To wait on your behest."

The Prince away to the greenwood rode,
And carved the runes with skill,
Such as might witch that gentle maid,
And make her do his will.

Then up and out spake Nicholas,
His best and dearest swain;
"This rune will surely cost your life,
"And bring your soul to bane."

"But little for my life I cared,"
'Twas thus the Prince replied,
"I little cared for life or soul,
"Were only she my bride."

He took the runes, that royal prince,
And so he threw them down,
That just beneath her cloak they leap'd,
Under her scarlet gown.

Nine nights she sat and nine long days
Out on the rocky fell.
And then back on the Prince again
She drove the runic spell.

And fain waB he, the royal prince,
To ride across the land.
And ask the maid in full Assize,
And plight her there his hand.

"I've knelt and sued proud Margaret's love
"Winters not less than three:
"Why should a poor young swain so long
"Have vainly bent the knee?

"I've sued proud Margaret's lily hand,
"Winters not less than five:
"Why should a swain sue maid so long,
"And in hi? suit not thrive?"

"Full five years earlier, noble Prince,
"My hand you might have won,
"If only, what you've done today,
"You from the first had done."

poems.title: Rosmer (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A lady once in Denmark dwelt.
And Hellelille her name;
A lofty castle there she built
And great that castle's fame.

Her daughter thieves had stolen away,
She sought her far and near:
The more she sought, the less she found.
And great her grief and fear.

She built a ship with gilded masts,
All rigg'd with silken sails,
And mann'd with knights, and a gallant crew
To face the Ocean gales.

Her three brave sons down to the strand
That noble lady brought;
And eight years long they roam'd the sea,
And still their sister sought.

Eight tedious years they wildly roar'd,
Since first they left the land,
And now they saw a lofty hill,
And anchored on the strand.

Then spake, as loud as she could call,
The lady Swanelille;
"Say who ye are, ye foreign knights,
Who visit this our hill?"

"Lady," the younger brother said,
So shrewd in speech was he,
"We're all a widow's three poor sons,
"Eight years we've roam'd the sea.

"Fair Denmark is our native land,
"Our mother Hellelille;
"We've sought a sister robbers stole,
"And seek that sister still."

"If born in Denmark thou hast been,
"And Hellelille thy mother,
"Then I am a sister dear of thine,
"And thou my youngest brother.

"But why, ray dearest brother, why
"At home didst thou not stay?
Tor haddest thou a thousand lives,
"Lost, everyone, were they."

She hid him in the smallest nook,
Where safely he might lie,
And begg'd him by the God above
To neither laugh nor cry.

Rosmer came stalking in from sea.
And straight began to ban;
"I smell, by my right hand I swear,
"The breath of a Christian man."

"A bird, that bare a Christian's leg,
"Across the courtyard flow;
"He dropp'd it down, but I caught it up,
"And away the carrion threw."

She made a bath so nice and warm,
Her lord the while caress'd;
"There's come to me my sister's son,
"O let him be my guest.

"There's come to me my sister's son
"From home across the sea;
"My lord! I've pledged my sacred troth,
"From harm he shall be free,"

"And is thy nephew come from home?
"Be quit of all alarm,
"I swear my great, my highest oath,
"To do the lad no harm."

Then was the mighty Rosmer heard
His servants twain to call;
"Go bid my lady's sister's son
"Come to the banquet hall."

All pale with fear the stranger grew,
When Rosmer called his name,
And trembling, and with beating heart,
Before his presence came.

King Rosmer took him upon his knee,
And kind and tender grew;
He tapp'd his guest so lovingly,
He left him black and blue.

"Stay, stay," said gentle Swanelille,
"Rosmer dear, take care;
"For heavy falls thy giant hand
"To tap a cheek so fair."

He there had stayed for fifteen years,
And then he pined for home;
"O give me aid, dear Swanelille,
"That I to Denmark come."

Before her giant Lord she stood,
"Let now your guest return,
"So many years he has been at sea,
"He now for home doth yearn."

"If here our guest has been so long,
"And pines for his native land,
"I'll help him forth, and give him too
"A gold-chest in his hand."

"And if you give him a chest of gold,
"From out your treasured store,
"Then be, dear Rosmer, kinder still,
"And bear them both ashore."

While thus spake gentle Swanelille,
She plann'd a knavish jest,
She emptied all the treasure out,
And crept inside the chest,

He took the chest between his teeth,
The man upon his hack.
And stoutly trod the Ocean depths
A long and weary track.

"And now I've borne theo to thy home,
"The land of sun und moon;
"I beg thee name not Swanelille,
"And ask no other boon."

As Rosmer sprang into the sea,
Cloud-high he dash'd the wave.
But found no more his Swanelille
To cheer his mountain cave.

He found no more his Swanelille;
His dearest wife was flown;
He wildly roam'd the mountain isle,
And turn'd to granite stone.

But in their mother's house was joy.
And all the country round,
That both her children, lost so long.
Had now at last been found.

poems.title: Rosmer (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Backlegs was there and Elfin-stone,
And more than I can say;
They built themselves a sturdy ship,
To Iceland steer'd away.

They launched the ship into the deep,
The sea growl'd like a bear,
The White Goose down to the bottom sank.
Some Trold was surely there.

Childe Roland left the sunken wreck,
And groped along the ground.
And leading towards Eline's bower
A little pathway found.

Childe Roland walk'd, till on a hill
He saw a fire's bright glow;
"Now hap to me, what happen may,
"To yonder fire I'll go."

And forward he childe Roland went.
And enter'd through the gate,
And there Eline, his sister, stood
Robed in a pall of state.

When Roland into the mountain went.
His hands he could not rear;
"Lord pity thee, poor luckless man!
"What can have brought thee here?

"Why?" spake the gentle dame Eline,
"Why hither art thou come?
"Tor be thy errand, what it may,
"'twere best to have stay'd at home.

"Into the chamber go, poor youth
"So dripping wet, and chill'd;
"But if the giant Rosmer comes,
"'Tis sure, thou wilt be grill'd.

"Sit down, thou poor unhappy man,
"And warm thy frozen feet;
"But if the giant hither stalks,
"He'll cut thee up for meat"

Home came great Rosmer Lengthylegs,
And fierce and angry grew;
"Some Christian man or wife is here,
"And coming here shall rue."
