Then forward stepp'd the fair Eline,
And solemnly she sware.
That o'er the house a crow had flown,
A deadman's leg-bone bare.

Rosmer he screeched and sprang about,
"A Christian here must be;
"Unless thou tellest me the truth,
"I'll make my steak of thee."

A purple mantle o'er her thrown.
Before hira stood Eline;
"There's here a youth from Iceland come,
"My very near of kin."

"If here is a youth from Iceland come,
"And of thy kindred he,
"I pledge my oath that while he stays,
"In safety he shall be."

Two years was Roland dwelling there,
But now desired to go,
For fair Eline became with child,
The source of coming woe.

Then went the gentle dame Eline
Before her lord to stand;
"Will ye this youth a furlough give
"To see his native land?"

"If home again this youth will go,
"And thou dost tell me true,
"I'll in a coffer lay for him
"Both gold, and silver too."

He took a heap of ruddy gold,
And stowed it in a chest;
Eline, she laid herself therein.
But that he never guess'd.

Under his arm he took the man,
The coffer on his back,
And dived beneath the salty sea.
For him an easy track.

"And now I've brought thee back to a land,
"Where shines the sun and moon,
"I'll give thee up the chest of gold,
"I trow no paltry boon."

"I thank thee, Rosmer, generous man,
Tor that my home I've seen;
"And now I'll tell thee news I've heard,
"With child is fair Eline."

Like falling dewdrops at the linn
Ran tears on Eosmer's cheek,
"But for my oath I'd gulp the down
"My rage on thee to wreak."

As fast he back to his mountain hied,
As hart pursues the hind,
But when he reached his cave again,
Eline no more could find.

Eline held on by Roland's hand,
The path that he might show;
They revell'd in their mutual bliss,
And talk'd of suffered woe.

Rosmer he wax'd so wroth of mood.
When her he saw not come,
He changed to a cold gray granite stone.
And lies there stiff and dumb.

poems.title: An Archer's Vengeance
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
I stood before my master's board
To pour the wine and mead,
And news was brought of a brother slain
By foul and murderous deed.

Soon as my lord and lady both
Had laid them down to rest,
I led me out my trusty steed.
And richly had him drest.

I led me out my trusty steed
With gilded bit and rein.
And ere I halted, fifteen miles
Had ridden o'er the plain.

I came to a house where troopers sat,
And drank their wine and mead.
And heard my dearest mother's voice
Wailing the murderous deed.

I strung my good and trusty bow.
And aim'd a shaft, and drew.
And left the king's twelve champions dead.
For they my brother slew.

And forth I rode across to court
Upon the judgement day,
And for my brother six men claimed,
For six a fine would pay.

Three several times I went to court
To pay what I might owe;
The Sheriff all my offers spurn'd,
And show'd himself my foe.

The Sheriff he and jurors twelve
Refused to set me free,
And doom'd me from my native land
An outlaw forth to flee.

I strung my good and trusty bow,
And aim'd a shaft and drew;
I shot the king's twelve Jury men.
And all the twelve I slew.

I left in haste the judgement court,
And mounted horse to ride,
And thought it well the wisest plan
In greenwood glen to hide.

An outlaw'd man for eight long years
I harbour'd in the wood,
And nothing else than leaves and grass
Had all that time for food.

I made my meals on leaves and grass,
No better was my fare.
Nor had I other bedfellow
Than savage boar and bear.

'Twas near the feast of Easter day,
That blessed holy tide,
And all in state the Swedish king
To church resolv'd to ride.

I strung my good and trusty bow.
And aim'd a shaft, and drew;
I drove it through his tyrant heart,
And so the king I slew.

And low he lay, that Swedish king.
Lay bleeding till he died;
To me they gave his'widow'd queen;
And she is now my bride.

poems.title: The Orphan Sister
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
I stood at wash beside a rill,
Under a mountain side
Two knights came riding down the hill.
How Hogen's sons can ride!

The one in silence went his way,
And one to chat with me would stay.

"O plight me troth, and, maiden fair,
"I'll give thee a gay gold band to wear."

"But should my fostermother scold,
"To see me wear a band of gold?"

"Say, walking out on yonder strand,
"Thou st found it glittering on the sand"

"And, pray, how should I frame my tale,
"If she should see my cheek grow pale?"

"Thy cheek grow pale if she should see,
"Tell her I mean to marry thee.

"But if thou wilt not hear of that,
"At least sit down with me, and chat.

"So place thee here upon the bank,
"And tell me what thy name and rank."

"At evening sunset I was born,
"My mother died at dawn of mora:

"The hour they laid her in her cell,
"Was rung my father's passing-bell;

"As him they left beneath the mould,
"For brothers and sisters too was told.

"And now were dead, all all were dead,
"All who should find me clothes and bread;

"Except Sir Swend my youngest brother,
"Who found for me a foster-mother;

"And she my childhood nurs'd and fed,
"Strange maidens taught me spin the thread.

"They taught me both to spin and sew,
"Virtue I taught myself to know."

"Fair maid, from this thy tale I hear,
"That thou art e'en my sister dear.

"So now, my sister, trust to me,
"I'll find a gallant knight for thee.

"Go dress and brush thy flowing hair,
"A brave rich knight shall be my care.

"Thy wedding feast shall be so grand,
"It's fame shall till our Danish land."

poems.title: Sir Ogey and Lady Elsey (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the versions of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Aage and Else" and George Borrow (1826), titled "Aager and Eliza".
poems.text:
Three maidens in their chamber,
The two were weaving gold,
And wept the third her bridegroom,
Lay buried in the mould.

It was the rich Sir Ogey,
He rode to an isle away,
He wooed the Lady Elsey,
And won that lovely may.

He won the Lady Elsey,
Betroth'd his gentle bride,
And on his very wedding night
Before her eyes he died.

So sorely wept the lady
And wrung her hands for woe,
The knight Sir Ogey heard it
Down in his grave below.

So sorely wept the lady.
So sorely beat her breast,
The knight Sir Ogey heard it.
Nor longer could he rest.

He rose, the knight Sir Ogey,
With coffin on his back,
And stagger'd towards her chamber
A dismal weary track.

He tapped her door with coffin,
He wore no robe of skin;
"'Wake up, my gentle Elsey,
"And let thy bridegroom in.'

Some while lay Lady Elsey,
And much in doubt was she;
"But can it be Sir Ogey
"Is hither come to me?"

Up spake the Lady Elsey,
And tears were on her cheek;
"Come, if the name of Jesus
"Thou still dost dare to speak."

"Rise then, dear Lady Elsey,
"And open me the door,
"For name I can Lord Jesus,
"As I could do before."

Uprose the Lady Elsey
And bitter tears she shed.
And let him in to her chamber,
The cold buried dead:

She took her comb, fair Elsey,
She comb'd his tangled hair.
And every lock she straightened,
She dropped on it a tear. "

"Now hear me, dear Sir Ogey,
"'The truth I pray thee tell,
"How under ground thou farest
"Down in thy cell."

"'Tis so down in that earth house,
"Where I must tarry now,
"'Tis as the joys of heaven,
"If happy thou."

"Then hear me, knight Sir Ogey,
"And grant the boon I crave,
"To go with thee, my dearest,
"And share thy grave."

"'Tis so down in that earth-house,
"My narrow lonely cell,
"Tis like to hellish torture,
"O cross thyself well I

"So oft as thou art weeping,
"And grievest thee so sore,
"Is brimming full my coffin
"With blood and gore.

"Above my head is growing
"The grass so sweet,
"But lothely snakes are twining
"About my feet.

"Yet when I hear thee singing,
"And thou art glad,
"Then is my grave's small chamber
"With roses clad.

"The white cock now is crowing,
"And down must I below;
"To earth wend all my fellows,
"And with them I must go.

"The red cock now is crowing,
"And down must I below;
"To earth must wend all dead men,
"And I too must go.

"And now the black cock's crowing
"Home I must go below;
"Unlock'd are all the portals,
"And I too must go."

Uprose the knight Sir Ogey,
Took coffin on his back.
And stagger'd towards the churchyard
A dismal weary track.

And what did Lady Elsey
So sorrowful of mood?
She walk'd beside her bridegroom
Across the murky wood.

But when she reach'd the churchyard,
She saw his. golden hair,
How pale it grew and paler,
That once had been so fair.

And when she had cross'd the churchyard
Up to the churches door,
Grew pale Sir Ogey's cheek too,
As roses red before.

At hand and foot Sir Ogey
Was fading away,
Fading his cheerful rosy cheeks
To clods of clay.

"Now hear me, Lady Elsey,
"Hear me, my bride so dear,
"No longer mourn thy husband,
"Nor drop for him a tear.

"But wend thee home, dear Blsey,
"In peace to sleep;
"No longer mourn thy bridegroom,
"No longer weep.

"See yon small stars above thee,
"How wanes their light;
"And see how fast is fleeting
"The hour of night"

She turn'd her towards the heavens.
The stars, she saw them wane,
But slipped to his grave the deadman,
She saw him not again.

He filipp'd away, the deadman.
And down he went below.
And full of grief his lady
Must homeward go.

Sorely she wept, fair Elsey,
And daily did she pray,
That live she might no longer
Than year and day.

So sick she grew for sorrow,
She laid her on her bed,
And, ere that month was ended.
Was on her bier, and dead.

poems.title: Sir Ogey and Lady Elsey (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the versions of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Aage and Else" and George Borrow (1826), titled "Aager and Eliza".
poems.text:
The knight it was, Sir Ogey,
Took horse and rode away.
And wooed the Lady Elsey,
And won that lovely may.

The Lady Elsey he betrothed
With all her heaps of gold;
But that day month Sir Ogey
Lay dead beneath the mould.

Then weep did Lady Elsey,
And all so wildly rave,
Sir Ogey heard her wailing
Down in his silent grave.

Uprose the knight Sir Ogey,
His coffin on his back,
And staggered towards her chamber
A dismal weary track.

Her door he tapp'd with coffin,
For mantle none had he,
"Arise, dear Lady Elsey,
"And open, love, to me."

"Nay," answered Lady Elsey,
"I'll open not the door,
"Till thou hast named Lord Jesus,
"E'en as thou couldst before."

"Rise then, dear Lady Elsey,
"And open me thy door,
"For name I can Lord Jesus,
"As I could do before."

She rose, the Lady Elsey,
While tears down-streaming ran,
And so within her chamber
Let in the spectre man.

Her golden comb she has taken,
And combs his tangled hair;
And every lock she straightens,
She drops on it a tear.

"Now hear me, dear Sir Ogey,
"The truth I pray thee tell,
"How under ground thou farest
"Down in thy narrow cell?"

"When thou, my dear, art cheerful,
"And easy in thy mind,
"The coffin where I slumber
"Is all with roses lined.

"But oft as thou Vt in sorrow,
"And bow'd with grief so sore,
"Is all that while my coffin
"Brim full of blood and gore.

"But hark! the red cock's crowing,
"And summons me away,
"The dead to th' earth must hasten,
"I dare no longer stay.

"The black cock too is crowing,
"To graveyard I must go;
"There's opening heaven's portal,
"And I must down below."

So took the knight Sir Ogey
His coffin on his back,
And stagger'd to the churchyard
A dismal weary track.

And rose the Lady Elsey,
For sad she was of mood,
And walk'd beside her bridegroom
Across the murky wood.

But when she reached the graveyard,
She saw his golden hair,
How pale it grew and paler,
That once had been so fair.

And when they from the graveyard
The church's threshold crossed.
His cheek, before so rosy,
It's fair fresh colour lost.

"Hear me, my gentle Elsey,
"Hear me, my bride so dear,
"No longer mourn thy trulove,
"Nor drop for him a tear.

"See yon small stars above thee,
"How wanes their feeble light,
"And see how fast is fleeting
"The murky hour of night."

But while the Lady Elsey
Was gazing on the skies,
Down sank the knight Sir Ogey,
And vanished from her eyes.

She turn'd her towards her chamber
With sorrow at her breast;
And that day month fair Elsey
"Was in her grave at rest.

poems.title: Little Kirstin's Dance
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
"Kirstin, fair Kirstin, come trip it with me;
"I've a gown all of silk, and I'll give it to thee."

"For gown all of silk, Sir, — as good I can buy,
"But dance not this year with the King's son will I."

"Kirstin, fair Kirstin, come trip it with me,
"I've shoes latch'd with silver — I'll give them to thee."

"For shoes latch'd with silver — as good I can buy,
"But dance not this year with the King's son will I."

"Kirstin, fair Kirstin, come trip it with me,
"I've a buckle of gold, and I'll give it to thee."

"For buckles of gold, Sir, — as good I can buy,
"But dance not this year with the King's son will I."

"Kirstin, fair Kirstin, come trip it with me,
"And half a gold ring, — see, I'll give it to thee."

"The half a gold ring, Sir, — as good I can buy,
"But dance not this year with the King's son will I."

"Kirstin, fair Kirstin, come trip it with me,
"Knives hilted with silver I'll give then to thee."

"Knives Lilted with silver as good I can buy,
"But dance not this year with the King's son will I."

"Kirstin, fair Kirstin, come trip it with me,
"My troth and my honour, I plight them to thee."

Fair Kirstin she tripp'd it so light and so neat,
Fifteen were the knights, that she danced off their feet.

Fair Kirstin so long mid the dancers would tread,
That over her shoes was the blood running red.

A mantle of scarlet around her was thrown.
And Kirstin was brought to the chamber of stone.

A mantle so blue there was spread on the floor.
And pretty and small were the children she bore.

And soon to the King is a messenger sped;
"Fair Kirstin sits nursing two children in bed."

He's gone to her chamber — "Now whom do you call
"The father to these pretty children so small?"

"Their father, so help me the God overhead,
"I know not, nor whether he's living or dead.

"My father, a poor simple creature was he,
"He built me a bower by the side of the sea.

"He built me a chamber below on the strand,
"Where boatmen were wont from their vessel to land.

"'Twas eight of those boatmen broke into my bower,
"And one of them left me disgraced from that hour."

"But tell me, fair Kirstin, o tell me, and say,
"What gave he, the price of thine honour to pay?"

"Of silk all embroider'd he gave me a dress,
"That ever adds new to my daily distress.

"Of shoes latch'd with silver he gave me a pair,
"Are daily renewing my trouble and care.

"He gave me a precious gold buckle and baud,
"There's found not a better in all the land.

"His gold ring he sunder'd, and half he gave me,
"Shame follow the villain wherever he be!

"He gave me two knives, with a rich silver hik,
"Would Christ with his knives that his hearts-blood were spilt!"

"O stay, little Kirstin, and curse him no more,
"For father am I to the children you bore."

He kiss'd little Kirstin again and again,
He crowned her, and gave her the title of Queen;

And now may fair Kirstin lay sorrow aside,
And nightly may sleep with the King at her side.

poems.title: The Brother and Sister
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A little sister full of love
Her brother came to woo;
And never heard I lovers yet
With warmer passion sue.

"I would thou wert the handsome knight
"Sat drinking at the board,
"And I the cup of ruddy gold
"That stood before my lord."

"Twere ill to be a drinking cup,
"And go the table round;
"There comes so many a drunken fool,
"Might smash it on the ground."

"Then thou shalt be the fairest knight
"That horse did ever ride,
"And I will be the polish'd sword
"Hung dangling at thy side."

" Tis just as ill to be a sword
"And hang beside a knight,
"There comes so many a drunken fool,
"May challenge him to fight."

"I would thou wert the finest dam
"Could stand upon the sand,
"And I would be a little stream,
"And trickle through the land."

"It were not good to be a stream
"And trickle o'er the soil;
"At early dawn the hunter comes
"Its silvery wave to soil."

"I would thou wert an antler'd hart,
"And roam'd the wood so wide,
"And I a little playful hind
"To frolick at thy side."

"It were not good to be a hind
"And frolick round a hart;
"The hunter to the forest comes,
"And strikes them with his dart."

"Then thou shalt be a graceful lime,
"And in a meadow root,
"And I a little tuft of grass
"Find shelter at thy foot."

"'Tis ill to be a tuft of grass
"Beneath a limetree's shade,
"The ox comes tramping o'er the mead,
"And breaks the tender blade."

"I would thou wert the finest tree,
"Could stand upon the waste,
"And I a gentle nightingale
"To built in it my nest."

"'Twere ill to be a nightingale,
"And sing upon a tree,
"There comes so many a listener,
"The warbler fain must flee."

"I would thou wert the finest church
"That glitters on a hill,
"And I an altar bright with gold,
"Where folk should come to kneel."

"Sister, if thou thy brother woo,
"Fine linen cease to wear,
"For barefoot thou wilt have to stand,
"Clad in a gown of hair."

poems.title: Fair Elsey
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
On grassy paddock they dance and fling,
Along the strand of the sea they go.
Their rioting wakes the chambered king.
He's lucky who never lias tasted woe,

The meadow they next so gaily tread,
Their revel is heard by the king in bed.

Sir Iver he leads the joyous band,
The liveliest knight in all the land.

Up starts from his midnight dream the king;
"What harper so skillfully strikes the string?"

"No harper was that, nor harpstring twang;
"With voice so thrilling Sir Iver sang."

"The midsummer night is mild and short,
"I'll up and ride there, and see the sport."

The king bids saddle his courser gray;
"I'll e'en to the mead, and see the play."

The king halts under a linden tree
Those graceful and active swains to see.

"A finer man I have never known,
"Nor is there in all the land but one.

"As slender is he as a crane and light,
"His skin it is like a swan's so white."

"Yet" answered the pageboy "rumour tells,
"That him his sister by far excels:

"So graceful, so lovely, so sweet and fair,
"She may with a princess well compare.

"And when in ermine she stands array'd,
"Is nobler than e'en a royal maid:

"As white as a lily, as fine as grass,
"For other maidens a looking-glass.

"By night she joins not the dancers' throng,
"Nor stands to list to the warbler's song."

The king twice round the meadow rode.
On Iver his special glance bestow'd.

Then sprang in amid the dancers' band,
And eagerly seiz'd Sir Iver's hand.

"Hark now, Sir Iver, youth so gay,
"And where is thy sister, Elsey, say."

"She works with gold in her lonely bower,
"And seldom she knows a cheerful hour.

"She sits in her bower, and weaves the braid,
"As well it beseems an orphan maid."

"Now hark, Sir Iver, thou well bred knight,
"Go fetch her hither to dance tonight."

"Thy wishes, my King, I am loth to cross,
"But dare not for fear of her honour's loss.

"For ill it becomes one gently bred,
"With drunken men in a dance to tread."

The king hi" prancing horse bestrode,
And homeward in -sullen temper rode.

The night long he tossed a sleepless head,
With thoughts of all that his page had said.

"Say, knave, if thou knowest a time and place,
"Where view we may catch of Elsey's face?"

"Five nuns tomorrow will take the veil,
"And she to be with them will not fail."

The king he dress'd, and his horse bestrode.
And off at once to the Abbey rode.

As walk'd fair Elsey in veil attired,
Her graceful figure the king admired.

The nuns stripp'd off their blyand small.
And clad themselves all in cloister pall.

Away their gold and brocade they threw.
And coarsest linen upon them drew.

The bishop before the altar stood,
And chatmted as march'd the sisterhood.

Around her curling and silky hair
A chaplet of pearl fair Elsey bare.

As back from the altar she turn'd her round,
Amid the gazers the king she found.

With reverence due she humbly bent.
But sorrow was in her bosom pent.

The king came forward and spake so free,
"Fair Elsey, give thy troth to me/'

"Nay, sire/' she answer'd with much despite,
"he child am I of a generous knight.'

She straight to her fostermother went,
Her fears to tell, and her grief to vent.

"O let me, mother, thy counsel hear,
"The king intends me some ill, I fear.

"And better be poor without a stain,
"Than wealth with a loss of honour gain."

She call'd to her maid "O haste," said she,
"Come hither and change thy dress with me."

"My mistress shall always find me true,
"Whatever she orders me to do."

Her maid in a silken dress she clad,
Herself in a coarse grey woollen plaid.

Her golden brooch to the maid she lent.
Herself in a menial raiment went.

"Now take thy seat in the gilded wain,
"I'll bid my servants to form thy train."

So proudly out of the church she drove.
That every eye to see her strove.

In costly raiment the maid was clad,
Her lady in cloak as coarse and sad.

The king stepp'd forward like humble swain.
And aided the maid to mount her wain.

The maid, she drove, and the king he rode,
Bat Elsey turned to her own abode.

Her plan she delay'd not a single hour,
But locked herself into a secret bower.

Its entrance was hidden within the wall,
That so it might be unknown to all.

Those others they reach'd the grove of rose,
And there would the king a while repose.

He took her up in his arms again,
To lift her down from the gilded wain.

"Fair Elsey, o let it not now displease
"To stroll with me under the linden trees.

"The road is weary, the daylight long,
"We'll stay and list to the warbler's song.

"We'll make us a couch of linden spray,
"And taste the sweets of a summer day."

"King, give over your warm caress,
"For I have in charge my lady's dress."

Her veil of blyand aside she threw.
And gray and wrinkled she stood to view.

"Away, wench! thee may the hangman fetch;
"Thy mistress I'll yet find means to catch.

"Nay tho' she journey from hence to Rome,
"I'll find her again, and bring her home."

The midsummer night was short and cold.
As rode the king in the wood and wold.

Himself he rode, and his servants run,
But trace of Elsey they found there none;

For hidden from sight in bosky dell
Was under the ground fair Elsey's cell.

But when they enter'd the Rosewood, hark!
They heard the sound of a lapdog's bark.

They roird the stones, they delved the ground.
And there the lily again they found.

They seized on her gold-embroider'd band,
And bound with it fast her fair white hand.

"Thy band we shall use to make a chain,
"Thou wilt not so easily slip again."

In horseman's mantle they wrapp'd the fair,
And lifted her up with tender care.

They rode with her off to the wood of rose,
And there would the king awhile repose.

"Virgin Mary, hear thou my cry!
"And undishonour'd oh! let me die."

Fair Elsey she scream'd so loud, the sound
Was heard by pirates who lay aground.

They heard her, as e'en they came from sea;
"Now what can that cry of anguish be?"

The king was riding along the strand,
And met on their march the pirate band.

"Hold still, Sir Knight, and thy valour prove,'
"Or give us in prize thy lady-love.

"Surrender at once the gentle maid,
"Or dead on the ground shalt then be laid."

"Take her, — I rather resign the wife,
"Than hazard for her to lose my life."

In sunder they cut the golden band,
And loosed the maiden's lily hand.

The mantle they doff'd that wrapp'd her round.
And gently placed her upon the ground.

In ermine and martin they dress'd the fair,
And off to their ship the maiden bare.

But while they were sailing, and while they row'd,
Her tears in silent anguish flow'd.

"Cease, beauteous lady, cease to grieve,
"A noble shall soon your hand receive.

"We carry you hence to the land of Spain,
"A noble lover you there will gain.

"You Ul into so rich a land be sold,
"With ladles they count us their heaps of gold."

They hardly had left the Danish shore,
Ere furious winds began to roar.

Amid the tempest's howl and hiss
Down sank the ship to the dark abyss.

The billows, that drown'd the pirate crew.
On England's coast fair Elsey threw.

Wet, sad, and weary, and all alone.
She sat to rest on a block of stone.

She sat there wringing her silken dress,
And wept with her pain and weariness.

In tears she was pacing the lonely strand,
As rode there a knight along the sand.

"Now tell me who are you, my lady fair?
"Whence come you, and why are you waiting there?"

"Abroad I have needlework been taught,
"And hither against my will been brought."

He wrapped in his mantle the maid so fair.
And lifted her up on his horse with care.

They rode, and they came to his courtyard gate.
Where waiting her son his mother sate.

"Hark, Adelman! tell me, my dearest son,
"That lovely maiden where hast thou won?"

"As e'en I was riding along the strand,
"I found the lady upon the sand.

"Abroad she has needlework been taught.
"And hither against her will been brought."

"If here with us she would like to stay,
"All honour will we the lady pay."

Three weeks she tarried with them, or four.
And daily they loved her more and more.

Some nine weeks longer she there had stay'd.
And better and better they loved the maid.

The knight and his mother, the worthy dame,
Were sitting at board to play a game.

"Now, Adelman, tell me, my dearest son,
"What thoughts in thy head so strangely run?

"Thou seemest to take of the Rookh no care
"In thinking about the lady fair."

"'Tis all the maiden from yon sea-side,
"But do not, mother, I prithee, chide.

"'Tis Elsey, 'tis she my heart has won,
"But knows not herself what she has done."

"But what wilt thou with a lady win,
"Who cannot lay claim to kith or kin?"

"And tho' she may have no kinsmen more,
"Her virtue alone is an ample store."

His mother was smiling beneath her cloak;
'Twas only to try her son she spoke.

"My wish any longer I cannot hide
"To see. thee take her to be thy bride."

Five months the banquet did they prepare.
And Elsey was living devoid of care.

A knight rode up to the courtyard gate.
As there Sir Adelman's mother sate.

"O tell me. Lady, has not for gold
"Been lately to you a maiden sold?"

"My son was riding along the strand,
"And found a maid on the lonely sand.

"We're e'en now holding their wedding day,
"Go in, and join in a group so gay."

As into the hall she saw him stride,
Beneath her mantle smiled the bride.

"My only brother, Sir Iver, see!
"He comes to me over the salty sea/'

"O give your consent" the bridegroom said,
"That I may your sister Elsey wed."

Sir Iver answer'd in courteous strain,
"No happier lot could maid attain.

"In this my sister behold your wife,
"In me a brother and friend for life."

They sold their lands and returned no more,
But stay'd for life upon England's shore.

poems.title: The Maiden Transformed to a Wer-wolf
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
My mother she bare me at eventide,
Ere crow of the cock herself had died.

Eight years my father would take no wife,
Lest cruel stepmother should plague my life.

But when those first eight years were fled,
Once more did he sorely long to wed.

He traversed the country far and wide,
And brought to his home a smiling bride.

He brought to his home the smiling dame,
But stepmother harsh she soon became.

As home they were driving her up the street,
I went to the gate the bride to meet.

I gently tapp'd on her robe so fine,
"O welcome home, dear mother mine!"

She spurn'd me back with a scornful heel,
"'Tis thou that shalt first my temper feel."

She changed my form to a scissars small"
And bade that I should not grow at all.

To maids and to matrons I was dear,
Their cloth with me they loved to shear.

But even the greater grew her hate,
The more that she saw my happy fate

She then to a sword-blade shaped my form,
And bade me to toil in battle's storm.

A sword-blade I was so keen and bright,
And dear to squire and to gallant knight.

Well pleased with me all, and proud they were
My blade in a gilded sheath to bear.

But still the greater grew her hate.
The more that she saw my happy fate.

As wer-wolf then by her cruel spell
She drove me to roam the wood and dell.

Eight years no other home I knew,
And many a gallant man I slew;

She bound me my form to take no more,
Till I should drink of my brother's gore.

And that she hoped that I ne'er should get,
For brother had I not one as yet.

Eight years I had passed in pain and care,
And still no child my stepdame bare;

But when the ninth was nearly spent,
She then with a little infant went.

One festival day, a holy tide,
To church she had ventured forth to ride.

But hidden behind a rock I lay,
Just where the dame must take her way.

I seiz'd the wretch's purple gown.
And out of her saddle dragg'd her down;

I hit the flesh from her left-hand side,
With claws I rent the opening wide.

I took the baby so small and good.
And hare him off to the murky wood.

I hit the hoy in his little toe,
And made a tiny streamlet flow;

But scarcely had drunk of brother's blood.
Before on my feet a maid I stood.

The boy myself to the font I bare.
And gave him then to a nurse's care;

And now in a cloister I go to live.
And all my days to Our Lady give.

poems.title: The Nightingale
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
I well know where a castle stands,
And richly it is dight
With silver and with ruddy-gold,
And marble polished bright.

Within its yard a linden stands
With tender leaflets hung,
And dwells therein a nightingale,
That sweetly tunes her tongue.

A gentle knight at midnight hour
Came riding there along,
And stood awhile in wonder lost
To hear the warbler's song.

"Now hark! thou little nightingale,
"A lay I prithee sing;
"And then thy neck I'll hang with pearl,
"With beaten gold thy wing/'

"I value not the plumes of gold,
"That you would have me wear;
"I roam the world a wild wood bird,
"Whom man shall never snare."

"And if a wild wood bird thou art,
"Whom man shall never snare,
"Must pinch thee hunger, cold and snow,
"When all the trees are bare."

"Me pinch not hunger wind or snow,
"Nor winter's bitter chill;
"But secret pangs of grief untold
"My heart with anguish fill.

"The brawling stream from mountain brow
"Deep in the dale is toss'd,
"But memory of one we've loved,
"Can never so be lost.

"A sweetheart once I had so dear,
"A brave and gallant knight;
"But hard stepmother grudged our love,
"And wreak'd on us her spite.

"Myself she shaped to a Nightingale,
"And drave me from my home,
"My brother a grisly wolf she made
"In forest wild to roam.

"In wolfish guise for seven long years
"He roam'd the murky wood;
"For bound he was in runic spell,
"Till he should drink her blood.

"One day, as through the Rose-tree grove
"All gaily dress'd she came,
"He slily watch'd her, lay in wait,
"And caught that hateful dame.

"He griped her fast with wolfish claw,
"And then with deadly bite
"Tore out her heart and drank her blood,
"And so stood up a knight.

"Myself I am still a little bird,
"That flies on heath so wide;
"And pass r in pain the weary hours,
"But most at winter-tide.

"Yet, thanks to God who sees my grief!
"I use my tongue anew:
"For five years I've not talk'd as much,
"As now I've done to you.

"While others slept, I've on ray bough
"Sung through the midnight hour,
"Nor ever found a better home
"Than in my greenwood bower."

"Now hark thee, little Nightingale,
"With this ray wish comply;
"The winter in my chamber sing,
"And off in summer fly."

"Thanks for your offer, gentle knight,
"Your room I cannot share;
"For that my mother's spell forbids,
"While feathered wings I bear."

As musing sat the nightingale,
Nor on his purpose thought,
He stretch'd his hand, and by the foot
The little warbler caught.

He took her home, and carefully
Shut door and window to;
And there she turn'd to beasts as strange
As ever came to view,

To lion and to bear she turned,
And many monsters more;
Or as an ugly lindworm laughed,
And seemed athirst for gore.

He cut her with his little knife;
And drew a stream of blood,
And there at once before his eyes
A blooming maiden stood.

"Then since I've thee from spell released,
"Thy tears of sorrow dried,
"Say, lady, what is thy descent
"On both thy parents' side?"

"My father was of Egypt king,
"My mother was the queen,
"My brother was a grisly wolf,
"That roam'd the woodland green."

"And was then Egypt's king thy sire?
"And was thy mother queen?
"Then thou art e'en my sister dear,
"Who long a bird has been."

And loud was over house and land
The voice of joy and song,
That he that little bird had caught,
In linden lived so long.

poems.title: The Maid as a Hind and a Hawk
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
As I was a little and tender child.
My own dear mother died;
And up the country my father rode.
And married another bride.

The night she came to her bridal bed,
A mother she seem'd so good;
The day that followed, the same next day,
A stepmother harsh and rude.

I sat me down at my father's board
With hounds and puppies to play;
In came my stepmother, stalking in.
To take my comfort away.

With roses and lilies I made a wreathe,
And sat at the board so still;
My stepmother grudged my guiltless joy.
For that was against her will.

She shaped myself to a little white hind,
And bade me to greenwood wend;
My seven little maids she turned to wolves.
And bade them my flesh to rend.

My seven little maids they loved me well.
My body they would not tear,
And much it my spiteful stepmother vex'd,
That harder I should not fare.

My trulove. Sir Orm, he served the king,
And handsome was he and bold;
He sorrowed for me both day and night.
But never his grief had told.

Sir Orm rode out from the royal court,
His gloom, if he could, to cheer,
And came to the wood with hounds and bow.
And purposed to chase the deer.

Sir Orm to the chase hallooed the hounds,
And near to the hind he rode,
But she for the yelp of the dogs fled not.
Such love for the knight she show'd.

The hounds they press'd the hind so sore,
For covert she fain must fly;
She shaped herself to a little wild hawk,
And flew to the clouds so high.

He fain would catch her, the good Sir Orm,
And laid in her path a snare.
But never could seize her, so quick was she,
So well of his wiles aware.

But down that little wild falcon flew,
And sat on a linden tree;
Beneath it Sir Orm, her trulove, stood,'
And bitterly wail did he.

Sir Orm on his shoulder brought an axe.
To fell the linden low;
There came the peasant, that own'd the wood
And parried the falling blow.

"If thou dost chop my ancestor's wood,
"And waste it in my despite,
"I'll write me a rune, shall work thy death,
"And make thee my loss requite.

"O let me but fell this single tree,
"Nor grudge me the boon I crave,
"For if that falcon I cannot catch,
"With grief I sink to the grave."

"Now listen, thou handsome active youth,
"A better device I weet;
"A falcon so wild thou wilt not catch,
"Except with a bait of meat."

A slice from his breast Sir Orm cut off,
And hung on a linden bough;
The breast it bled, and the steak it crack'd,
'Twere hard if they miss'd her now.

And down from her branch the falcon flew
And clapp'd with her wings so quick;
And slily she laugh'd to herself with joy,
She well understood the trick.

She hack'd and peck'd at the meat so fast,
She seemed to relish the treat;
For still the longer she ate thereof,
The more she wanted to eat.

Then flitted that falcon so wild away,
And sat on the glittering sand;
And there she changed to a maid, as fair
As any in all the land.

And now she stood at her trulove's side,
From trouble and sorrow free,
And much they told of their mutual grief
Beneath the linden tree.

He took her so gently within his arm,
And then her lips he kiss'd;
"Thank God! I find thee so sound and fresh,
"So long as I thee have miss'd."

And while she was standing beneath the tree,
And combing her flaxen hair,
Her seven little maids, that wolves had been.
Came running her joy to share.

"Now plight me thy troth, fair gentle maid,
"And give me in pledge thy hand;
"And say, if ready to go with me
"Afar to my native land/'

"O thanks for thy goodness, thou brave Sir Orm,
"And thanks for the dainty steak;
"Henceforth, so long as I live and breathe,
"I never will thee forsake.

"My gratefullest thanks, thou brave Sir Orm,
"Who saved me from all my pain;
"Henceforth thou never, but at my side,
"Shalt slumber or sleep again."

The gallant Sir Orm redeem'd his word.
Like a true and loyal knight.
And held in a month his wedding feast
To drink the nuptial rite.

And so has the fair and gentle maid
Overcome her trouble and pain;
Has found her trulove, the brave Sir Orm,
And is in his arms again.

poems.title: The Lindworm
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Signelille in her cheerful bower
With golden harp beguiled the hoar.

But while the strings her finger swept,
A lothely Lindworm towards her crept.

"Fair maiden, plight thy troth to me,
"And heaps of gold I'll give to thee."

"Protect me, God, from that sad fate,
"To be a writhing Lindworm's mate!"

"I'll will at least thou wilt not show,
"So kiss me once, and let me go."

So on his mouth a cloth she laid,
And kiss'd it, as e'en the Lindworm bade.

He ruffled up his horny scale,
And blood ran dripping down her veil.

As from her bower the Lindworm crept.
She followed, wrung her hands, and wept.

But when she reach'd the chamber stair.
Her brothers seven were standing there.

"Dear Signelille, how find we thee
"Keeping the Lindworm company?"

"I needs must follow the Lindworm's lead,
"Because my fate has so decreed."

Into the cave the monster crept,
She followed, wrung her hands, and wept

Then knelt on her bare knee and pray'd;
"O lend me, Mary's son, thine aid."

Soon as the cave he came within,
He cast aside the Lindworm skin:

Threw off the vermin's horny scale,
And stood a knight in coat of mail.

"I thank thee, sweetest Sidselille,
"I'll live and die to do thy will."

And now, reliev'd from all alarm.
She nightly sleeps on a Prince's arm.

poems.title: The Maiden in the Shape of a Snake
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There stood a fair and a courtly maid
Beside Sir Jenus bed,
And proffered him five good silver bowls
And gifts of the gold so red.

"Five silver bowls were left with me,
"These all will I give to you
"What time my brother divided goods,
"He nothing about them knew.

"I'll give you the whole of my coffer'd store,
"Both gold and jewels rare;
"My brother, when we divided goods,
"Was nothing of them aware.

"I'll give you beside the twelve fleet foals,
"That out in the forest race;
"Reliance upon my plighted word,
"Sir Jenus, you may, place.

"I'll give you besides my twelve stout boats
"Are anchor upon the strand;
"I would, if I were a knight like you,
"Accept such a lady's hand."

"Twas near on the stroke of midnight hour,
The cock had struck on the beam;
"I' faith 'tis time that you help me now,
"Ere daylight begins to gleam."

'Twas just on the stroke of midnight hour,
The cock he had clapp'd his wing;
She changed from a maid to a creeping snake,
And into the grass did spring.

So fast and so sound Sir Jenus slept,
He nothing had seen or heard;
But wakeful was lying the little page-boy,
And told to him every word.

"Now list, Sir Jenus, dear master mine,
"In dreams thou art deeply read;
"There came hereof a fine and gentle maid,
"Was standing beside your bed.

"Eich gifts of the gold she proffer'd you,
"And five fair silver bowls,
"And coursing upon the forest lawn
"Twelve fleet and highbred foals.

"She proffer'd you all her twelve stout boats,
"Are anchor'd upon the strand;
"She would, if she were a knight like you,
"Accept such a lady's hand.

"'Twas near on the stroke of midnight hour,
"The cock had struck on the beam;
"She said, it was time to give her aid,
"Ere daylight began to gleam.

"'Twas just on the stroke of midnight hour,
"The cock he had clapp'd his wing,
"And then she changed to a creeping snake,
"And into the grass did spring."

Sir Jenus he called his servants twain,
And thus he was heard to say;
"Up knaves, and upon my good grey steed
"My best gold saddle lay."

Sir Jenus he went by a lonely road
Along the mountain side,
And there he beheld the creeping snake
Through herbage and bushes glide.

Sir Jenus over the saddle bent.
The bright little snake he kiss'd.
And straight there was smiling a lovely maid.
Where even a snake had hiss'd.

"Sir Jenus, for this great honour done
"My gratefullest thanks are due;
"Whatever the favour you ask of me,
"I gladly will grant to you/'

"I thank you heartily, gentle maid,
"Nor will I your offer slight,
"But here I will make you my trulove dear,
"If you will pledge a knight"

"Then hear me, Sir Jesus, the words I say,
"There's no one so dear as you;
"And gladly I'll pledge you before the world
"To you to be ever true."

And there Sir Jenus upon the spot
He plighted the maid his troth,
And soon there was held the marriage feast
With joy and with peace to both.

poems.title: The Maid in the Linden Tree
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A maiden went in mantle blue
To where a graceful linden grew.
Against so blithe a summer,

Oak trees and beech she there might see,
But green as leeks the linden tree
Against so blithe a summer,

"Good morrow, linden! fresh and fair!
"How bright as gold the leaves you bear!"

"To me is no such flattery due,
"With better luck God blesses you.

"For you sit warm with fire and light,
"And I stand freezing through the night.

"While we were children, young and small,
"Our mother left us orphans all.

"A new wife then my father sought,
"And home a harsh stepmother brought.

"She changed us, some to fleeting deer,
"And some as hawks bade skim the air;

"Myself a linden tree she made,
"And set to grow on a green-wood glade.

"Alike the summer breezes blow,
"Or chill me winter's frost and snow;

"I no relief may hope to find,
"Till comes a prince to kiss my rind.

"Tomorrow a suitor kneels to you,
"But me to chips the woodmen hew.

"To you a suitor comes from Scone,
"But I by woodmen shall be thrown.

"They'll cleave, and build a boat of me,
"And launch me on the salty sea.

"Perchance, as some confessor's chair,
"I hear false wives their guilt declare.

"Perchance, become a bedstead amo,
"Hear whisper many a deed of shame."

"Wait here, poor linden, wait in peace;
"I'll pray to God for your release."

Her brother dwelt in a foreign land,
To him she wrote with lily hand.

Her letter read the knight and cried,
"In this affair be God ray guide!

"Befall myself what he decrees,
"I'll e'en in this my sister please."

He hoisted high his silken sail,
And crossed the sea with gentle gale.

He dress'd in costly mantle blue,
And went to where the linden grew.

He found the linden, kiss'd her wood,
And there at once a maiden stood.

With rosy cheek and flowing hair
Retired for shame the blushing fair.

O'er her bare charms his cloak he spread,
And then the maid to his sisters led.

Up to his sister's bower he went,
In courtesy she rose and bent

"Sister, the lily here behold,
"Of whom thy letter lately told.

"I've set her free from thrall and woe;
"On whom wilt thou her hand bestow?"

"Hear then my wish, dear brother mine,
"And let the lovely maid be thine."

He gave her first a golden band.
And then in troth pledged her his hand.

He made the blushing rose his bride,
And both have laid their cares aside.

Brother and sister both are gay,
They married, both, the selfsame day.
Against so blithe a summer.

poems.title: The Little Horseboy
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
"Come bring the board, my gentle page,
"And venture a game with me,
"I've here no glittering gold in purse
"To stake it at play with thee:

"But wager thou that dandy hat,
"Tho' true it is somewhat gray,
"And I'll put up my necklace pearls,
"To win, if thou canst, away."

A first time upon the checquer'd board
The golden cubes have run,
The Page it is has lost his stake,
The Lady it is has won.

"Come bring the board, my gentle page,
"And venture a game with me,
"I've here no glittering gold in purse.
"To stake it at play with thee:

"But wager thou that holiday coat,
"Tho' true it is somewhat gray,
"And I'll put up my crown of gold,
"To win, if thou canst, away."

A second time on the checquer'd board
The golden cubes have run,
The Page it is has lost his stake.
And Lady it is has won.

"Come, bring the board, my gentle page,
"And venture a game with me,
"I've here no glittering gold in purse
"To stake it at play with thee:

"But wager thou thy scarlet hose,
"Thine hose and a pair of shoes,
"And I'll my honour and troth put up,
"And truly pay if I lose/'

A third time upon the chequer'd board
The golden cubes have run.
The Lady now has lost her stake,
The Page it is has won.

"But hark thee now, little horseboy dear,
"Up, leave me, I pray, and go;
"And then my silver-mounted knives (
" "On thee I will all bestow."

"Now as to thy silver-mounted knives,
"I'll take them too, if I may,
"But 'faith I'll have the pretty maid,
"I fairly have won in play,"

"But hark thee now, little horseboy dear,
"Up, leave me, I pray, and go;
"And then these silk-embroider'd shirts
"On thee I will all bestow."

"Now as to thy silk-embroider'd shirts,
"I'll take them too, if I may,
"But 'faith I'll have the pretty maid,
"I fairly have won in play."

"Nay! hark thee now, little horseboy dear,
"Up, leave me, I pray, and go:
"And then my palfrey and saddle too,
"On thee will I both bestow."

"Now as to thy palfrey and saddle too,
"I'll take them both, if I may,
"But 'faith I'll have the pretty maid,
"I fairly have won in play."

"Nay, hark thee now, little horseboy dear,
"Up, leave me, I pray, and go;
"And then my castle and all its towers
"I'll gladly on thee bestow."

"Now as to thy castle and towers and all,
"I'll take them too, if I may,
"But 'faith I'll have the pretty maid,
"I fairly have won in play."

The Lady alone in her chamber stands,
To comb and to dress her hair;
"God pity and better me simple maid,
"And me for the match prepare."

The page is standing in castle yard.
And leans him upon his sword;
"As good a marriage wilt thou have made,
"As doth with thy birth accord.

"Nor Page nor Horseboy at all am I,
"Tho' mean may have seem'd my birth,
"But son of one as noble a king,
"As ever held rule on earth/'

"A son of one as noble a king,
"As ever held rule on earth?
"Then thou my honour shalt have and troth,
"And all that beside I'm worth."

poems.title: Sir Thor and Lady Silvermor
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The young Sir Thor and Silvermor
Were playing chess in lady's bower.

The more they play'd, more kind they grew,
Till love stole in between the two.

"But, Silvermor, how long, I pray,
"At borne unmarried would you stay?"

"If but my kinsmen do not chide,
"Nine years for you I'll bere abide."

"I ask you not so long to wait,
"Stay for me only winters eight."

Those long eight years away have roll'd;
Her kinsmen now a meeting boN.

"We'll wed the maid, we'll wait no more
"She shall not have the young Sir Thor;

"There come to woo from east and west,
"The richest come, and eke the best;

"And when a count so wealthy sues,
"His offer let us not refuse."

Her hasty father scorn'd delay,
And married her that very day.

It was a Sabbath's holy tide.
And richly clad for church the bride.

As on her balcony she stood,
She saw the vessels skim the flood.

Beyond the rocks she turn'd her gaze,
And ships saw steering through the haze.

She look'd along the mountain side,
And saw the gilded ro wheats glide.

"Each knight comes to his lady home,
"And will my trulove never come?

"O brother Salman, wouldst thou ride,
"To pleasure me, to yon sea-side?"

As Salman rode along the sand,
Sir Thor his vessel steer'd to land.

"Tell me, young swain, who ridest there,
"How all the island maidens fare?"

"One after eight years' long delay
"Will drink her wedding feast today.

"She wrings her hands for grief at heart,
"And oft is seen the tear to start."

Still stood the knight, and heard the news;
He thought his senses he should lose.

He went, and in his coffer sought.
And gilded harp and chessboard brought.

All with his gilded harp in hand
He went before the maid to stand.

First one, and then another lay,
The lady sat and heard him play.

"That," thought within herself the bride,
"Is my Sir Thor; tis none beside."

Sir Thor, with head wrapt in his cloak,
Enter'd the bridal hall, and spoke;

"Is any chess-player here within,
"From foreign swain a purse will win?

"Is any here, a knight or dame,
"Will sit with me and play a game?"

Silent sat all the knights aside;
Her father rose, and thus replied.

"There sits at present none within,
"Who prize at chess may hope to win;

"Except fair Silvermor, the bride,
"And she must at the board preside."

Her mother Torfred rose and spake;
She little knew the prize at stake.

"Yet, sure, this long midsummer day
"The bride a game or two may play.

"Fair Silvermor, from table rise,
"If you at chess will win a prize."

The maiden smiled within her sleeve;
"I'll first go ask my father's leave."

She wrapp'd herself in scarlet cloak.
And up to her father went, and spoke.

"Father, your leave I come to pray,
"Before I go at chess to play.

"May I sit o'er the board awhile,
"And so the tedious hours beguile?"

The knight his daughter led aside,
And long with solemn lecture plied.

"One small short hour thou may'st remain,
"But win no gold from foreign swain.

"And of that knight. Sir Thor, take care;
"I fear he plots some crafty snare."

The bride in mitfitle wrapped her head,
And up to the banquet-chamber sped,

Soon as she came within the door,
Rose up with due respect Sir Thor.

At first, as they their game begun.
It was the young Sir Thor, who won.

"The grisly wolf roams in the wood,
"And thinks to make the deer his food.

"He rends the one, lets others lie,
"And many wounded leaves to die.

"Gold it is hard enough to win,
"And quite as hard a faithless quean."

But when they play'd a second game.
That fairly won the youthful dame.

Fair Silvermor to his taunt replied,
And sad her tone, and deep she sigh'd.

"High o'er the heath the eagle flies,
"And proudly storm and wind defies.

"Perch'd on a rock he takes his rest,
"And feathers well his airy nest.

"True to their word would many be,
"Could they but rule their destiny."

"If you, fair maid, to your troth are true,
"Here sits a swain as true to you.

"If you, fair maid, will follow me,
"I'll face for you the roughest sea.

"My horse impatient paws the sand;
"My ship lies ready on the strand."

"Sir Thor, do you to your vessel go;
"To follow I shall not be slow."

By th' eastern door he left the hall;
The bride came round the western wall.

Soon as she reach'd the glittering sand,
Sir Thor held out to her his hand.

He caught her up, and was not slow
To place her on the gilded prow.

High on the yards they spread the sail,
And put to sea before the gale.

The news to her father soon was told,
"Sir Thor has Silvermor cajol'd."

Her mother sware a cruel oath.
Deep in the sea to sink them both.

"A storm I'll raise, and manage so,
"That both shall down to the bottom go."

And hardly had they left the strand,
Ere came a blast from off the land.

The ship no longer they could steer,
And pale grew every face with fear.

So rock'd their vessel, pitch'd and roll'd,
No sailor could the rudder hold.

Not one on deck could even stand.
But the fair bride with lily hand.

And as the helm she stood to hold,
She wore her precious crown of gold.

In her the crew a pilot found,
And what her mother loos'd, she bound.

"Now up the mast, my page, and see,
"If land we are nearing on the lea.

"But as thou goest aft or fore,
"Take care to tread not on Sir Thor."

"Lady, His Norway's rocks I see,
"God bring us there from danger free,"

"If all is true, that thou dost say,
"Thy tidings richly I'll repay;

"I'll thee with me at table seat,
"And courteously and kindly greet.

"And give thee a kirtle rich with lace,
"And horse of wild and fiery race."

"Aye!" said Sir Thor who lay below,
"Many see land, nor promise so."

They cast their anchor upon the sand;
Sir Thor the first stepped out on land.

The good Norse people, all, on shore
Greeted with cheers the rich Sir Th.

Their joy they show'd on every side,
And cheer'd no less his lovely bride.

To Ager-house he brought his spouse.
And wedded her with great carouse.

poems.title: Signelill
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Malfred bade her maiden speak,
"Signelill, my maiden!
"Why so sickly pale thy cheek?"
But sorrow pinches sorely.

"No wonder if so pale I grow,
"Malfred, oh my lady!
"It is the long long hours I sew."
And sorrow pinches sorely.

"Thy cheek was once like roses red,
"Signelill, my maiden,
"But now it's like the very dead."
But sorrow pinches sorely.

"I'll hide no more the truth from thee,
"Malfred, oh my lady!
"Thine eldest son has wheedled me."
And sorrow pinches sorely,

"And did my son thy love betray,
"Signelill, my maiden?
"Then how did he thy favours pay?"
For sorrow pinches sorely.

"He gave the silver-buckled shoes,
"Malfred, oh my lady!
"That daily still with shame I use."
For sorrow pinches sorely.

"He gave me too a silken dress,
"Malfred, oh my lady!
"That still I wear in great distress."
For sorrow pinches sorely,

"He gave me a ring of gold so fine,
"Malfred, oh my lady!
"More costly are not even thine."
But sorrow pinches sorely,

"And what will all his gifts avail,
"Signelill, my maiden,
"If yet to wed thee he should fail?"
For sorrow 'pinches sorely.

"To wed me, aye! that did he swear,
"Malfred, oh my lady!
"In pledge he gave me these to wear."
But sorrow pinches sorely.

"And what will secret vows avail,
"Signelill, my maiden?
"He tells so many more the tale."
And sorrow pinches sorely.

"If I but take my harp on knee,
"Malfred, oh my lady!
"My lord will wake and send for me."
For sorrow pinches sorely.

And scarcely she a string had stirred,
Signelill the maiden,
Before the knight her music heard.
But sorrow pinches sorely.

"Bring me,' bade the knight his groom,
"My mother's gentle maiden;
"Haste and bring her to my room."
For 'sorrow pinches sorely,

Towards his bedstead rail he drew
His mother's gentle maiden;
"Now seat thee here, there's room for two."
And sorrow pinches sorely.

"O no, my lord; that would not dare
"Thy mother's humble maiden;
"I never yet have sat me there."
And sorrow pinches sorely,

"Seat thee; why this coyness feign,
"My Signelill, my maiden?
"For thou hast in my bosom lain.
And sorrow pinches sorely,

"Seat thee; thou shalt be my bride,
"My Signelill, my maiden,
"Shalt every night sleep at my side."
For sorrow pinches sorely.

poems.title: The Elf and the Farmer's Wife (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
'Twas in a wood on a Western isle,
A farmer chose his ground;
He thought to spend the winter there.
And brought his hawk and hound.

He brought with him both hound and cock,
For long he meant to stay,
And much the deer, that roam'd the wood.
Had cause to rue the day.

He fear'd the oak, he fell'd the "birch,
Nor beech nor poplar spared,
And much was griev'd the sullen Elf,.
At what the stranger dared.

He hew'd hira balks, he hew'd him beams,
With eager toil and haste;
"Who," ask'd the Elves in the mountain cave,
"Who's come our wood to waste?"

Then up and spake the tiniest Elf,
As emmet small and slim;
"There's hither come a Christian man,
"Leave me to manage him."

And then' spake up the biggest Elf,
And grimly roll'd his eyes;
"We'll march our troop to the farmer's house,
"And hold on him Assize.

"He is hacking down both wood and bower,
"He shows us great disdain;
"His housewife he shall give me up,
"And taste of shame and pain."

And all the Elves from out their cave
Began to dance and spring.
And marching towards the farmer's house
Their lengthy tails to swing.

The dog howl'd in the farmer's yard,
The herdsman blew his horn.
The falcon yell'd, and crow'd the (Tock,
For e'en he had had his corn.

Seven hundred Elves from out the wood, '
And foul and grim they were,
Would at the farmer's hold a feast
His meat and drink to share.

The farmer out of his window look'd
This host of Elves to see;
"O help me, Jesus, Mary's son!
"These Elves will visit me."

In every nook he made a cross,
But most about his room,
And off flew many a frighten'd Elf,
Back to his forest gloom.

Some flew to th' East, some flew to West,
Some flew to the North away,
And some down into the deep ravine,
Where still I hope they stay.

But one, the smallest Elf of all.
In through the doorway strode;
No fear had he for sign of cross.
But great the grudge he ow'd.

The housewife took the wisest plan,
She set him down to board.
And fed him well with ale and meat
And many a coaxing word.

"But hark, thou farmer of Willenshaw,
"What now I say to thee;
"Who gave thee leave to build a house,
"And settle here with me?

"Yet if thou wishest here to dwell,
"The treaty bear in mind;
"From this day forth thy wife so dear
"To me must be resigned/'

"Ah! nay," the unhappy farmer spake
In all his depth of woe,
"Eline, the comfort of my life,
"I never will forego,"

He sooth'd the Elf, as best he could;
"Leave me my housewife dear,
"And, for the rest, take what thou wilt,
"My gold and all my gear."

"Then both Eline and thee I'll take,
"And trample both of you;
"And bury underneath my cell
"Your gold and silver too."

The farmer, maids and serving men
In dread and fell despair.
Thought better, she alone were lost.
Than all in ruin share.

The farmer wild and frantic rose
With bitter grief and keen.
And gave to the little hateful Elf
His wife, his dear Eline.

He clasped her in his arms with joy,
And round in circles sprang;
But pallid grew the housewife's cheek.
For sharp she felt the pang.

She spake, poor woman, full of woe,
With many a falling tear;
"Lord! in mercy send relief,
"My fate is hard to bear.

"My husband was a man, as fine
"As one on earth might see;
"And now to such a lotliesome Elf
"The leman I must be."

He kiss'd her once, and then again.
So sad and woebegone;
The ugliest little Imp he was.
That eye could look upon.

But when a third kiss he would take,
On Mary's son she cried;
And straight, instead of a lothely Elf,
A knight was at her side.

'Twas under a linden tree so green
His shape he found again.
And that to no one's hurt or loss.
But joy to both the twain.

"Now list, my dearest sweet Eline,
"My housewife thou shalt be;
"In England lies a heap of gold,
"I'll give it all to thee.

"While I was still a little child,
"And dead my mother lay;
My stepdame I was driven from home,
"And turn'd to an Elfin gray.

"And now I'll make thy husband great,
"I'll give him gold and fee;
"But thou, Eline, the farmer's wife,
"My housewife thou shalt be."

"Nay, noble knight, for this relief
"Th' Almighty let us thank;
"Choose thou to live in bliss with thee
"Some maid of equal rank."

"If then I get not thee to wife,
"Thy daughter I will take,
"Since recompense for thy good deeds
"No other I can make.

"To thee, Eline, thou wise good wife,
"All honour I will pay;
"But since I cannot win thy love,
"'Tis best thou shouldest stay."

The farmer now on his island dwells
From care and trouble free,
His daughter in England wears a crown.
And happy days has she.

Eline, she too, the farmer's wife,
Is quit of all alarm.
Proud to be mother of a queen,
A king folds in his arm.

This queen she first a daughter bare,
And then a little king;
And every hour she praises God,
From whom such blessings spring.

And there Eline's fair daughter sits,
A kingdom owns her sway;
And she, that honest farmer's wife,
May with her good man stay.

poems.title: The Elf and the Farmer's Wife (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Out in the West sea lies an isle,
Where once a farmer came,
And brought with him his hound and hawk,
And there his house would frame.

He fear'd the oak, he fell'd the beech,
He built his house so fast;
"And shall then," said the cavern Elf,
"This farmer's bragging last?"

Out came the very smallest Elf,
An ant were scarcely less
"And shall this Christian cart our wood,
"And cause us all distress?"

Seven hundred ugly Elves there were
Met in a ring so bold,
And flew away to the farmer's yard,
And there their court would hold.

The farmer out of his window look'd,
And saw their troop so near;
"O help me, God in heaven above,
"How much these Elves I fear!"

The housewife took the wisest plan.
She set them all at board,
And fed them well with meat and ale.
And many a coaxing word.

The first who spake, the grimmest Elf,
The farmer thus addressed;
"Farmer, thy housewife I will have,
"And then I'll take the rest."

"O leave me but my gentle wife,"
In grief the farmer spake,
"My house and yard are in thy power,
"These thou may'st freely take."

"Nay," said the Elf, "have me she shall,"
And took her in his arm;
Her face, as red as any blood,
Betray'd her heart's alarm.

Him must she take in arms, and kiss,
And keen she felt the pain;
For ill and strangely he was shaped,
As eye shall see again.

The housewife's heart was like to break,
"O give me, God, thine aid:"
The third time she must kiss his mouth,
A knight that Elf was made.

"Now thanks, thou noble farmer's wife,
"I'll prize thee, while I live;
"Wilt thou thy farmer have or me?
"The choice to thee I give."

"O knight, thank rather thou thy God,
"Who made thy sorrow cease;
"Betrothe some knight's fair daughter thou,
"And live in joy and peace."

poems.title: The Elf and the Farmer's Wife (C)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Out in the West sea lies an isle,
There once a farmer came,
And with him brought his hawk and hound,
And house began to frame.

He fell'd the oak he fell'd the beech,
He built his house so fast;
"And shall then' ask'd the cavern Elf,
"This farmer's bragging last?"

Up rose and spake the smallest Elf,
"In circle let us meet,
"And march away to the farmer's house,
"And yule-feast with him eat."

The hound he howl'd in the farmer's yard,
The herdsman blew his horn.
The cock leap'd up on the bench, and crow'd.
As if he had his com.

The farmer out of his window look'd.
And humbly cross'd his breast,
"O help me, Jesus, Mary's son,
"The Elf will be my guest."

He made a cross in every nook,
About his room the most,
And some flew east, and some flew west,
And some to Norway's coast.

Some flew to the east, and some to west,
And some to the north away,
But one, the grimmest Elf of all.
Would with the farmer stay.

The farmer, as he was wont to do.
His people at table placed;
The Elf he took the foremost seat.
Their meal they dared not taste.

The farmer had so fair a wife,
On earth was scarce he? peer.
And her that foul and lothely Elf
Would take for his leman dear.

"For husband I have as good a man,
"As one on earth may see;
"Great God, forbid that now to an Elf
"The leman I should be."

"Hark, woman! dear thou art to me,
"Yet if this boon's denied,
"I'll sink thee down to the lowest pit,
"Thy house and land beside."

She took him gently within her arms.
His Elfish lips she kiss'd,
And straight he grew to as tine a knight,
As doth on earth exist.

"And now, good honest farmer, hear,
"'Tis much to thee I owe,
"And lifelong every day and hour
"My love to thee I'll show.

"With wealth I'll day by day reward
"Thee and thy gentle wife,
"So rich shall be no knight on earth,
"For thou hast saved my life."

poems.title: Redeblack
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The emperor's daughter dwelt at Rome,
Her hue was like the rose in bloom.
So proudly he runs amid the fair damsels.

A maid on deeds of kindness bent,
A gift to Denmark's king she sent.

Five foals she sent from out her stall,
And Bedeblack the best of all.

Nine foals she sent, and all so fine;
Yet best was he of all the nine.

That fiery steed no stall could hold,
But while he champ'd on bit of gold.

No other food he deign'd to eat
But sifted grain of finest wheat.

He went not where the river flow'd.
Save when his back a prince bestrode.

And if he then would quench his thirst,
A prince must fetch the bucket first.

The king to war would march away.
His queen and Bedeblack should stay.

The sail of silk and golden oar
Down to the sea the sailors bore.

The king steer'd off his bark from land.
The queen stood waiting on the strand.

"Guide thou my realm, and guard my coast,
"But care for Bedeblack the most."

The queen to her palace hasted back.
And sought the stall of Bedeblack.

She took away his sifted wheat.
And made him fire and venom eat.

In stall would be no longer stay,
But to the sea-shore took his way.

The king gAzed from the heaving tide,
And there his Bedeblack descried.

The king to his aged steersman spake,
"Turn thee and landward steer my snake."

The king the foremost stepp'd on land,
Saw Bedeblack dead on the sand.

"Were it not sin, the monks should sing,
"And bells for Bedeblack should ring.

"Aye! but for what the world would say,
"His bones in Christian soil I'd lay."

They buried Bedeblack on shore;
The king smiled on his queen no more.

poems.title: The Baffled Suitor
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The knight took hawk and his swain took hound
And off they rode to the hunting ground.
My friends they are so few.
Among a score one finds not more
Than one good man and true,

And under a linden's dusky shade
They found in hiding a lovely maid.

"My greeting, lady so blithe and fair!
"But why then here in the cold night air?"

"I've stood in the dark and cold so long
"To list to the nightingale's tuneful song."

"You listened not after the bird so sweet,
"But steps of the knight you're come to meet"

"The truth of the matter I'll not disown,
"I've plighted my hand to a knight of Scone."

"Then list to the offer that now I make,
"And plight it to me, and him forsake.

"Ah! were your birth as your features fair,
"Were none so worthy a crown to wear!

"But pledge me your troth, to me be true,
"My hand and my honour I pledge to you.

"I'll give you castles and gold beside;
"Be kind to me, maiden, and be my bride."

"It ne'er shall be said of me, while I live,
"That I to two men my troth could give;

"And you, if your knighthood you would not stain,
"Will take me unhurt to my home again."

"For honour I've harder tasks essay'd
"Than led to her bower a gentle maid."

Great honour was that to the lady done,
She rode on his horse, and the knight must run.

He ran and he walk'd, but on she rode,
And came the first to her own abode.

She fastened her door with bolt and bar;
"And there you may stay. Sir, where you are."

The knight he mounted, and wroth was he,
But laugh'd the lady with hearty glee.

IS The knight rode back again down the street,
And there had banter and jests to meet.

He told his mother the maid's sly plot,
But small was the comfort from her he got.

She warn'd him another time well to look.
What maid in his hand to dance he.took.

"For early and late they are all awake
"To guard the honour they have at stake.

"They'll out of your hand as slily steal,
"As when by the tail you grasp an eel.

"And trust to their words, you'll he misled,
"As when on a worm-eaten bridge you tread."

poems.title: The Foundling
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A daughter fair of England's king,
Without a tear she had spent her youth,
But sorrow now her heart shall wring,
For young Sir Styge has had her troth,

In honour and virtue wont to live
Without a tear she had spent her youth
And only to him her hand will give,
For young Sir Styge has had her troth.

Nor sooner were forty weeks gone by,
Than loudly the fair was heard to cry.

She muffled her up in mantle blue,
And down to the room of stone withdrew.

Alone she is all in secret gone,
And there she has borne an infant son.

Her child in linen so fine she dress'd,
And secretly laid in a gilded chest.

And since he had never had church's rite,
She set in it hallowed salt and light.

She muffled a cloak about her head,
And down to sea with her infant sped.

She paced for a while the silent strand,
And off the casket she pushed from land.

She drove it to sea with all her might,
"To Christ I trust thee, my little wight:

"May He from all evil keep thee free,
"A mother no longer hast thou in me."

The King was hunting and reached the strand.
And found the chest, as it drove to land.

He opened the lid, and saw a child,
And fair was the babe, and sweetly smiled.

He raised it out of its little chest.
And had it as Christian dipped and bless'd;

Then took the money from out his purse.
And put the baby so small to nurse.

"See, dame, to rear him with utmost care,
"For nobly born is a child so fair."

She nurs'd five winters his tender age,
And then he was made the king's own page.

He grew, till he reach'd his eighteenth year,
And then he the royal banner bare.

The king had given him forts and land.
Would give him to boot his daughter's hand.

The good old King to his daughter spake;
"When wilt thou, my child, a husband take."

"Whenever it be my father's will,
My duty gladly will I fulfil."

"Sir Carl is my best and bravest knight."
"But, father. Sir Styge is my delight."

As drew the day of the wedding near,
Could nothing the lady's sorrow cheer.

Five days they were drinking the bridal wine,
And still she would not her seat resign.

But soon as a sixth day too had fled,
They carried her off by force to bed.

Nor long had waited the weeping bride,
Ere gallant Sir Carl was at her side.

He tapped her gently the lily cheek,
"Now turn thee, my dearest, to me, and speak."

"Hush! hush! now. Sir Carl, my son, and see
"A mother and not a wife in me,

"Foul shame it would be to my father's land,
"That mother should give a son her hand."'

"And shame were it too, should that be told,
"That you, a mother, wear crown of gold."

The King he came with the morning light,
To ask of them how they spent the night.

"For all his kindness I thank my King,
"Yet nothing but scorn this match will bring.

"The King would on me his favours shed,
"But bere he has made me my mother wed."

"We'll bum her to death on faggot pile,
"Or send her off to a paynim isle."

"O spare her, my liege, nor treat her so,
Without a tear she has spent her youth
But on Sir Styge her hand bestow.
For he Sir Styge has had her troth.

poems.title: Duke Henry and the Maiden Malfred
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
One balmy night in summer,
All sparkling lay the dew,
As struck his harp Duke Henry,
And music from it drew.

Fair Malfred on her balcon
Had heard his soothing lay;
"Oh heavens! that brave Duke Henry
"Would only come this way.

"Then, should he wish to slumber,
"On me he might recline;
"And should his lips be thirsty,
"'Tis I would pour his wine."

As spake the maiden Malfred,
Her foster-mother came:
"Hush hush! my dearest Malfred,
"You'll bring yourself to shame.

"Too young are you and tender
"To think of wedlock's band,
"Nor will for three years longer
"Your father give your hand."

"And let me be so tender,
"And let me be so young,
"This evening he were welcome,
"Who such a lay has sung."

So guileless spake the maiden.
She thought none other near.
But stood below Duke Henry,
And lent a listening ear.

'Twas late one summer evening.
And dew lay on the mead;
The Duke from out his stable
Himself led out his steed.

He girt on him the saddle,
He rode away alone;
No squire or groom might follow.
Of them he trusted none.

His saddle all of silver,
His bit with gold so red,
He chose a little greenpath,
That up to her chamber led.

"Oh, rise, dear maiden Malfred,
"Admit me to thy bower;
"'Tis I, thy true Duke Henry,
"Beneath thy chamber tower."

"You lord it over castles,
"Have men at your behest;
"I've not the means at evening
"To treat so rich a guest."

"O spread for me no dainties,
"Nor pour for me the wine,
"But in thy bosom lay me,
"And call me, Malfred, thine."

"Should I unbar my chamber,
"Or should I call you dear,'
"How wroth would be my father,
"If he the news should hear!"

"To talk with thee, dear Malfred,
"I've hither spurr'd my steed;
"If now I may not enter,
"I come no more to plead."

"'Tis not your steed I care for,
"Or what the pace he came,
"But only for my honour,
"And not to lose my name."

"Oh! rise, dear maiden Malfred,
"And kindly let me in,
"I'll ride and see thy father,
"And try thy hand to win/'

"A thousand thanks, Duke Henry!
"I'll not admit you here;
"Go first and ask my father,
"And all my kinsmen dear."

Away he rode, Duke Henry,
And angry too of mood.
But laugh VI the maiden Malfred,
As in her bower she stood.

Well done the maiden Malfred!
For well had she replied;
He rode and pray'd her father
To give him her for bride.

Well one the brave Duke Henry!
The maiden's worth he found,
And pledged her troth on Courtday
With all her kinsmen round.

And so the maiden Malfred
The meed of virtue gains,
And now a wealthy princess,
O'er many a castle reigns.

poems.title: Hedeby's Ghost
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of George Borrow (1826), titled "The Heddybee-spectre".
poems.text:
At fall of night I ceas'd to ride,
And so my horse in tether tied.
The talk of U spreads around.

Down on a tump I laid my head,
And made the grassy sward my bed;

I scarce my first short nap had slept,
When up to me the dead man crept.

"If thou art of my name and race,
"Thou shouldest take in hand my case.

"Do thou to Hedeby repair;
"My kin, all ten, are living there.

"'Tis there my father and mother dwell,
"My brother and sister too as well;

"And there lives Kirstin, once my wife;
"Who, wicked traitress, took my life.

"With five her maids, on silken bed
"She stifled me, and left me dead.

"My corpse they then in haybands roll'd,
"And cast me on the cheerless wold.

"The swain, on whom I most relied,
"Now takes my horse himself to ride;

"Carves with my silver-mounted knife,
"And nightly sleeps beside my wife;

"With wine and meat his heart he cheers,
"And all the while my children jeers;

"With niggard hand he doles their bread,
"And flouts them, now their father's dead;

"He rides my horse, he hunts my hounds,
"And deer he chases through my grounds.

"Each one, that through the thicket breaks,
"Me in my grave from slumber wakes.

"Be sure, if home to him I go,
"My visit brings him bitter woe."
The talk of il spreads around.

poems.title: Peter Gudmanson and the Dwarfs
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was Sir Peter Gudmanson
Bade saddle up his grey;
"I'll mount, and to my lady-love
"A visit ride and pay."

The knight Sir Peter Gudmanson
Was riding through the grove,
And happy he, for all his thoughts
Were of his lady-love.

The knight Sir Peter Gudmanson
Rode over wood and lawn,
And in the forest lost his way
About the morning dawn.

And where he tried the devious paths,
With silk he found them spread,
And thus Sir Peter Gudmanson
Into the cave was led.

The knight Sir Peter Gudmanson
Enter'd the mountain cave,
And up to meet him rose the dwarf,
And a hearty welcome gave.

"Welcome, Sir Peter Gudmanson,
"To this our Elfin land!
"The nutbrown mead, the sparkling wine
"We'll pour with bounteous hand.

"The nutbrown mead we'll pour for you,
"The sparkling wine as well,
"But here, Sir Peter Gudmanson,
"A twelvemonth you must dwell."

"I've to a maiden plighted troth,
"She lives beyond the heath,
"And if for a year I stay with you,
"She pines herself to death."

Sad was.Sir Peter Gudmanson,
And sorely did he grieve;
The dwarfs fair daughter barr'd the door,
The cave he could not leave.

"I care not I for dames and maids,
"Or all their glittering train,
"But you shall in our Elfin cave
"A year with us remain/'

At last that wild and salvage dwarf,
On warfare forth would roam;
Glad was Sir Peter Gudmanson,
That he might stay at home.

The knight Sir Peter Gudmanson,
His head wrapp'd in his hood,
And to the dwarfs fair daughter went.
And in her chamber stood.

"Dwarfs daughter, hail, thou peerless maid!
"Like rose's queenly bloom!
"O teach me 'scape by runic spell
"This cavern's dreary gloom!"

"No child of Elfin dwarf am I,
"Tho' such I may appear,
"But, born of good and Christian blood,
"Was brought an infant here.

"I'll gladly teach thee runic spells,
"Shall ope for thee the door,
"But fear that thou in foreign lands
"Wilt think of me no more.

"Aye truly I will teach thee runes
"How from the cave to flee;
"When thou'rt again with dames and maids,
"I charge thee think on me."

"And wilt thou really teach me runes,
"How from the cave to flee?
"Then, maiden, on my Christian oath
"Forget I never thee."

When home the wild and spiteful dwarf
Came from his wars at last,
Up stood Sir Peter Gudmanson,
And runes against him cast.

So soon as rose the morning sun,
And shone abroad so brave.
Much long'd Sir Peter Gudmanson
To leave the Elfin cave.

Alas! his hope to leave the cave
Turned but to grief and pain;
The dwarfs fair daughter wrote rune.
And fetched him back again.

As stepped Sir Peter Gudmanson
Into the mountain cave,
Rose from her seat the Elfin maid.
And him a welcome gave.

"Welcome, Sir Peter Gudmanson,
"All honour be your due!
"I cannot let you leave my side,
"Such love I feel for you."

"O let me see the fields again
"For but one single day,
"And on my honour, Elfin maid,
"Thy goodness I'll repay."

She gave a lingering slow consent,
That he the cave should leave;
And truth it is, the Elfin maid
Had bitter cause to grieve.

Sir Peter stoop'd and wrote a rune
Down on the threshold floor,
And left the cave, and thank'd his God,
He dwelt therein no more.

As rode Sir Peter Gudmanson
In through his homestead gate.
Stood at the door his lady-love
Array'd in robe of state.

Oat stepped that fair and gentle maid
Her trulove knight to greet;
"Now praised be God, who sits in heaven,
"That once again we meet!"

"With. Elves and Dwarfs in mountain cave
"I spent a tedious year,
"But ever was my greatest grief,
"What you for me might fear."

The knight Sir Peter Gudmanson
His mantle o'er him spread.
As up into the lofty bower
The way his lady led.

And soon they held their wedding feast,
That happy youthful pair.
And live in peace and mutual love
Devoid of pain and care.

Thero pines to death the mountain dwarf
Bound in a runic spell;
And here Sir Peter Gudmanson
May with his trulove dwell.

So is Sir Peter Gudmanson
From pain and sorrow free,
Sleeps in his faithful lady's arms,
And happy man is he.

poems.title: The Knight in Bird-Dress
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There lives a maiden within a bower,
I'll venture my life, will I,
As graceful, she, as a lily flower.
I'll venture my life for a lady.

There lives on a neighbouring isle a knight,
Who fain with the maid his troth will plight.

Her hand this lady will give to none,
Except to a flying knight alone.

The Master Hildebrand that had heard,
And learnt to dress him in guise of bird.

With plumes of silver and wings of gold
He flitted around and about so bold;

Both over and under her bower he flew,
And gazed on the maiden he came to woo.

So soon as the gentle bird she saw,
There seem'd her a something to him to draw;

And out she ventured, that lily flower,
To lure him within her maiden bower.

A dainty morsel as bait she threw.
And nearer the bird and nearer drew;

He flitted in, and he came so near.
And seem'd so gentle and free from fear.

"O bird, pretty bird, wert thou but tame,
"I'd seat thee hero on my broidery frame.

"Oh bird, pretty bird, wert thou but mine,
"I'd set for thy porch my gilded shrine."

'Twas evening twilight, the dew had spread.
And soon the lady retired to bed.

The bird he sat on her mantle pole,
And tardily seem'd the hours to roll.

The morning bell to the matins rang,
And up and twitter'd the bird and sang.
