With wonder and fear the lady woke,
"Now who is here in the bower, and spoke?"

"Nay," answer'd her maid, "the voice you heard,
"Was only your pet, your pretty bird."

And down from his pole he flew below,
And strutted him boldly to and fro;

He flew and perch'd on the lady's bed.
And hopp'd and chirruped about her head;

He play'd with her hair, her pearls, and band,
And gently he peck'd the lady's hand.

"Dear bird, wert thou from feathers free,
"None other I'd take to wed but thee."

"You've plighted your word, and now be true,
"Give hither your hand, my claw take you."

The lady she gave the bird her hand,
And free from feathers she saw him stand.

He shook his limbs from the plumage free.
And straight a gallant young knight was he.

"By day in thy cage thou still shalt keep,
"By night shalt here in my bosom sleep."

So long did the knight her chamber share,
Till Ingelille two little babies bare.

For summer amusement the lady won
A bonny fair maid and a comely son.

Her father came in the babes to see,
And thus to his daughter dear said he.

"O say, my daughter, whom thou dost call
"The father to these pretty babes so small?"

"Dear father, to you the truth I'll tell,
"I found them both in a woody dell.

"I rais'd them from off the cold damp ground,
"And here have a foster-mother found/'

"Well well, my daughter, so let that be;
"The babies perhaps belong to thee."

At th' evening hour flew home her pet.
Whom she with a kindly welcome met.

"(to sue for me now to be thy bride,
"For here can I thee no longer hide."

The Master, Sir Hildebrand, donn'd his cloak,
And up to her father he went, and spoke;

"J,ist, worthy good knight, to my demand,
"And give me your gentle daughter's hand."

"What ails thee my Ingelille's hand to claim?
"She bears no better than leman's name.

"But if to thy word thou yet wilt hold,
"I'll give her for dowry two casks of gold.

"If thou wilt wed her, and wilt be true,
"Fifteen estates will I give her too."

"O keep your estates and all your store,
"And give me your daughter, and nothing more."

And now she may lay her griefs aside,
The Master Hildebrand's lawful bride;

For joke and banter no longer care,
The knight she has wedded can wing the air.

poems.title: Fair Hillelille and Sir Judah
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
There lay and dreamed fair Hillelille
Alone in her bower so high,
She never should be a wedded wife,
And yet would in childbed die.

At dead of the night fair Hillelille
From heavy sleep awoke.
And, all so vivid had been her dream,
In fright to her mother spoke.

"How strange, dear mother, the dream I dreamt,
"As e'en I was sleeping here!
"What anguish I feel, God only knows,
"Or what I may have to fear.

"Oh! strange, dear mother, my midnight dream,
"Th' Almighty my conduct guide!
"All through my body I seem'd to feel
"The sword of Sir Judah glide/'

Awake her listening mother lay,
III dreams her especial skill;
"Oh heed thee well, my daughter dear,
"It surely must bode some ill.

"Oh! heed theo well, my daughter dear,
"Beware of a scheming foe;
"Sir Judah against thy honour plots,
"As falcon besets a roe."

"My troth Sir Judah shall never gain,
"His suit I shall aye repel,
"And rather will take what wealth I own,
"And live in a cloister cell/'

"Oh grieve me not, Hillelill, daughter mine,
"By taking the fatal vow,
"My pride, and the fairest of all our isle,
"My only child art thou.

"But seat thee awhile in thy maiden bower
"To broider with golden thread,
"Till he. Sir Judah, has plighted troth
"Some other fair maid to wed."

And there eight weary years she sat
So tedious and so long,
And never could hear in all that time
A mass or a vesper song.

Sir Judah wrote to his friends around
He would on a journey ride,
But came at nightfall, and lay in wait
In under the mountain side.

The gentle Hillelill left her bow'r
Her mother for leave to pray;
"And now may I safely drive to church,
"Sir Judah is far away!"

"Aye! go thou mayest, dear daughter mine,
"For danger is none at hand;
"The knight to a widow has plighted troth
"Afar in a foreign land/'

Fair Hille was driving so glad to church,
Was passing the greenwood shaw,
As under a tree in evil hour
Sir Judah himself she saw.

"Good morrow, my gentle Hillelill,
"And whither then all alone?
"Say wilt thou show me the same contempt,
"And ever my claim disown?

"Three times so humbly I made my suit
"With all my kith and kin,
"Your hand, you have sworn by all that's good,
"I never may hope to win."

"Now hark thee, my dearest Sir Judah, hark!
"And let me this journey ride,
"And then by all that is good I swear
"To hold me thy trothplight bride."

"And faithful thou mightest a month remain,
"Aye two regard thine oath,
"But comes the suitor thou lovest more,
"Thou givest to him thy troth.

In greenwood was Hillelille's bridal bower,
Her bed of the linden leaf, "
And two little sons she bare the knight.
But died at their birth, of grief.

"With all my kindred with due respect
"Three times I have come to woo,
"You said that I had no morning gift,
"None such as to you was due.

"Go now to your home, fair Hillelille,
"Sit down at your mother's board;
"You never shall see the happy day,
"I greet you with e'en a word."

"But" answered the gentle Hillelille,
Poor sorrowful hapless wife;
"Should once to my kin the tale be told,
"This outrage will cost your life."

"Now as to your kin and all their wrath,
"To fear it I do not need,
"For off on the salty sea I sail,
"And vengeance I little heed."

The gentle Hille went weeping home.
Tore off her crown of gold,
And deeply and bitterly sigh'd and sobb'd,
But could not her tale unfold.

Her kind good mother to Hille came
To welcome her home again;
"But what has the priest in his sermon said
"To cause thee so bitter pain?

"Speak to me, dearest daughter mine,
"And tell me where hast thou stay'd;
"For other folk, all, who went to church,
"To bed and to sleep are laid."

"Sir Judah it is has wrought me shame,
"And lifelong and daily care;
"Ah! luckless it was and doom'd for ill,
"That me any mother bare!"

"But cease thy plaining, dear daughter mine,
"As ill as thy journey sped,
"For soon as thy kinsmen hear the tale,
"The villain Sir Judah's dead."

"Ah! mother, in vain ray kinsmen threat
"His outrage to make him rue,
"Sir Judah is sailing the salty sea,
"Nor cares he what they may do."

For many a long and weary week
She neither had laugh'd nor play'd.
Nor pastime nor kindly words avail'd
To cheer the drooping maid.

Sir Judah he steer'd his bark from shore.
And sail'd on the salty tide.
Nor came to his native land again,
Till after the maid had died.

Fair Hillelill, when the forty weeks
In tedious course were gone,
Slie ask'd of her dearest mother leave
To go to the room of stone.

And into the room of stone she went,
I do but the truth declare,
The hapless mother in childbed died
With two little sons, she bare.

Sad scene it was in the room of stone,
And tears in every eye.
As laid was on Hille's tender lips
A gag to check her cry.

The gentle Hillelille spake but this,
And e'en with her dying breath;
"Go bid ye a thousand times farewell
"To him who has caused my death.

'And send Sir Judah my infant boys,
"And set them before his board,
"The' he, in return for the woes he caused,
"Would give me no friendly word."

That night she turn'd to the chamber wall,
And sank to a guiltless death;
She lean'd her back in her mother's arms.
And calmly resigned her breath.

That very same night Sir Judah woke.
Where far far off he slept.
And scared with a vivid and fearful dream
His silence no longer kept.

"Methought to a church with all my men
"A mass I had gone to hear,
"And fell my clothes on the pavement down,
"And there was my body bare."

Awake by his side his comrade lay;
"'Tis this that thy dreams portend;
"The loss of thy clothes will plainly say,
"Thou losest thy dearest friend.

"And that thou hast dreamt that thou wast bare,
"Lost even thy scarlet pall,
"It means that thy lady the first shall die,
"And thou the next of all."

As steer'd Sir Judah his bark ashore,
He heard the island bell;
"Grant heaven it be not for Hillelill
"Is tolling that doleful knell!"

Sir Judah in haste with all his men
To th' island churchyard hied.
And saw on her bier, a clay-cold corpse,
His Hille, his gentle bride.

"Sir Judah, 'tis thou" the mother said,
"'Tis thou that the maid beguiled;
"Through thee she lies on her bier a corpse,
"My dear and my only child.

"And, villain," the poor sad mother cried.
And fiercely she drew her knife;
"Had not my daughter so pray'd for thee,
"This outrage would cost thy life."

"Ye let my infants to church be brought,
"And rear them in Christian lore;
"I go with my Hille to church today
"And come from it back no more.

"There's nothing left me, but this cold steel,
"To lessen my sorrow's smart."
He fix'd it firmly against a stone,
And drove it through his heart.

Yet spake Sir Judah, as on the ground
All bleeding he lay and cold;
"These infant boys are my own true sons,
"And heirs to my land and gold."

poems.title: How Sir Hylleland Wins His Bride
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The good King Loffer had launched his ship,
And sail'd the billowy main;
There came a Trold, and his daughter seiz'd,
And bitter his grief and pain.
Sir Hylleland fetches his bride.

Sir Loffer, her father, that good old king,
At banquet table sat.
And talked to his men of times gone by
In cordial hearty chat.

"Whichever of you, my faithful men,
"Will bring me my child again,
"Shall wed the maiden, and share with me
"My castles and wide domain.

"If any will rescue my daughter dear,
"If any will ease my grief,
"I'll give him to wife the gentle maid
"With castles and ample fief."

All silent they sat, good honest men,
From danger they seem'd to quail;
Nor one but the gallant young Hylleland
Would offer himself to sail.

Up rose that gallant young Hylleland,
And sprang across the board;
"'Tis I will bring you your daughter back,
"Hold you, my lord, your word."

'Twas he, the gallant young Hylleland,
Sail'd Norway's shore along,
And there at her cave the mermaid found,
Who wrought them so grievous wrong.

"And here thou art sitting, thou lothely witch,
"Aye stirring a smoky brand;
"Go fetch me the maiden Hyllensborg,
"And bring her to yonder strand."

"The fair young maiden thou wilt not gain,
"Of that there is little doubt,
"Unless alone to the cave with me
"Thou goest to fetch her out.'"

And into the cave he boldly stepp'd,
And held in his hand his blade;
And there sat one he had known so long,
'Twas even the lovely maid.

Uprose to meet him the gentle fair,
And blush'd as a rose in bloom.
And wonder'd enough to see the youth
That into the cave was come.

"Stranger," said then the lothely witch,
"Thou winnest not her for bride,
"Until three truths thou hast told to me
"That never can be denied."

"There's money lying upon the floor,
"The walls are gleaming with gold,
"And thou art thyself the lothesomest witch,
"Mine eyes did ever behold."

Up then and answer'd that lothely witch
And angrily answered she;
"What sort of a footman boy is this,
"Come hither to rail at me?"

"A trooper am I, and serve the king,
"Sir Hylleland is my name,
"And who-so calls me a footman boy,
"I'll teach him to rue the same."

"This night together I'll let you sleep,
"Since such is your mutual will;
"Tomorrow you surely shall lose your life,
"Ere sun shines over the hill."

At evening was standing beside his bed
The maiden so fair and bright;
"Would God, that, as long as five, could last
"So happy and sweet a night!"

The young Sir Hylleland turn'd him round,
And smiled to the gentle maid;
"Regard not, my dearest, a witch's spite,
"Nor be of her threats afraid.

"Lie down, lie down there, my lovely fair,
"And quit you of all alarm;
"I've skill to write such a potent rune,
"That nothing shall do us harm."

So soon as had dawn'd the morning light.
And sun shone over the lea,
Uprose from her lair the lothely witch.
And sharpened her knife with glee.

Sir Hylleland laid the potent runes
Just under the threshold floor;
So soon as the witch had trodden thereon.
She threatened their lives no more.

She gently stepp'd to the bedstead side,
Her malice and spite repress'd;
And threw on the bed a quilt of silk,
And bade them in peace to rest.

"Arise from your bed, fair Hyllensborg,
"In gayest of raiment dight,
"And go with Sir Hylleland off to sea,
"For be is a gallant knight."

She bade them to bring the gilded shrine
All fill'd with the brightest gold:
"And that is for you. Sir Hylleland,
"As merits a heart so bold."

She bade them to bring a second shrine,
And ruddy the gold there lay,
"And this shall be your's, my lady fair,
"Your season of grief repay."

Right joyous were both the gentle maid,
And gallant Sir Hylleland,
And gladly they took the witch's gold,
And went to the ocean strand.

The knight in his arms the lady rais'd,
And down in his vessel stow'd.
And steering back to his native land
The prize of his valour show'd.

The king stood up on his castle tower,
And gazed on the sea so wide;
"She's coming — my daughter — her ship it is-
"Is speeding across the tide."

The good king Loffer was glad at heart
His daughter to see again;
And gave her to young Sir Hylleland,
With castles and wide domain.

poems.title: The Maid in the Wood
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The knight took hawk, and his swain took hound,
And rode to the chase away,
And game they started both great and small,
That skipp'd on the heath at play.
In summer-tide.

Beneath a linden he found a hind,
A maiden beneath a rose,
And laid on the ground his cloak so bine
To taste of a sweet repose.

And there they lay the night so long
To nobody's harm or grief;
And all the while the linden tree
Was hiding them under its leaf.

They lay in comfort the night so long,
And nobody knew they were there;
And sheltered them both the linden tree
With branches so green and fair.

But soon as morning began to dawn,
And shrilly the cock to crow,
The lady she tapp'd the knight's fair breast;
"Tis time for you now to go.

"So over the bridge and gallop away,
"And carefully cross the heath,
"My seven bold brothers avoid, if you can,
"Or surely they'll be your death."

"Now whether thy brothers are seven or ten,
"Or ever so handsome and tall,
"If me for a comrade and friend they take,
"I'll not be the worst of them all.

"And if to me they are staunch and true,
"A brother they'll find in me;
"But if they will rather my life and blood,
"A match for them all shall see"

"But oh! now, hear me, my dearest knight,
"So earnest and hard I sue,
"And turn thee and ride some other road,
"If ever they come in view."

"Nay, that shall never be told at court,
"That I have skulk'd away:
"Nay, tho' there should meet me three times seven,
"I'll prove me as good as they."

The knight he donn'd his coat of mail.
And belted sword to side;
A thousand adieus, as he rode away.
He bade to his weeping bride.

He plied the spur to his courser's flank.
So fiery was he of mood.
And soon he had reach'd the forest's edge,
Where seven brave horsemen stood.

"Well met! well met! thou gallant young knight,
"Tis early we find thee here!"
"I've ridden in greenwood at early hour,
"And hunted the forest doer/'

"But where is thy hawk? and where thy hound?
"And game that thou there didst slay?"
"I gave them all to a very good friend,
"Who met me at dawn of day."

"Nay never has that been knightly use,
"To give to a friend one's game;
"But thou with our sister has slept tonight,
"Unmindful our leave to claim."

"I rode to the wood to chase the deer,
"Nor sister of your's had known,
"I chased and I caught the first I saw,
"So pretty and all alone.

"It crept so sweetly beneath my cloak,
"So well was it pleas'd with me,
"And I was as glad and well content,
"How could I but let it be?

"The deer they had run before my hounds,
"To thickets had made their flight;
"The pretty tame hind to my breast I drew,
"And gaily we pass'd the night.

"A lady was she, a graceful maid,
"As mortal with eyes may see;
"If she is your sister, your leave I pray,
"That wedded she be to me.

"A faithful brother I'll be to you,
"For you will I risk my life;
"And her with all honour and love will treat;
"What more can I promise a wife?"

"No! never shalt thou our sister gain,
"Thy wedding we'll here prepare;
"Confess thee now at the linden tree,
"Confess to the birds in the air.

"And say if thou rather wilt stand or my?
"Or thee to the wood betake?
"Or boldly with arms defend thy life
"And fight for the lady's sake?"

"Then here will I stand, and scorn to fly,
"Or me to the wood betake,
"I'll boldly with arms defend my life,
"And fight for my lady's sake."

He first slew one, and he then slew two.
Such prowess and skill he show'd;
His lady's brothers he slew them all,
As gallant as they were proud.

But bitter the tears the lady shed
At news of the dismal fight;
She wept for her seven bold brothers slain.
But most for the handsome knight.

poems.title: Sir Swerkel
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
In Swerker's house the fairest there
Fair Christel danced with flowing hair.
So modest and good the maid,
Who holds my heart in thrall.

Danced King and court, and all so gay,
And little Christel sang the lay.

Sir Swerkel gave the maid his hand;
"Fair Christel, deign with me to stand."

He pressed her hand, he drew her near,
"Christel, be my trulove dear."

Her foot he trod, her hand he press'd,
"Fair Christel, are my wishes guess'd?"

They danced within the chamber both,
And there she plighted him her troth.

The knight his mantle o'er him threw.
And off to his mother's chamber flew.

"Hark mother! Christel, lovely may,
"Has plighted me her troth today."

"Now heaven forefend," the dame replied,
"That sister be her brother's bride!

"Wedded may ye two never be,
"Ye're both my children, thou and she."

"O speak, and tell me, mother dear,
"When didst thou little Christel bear?"

"Whilst thou wast at the court of Rome,
"First saw the light that budding bloom.

"Whilst thou wast at the Holy Grave,
"Birth I to that bright mirror gave.

"But bred at court, since she was born,
"The maid has fur and scarlet worn."

"O mother dear, thy counsel give,
"How without Christel I may live."

"Go then, and hunt the hart and hind;
"So banish Christel from thy mind.

"Go, hunt the stag, go hunt the roe,
"And every thought of love forego."

He hunted both the hart and hind,
But she was ever in his mind.

He hunted both the stag and roe,
But thought of her could not forego.

So him they forced to quit the land.
And she to cloister pale was banned.

But not a bird approached her cell.
She pray'd not news of him to tell.

Not one could o'er his island glide,
He did not ask, how fared his bride.

poems.title: Elfin Hill (A)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of George Borrow (1826), titled "Elvir Hill".
poems.text:
I once was an innocent poor young swain,
And, riding to meet my love,
I felt so weary, I longed to rest,
On lawn of the rosetree grove.

So down on a hillock I laid my head.
And sleep on mine eyelids fell,
When out of their cave three maidens tripped
Their treacherous tale to tell.

The one came towards me, the other went fro,
And whispered the third in my ear,
"Up, pretty young swain, to the dancers come,
"And join in our woodland cheer.

"O do as I bid thee, my pretty young swain,
"And join in the dancers' ring;
"My maiden shall time it with sweetest strain,
"Lips ever were heard to sing."

They brought from a cave a golden chair.
As seat for their Elfin queen;
And now, if I freely the truth declare.
Entranced I had nearly been.

She cleared her voice, and a song began,
And sweetly she tuned her lay,
The brook, that was wont so fast to flow,
Its torrent was fain to stay.

The brook, that was wont so fast to flow,
Its torrent was fain to stay.
The fish stood still in the crystal wave.
And ceas'd with their fins to play.

The pearly fish in the crystal wave
Lay still, as the maiden sang;
The deer, that roam'd in the greenwood shaw,
No longer or skipp'd or sprang.

The deer, that roam'd in the green wood shaw,
Forgot them to caper and bound,
The birds, that sat on the boughs above.
Were still at the soothing sound.

And each with her trulove, and all so gay.
Were dancing there, out and in;
But silent' sat, the poor young swain.
My hand held under my chin.

Then came there a maid with a silver can.
Came tripping from out the crew,
But down at her foot she spill'd the mead,
The maiden right well I knew.

"O listen and say, dear sister mine,
"The wine shall I drink, or no?"
"Nay raise it, but let it not touch thy lips,
"But down on thy bosom flow.

"Raise but to thy lips the silver cup,
"The wine in thy bosom spill;
"For sad is the life with an Elfin quean
"In cavern beneath the hill."

I rais'd to my lips the silver cup,
The wine on my breast let flow;
The Elf-queans merrily clapp'd their hands,
They thought they had won me so.

"Now hark to me, dearest sister mine,
"Up mount thee with me and ride;
"I'll bear thee to where afar from Elves
"In safety thou may'st abide."

"Thou would'st not in all the livelong day
So distant a gaol have won,
"That hither I came not back again
"At rise of the morning sun."

God had not help'd me in time of need
With crowing of cock so shrill,
I surely had stay'd with these Elfin queans
In cavern beneath the hill.

And therefore I counsel all good young swains,
Whoever an errand ride,
They lay them not down upon Elfin hill.
Lest them such a fate betide.

poems.title: Elfin Hill (B)
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the version of George Borrow (1826), titled "Elvir Hill".
poems.text:
On Elfin lull as I laid my head,
A trance on mine eyelids fell;
And forward tripp'd with a lively tread
Two maidens their tale to tell.

With gentlest hand they smoothed my face,
And whisper'd it into my ear;
"Up, pretty young swain, a dance to pace,
"And strains of our music hear.

"Wake up! wake up! thou pretty young swain,
"Join hands in our dancer's ring,
"And tread to the time of the cheerful strain,
"My maiden for thee shall sing."

As soon as the one her lay began,
A lovely and peerless maid,
The brook that before so swiftly ran,
It's eddy and brawling stayed.

The brook that was wont so fast to flow.
It's eddy and brawling stay'd,
And fishes down in the waves below
Their fins to the cadence play'd.

The fishes down in the limpid flood
Were sporting with pearly tail;
And birds came flitting from out the wood,
And twitter'd in all the dale"

"Stay thou with us here, my pretty young wight,
"And gaily we'll pass the time;
"We'll teach thee to read, we'll teach thee to write,
"And many a Runic rhyme.

"We'll teach thee to tame the boar and bear,
"And tie them up to a tree,
"And force the Dragon to leave his lair, -
"His treasure forsake, and flee."

But all the while that the Elfin train
Was tripping it round and round,
On sword-hilt I lean'd me, the fair young swain,
And silent sat on the ground.

"Now wilt thou not answer us e'en a word?
"Nor take in our dance a part?
"Then soon shall thy.glittering knife and sword
"Bear death-sleep into thy heart."

That moment there crew the cock so shrill,
Sure Jesus my soul would save,
For else had I stay'd on the haunted hill,
And been to the Elves a slave.

So list to me, every gentle wight.
And wisely my counsel keep.
You ride not on Elfin hill at night.
Nor lay yourselves there to sleep.

poems.title: The Three Robbers and Their Three Sisters
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Truel he dwelt beside the sea,
Far out on an island west
And with him his graceful daughters three,
The roses in silk were dress'd

"i Dame Mettelille wakes her daughters three
Far out on the &c.
"Get up, my daughters, and come to me.
The roses c.

"Get up, my daughters, you've slept so long,
"You've miss'd the sermon and morning song."

"Then if the matins we miss'd today,
"We'll much the longer at high-mass stay."

Dame Mettelille comb'd her daughters' hair,
Nor dream'd how ill they were doom'd to fare.

She clad them each in a mantle blue,
And sent them to church to Horbelew.

There, just as they reach'd the Tostrup shaw,
The robbers' dog in the path they saw:

Nor sooner had enter'd the Tostrup wood,
Than all three robbers before them stood.

"Now, say, will you rather be robbers' wives?
"Or here on the instant lose your lives?"

"We never will be three robbers' wives;
"We rather will all of us lose our lives/'

They murder'd one, and they murder'd two,
Hard strove the third one, ere her they slew.

"Then grant us this for our honour's sake,
"Tonight at Sir Truel's your rest to take/'

'Twas late as they came to Sir Truers house,
And there they halted and held carouse.

They feasted so long, they drank so deep,
Sir Truel retired to his bed to sleep.

"Now hark, Dame Mettelille, what we say,
"And plight us your favour, nor say us nay."

"Before I plight me to all the three,
"I fain would first in your wallets see."

She open'd their wallets, and saw therein
Her daughters' brooches and golden pin.

"Now tarry a moment and take your rest,
"I go but to fetch my treasure chest."

She fasten'd the door, as out she pass'd;
With bars of iron she made it fast.

She mantled her head, and up she stepped
To where in his loft Sir Truel slept.

"O wake. Sir Truel, and come with me;
"These robbers have murder'd our daughters three."

Sir Truel he hasted his men to wake,
"Up! up! my troopers, your weapons take.

"Up! buckle upon you coats of mail,
"These robbers are not the men to quail."

"Now speak and tell us, ye robbers three,
"Who are ye, and who may your fathers he?"

"Our father had seat us 'all to school,
"But us poor children the robbers stole.

"With them we have dwelt these fifteen years,
"And eaten our bread with grief and tears.

"Those older robbers are now all dead,
"And we on the highway seek our bread.

"One only crime we have dared to do,
"We yesterday night three maidens slew."

Sir Truel in tones of anguish griev'd,
"Of all my children I'm now bereav'd.

"Your mother it was ye wish'd to plight,
"Your sisters it was ye slew last night.

"Three suits of clothes for you I will buy,
"But out of the town and country fly."

"O nay! dear father, that will not we;
"Nay! 'Life for Life' is the law's decree."

They fetter'd and led them out of town,
And better at once had hewn them down,

The two were rack'd on a pole and wheel,
But one made off to the woods to steal.

poems.title: Sir Luno and the Mermaid
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Luno he built a ship so grand, '
As never was seen on sea or land.
They gather gold in Greenland.

'Twas gilt all over from stern to prow,
The name of the Virgin on either bow.

'Twas gilt all over from deck to floor,
And blazon'd the name of Jesus bore.

The sails were of silk, so bright and new,
The one was yellow, and one was blue.

The yards they were all with silver bright.
The mainmast top with gold was dight.

Sir Luno bade, and they down to shore
The anchor bare and the slender oar.

As steer'd Sir Luno across the sea.
There met him a Mermaid, and wroth was she.

"Hark thee. Sir Luno, and wend thee back,
"Or high on a rock thy ship I'll wrack."

"Foul witch, thou never the day shalt live,
"That I should place to a Mermaid give."

The very first wave the Mermaid cast.
Asunder were rent both sail and mast.

The very next wave that the Mermaid threw.
The sails to the sea in tatters flew.

Said then the steersman, "lias none the skill
"With Runes the Mermaid's wrath to still V"

Up spake Sir Luno, that worthy knight,
"The Runes myself I have learnt to write."

On staff so slender he wrote the Rune,
And bound the struggling Mermaid down.

He wrote the Rune on a twig so small,
Yet bound her fast on a stone withal.

"Sir Luno, Sir Luno, oh set me free,
"Seven tons of silver I'll give to thee.

"Seven tons of silver and eight of gold;
"Have mercy, Sir Luno, and loose thy hold!"

"Sit thou and famish in cold and pain;
"The spell I never. will loose again.

"Sit there, and all who come near thee, tell,
"How thou hast been bound in Sir Luno's spell."

Sir Luno is home to Greenland gone.
The Mermaid is fast on a reef of stone.

poems.title: Proud Eline
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the handsome Sir Remold
He rode away.
And won Sir Bonders daughter's hand,
A lovely may.

He brought Sir Bonders daughter home
To his abode;
The Archbishop and the King himself
Beside them rode.

In state they brought that gentle bride,
To Sir Remold,
Nor for the minstrel stinted they
The ruddy gold.

They led the bride to banquet room
From out her wain,
There follow'd her both knights and squires
To hold her train.

They seated her, the lovely bride,
On bridal chair.
And walked in front both knights and squires
Her robe to boar.

Uprose with silver cup in hand
The proud Eline,
And all the day she pour'd the wine
Till dusk of e'en.

All the day long she serv'd the wine
From man to man,
But snatched in anger from the bride
The silver can.

She pour'd the bright and sparkling wine,
While yet was light;
The bride was led in state to bed
At fall of night.

From banquet hall to bridal house
They led the fair;
In front there march'd both knights and squires
The torch to bear.

They seated on her bridal bed
The gentle bride,
And he from table rose, and soon
Was at her side.

The rest they left the bridal house.
Friends all, so kind.
But crept beneath the silk Eline
And stay'd. behind.

Then spake the handsome Sir Remold,
As there he lay,
"One thing, my dear and gentle bride,
"I prithee say:

"Tell me between our own two selves,
"Are you not loth
"To sleep beside a faithless man,
"Who brake his oath?

"My Christian faith, my hope in God,
"My honour too,
"Was plighted all to proud Eline,
"Ere given to you/'

"While one you had at home so fair
"As here I see,
"Why rode you to my father's house
"To wed with me?

"While here so lovely a one you had
"Your home to share,
"Why ride across to plight to me
"Those vows you sware?"

"I would no longer lead with her
"A graceless life,
"And therefore, Loumor, wedded you
"To be my wife."

"And yet methinks," fair Loumor said,
So good was she,
"Might surely claim the proud Eline
"Your match to be."

While so they spake, thought Sir Remold
None other near,
But in the bride-house stood Eline
With listening ear.

When on his pillow Sir Remold
Sank down and slept,
The proud Eline to the bridal bed
For vengeance crept.

Her golden-hilted knife she drew
From sleeve so red,
And therewithal she stabb'd the knight,
Till he was dead.

From sleep awoke the gentle bride,
And weeping spake;
"Forbear, by all that's good in heaven,
"My life to take."

"But that e'en now I heard thee say
"Kind words for me,
"The selfsame death as Sir Remold
"Awaited thee.

"Put on thy maiden crown again,
"And band of gold,
"The bride thou wast but not the wife
"Of Sir Remold."

Back to her father's went the bride
In saddest mood.
And left the handsome Sir Remold
Drench'd in his blood.

poems.title: The Water-Sprite's Treachery
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The maids at the palace they danced away,
With hair all flowing so blithe and gay.

With hair all flowing there danced the maids,
There danced the knights with their naked blades.

The knights they danced, and their sword blades rang,
The measure the king's own daughter sang.

The maiden was proud, and her voice so clear
All under the ice the sprite could hear.

Up heaved him the sprite, and clothes put on;
"That maiden so proud is mine anon."

He clad him in dress of gold and green,
Took Allfast, the Prince's, name and mien.

A black and white horse he then bestrode,
And off on a golden saddle rode.

As up to the courtyard gate he came,
They tripp'd a dance, as in chase of game.

His horse to the churchyard rail he bound.
And entered and danced to the tuneful sound.

The maiden her hand held out to the sprite;
"Come dance with me, Allfast, my trulove knight."

"I will not join in the dance with thee,
"Unless thou wilt come to my home with me.

"O maiden, no longer thy love withhold,
"I'll grace thy head with a crown of gold:

"I'll give thee so precious a golden band,
"As never was seen in all this land.

"Tho' rules thy father so many a town,
"He gave thee never so rich a crown;

"Tho' king thy father o'er all the land,
"He gave thee never so rich a band."

"But how shall I 'scape from the castle yard,
"Where kinsmen so many hold watch and ward?"

"Tho' guard thee thy kindred by night and day,
"Thy troth thou hast plighted, and must away."

His horse so gentle was standing there,
And up on its back he rais'd the fair;

He gallop'd away o'er heath and wold.
And gleam'd afar with a blaze of gold.

His horse rush'd onward o'er holt and hill,
And first at a roaring stream stood still.

"Now tell me then, Allfast, my knight so true,
"What will you to cross that water do?"

"No trulove of thine, tho' such I seem,
"My home is here in the roaring stream."

With fifteen nails in the four gold shoes
Down sank the steed in the stifling ooze;

And far they could hear on the mountain side,
How under the water the maiden cried.

poems.title: Mar Stig's Daughter and the Merman
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
"O mother, give me thy rede herein,
"Mar Stig's fair daughter how I may win."

Of water she made him a horse to ride,
Of sand a saddle and reins beside.

Himself she shaped to a knight so proud,
And off to St. Mary's church he rode.

His horse to the churchyard rail he bound.
And twice the church walked wrongways round.

He entered the door, and one and all
Turn'd round at the sight the statues small.

The priest who before the altar stood,
Ask'd who he might be, that knight so proud.

Said Mar Stig's daughter with downcast eyne;
Would God that the gallant knight were mine!"

He stepp'd over one stool, stepped o'er two,
"Be mine, Stig's daughter, to me be true."

He stepp'd over three seats, stepp'd o'er four;
"O come to my home on yonder shore."

Up rose the maid and her hand gave she;
"I plight thee my troth and follow thoe."

They walk'd from the church in bridal train,
And danced so joyously both the twain.

They danced till at last they reached the shore,
And no one was left beside them more.

"Mar Stig's fair daughter, hold thou my steed,
"For here I must build us a ship at need."

So soon as they came there and trod the sand,
The little boats all turned round to land.

They hardly put off and left the bank.
Ere down to the bottom Stig's daughter sank.

The far off dwellers about the creek.
Heard under the water her drowning shriek.

So list to my rede, ye maidens good.
And go not to dance in so proud a mood.

poems.title: The Two Sisters Who Avenged Their Father
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A sister thus to a sister spake,
My trulove who secretly had my vows

"And never wilt thou a husband take?"
Is sheltering under the greenwood boughs.

"Nay wed will I never a living swain,
My trulove (c.
"Till vengeance I've had for a father slain."
Is sheltering c,

"But what will our own two hands avail?
"No sword have we here, nor coat of mail."

"These wealthy farmers, who near us dwell,
"Will lend us mail and a sword as well."

On cloak and collar they plied their shears,
And made them dresses for cavaliers.

They d'onn'd their mail, girt sword to side,
And mounted horse to the court to ride.

When up to the courtyard gate they came.
There stood beside it Sir Erland's dame.

"Our greeting. Sir Erland's wife! now say,
"Is he, Sir Erland, at home today?"

"Sir Erland sits in his hall to dine,
"With guests around him is quaffing wine."

As enter'd the hall those maidens two,
He rose to meet them with honour due.

The purple cushion Sir Erland pressed,
"Come hither, sit down, young men, and rest."

"We're not so weary, nor are we tired,
"And yet were a little rest desired."

"Now say, are ye married men, ye two?
"Or stealthily ride ye out to woo?"

"We are not married, nor have we bride,
"But hither to woo by stealth we ride,"

"Then hark ye, young gallants! for I can tell,
"Where two rich fatherless maidens dwell."

"But if so rich are these orphans two,
"Say, why for their favour did you not sue?"

"Their favour myself I had gladly sought,
"If hindered me not a crime, I wrought;

"The maidens' father had I not slain,
"And then with the widowed mother lain/'

"ris true, by thy hand our father died,
"But touching our mother 'tis foully lied."

With maidenly grace their swords they drew.
With manly courage the knight they slew.

They hack'd Sir Erland to bits as small,
As chips from a woodman's hatchet fall.

With teardrops many, and rueful face,
The maids to their shrift were seen to pace;

But all the penance the father bade,
Three Fridays on bread and water paid.

poems.title: Sir John
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the versions of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Lovel and John" and George Borrow (1826), titled "Sir John".
poems.text:
As home Sir Peter came from town,
Ye're bidden every one!
All eagerly rushed his daughter down
To ask about Sir John.
So bind a golden helmet on,
And come along with John,

"Dear father, welcome home at last!
"Now tell me what at court has passed,
"And all about Sir John/'

"My dear, the news I bring is grand,
"The rich Sir Lave gets your hand,
"And not the rogue Sir John."

"And if he does, then I can tell,
"For him it we'nt turn out so well,
"If still alive Sir John."

His news Sir Peter had hardly told,
When up Sir Lave rode so bold,
Alas! 'twas not Sir John.

Sir Lave made his marriage feast,
Sir John got shod his trusty beast,
"I'll soon be there," said John.

Sir Lave rode to an isle away,
Ye're bidden every one
And there betroth'd a lovely may;
"I'll ride with them," said John.
So hind a golden helmet on
And come along with John,

Sir Lave brought him home his bride,
And knights and squires to meet them hied,
"And here am I," said John.

They set her down on bridal chair.
To deal the wine Sir John was there.
"Now drink away," said John.

They took to bed the blushing bride,
But left by chance her stay-lace tied;
"Come, I'll loose that," said John.

He lock'd the door with hearty glee,
"Sir Lave wish good night' from me,
"For here I stay," said John.

"Sir Lave, haste map! haste!" they cried,
"Sir John's up stairs and with the bride;"
"Aye! that I am," said John.

Sir Lave tapp'd the chamber door,
"Come out. Sir John, and jest no more;"
"Now wait a bit," said John.

With spear and shield he made a rout,
"Up. up, Sir John! this instant out."
"See if I do," said John.

"Unless at once you leave my bride,
"Before the King I'll have it tried."
"And that you may," said John.

The morrow morn at dawn of day
To court Sir Lave bent his way;
"And I'll go too," said John.

"I wooed and brought me home a bride,
"Sir John has stolen her from my side;"
"That's very true," said John.

"If she's to both of you so dear,
"Then go like men, and break a spear."
"With all my heart," said John.

The morrow, soon as it was light,
Went knights and squires to see the fight.
"I'm ready, boys," said John.

They rode and charged with all their force,
And knuckled down Sir John's good horse.
"God help me now!" said John.

They rode again and grappled well.
And on the ground Sir Lave fell.
"There let him lie," said John.

As reach'd Sir John his castle gate.
There waiting him his lady sate.
"You are mine then now," said John.

And so Sir John, apart from strife,
Can live in comfort with his wife.
"I've got her safe," said John.

poems.title: Lady Bodild
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The Linden stands on Lindenhill,
Stands bending towards the ground;
For Lady Bodild's wasting grief
A cure can not be found.

The linden stands on Lindenhill,
And gaily spreads its leaf,
But still to Lady Bodild's heart
No season brings relief.

It was the gallant knight Sir John
Awoke, and told his wife,
"I've dream'd tonight a wondrous dream,
"And fear I lose my life.

"I dream'd I rode to hunt the wolf
"Out in the forest shaw,
"And slain, and rent in morsels small
"Fell mangled from his jaw."

"And have you dreamt this frightful dream?
"God guide us for the best!
"Get shriven before you take the field,
"And have your banner bless'd."

Sir John in church is duly shriven,
And off to the war is gone;
The first, that in the battle fell,
Was even he Sir John.

Sir John, he with his king had march'd
To meet his country's foes.
And in the van his banner bare,
And fell, and never rose.

Three months went by, and peering out
The Lady Bodild stood;
"A hearse comes hitherward from south,
"I see the gilded wood.

"Bright glittering over Lomberd hill
"That hearse comes moving on,
"And either 'tis the King himself,
"Or else my lord, Sir John."

The Lady Bodild call'd her men;
"Ye servants twain, come near;
"Go saddle me quick my good grey horse,
"I'll ride to meet the bier."

Then thus Sir Peter, gallant knight,
No guile was in his heart;
"'Twas I that won his wife's consent
"To let Sir John depart."

Off to the van, where rode the king.
Sir Peter went, and spake;
"See here my sister Bodild comes;
"What answer shall we make?"

"O tell her 'tis Sir John's small page
"That on the bier is lain,
"Before next candlemas is past,
"Sir John comes home again."

The Lady Bodild heard the news,
But gave it no belief,
And wept, and wildly clapp'd her hands
In bitterness of grief.

"Set down, set down that gilded bier,
"I'll see what may be there,
"For better I can trust my eyes,
"Than what my kinsmen swear."

She looked, but knew Sir John no more,
Nor aught of him could see,
For tied up in a linen cloth
All chopp'd to bits was he.

She first of all his fingers viewed,
Then on his eyes would pore;
"Wert thou the only man on earth,
"I should not know thee more."

His little finger again she view'd,
And there she found a scar,
That with her scissars she had made
Herself in playful spar.

"'Tis thou indeed, my dear Sir John,
"All mangled tho' thou art;
"I ne'er shall see that happy day,
"That anguish quits my heart."

His clay-cold cheek she gently tapp'd,
A tender tear let fall;
"Forgive thee God, my brother dear,
"But thou hast caus'd it all."

She gently through her fingers drew
His long soft yellow hair;
"How often with my silver shears
"I clipp'd these locks so fair."

She rais'd his hand, his dear right hand,
And kiss'd his lips so cold;
"O pity, Lord, a widow's grief,
"My happy days are told."

Then kindly spake the Danish king,
Nor longer could refrain;
"My noble lady, why thus weep,
"Where sorrowing is in vain?

"Cease, lady, cease to mourn and sigh
"For what is lost and gone;
"I'll find thee soon another man
"Much richer than Sir John."

"Nay, gold and silver lack I not,
"I still have both in store,
"But friend so true, as was Sir John,
"I find me nevermore.

"And thanks for other rede you gave,
"But surely spoke in jest;
"There's one above can venge the wrong'd,
"And give the troubled rest.

"On me, a weak defenceless wife,
"You've wreak'd your wrath and spite,
"But look to what the proverb says
"Shall you for this requite."

In angry mood rode off the King,
To church the lady drave,
And weeping there slie left Sir John
Closed in his silent grave.

She little cared for Denmark's king.
Or gave his counsels heed.
But ever sat on widow's bench,
And -dress'd in widow's weed.

Nor knight was there in all the court,
Despite the king's command,
Could ever cheer her lifelong grief.
Or ever gain her hand.

poems.title: Fair Signild and the Brother Whom She Rescued
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Signild had brew'd and mix'd the wine,
The rime begins to fall
And ask'd her brother to come and dine.
Up! don your harness, all!

The mead and the wine they set to run,
As long as was shining the cheerful sun.

Her brother, he then would homeward ride,
And swains she would give him his course to guide.

"What need have I now your swains to take?
"So late my foes are no more awake."

But just as the town from sight he lost,
His path seven foes, his bitterest, cross'd.

When round to the thickset wood he turn'd,
He there more plainly his foes discern'd.

"Now grant me, my foes, a boon, my last,
"On gilded cornet to sound a blast."

"Thereto we give thee a short reprieve,
"So blow, as thou wilt, thou hast our leave."

He blew on his horn, he blew so hard,
Fair Signild heard him in castle yard.

His horn so long and so loud he blew.
Its tone in her bed fair Signild knew.

O'er all the castle was heard her call;
"My palfrey bring me from out his stall.

"Aye bring from his stall the gallant gray;
"'Tis seven years, since he has seen the day.

"'Tis seven, since he the sun has seen;
"Since saddle he bare, at least fifteen.

"Bring forth my spear, and bring my brand,
"They've eighteen years not been in hand."

Fair Signild she urged her gallant steed.
And off he sprang at his utmost speed.

Fair Signild she call'd with voice so high,
"If living, my brother, make reply."

"I still am unhurt, nor think to bend,
"But yet, if thou canst, some succour lend,"

She charged his foes, and she cut them down.
And living she brought him back to town:

And though there had twice as many fought,
Their death had the fearless maiden wrought.

poems.title: Sir Norman and Christine
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Some knights, while at an isle they stay'd,
Wrangled about a pretty maid.

"I'd wager all my gold so red,
"Christine cared not, were Norman dead.

"I'd wager gold and neckbone too,
"Christine is not to Norman true."

Sir Norman all their doubts had heard,
"Come now, my friends, I'll prove your word."

Sir Norman, clothed in silk so red,
Lay down, stretch'd out, as he were dead.

The King's men steer'd their ship to land,
Where paced Christine along the sand.

"Welcome, ye King's men, home again!
"How have ye fared in this campaign?"

"Dear has our troop this voyage cost,
"So fine a man we've lately lost.

"We've lost a handsome gallant knight,
"The young Sir Norman he was hight."

The news she scarcely heard them tell,
Ere fainting on the ground she fell.

"And is it true that Nonnan's kill'd?
"Then o'er his corpse a church I'll build.

"Its walls shall be of marble stone,
"The tomb of whitest whalefish bone.

"His coffin I'll with silver dight,
"And golden letters on it write;

" So there' shall say the passers by,
" The bones of Christine's lover lie.' "

Her sorrow he could bear no more,
But rose and kiss'd her o'er and o'er.

Good loyal knight, without delay
Sir Norman fix'd the wedding day.

Well done the gentle lady too!
She show'd herself so good and true.

And now she is free from all alarm,
And nightly sleeps on Norman's arm.

poems.title: Gundelille and Sir Palle
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the maiden Gundelille
Her mother's rede would know,
Might she to drink her Yule-tide draught
To young Sir Palle go.
The leaves are hur sting out so green,

"My daughter, surely as thou shalt dare
"With him thy Yule to keep,
"He'll do what he so long has tried,
"And give thee cause to weep/'

Sir P. "O listen, maiden Gundelille,
"My tender love requite,
"And all the days, I have to live,
"I'll prove thy faithful knight."

"Now hark. Sir Fa6, gallant knight,
"If me no harm you do,
"As soon as Mass is duly sung,
"Home I will go with you.

"Yes, hark, Sir Palle, gallant knight,
"From troubling me refrain,
"And when the Priest has sung the mass,
"Mount with me in my wain."

But when the Mass was duly sung,
And people gone away,
Did still the maiden Gundelille
In church awhile delay.

In scarlet cloak of finest cloth
Her coachman boy she clad;
Herself, the maiden Gundelille,
Disguis'd her like the lad.

She took the reins, and towards the house
Drove off the buxom maid,
And there the rich Sir Palle stood
In marten robe array'd.

Sir Pall he, like gallant knight,
Stepp'd to the lady's wain,
And gently folded in his arms,
And lifted down the swain.

And then with graceful courtesy
Led to his room the lad;
Behind them follow'd Gundelille
In driving mantle clad.

There at the board they seated him
On bridal bench to dine;
The maiden Gundelille herself
Pour'd out and serv'd the wine.

And while he sat, that coachman boy,
And quaff'd the brimming horn.
Went Gundelille and gave the steeds
Their water and their corn.

But now with evening's chilly mist
The fields were overspread.
And time the lady's coachman boy
Should rise and go to bed.

They led him off to the bridal house,
That coachman boy so fair,
And in the van march'd Gundelille
The bridal torch to bear.

So soon as in the bridal bed
The lady's coachman lay,
No longer could the gallant knight,
Sir Palle, stay away.

Down in the bridal bed he sat,
And tapp'd him on the cheek;
"Turn round, my lovely Gundelille,
"Turn round to me, and speak."

"I'm not the maiden Gundelille,
"I do but drive her wain;
"Sir Palle, pry thee, gracious knight,
"Forgive an humble swain."

"Art thou not maiden Gundelille,
"But only hired to drive?
"Then never from this bridal bed
"Shalt thou come out alive."

To find a weapon, knife or spear,
Sir Palle turn'd him round,
And out of window sprang the lad,
And lighted on the ground.

Into the courtyard leap'd the lad
From off the window sill,
Where, waiting in her carriage, sat
The maiden Gundelille.

And off and through the courtyard gate
She drove her gilded wain,
And turn'd her round, and gaily laugh'd,
And gave her steeds the rein.

Anon with sundry courteous notes
The unhappy knight she teaz'd;
"Would know, if with his coachboy bride
"The gallant knight was pleas'd."

With cruel jokes and daily pranks
She drove him nearly wild;
A cradle sent and baby clothes
To rock and wrap the child.

The knight Sir Pall, vex'd was he,
And keenly felt her jest:
"O would to heaven I were but dead,
"And in my grave at rest!"

So vext was he, the baffled knight,
He broke his heart and died;
But she lives on, fair Gundelille,
In all her maiden pride.

poems.title: Fair Anna
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The rovers sail'd in search of spoil,
And far from home they came,
And stole a daughter of England's king,
Fair Anna call'd by name.

They took her off to a distant land,
And Anna there they sold;
A Duke's son he that bought the maid
With heavy sums of gold.

And while eight years with him she liv'd,
Seven sons Fair Anna bare,
And through her modesty and worth
He won a crown to wear.

This lord was born in Mecklenburg,
Of princely race and old;
And him the child of England's king
Was by those rovers sold.

But when eight years were past and gone,
Could Anna not mistake.
That he would wed another maid.
And her at last forsake.

Before his mother's chair she stood,
And, "Mother dear," said she;
"O pity me, and pray your son
"To marry none but me."

"That, Anna, gladly I will do,
"Will ask him even now;
"No other maid, that he could wed,
"Were dear to me as thou."

She went and stood before her son
Fair Anna's cause to plead;
"How long designs my lord and king
"This graceless life to lead?

"Your wife, your wedded wife and queen
"The faithful Anna make,
"And let your seven fair children too
"Their rank and station take."

"Nay, mother, nay! that will I not,
"With money she was bought,
"Nor know I, who her parents are,
"Nor whence the maid was brought."

The King his marriage-letters wrote.
And sent them up and down,
To name the lady he would wed.
And for his queen would crown.

Fair Anna heard up in her bower
The words the barons spake;
"O heavenly father, grant my prayer,
"That my poor heart may break."

There came the king, and Anna found,
And, "Anna," said the king;
"What gift, what worthy gift wilt thou
"My bride and princess bring?"

"I'll give her good and precious gifts,
"My lord and king," said she,
"I'll give her all my seven fair sons,
"Her pages they shall be."

"That is no precious gift to give,
"Anna, my gentle dove;
"Some other richer one bestow,
"Wilt thou retain my love."

"A richer gift than that I'll give,
"And very ill can spare,
"Thy own dear person to be her's,
"And try my loss to bear."

"That is no very precious gift,
"Anna, my gentle dove,
"Thy best gold buckle thou must give,
"Wilt thou retain my love."

"My best gold buckle gets she not,
"For never will I spare
"What eight years since as morning gift
"Yourself you bade me wear."

Then stood the king before his bride;
"Fair Princess, fain I'd know,
"On Anna, long my leman dear,
"What gift will you bestow?"

"A very good and fitting gift,
"My lord and king" said she,
"A pair of old and cast off shoes,
"As suits her base degree."

"My noble Princess, and my bride,
"That were not good or kind,
"Some better gift than that bestow,
"My love if you will find."

"So shall I give her richer gifts,
"My lord and king" said she,
"I've seven fine mills across the Rhine,
"And her's those mills shall be.

"Well built are all those mills, and deck'd
"With many a choice device;
"And rich indeed the rents they pay,
"They grind both wheat and spice."

Fair Anna stood before her lord;
"O grant me this request,
"That I may go to the bridal bower,
"To see your pretty guest."

"Nay, Anna, that thou mayest not,
"From all such thoughts forbear;
"For angry should I be to learn,
"That thou had'st enter'd there."

Before his mother then she stood.
And, "Mother dear she cried,
"I'd fain within the bridal bower,
"To see the pretty bride."

"Right welcome that to do art thou,"
'Twas thus the mother spake,
"But dress thee in thy richest suit,
"And all thy maidens take."

Fair Anna stepped within the door,
With anxious heart and sad:
Before her walk'd all seven her sons
In scarlet richly clad.

Fair Anna pour'd the bride a draught
From out the silver can,
And one may think, how down her face
The tears of sorrow ran.

Then went and stood before her lord
The fair and royal bride;
And ask'd him whence the lady came,
And why she wept and sigh'd.

"That lady then, my fair young bride,
"If I the truth should tell,
"Is but a niece, that from afar
"I fetched with me to dwell."

"Nay! nay! my lord, it is not so,
"Why such untruth pretend?
"Your leman, once so dear, is she,
"God knows how that may end."

"If to her pain and sorrow then
"The truth must needs be told,
"She from abroad was sent to me,
"For money she was sold.

"Her sons and mine those seven fair boys,
"Who stand before your chair;
"To see her children serving you,
"lias brought her to despair."

"I had a little sister once,
"And her name Anna too,
"Was stolen away and sold abroad,
"But where we never knew.

"By pirates she was stolen away
"In childhood's early years,
"And bitter was her parents' woe,
"And ceaseless were their tears.

"That sister Anna thou must be,
"That rosebud now in bloom;
"Thy mother has never smiled again,
"Since thou wast stolen from home.

"It is that sister's voice I hear
"Too plainly to be wrong;
"Keep now thy lord; God grant you both,
"Happy to live and long!"

Great was the joy and merriment
That through the palace spread,
To see, in all his royal state,
The King fair Anna wed.

Anon the fair young bride return'd
Back to her home again.
And took her sister's youngest boy
And all her bridal train.

poems.title: Sir Tideman and Blidelill
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
It was the knight Sir Tideman
Sat quaffing wine at board.
And gaily among his comrades joked
With many a merry word.
It is dawning under the hill.

"If I win not fair Blidelil
"With gift or word of lip,
"I'll write and send her runes so strong,
"Shall lure her aboard my ship."

He wrote a 'pair of potent runes,
And toss'd them towards the land,
And bade them both to float ashore
To Blidelil's fair hand.

There went the maiden Blidelil
To walk along the Sound,
And saw two little scribbled chips,
Lay thrown upon the ground.

She gather'd up the little chips.
And stuck them in her sleeve.
And on her pillow laid them down,
As home she came at eve.

That night the maiden Blidelil
At midnight hour awoke,
And scar'd with wondrous dreams she had dream'd,
She thus to her mother spoke.

"I know not whence this longing comes,
"Or how it well can be;
" Tis after one Sir Tideman,
"I never chanced to see."

"Spread over her a silken sheet,
"And velvet counterpane;
"Perhaps our little Blidelil
"May fall asleep again."

But rose and dress'd fair Blidelil,
And left her mother's bower.
And went to walk along the strand
Alone at midnight hour.

As stepp'd the gentle Blidelil
On board the gilded prow,
Up rose the knight, Sir Tideman,
And made the maid his bow.

"Welcome, dear maiden Blidelil,
"Right welcome to my hand!
"And was there then no knight or squire
"In all your father's land?"

"Aye! truly knights there are, and squires,
"And gallant men at home;
"'Tis through the potent runes, you wrote,
"That here you see me come/'

Vex'd was the gentle Blidelil,
Sore vex'd at what he said,
And took the little grassy path.
That to the deep sea led.

Crosswise she spread her arms, and leap'd
From off the rocky bank.
And down beneath the billows blue
To th' Ocean's bottom sank.

Long stood the knight. Sir Tideman,
Lost in sad thought was he;
"And could the gentle Blidelil
"Have drown'd herself for me?"

Long musing on her mournful death
The knight in anguish stood;
Then toss'd aside his purple cloak.
And plunged into the flood.

Ill written were those runes, and sad
The doom that o'er them hung,
That both so soon their death should find,
So highborn and so young.

poems.title: Fair Christel and the Heathen King
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Christel she serves the royal hall,
Fair Christelille of Fuen,
She robes her in silk and sable pall,
And well she eludes the Rune.

She wins the favour of knight and squire,
Fair Christelille of Fuen,
Wakes even the Danish king's desire,
And well she eludes the Rune,

"Dear Christel, would heaven the queen had died,
"And thou, my Christel, shouldst be my bride!"

"O hush, my king, hush! and say not so;
"Compare not to her a maid so low;

"For fairer would she he turn'd to clay,
"Than I in my scarlet on gala day.

"Aye! fairer would she be upon her bier,
"Than I am in health and best of cheer."

Now while they thought they were all alone.
The queen had listened to every tone.

The queen she spake to her servants twain,
"Go summon me Christel back again."

Fair Christel she stood before the board;
"My gracious Queen, you have sent me word?"

"What was it thou told'st the king of me,
"As he last evening spake with thee?"

"Naught else but only, so help me heaven!
"That thou art to every virtue given."

The queen with her kinsmen thought awhile
To burn her to death on faggot pile.

"Nay, burn her, that were too harsh amend;
"The maid to the Paynim ' sultan send.

"And let him roast her, or boil, or burn,
"Whatever he chooses, will serve my turn."

She lost not a moment, but wrote a brief,
Should bring little Christel into grief.

She gave them into her servants hand
To carry them both to a heathen land.

But when they were near the Paynim shore,
That hateful letter the servants tore.

They wrote in a new one to pray the king
To take for his wife the maid they bring.

Fair Christel she entered the castle gate,
Where wrapt in ermine the sultan ate.

"Now sooner than be that Paynim's wife,
"I gladly this instant would lose my life."

"Then rather than miss a maid so fair,
"Baptize me your Christian faith to share."

On Saturday night baptized was he.
On Sunday was married with games and glee.

Bright gold on the altar Christel laid.
And two full measures her servants paid.

"Salute me the King with as oft good bye,'
"As glitter the stars in a winter sky.

"But ban on the queen as many sad cares,
"As linden has leaves, or the hind has hairs."

poems.title: Sir Rosmer in Elfland
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Bund had dwelling beside the sea
Two daughters, as fair as fair could be.
The linden is all in leaf.

Five sons he had too, fair youths and tall,
But Rosmer the fairest by far of all.

An elfquean that lived upon the shore,
Had loved him for fifteen years or more.

For fifteen winters on plans she thought,
How Rosmer might be most safely caught.

One evening late, as fell the dew,
The elfquean wrapped her in mantle blue.

Well wrapped in her mantle, in she stepped,
And up to the room where Rosmer slept.

She tapp'd at his door with muffled knock,
"Get up. Sir Rosmer; the door unlock."

"No meeting tonight have I to keep,
"I let in nobody, while I sleep."

Her fingers were all so small and fine.
As into the wards of the lock to twine.

With tiny finger the bolt she drew.
For well the trick of his door she knew.

She seated herself beside his bed,
And play'd with the locks of Sir Rosmer's head.

She seated herself on his bedstead rail,
And soothingly told her wily tale.

"Now promise to meet me, nor say me nay,
"And be at the stone-bridge at break of day."

Sir Rosmer at midnight hour awoke.
And thus of his dream to a comrade spoke.

"A lovely maiden I seem'd to see,
"As fair and tender as wax was she.

"Methought she sat in my bedside chair,
"In kirtle of silk and flowing hair.

"I've pledged my promise, at dawn of day
"To meet at the bridge the lovely may."

"Lie still, Sir Rosmer, nor give it heed,
"Some elfquean surely will thee mislead."

"The dream turn out, as it pleases heaven!
"But stand I must to the pledge I've given."

As soon as the sun in his chamber shone,
Sir Rosmer rose, and his clothes put on.

He first a shirt on his shoulders drew,
And then a jacket of velvet blue.

And then he fitted a buckskin boot
And gilded spur upon either foot.

Sir Rosmer his servants was heard to call;
"Go fetch me my steed from out his stall.

"Up! saddle me quickly and rein the grey,
"For I must e'en to the bridge away."

He girt on his side his trusty brand.
His mother was near and wrung her hand.

As out of the yard Sir Rosmer rode.
The tears on the cheek of his mother flow'd.

But while he was crossing the bridge of stone,
His horse tripp'd up on his golden shoon.

His horse tripp'd up on the nails of gold.
And into the torrent Sir Rosmer roll'd.

Sir Rosmer he swam the eddying flood,
To where on the bank an elfquean stood.

"O welcome, Sir Rosmer! come home to me,
"I've brewed the mead and the wine for thee."

"The wine and the mead thyself may cheer;
"Unhappy am I to have landed here."

"Now tell me, Sir Rosmer, as gallant knight,
"The name that the land of your birthplace hight."

"In Denmark have I from my childhood grown,
"And there was my clothing cut and sewn.

"And there dwells also the gentle bride,
"With whom I had willingly lived and died."

She turned to her maid, "Go thou with speed,
"And fetch me hither the horn of mead.

"Bring hither the goblet of red-deer horn,
"And cast in it grains of elfin corn."

The maid came in at the chamber door,
A goblet of horn in her hand she bore.

"Now pledge me. Sir Rosmer, a friendship's en p."
"If such is thy pleasure, I drink it up."

He swallow'd the juice of the elfin grain;
The world was lost to his wilder'd brain.

His father and mother he clean forgot,
His sisters and brothers remembered not.

Forgot his trulove, the gentle bride,
With whom he would gladly have lived and died.

"Now tell me, Sir Rosmer, as gallant knight,
"The name that the land of your birth-place hight."

"Elfland, and here from a child IVo grown,
"And here my clothing was cut and sewn.

"And here you are standing, the winsome bride,
"I'm ready to live and die beside."

The elfquean has now her mind at rest.,
May daily repose on Sir Rosmer's breast;

But much have his father and mother cried,
His brothers and sisters, and eke his bride.

poems.title: Axelwold
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The King's men out to the forest ride
To chase the hart and hind,
And under a linden tree so green
An infant boy they find.

All wrapped and roll'd in mantle blue
The little babe they bare,
And gave him in the royal court
To foster-mother's care.

To holy church they carried him,
They christen'd him by night,
They call'd his name Young Axelwold,'
And hid him out of sight.

They nurs'd him all the winter through,
They nurs'd him winters three.
Till he the finest lad was grown,
That one on earth might see.

They rear'd him yet some fifteen years
To manhood's strength and height;
Nor rode there in the royal guard
More brave or graceful wight.

The King's men went to try their skill
At pitching bar and stone.
But forward stepp'd young Axelwold,
And beat them every one.

"Go to the Ladies' chamber thou,
"And learn thy mother's name!
"'Twere better than on target ground
"To put us so to shame."

With bloodless check made he reply,
So ill their taunts he bore;
"Till I to name my mother learn,
"I join your game no more."

Silent and sad young Axelwold
From castle-yard withdrew,
And bade his foster-mother tell,
What of his birth she knew.

"Hear me, my foster-mother dear,
"What now I come to say;
"If of my mother aught you know,
"Tell it without delay."

"But tell me thou" dear Axelwold,
"Why sadden'd thus thy brow?
"If lives thy mother, or is dead,
"Ffaith I do not know."

"Nay then," replied young Axelwold,
And drew his glittering knife,
"My mother me this instant show,
"Or this shall end your life."

"Go then, but go with studied speech,
"Up to the ladies' hall,
"And her, who wears a crown of gold,
"Thy mother thou may'st call."

He turn'd about, young Axelwold.
And round him wrapp'd his cloak,
And where the maids and matrons sat.
His silence thus he broke.

"My greeting, matrons all, and maids,
"And dames of high degree!
"My greeting, dearest mother, too,
"If here with you she be!"

Silent those other ladies sat,
Nor answer'd him a word;
Eline took off her crown of gold,
And laid it on the board.

"You then, who work with lily hand,
"And dare that crown to wear,
"My rightful mother, you I ask,
"Whore is the son you bare?"

Long sat in silence proud Eline,
Nor what to answer knew.
The while her cheek, so red before,
Now pale and paler grew.

She stripped her gorget off her breast.
So much was on her mind;
"No son have I in secret borne,
"So God to me be kind!"

"Now think you, dearest mother, think,
"Is't not a crying shame,
"So long to hide my birth from me,
"And such a son disclaim?

"Hear, dearest mother, hear my prayer,
"And let the truth be told,
"If to yourself my father's known,
"The whole at once unfold."

"Go then, but go with studied speech,
"Up to the banquet hall,
"And him, whom serve the knights at board,
"Thy father thou may'st call.

"Go to the hall, where sits the king
"'Mong knights and men of fame,
"And if Prince Erland thou shalt see,
"Him for thy father claim."

With haughty mien young Axel wold
Robed him in scarlet cloak,
And in the hall of Denmark's king
Addressed the Prince, and spoke.

"Hail, all ye courtly knights and squires,
"Who drink of wine and mead!
"You too, my dearest father, hail!
"If here you are indeed.

"While you're so proud at banquet sit,
"A 'foundling' me they name;
"Now is not, think you, my reproach
"For you a crying shame?"

The courtiers all in silence sat,
Prince Erland only spake;
"I'm not thy father, Axelwold,
"Such claim tho' thou may'st make."

He turn'd him round, young Axelwold,
And sternly drew his knife;
"Hear me! My mother you shall wed,
"Or this shall cost your life.

"Among your knights and very squires
"I've been a jest and scorn,
"Been treated as a leman's brat,
"And yet so princely born."

"True Prince thou art, young Axelwold,
"Put up that murderous knife;
"Eline thy mother give thou me,
"And she shall be my wife."

A merry scene was that at court,
And talk'd of o'er the land,
As Axelwold his mother gave
Into his father's hand.

He waved his hat, young Axelwold,
So glad was he and gay;
"But yesterday a foundling boy,
"A Prince I am today."

poems.title: Agnes and the Merman
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.note: Also in this archive in the versions of E. M. Smith-Dampier (1920), titled "Agnes and the Merman" and George Borrow (1826), titled "The Deceived Merman".
poems.text:
Fair Agnes, on Hoveland bridge she stands,
As up from the sea a Merman lands.
Ha! ha! ha!
And up from the sea a Merman lands.

"O turn thee, my Agnes, and list to me;
"Say wilt thou come and my trulove be?

"Aye gladly I will, and at once I go,
"If thou wilt take me with thee below."

Her ears he stopp'd, and her mouth he stopp'd,
And down to the bottom of ocean dropp'd.

Eight years she dwelt with the Merman there,
And under the sea seven children bare.

But while at her cradle she sat to sing,
"She heard church-bells in England ring.

Before the Merman she went to stand;
"O may I not go to church on land?"

"Thou'rt welcome, my Agnes, to church to go,
"But back to thy children return below."

He stopp'd her ears, and her mouth he bound,
And landed her safely on English ground.

Her steps to the church fair Agnes bent,
And close behind her her mother went.

"O hear me, my Agnes, and still my fears;
"Now where hast thou lived these eight long years?"

"In th' ocean, dear mother, and on its floor
"I seven small sons to the Merman bore."

"The day that he took thee with him to live,
"To pay thine honour what gift did he give?"

"He gave me of gold as rich a band,
"As any that glows on the queen's own hand."

In strode the Merman: the statues all
Turn'd round their face to the church's wall.

His hair it glitter'd like purest gold.
And blithe and joyous his eyes he roll'd.

"Now hark thee, my Agnes, and come with me,
"Thy seven little children all long for thee."

"And long as they may, their longings are vain,
"I'll never go back with thee there again."

"O think of the big ones, and think of the small,
"And think of the infant can hardly crawl."

"I think not of big ones, I think not of small;
"Of th' infant in cradle think least of all."
Ha! ha! ha!
"Of th' infant in cradle think least of all."

poems.title: Agnes and the Hill-King
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Agnes went out to the field and cried.
The birds were singing sweetly
The Hill-King listened at Agnes' side
Beautiful Agnes!

"Agnes, come into the cave with me,
"The ruddiest gold I'll give to thee."

Thrice went fair Agnes the mountain round,
And entered the cave beneath the ground.

Three times throe years in the cave was she,
And sorely she long'd green fields to see.

As Agnes was sitting and Lullaby sang,
The bells so merry in England rang:

She went to her lord; "I were so fain
"In England to go to church again."

"To church in England I let thee go,
"But leave thy jewels and gold below.

"And when in the churchyard, bear in mind,
"Thou shalt not thy golden hair unbind.

"And when thou kneelest at church to prayer,
"Apart from thy mother place the chair.

"And when the Highest of Names is heard,
"Kneel thou not down at the Holy word."

She deck'd her with gold and jewels rare.
And over her shoulders she toss'd her hair.

She reach'd the church at a holy tide.
And took a seat at her mother's side.

So oft as she heard God's Holy Name,
Her knee on the marble pavement came.

And mass and sermon at last are done.
And she is home with her mother gone.

"Agnes, my Agnes, come back to me,
"Thy seven small children they wail for thee."

"TIie children may wail, as they will, and cry,
"With them nothing more to do have I."

He smote her with sickness and pangs of death;
And the birds were singing sweetly
That hour breath'd Agnes her latest breath.
Beautiful Agnes!

poems.title: The Lady and the Dwarf-King
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Hermeline ask'd her father dear,
The time drives on so slow
"O might I to church, a mass to hear?"
So heavy the weight of woe,

"Yes surely, my daughter, I grant thy prayer,
"But be of the mountain dwarf aware."

In purple and gold the maid was diglit,
And all her fingers with gold were bright.

Fair Hermeline went by a small green lane.
The Dwarf by the highroad across the plain

Away to his cavern he drew the maid,
And eight long years in the hill she stay'd.

She lived in his cave eight years or more,
And there to the Dwarf seven sons she bore.

Fair Hermeline came and bent her knee;
"O may I my father go and see?"

"Yes surely thou may'st to thy father go,
"But say not a word of thy fate below"

"Nay that will I not: have thou no fear,
"That any thing reach my father's ear."

Fair Hermeline came to her home once more,
Her father was standing before his door.

"O! Hermeline, answer, my child, and say,
"Where hast thou been living so many a day?"

"I've dwelt so long in a mountain cave,
"And borne to the Dwarf seven sons so brave."

"Go then to the table, my child, and eat,
["'Tis long thou hast tasted no Christian meat."

Fair Hermeline went to the board and ate,
The Dwarf knock'd loud at her father's gate.

"What is it fair Hermeline talks of me?"
"'Tis nothing at all I have said of thee.

"I say that all honour to me he shows,
"I say that his heart no malice knows."

The Dwarf on her lap gold apples threw,
[That home to the cavern his lady drew.]"

Fair Hermeline up from the table sprang,
The apples of gold they clash'd and rang.

As Hermeline came to the mountain cave,
The Dwarf on her ear a buffet gave.

As came fair Hermeline under ground,
To welcome her stood her children round.

He whipped her on with a birchen rod,
And sullen and vengeful in she trod.

Her first little boy, he brought a chair.
The second, he pray'd her be seated there.

The third to his mother the water gave,
The fourth, he pray'd her therein to lave.

The fifth with a napkin was near her side.
The sixth stood by, till her limbs were dried.

The seventh was her comfort, for he in time
Will surely avenge his father's crime.

poems.title: Sir Magnus and the Elf-Maid
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The maiden wooes the handsome knight
To plight to her his troth,
Would give him gifts to sleep with her
Of gold and silver both.
"Magnus plight thy troth to me
"So' longingly I pray:
"And thou canst answer 'nay' or noy'
"Or yea and yea and yea,' "

"I'll give thee a richly broider'd shirt,
"As fine as e'er was bought,
"And every seam, there is therein,
"With silken thread is wrought.
"Magnus &c.

"I'll give thee too a horse to ride
"So stout of wind and bone,
"He walks as well on billows blue
"As on the hardest stone.
"Magnus &c.

"I'll give thee a ship with gold belaid;
"Will stem the roughest seas;
"Its sails arc all of scarlet cloth,
"It flies with every breeze.
"Magnus &c.

"I'll give thee a costly sword of gold,
"The hest thou couldest wield;
"With it the victory shall be thine
"On every battle field. -
"Magnus &c.,

"And hark! lUl give thee a falcon blue,
"No swifter sits on bough;
"Such precious gifts would I not miss,
"Were I a knight as thou."
"Magnus &c.

"Thee would I gladly wed, wert thou
"Like other woman-kind;
"But thou'rt as foul a mountain Elf,
"As one on earth may find."
"Magnus &c.

The Knight girt up his good grey steed.
To Kendsborg he would ride,
But seiz'd his skirt the Elfin maid,
"Nay here shalt thou abide."
"Magnus &c.,

The Knight he drew the costly blade,
That at his side he wore,
And chopped the maid to bits as fine
As sand on ocean shore.
"Magnus c.

The maiden turn'd to a blazing fire,
And rose in angry flake,
And made the mightiest forest trees
To tremble all and quake.
"Magnus plight thy troth to me
"So longingly I pray,
"And thou canst answer 'nay' or 'no
"Or yea and yea and yea. '

poems.title: Ingfred and Gudrune
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Two sisters, Ingfred and Gudrune,
Were seated in their bower alone,
So fair it is at summer tide.

Fair Ingfred wove a web of gold,
But tears her sister's sorrow told.

"O speak, Gudrune, my sister dear,
"And say, why sheddest thou the tear?"

"Much cause I have to weep and sigh,
"For heavy griefs to bear have I.

"Hear, Ingfred, hear now what I say,
"Do thou be bride for me to-day:

"And this my wedding dress so fine,
And all my dowry shall be thine."

"Unless thy bridegroom I may keep,
"As bride with him I will not sleep."

"Then doom me heaven to weal or woe,
"My bridegroom I will not forego."

In silk attire was clad the bride,
And led to church in all her pride.

The priest in golden stole was dress'd,
And her and Samsing join'd and bless'd.

Away they drove across the mead,
Where sat a herd his flock to feed.

"Ye gentle maids, be on your guard,
"And enter not Sir Samsing's yard;

"For there he keeps two nightingales,
"Will tell of ladies secret tales;

"Will sing with little treacherous bill,
"If dame they be, or maiden still."

They drove aside to a greenwood glade,
And change of all their dresses made.

But tho' they clad themselves anew,
They could not change their faces hue.

"To Samsing's hall the bride was led,
And gold abroad in handfuls shed.

They placed her high on bridal chair,
And knights were proud her cup to bear.

Up spake the Minstrel, spake so free,
"Methinks 'tis Ingfred's face I see."

The maiden doff'd her golden ring.
And fee'd him something else to sing.

"Twas but in silly jest I spoke;
"Heed not, I pray, a minstrels joke/'

It now was late, and fall'n the dew.
And time the bride to bed withdrew.

And then to his birds Sir Samsing cried,
"Talk, pretty birds, before my bride.

"Sing me your song, and truly say,
"If to my bed is gone a may."

"'Tis Ingfred lies in bed as bride,
"Gudrune it is stands at the side."

"Up then, fair Ingfred, leave the bed,
"And thou, Gudrune, lie there instead.

"And say, Gudrune, my dearest, say,
"Why she and not thyself there lay,"

"My father dwelt beside the strand,
"Where lawless violence ruled the land.

"Eight rovers came at midnight hour,.
"And broke into my lonely bower.

"And one there was of high degree,
"Brought me to shame: — a knight was he."

He kindly tapped her cheek, and cried,
"Weep thou no more, my dearest bride;

"For, sent by me at midnight hour,
"My swains were they who broke thy bower;

"My swains and I it was who came,
"Myself the knight who wrought thy shame."

The seeming bride, fair Ingfred, too
A royal courtier came to woo.

As bride she had been so gaily dight,
She married too a wealthy knight.

poems.title: Sir Verner's Escape
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The banquet was spread at Lindholm house,
The troopers were drinking a full carouse.

The troopers were drinking, and glad were they,
And singing Sir Verner in dungeon lay.

Dame Ingeborg woke, and heard his strain;
"Now singing is which of my maiden train?"

"So sweetly not one of your maidens can;
"Nay., that is Sir Verner, the captive man."

She call'd two pages, who serv'd her bower;
"Go fetch me Sir Verner from out the tower."

Sir Verner enter'd, and him to greet
Dame Ingeborg rose with courtesy meet.

Sir Verner he stood before the board;
"My Lady, you see me; you sent me word!"

Dame Ingeborg kindly the cushion press'd,
"Come hither. Sir Verner, sit down and rest.

"Now listen. Sir Verner, to what I say;
"You sing me of love some tender lay."

"Full fain would I sing one at your behest,
"But lovesong I cannot; I'll try my best."

Sir Verner he chanted so soft a strain,
He lull'd the ladies in chamber lain.

He liiird the ladies and maids to rest,
He liiird the dame in her scarlet dress.

Sir Verner saw hanging on chamber wall
The keys of the castle, the great and small.

Sir Verner so quick from the door withdrew,
He stay'd not to wish the dames Adieu.'

But soon as he came on the open plain,
He struck up as gaily his lay again.

Sir Verner he waved his hat on high,
"Go wish the lady for me Good bye.'

"And, watchman, in pacing here to and fro,
"Give ear to the songs of those below.

"A bushel of gold she scorn'd last night,
"Now gets not a doit for the captive wight/'

Sir Verner so quick from the door withdrew,
He stay'd not to wish the dames Adieu.'

poems.title: The Knight Disguised as a Hart
