poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
"Up hoist, my lads, the silken sail,
"We'll steer to an isle away;"
The swain was dreaming all the night
About a lovely may.
All the night long has dreamt the swain
About that lady fair,

Sir Lavy dwells beside a stream,
And loves to row and sail.
And cheats full many a simple maid
With false and wily tale.

Sir Lavy call'd two faithful squires
Ready to do his will;
"Entrap for me with honied words
"The maiden Elselille."

In came to her bower the table squires.
And stood before the board.
And ready men of speech were they
To choose the fittest word.

"O rise, fair maiden Elselille,
"In richest raiment dight,
"And come with us on board our ship
"To meet a gallant knight."

"That will no welbred maiden do,
"To go on board a ship,
"And make herself a jest and scorn
"For every sneering lip."

Home rode again those faithful squires,
And thus to their lord replied;
"We could not catch fair Elselille
"With all the arts we tried/'

"Could ye not catch that wary maid
"With all your art and skill?
"Within a day, live I so long,
"I'll win fair Elselille."

With that Sir Lavy in dappled skin
His head and limbs array'd,
And like a tame and gentle hart
Before her window play'd.

As open stood the courtyard gate.
In skipp'd the spotted doer,
And ran the lady's lapdogs all
Beneath her robe for fear.

Fair Elselille to her window stepp'd,
And stood awhile to gaze;
"Whose is the tame and pretty hart,
"That in the courtyard plays?

Then answer'd her the waiting maid,
She fear'd some crafty snare;
"When have you seen a hart or hind,
"That golden antlers bare?"

With playful bound and graceful gait
The hart ran towards the strand,
And after him went Elselille
Waving her lily hand.

"Would heaven, dear hart, that thou wert tame,
"And that I thee could keep!
"And then thou shouldest every night,
"On scarlet mantle sleep/'

He toss'd aside the hartskin dress,
A man again became;
"And now, fair maiden Elselille,
"Behold the hart is tame."

"Had I but only known before,
"You were so brave a knight,
"I ne'er had wish'd to other swain
"My hand and troth to plight."

But Elsey planned a crafty scheme,
While she the knight cajoled;
"Sir Lavy, I shall show you now
"My father's buried gold.

"While I was still a little child,
"My father brought his store,
"And buried it deep in the earth
"Just at my chamber door.

"Now could we take that gold with us,
"Before I leave ray home,
"The little children, we may have,
"To want could never come.

"Do you and all your active swains
"Push off your ship from land,
"While with my maids the treasure gold
"I dig from out the sand."

They grubb'd the earth, they hack'd the stone.
They nothing won but clay;
"'Tis hard to dig a treasure up,
Where treasure never lay.

The lady a lucky moment saw,
To seize it was not slow,
And up the stairs to her chamber ran,
And left the knight below.

She stood and call'd from out her bower
In gay and bantering tone;
"Good bye, Sir Lavy; all your gold
"Seems turning into stone!

"And hark. Sir Lavy, naught but dirt
"Is lying there in store;
"And so a thousand times Good bye!
We meet again no more/'

poems.title: Sir Peter and Christine
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Christine and Sir Peter sat at board,
Our love we'll now maintain for ever
And joked with many a pleasant word,
My dearest Thee forsake I never,

"Now hark, Sir Peter, what I say,
"You'll ask me on your wedding day?'

"Where I must go to fetch my bride,
"Is much too far for you to ride."

"And tho' your wedding be at Rome,
"Ask me. Sir Peter, I shall come."

"But if, Christine, you will be there,
"Your glittering gold you must not wear."

"To wear it there I need not shun,
"'Twas gold by no dishonour won."

While he prepared his marriage feast,
Christine got shod her trusty beast;

And, mounted on that good grey horse.
Straight to Sir Peter's bent her course.

Christine within the courtyard rode.
Where richly dress'd Sir Peter stood.

"Hark ye. Sir Peter, fair and fine,
"And may I pour you out the wine?"

"Though bride-gift there be none for you,
"A leman's seat is still your due."

Christine in sorrow dropp'd a tear;
"Contempt is hard indeed to bear."

As went her knight to banquet hall,
She followed him in costly pall.

With glittering gold her dress was dight,
With gold her every finger bright.

So soon as into the room she came,
Rose up to greet her maid and dame.

She took the can of silver fine,
And pour'd the knight a cup of wine.

The bride would know what maid so fair
Was she the silver wine-can bare.

"That," said her maid, "dear lady mine,
"That is Sir Peter's concubine."

"If one so fair he had at home,
"Why did he to my father's come?

"While she still in his bosom lay,
"Why come his court to me to pay?

"More gold she bears upon her hand,
"Than worth is all my father's land."

As came the night and hour for bed.
The bride.would to her room be led.

All in the van before the fair
Christine the blazing flambeau bare.

And soon in bed was laid the bride,
And he, Sir Peter, at her side.

Christine the coverlet o'er them spread,
"There lies the youth I thought to wed."

But ere she latch'd their chamber door,
"Good night!" she wish'd them o'er and o'er.

She closed the bower, she turn'd the key;
"And so God's will be done!" said she;

Then went, with sorrow on her brow,
And hung her on an apple bough.

In rush'd a page, the bridegroom told,
"Christine is hanging dead and cold."

Sir Peter rose — grief in his look —
A sword beneath his mantle took;

Against a stone made fast its hilt.
And his heart's blood for sorrow spilt.

But little could the chilly steel
That house's pain and anguish heal;

For to the bride the tidings spread,
"Sir Peter's in the orchard dead."

'Twas hardly told, ere sank and died
For sorrow too the tender bride.

So on the morn at dawn of day
In one sad house three corpses lay;

The bride, that late so gay had been,
Sir Peter, and the fair Christine.

poems.title: The Count of Vender's Daughter
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A little babe 'mong dames and maids
In chamber I was bred.
And richly swathed in finest silk
And scarlet cloth so red.
But none may all my trouble know.

But soon a hard stepmother came,
Small favour show'd she me;
She laid me in a gilded chest,
And toss'd me on the sea.

One wave would drift me out afar.
Another hack to land;
Till God should rule it, that at last
I stopped upon the strand.

The flood would carry me ashore.
The ebb afar to sea;
No royal child did breeze e'er drift
So strangely on, as me.

But God had guided so my luck,
The sea threw me on land.
As prowling came a grisly wolf,
And paced along the strand.

Prowling came by a wild grey wolf,
And took me in his jaw.
And all so gently bare me off
Into the greenwood shaw.

Beneath a tree that friendly wolf
Had laid me down with care.
When skipping came a nimble hind,
And took me to her lair.

She fostered me the winter long,
Aye did she more than one;
And first I learnt to creep about.
And then on foot to run.

There eight so happy peaceful years
In greenwood I was kept,
And many a slumber, sweet and sound,
I've in her bosom slept.

No other dress than linden leaves
To clothe me could I find;
Nor other nurse to foster me,
But her, the gentle hind.

One day there came a gallant knight,
A hunter he, so keen,
And shot my foster-mother dead
All in the wood so green.

He shot my foster-mother dead,
While skipping in the field;
But me he wrapped in mantle blue,
And laid me on his shield.

In his own room he fostered me,
That gallant handsome knight.
Till I had grown to be his bride,
And could his love requite.

My father was, as he had heard,
A count of high degree;
And castles held in Vendel's land,
A sovereign lord and free.

Our very first, our wedding night
Began my tale of pain;
Into the court-yard rode his foes,
And he my knight was slain.

That first, the wedding night, I pass'd
In anguish and alarm;
His foes brake down the chamber door,
And slew him on my arm.

My kinsmen then in counsel met,
And me a husband gave;
And he was e'en the cloister Prior,
Sir Nilus, good and grave.

But soon as I to cloister came,
The nuns they.rais'd a din;
By God's high name they swore the Prior
My very near of kin.

They led him out beyond the town,
They stoned him there with stones;
And weeping I stood looking on,
And heard his dying groans.

My friends in council met again.
And husband found for me;
A prince, the son of England's king.
Sir Engelbert was he.

We lived together a winter long,
We lived through winters nine;
And ten sons had I borne my lord.
All gallant youths and fine.

At last broke war upon the land.
And brought.me grief again.
For with my lord, Sir Engelbert,
Nine of our sons were slain.

My sons and husband both were kill'd,
For that I grieve so sore,
The tenth they took to a foreign land,
I never saw him more.

As numerous now my sorrows are
As threads, that maidens spin;
God bless in heaven Sir Engelbert,
So pure his heart from sin!

And now in cloister I will dwell
Apart from worldly care,
And never more a husband wed,
But pass my life in prayer.

And here I'll learn me under foot
To tread my useless grief;
For all the more I mourn and sigh,
The less I find relief.

poems.title: Sir Helmer Blaa and His Bride's Brothers
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Helmer Blaa with hawk and hound
Was riding through the forest ground.
So well he sits in saddle,

He saw just under a mountain side
His lady-fair's seven brothers ride.

Sir Helmer ask'd his squire so true,
"What thinkest thou were best to do?"

"Twere best, the truth if I may say,
"o spur our steeds and ride away."

"That to my bride shall ne'er be said,
"That I before her brothers fled."

No coward he. Sir Helmer Blaa,
He boldly rode and met his foe.

"Sir Helmer, meet we thee again?
"Our honoured uncle thou hast slain:

"Thou, thou, it was, our uncle slew,
"And never paid what fine was due.

"And now thou hast made our sister thine,
"Our leave unask'd, unpaid the fine."

Safe in my treasure chest I hold,
"To pay the death, ten marks of gold."

"We'll take of thee but one amend,
"Thy left foot and thy dexter hand."

"Ere ye shall get my hands or feet,
"Some other fate yourselves may meet."

Sir Helmer Blaa his sabre drew,
And at a stroke Sir Ebbe slew.

When Lang and Ove slaughtered lay,
His sword had just come into play.

He then kill'd Wolf and Edgar White,
And so were four in equal plight.

Torkild and Thor the next he sped,
So lay in all six brothers dead.

Then rose as red as blood Sir Paul,
A courteous man belov'd by all.

"Sir Helmer, lay this feud aside,
"My sister I'll give thee for bride."

His terms with joy Sir Helmer heard,
And in the greensward stuck his sword.

"Thanks, good Sir Paul! and I agree;
"Henceforth a brother see in me."

Like loving brethren home they rode,
Such courtesy each the other showed;

And when Sir Helmer reach'd his hall,-
His sister too he gave Sir Paul.

Gaily they drank their wedding feast,
Nor has their friendship ever ceas'd.

poems.title: Hogen's Dance and Song
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
The King he sits at Ribe,
And quaffs his wine so gay;
"Up, now, my Knights of Denmark!
"Well make a merry day.
So gloriously dances Hogen,

"Up, up, my squires and horsemen!
"And ye my knights so keen!
"Up all, and leave the banquet
"To dance upon the green."

Now lists the King of Denmark
To dance the rest among,
And off goes Hero Hogen,
And leads them with a song.

Up wakes the Queen of Denmark,
As in her bower she lies;
"Now which of all my maidens
"The harp so sweetly plies?"

"'Tis none of all your maidens
"Is touching so the string;
"There's none but Hero Hogen
"Such lay as that can sing."

"Wake up, wake up, my maidens,
"With roses bind your hair,
"And out with me to the greensward,
"And merrily dance we there."

First rode the Queen of Denmark
In scarlet robe so red.
And then her maids and ladies
So high and nobly bred.

And there the Queen of Denmark
Rode round and round the dance;
But still on Hero Hogen
Was ever turn'd her glance.

Till came the Hero Hogen
And held her forth his hand;
"Now lists my. gracious lady
"In dance with me to stand?"

Off tripp'd the Hero Hogen,
And gaily tripp'd the Queen;
And sooth to say, their gladness
Was in their faces seen.

But came a little maiden
All in a kirtle blue;
"Beware of newsy tattlers,
"That listen after you."

Then ask'd the King of Denmark
With angry voice and roien,
"To dance here on the greensward
"What business has the Queen?

"'Twere better in her chamber
"To strike the tuneful string,
"Than here amid the dancers
"With Hogen so to fling."

Then came a little maiden
All in a crimson gown;
"Haste home, my gracious lady,
"The King begins to frown."

') "'Twas late I join'd the dancing,
"But, faith! I'll see the end;
"So let him, if he is angry,
"His manners learn to mend."

Then came and lightly whispered
A little Page in green;
"The King is riding homeward,
"O hasten home, my Queen."

Fie! fie! on Hero Hogen,
And on his honied tongue;
Close pent within her chamber
She rues the song he sung.

poems.title: Childe Engel
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A daring wight, Childe Engel,
He up and mounted horse,
A lady seized in Upland,
And bore her off by force.

He ask'd no leave of kinsmen,
He car'd not he for right,
But took her home to Westerns,
And slept with her the night.

But out of sleep Childe Engel
At dead of night awoke,
His dreams had been so frightful,
He turn'd to her and spoke.

"A gaunt and hungry wolfs whelp
"And mother wolf so gray
"My heart methought were munching,
"As wide awake I lay."

"Childe Engel, 'tis no wonder,
"Your dreams should be so sad;
"You've torn me from my kinsfolk,
"Their leave have never had,"

In stepp'd young Sauley Johnson,
And stood before the board,
A cunning man in parley
To find the fittest word.

"Childe Engel, up from table!
"Up, mount thee quick and ride!
"Here's come Sir Judah Lowman
"With men from every side."

"I tremble not for four men,
"I tremble not for ten,
"Nor yet for Judah Lowman
"And all his thirty men."

"But more there are than four men,
"Aye more there are than ten;
"There's with Sir Judah Lowman
"A hundred armed men."

In haste arose Childe Engel,
His lady towards him drew;
"For God's sake think, dear Malfred,
"And tell me what to do."

In sore distress Childe Engel
He tapped her on the cheek;
"What means are left of safety?
"O hear me, dear, and speak/'

"This counsel then I give thee,
"As best to serve our turn,
"St. Mary's church we'll purchase,
"For that they dare not burn.

"We'll spare not of your silver,
"We'll ladle out your gold,
"Give both to buy St. Mary's,
"Tomorrow get it sold.

"With all your brave retainers,
"Your bread with you who share,
"We'll while the danger urges,
"To yonder church repair.

"And all your gallant horsemen, ".
"Your steeds are wont to ride,
"Take all within St. Mary's,
"And there the storm abide.

"Such plan I deem the wisest,
"A poor weak wife am I,
"To lock us in St. Mary's,
"And there their threats defy"

In haste arose Childe Engel,
And into church he went,
And soon Sir Judah Lowman
His horsemen thither sent.

Five months so long and weary
They lay before the place,
And daily greater anger
Was in Sir Lowman's face.

Then spake fair Malfred's mother,
Nor could her spite withhold;
"Burn down the church and steeple,
"And build it up with gold."

The blaze began to sparkle,
And playful in it flew;
The lily cheek of Malfred,
From pale to paler grew.

It scalded in the churchyard,
It glow'd so fiery red;
Inside it still was hotter,
As ran the molten lead.

Then spake the lady Malfred,
Full sad was she of mood;
"We'll slaughter all our horses,
"And cool us in their blood."

"Alas!" Childe Engel answered,
Beneath the blazing aisle;
"Their blood will serve to cool us
"A very little while/'

"Kill them not" said the groomboy,
He loved them far too well;
"'Twere better Lady Malfred
"Herself the victim fell."

Childe Engel clasp'd his Malfred,
And "No, my dear" he cried,
"Of death art thou not worthy,
"My gentle dearest bride.

"But listen now, my Malfred,
"And grant me this my prayer,
"If son this year thou nursest,
"My own name let him bear."

They laid her on a buckler,
And lifted it with spears,
And up to the window rais'd her
All trembling and in tears.

Through churchyard went fair Malfred
Amid the smoke and glare,
All singed her scarlet mantle
And burnt her flowing hair.

There sank the Lady Malfred,
And pray'd on naked knee;
"Grant heaven I bare a son this year,
"And vengeance on them see!"

They took the lady Malfred
All in her mantle clad,
And raised her on her palfrey
So sorrowing and so sad.

"There," said the lady Malfred,
When to the mead they came,
"St. Mary's church is burning
"And brave men in the flame.

"There, there the church is blazing,
"And 'mid the cinders lain
"So brave a man, as never more
"Will here be seen again."

That year fair lady Malfred,
Ere many months were run,
Retired within her chamber,
And bare an infant son.

To holy font they brought him.
They christen'd him at night.
Him too they named Childe Engel,
And hid him all they might.

She nurs'd him through the winter,
She nurs'd him winters nine.
No lad in all that country
So fair as he and fine.

In grace and strength and beauty
Seven winters more he grew;
"Now hark!" said she, "thine uncle,
"'Twas he thy father slew."

And (lay by day she told him
For other winters five,
"Thine uncle slew thy father,
"Or he were still alive."

"Now hear me, dearest mother,
"All robed in costly" pall,
"I'll serve the king of Denmark,
"A trooper in his hall."

"Ride then and serve as guardsman,
"Be brave and earn thee fame,
"But think upon thy father,
"I need no more to name."

He serv'd the king of Denmark,
And won the royal grace.
But laugh as might his comrades,
Was sadness on his face.

Well marked the king of Denmark
The grief upon his brow;
"Come hither, speaks Childe Engel,
"And what thy grief, avow.

"Like some lone bird on branchlet,
"I hear thee ever moan;
"Like one who claims no kindred,
"Thou mop est all alone."

"Ah! hear then, King of Denmark,
"The reason why I pine;
"My uncle slew my father,
"And never paid the fine."

"To venge thy murder'd father
"To Upland thou shalt ride;
"I'll lend thee trusty guardsmen
"To combat at thy side.

"To venge a murder'd father,
"As right it is to do,
"I'll lend thee arm'd and mounted
"Three hundred good and true.

He mounted horse, Childe Engel,
And rode to the green-wood lawn;
And arm'd his gallant troopers,
And off at early dawn.

In came a little page boy,
And stood before the board,
And cunning he in parley
To choose the fittest word.

"Sir Judah Lowman, listen,
"Up, mount thee quick and ride,
"For here's Childe Engel marching
"With men from every side.

"From all four roads Childe Engel
"Is riding through the land,
"His face so full of anger
"His drawn sword in his hand."

"To Council and Assizes
"I've ridden far and near;
"But yet that name, Childe Engel,
"Has never reached my ear."

Then call'd his page Sir Lowman,
And tapp'd him on the cheek;
"If counsel thou canst give me,
"Be quick, my page, and speak."

"For shelter then betake thee
"To yonder room of stone;
"To me no other counsel,
"No refuge else is known.

"It's walls are all of marble,
"Of metal forged the gate,
"And hard shall be the struggle
"Ere foe break through the plate."

A moment checked Childe Engel
His troopers on the heath,
"In yonder church, St. Mary's,
"My father met his death.

"And there I see the mansion,
"My uncle dwells within:
"God guide us what atonement
"We have therein to win."

On all four sides Childe Engel
Besat that room of stone;
The first in every danger,
He made his valour known.

Then peer'd Sir Judah Lowman
From out the window loop;
"And who then is the captain,
"So boldly leads your troop?"

Childe Engel made him answer
Beneath his cloak so fine:
"'Tis I myself, Childe Engel,
"A sister's son of thine."

"Aye!" spake Sir Judah Lowman
With anger on his brow,
"And small the ground for glory;
"A bastard son art thou."

"And tho' I'm born a bastard,
"My birth I need not hide,
"I've gold in store, and silver,
"And gallant steeds to ride.

"Let be, I am born a bastard,
"For that art thou to blame,
"Green woods I have and meadows,
"And towers to guard the same.

"My father thou hast murder'd,
"And never paid the fine,
"And darest thus upbraid me!
"But vengeance now is mine.

"My friends, what profits hoarding?
"Our chest with gold is fill'd,
"We'll burn this room to cinders,
"And soon another build."

The anteroom was scalding.
All molten ran the lead,
But hotter was the chamber.
Where now the fire had spread.

Awhile he stood, Childe Engel,
His steed he turn'd not round;
"I'll stay but till the chamber
"Lies smouldering on the ground."

And then rode off Childe Engel,
And waved aloft his hands,
He saw his uncle burning
To cinder 'mid the brands.

He smiled and spake, Childe Engel,
As redder glow'd the fire;
"Now feelest thou the torment
"Thyself didst cause my sire."

He mounted horse, Childe Engel,
And up to his mother's rode,
And found her, robed in martin,
Before her own abode.

"Hail thou, my. dearest mother,
"In robe so richly drest!
"I've ridden up to Upland,
"I've done thy stem behest."

"Aye?" answered lady Malfred,
And tears she shed anew,
"Before I had but one grief,
"And now I weep for two.'

"I've done what thou hast bidden;
"Why drop those idle tears?
"Why weep for what thou badest?
"How woman's temper veers!"

Childe Engel turn'd his charger,
Nor longer would he stay,
But left his mother weeping.
And rode to Court away.

Before the royal mansion
He check'd his horse's rein,
Where stood the king of Denmark
To welcome him again.

Beside the king of Denmark
In to the Court he went,
And thank'd him well and warmly
For all the men he lent.

"I've taken now my vengeance,
"And in his marble-room
"The wretch, who burnt my father,
"Himself has met his doom.

poems.title: Esbern and Sidselille
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Esbern he serv'd the King at court,
So long in his troop he rode.
The King at the last he dubb'd him knight,
And fiefs on him too bestowed.

So well and so truly he serv'd the king
With bravery and with skill,
He gave him besides a maid to wife,
The beautiful Sidselille.

They lived together the winter through,
Together for five whole years;
And nowhere a truer or tenderer love
Has man ever seen than their's.

They dwelt together in joy and peace
For more than winters nine.
Nor ever exchanged an angry word,
Nor ever did they repine.

Sir Esbern was wont to pace his yard
And flourish his silvered brand,
And often there came to his mind a vow
To go to the Holy Land.

"God bless thee, my gentle Sidselille,
"Who sittest to spin thy gold;
"My vow to visit the Holy Land
"In duty I'm bound to hold."

"You've gold in your chest, an ample store
"Of gold and of silver too;
"Now send on your errand your faithful squire,
"For ill can I part with you.

"You've silver and gold enough in store,
"Long treasur'd within your chest,
"Your squire may go on the pilgrimage,
"And you at your home may rest."

"O prithee, my gentle Sidselille,
"To this my design agree,
"For thither I must, and keep my vow,
"I'll soon be again with thee."

To church Sir Esbern on Sunday rode
At the holy hour of prayer,
And call'd aloud on his kinsmen all.
Were bidden to meet him there.

"If any among you I've ever wrong'd,
"Or wrought on you aught of ill,
"I pray you avenge it on me today,
"And not on my Sidselille."

Sir Esbern made ready to launch his ship,
That riding at anchor lay;
His lady was sitting with tearful eyes
And wailing the livelong day.

She down to the strand with her husband went,
So running her cheek with tears;
"Remember I am but a poor weak wife,
"Forgive me a woman's fears."

She press'd to her bosom the noble knight,
A thousand times bade 'Adieu,'
"Remember, my lord, in a distant land,
"There's one at home thinks of you."

"God bless thee and keep thee, my dearest wife,
"Whom here I must leave behind!
"Wherever I wander the world so wide,
"Thine image I keep in mind."

The gallant Sir Esbern stepp'd on board,
His row-boat he steer'd from land;
He manfully stood to the wild wide sea,
As loudly as roar'd the strand.

He thought he should on that pilgrimage
A year and a month remain;
It lasted him fully fifteen years,
Before he was home again.

'Twas hardly a month the gallant knight
Had sail'd from his native shore,
Ere Sidselille up in her lofty bower
A fair little daughter bore.

Full eighteen years was Sir Esbern gone
Still leading a pilgrim's life,
And often and sorely for home he long'd,
For home and his gentle wife.

Full eighteen long and weary years
Away did the knight remain,
And well we may think how pined his wife
To see him at home again.

At last when eighteen years were gone,
He came to his native land,
And there Sir Esbern a herdsman saw,
Was pasturing near the strand.

"Now hark thee and say, good honest man,
"Adriving thy cows to dell,
"Say truly what I would so gladly know,
"Does here any widow dwell?"

"Hard by there is living a widow hero,
"Caird Lady Sidselille;
"'Tis eighteen years that her husband left,
"And him she is mourning stilL"

"Now tell me how fares the country folk
"Around her and far and near;
"How Sidselille too, the Lady fares,
"For she is to me so dear."

"'Tis well is faring the country folk
"Of all and of each degree,
"And well is the Lady Sidselille,
"The worthiest dame is she."

In baste Sir Esbern he left his ship
To tread on his native ground.
And sought the lady he loved so well,
And her at her door he found.

A pilgrim's wallet was on his back,
A staff in his hand he bore;
A stranger be enter'd his house and home,
And nobody knew him more.

He greeted the lady in courtly tone,
As due to her rank and right,
"Now all for your husband Sir Esbern's sake
"Give lodging to me tonight."

"Full gladly," said Lady Sidselille,
In tears to the man she spake,
"Full gladly I lodge you in Jesus' name
"For dearest Sir Esbern's sake."

"God bless you, good Lady "Sidselille,
"So courtly of tone and air!
"But let for the same dear husband's sake
"A bath-room for me prepare."

Herself she fetch'd him the cleansing lye,
Herself the water too;
Just as she had bathed in former times
Her husband so good and true.

"A daughter I have, is his and mine,
"Eighteen she now must be,
"Her father's face she has never yet seen,
"And never, I fear, will see."

The Lady Sidselille all this time
Stood washing his hands so white;
"Let him, who longer could hide the truth,
"Be shorn of the name of knight/'

He clasp'd her hard to his heaving breast,
He call'd her his dearest dear;
"And now I shall tell thee a joyful news,
"Thy husband is standing here.

"No longer could I the truth conceal,
"My purpose thy love overcame;
"I'm here thy husband, Sir Esbern's self,
"And thou art my faithful dame."

She led him above to the ladies' bower,
So soon as she heard his tale,
And brightly her smiles lit up the check,
Had been with her grief so pale.

And all was glad in Sir Esbem's house;
His daughter she came anon,
And stood before him the fairest maid,
That ever the sun beshone.

Sir Esbern he gave his daughter's hand.
As fair as the very light,
He gave her hand to the young Sir Carl,
As gallant and good a knight.

poems.title: Cloister-Robbing
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
I'll sing you now a story,
Who listeth, hear my lay,
Of how the young Sir Morten
Betroth'd a lovely may.
The lilies and roses they grow so well,

And full of grace and goodness
The gentle girl he won,
Yet much it vex'd his kinsmen.
For riches she had none.

The lady's kinsmen, they too,
When news of it was spread,.
Swore all by God Almighty,
That her he should not wed.

Him sent from home his father
Beyond the salty Rhine,
And her shut up her kinsmen
In cloister cell to pine.

Sir Morten stay'd the winter,
For winters nine he stay'd,
And all the while was longing
To see his. trothplight maid.

So sorely long'd Sir Morten
To see his lovely bride.
That stay he could no longer,
Tho' for it he had died.

And home he came, Sir Morten,
Back to his native land;
But painful were the tidings
He heard on every hand.

But what of all those tidings
Griev'd him the most of all,
He heard that she, his trulove,
Was doom'd to cloister thrall.

He sought his dearest father;
"My trouble let me tell;
"The maid to whom I'm plighted,
"They've shut in cloister cell."

"Hear thou a father's counsel,
"For her no longer pine,
"But wed this other maiden,
"She's twice as rich as thine.

"Give way no more to borrow,
"But take a father's rede;
"Thine Adelaide has little gold,
"And less of grassy mead."

"I'd rather have my trulove
"In but her scarlet gown,
"Than knight Sir Stige's daughter
"With all that she may own.

"I care not I for treasure,
"Still less for grassy land;
"To Adelaide I've plighted troth,
"And fain would have her hand.

"I caro not I for kinsmen,
"The they were many more;
"I'll keep the word I've plighted,
"The driven to foreign shore."

Off went the young Sir Morten,
And ask'd his brother rede;
"O say how shall my trulove
"From cloister thrall be freed?"

'Go, get thee swathed in grave-clothes,
"And lay thee in thy shell,
"And I will to the cloister ride,
"The gloomy news to tell/'

He laid him down in grave-clothes.
The news was widely spread;
Sir Nilus to the cloister rode,
And wail'd a brother dead.

"My greeting, fair young maidens,
"I'll richly you repay,
"If here within your cloister
"My brother I may lay."

This heard those holy maidens,
And sat there silent all;
But one, the maiden Adelaide,
Let work and scissars fall.

And she it was made answer.
The tears upon her face;
"Here in our cloister chapel
"Make you his resting place.

"Iii this our cloister chapel
"Inter his corpse you may;
"And I, to please his kinsmen,
"Will go there every day.

"In tender years of childhood
"I plighted him my love,
"And how I grieve to lose him,
"Knows only God above:

"That pent I was in cloister,
"Was much against my will;
"Him too his kinsmen banish'd
"Our glowing love to chill."

Then kindly spake Sir Nilus,
And tapp'd her cheek so fair;
"O weep not, maiden Adelaide,
"But banish grief and care/'

"I ne'er shall still my sorrow,
"Or solace ever see,
"For gone is dear Sir Morten,
"Who best could comfort me."

So sorely wept the maiden.
So.frequent fell the tear,
While to the cloister chapel
They bore Sir Morten's bier.

She pray'd beside his coffin
All bending on her knee;
"Christ save thy soul, Sir Morten!
"How dear wast thou to me!"

Two tapers then she lighted,
And bitterly she cried;
"O would that in my cradle
"I long ago had died!

"I've nine long weary winters
"In pining for thee passed;
"Mine eyes had scarce beheld thee,
"And see thee a corpse at last."

While wept that lovely maiden,
And wrung her hands so white,
Her wailing heard Sir Morten,
And laugh'd" and rose upright.

No more could bear Sir Morten
To see her so distrest;
But tossed aside the grave-clothes.
And clasp'd her to his breast.

"Now hear, my dearest trulove,
"Away with grief and care!
"And off with me from cloister,
"As fast as horse can bear.

"In churchyard stand the horses,
"And dark they are of hue,
"And mail-clad all my troopers,
"Will follow thee so true"

He wrapped her up, Sir Morten,
In costly sable pall,
And led her off so gaily
Outside the cloister wall.

The pious nuns around her
Stood reading in their book,
They thought 'twas some good angel,
Their sister from them took.

There stood those holy maidens,
And warmly did they pray,
"Would God there came such angel
"Me too to fetch awayT

Bravo the young Sir Morten!
He wavered not the least,
But to his dwelling brought her.
And made his marriage feast.

And now with maids and pages,
And honour'd and caress'd,
She lives Sir Morten's darling
In costly sable drest.

poems.title: The Lady's Rejoinder
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
A group of gay and gallant knights
At the Queen's table sat,
Among her maidens pass'd the time
In light and lively chat.
"You wait for me under the linden.

They talk'd not, they, of priest or church,
Nor yet of cloister cell,
But of the dames, who daughters bad,
And such as bred them well.

Then up Sir Peter rose and spake,
His notions were so grand;
"No maiden I to wife will take,
"But who has house and land.

"My bride in broidery shall be skill'd
"To sew her silken gown;
"But such I'll never take to wife,
"As gads about the town,

"Her household duties she must know,
"And how the board to spread,
"Nor be too flippant of her tongue,
"For such I'll never wed."

All still those handsome maidens sat.
And utter'd not a word,
Till spake her mind the fair Christine,
Who served the Queen at board.

"Now were I once a woman grown,
"And suitor came to woo,
"I'd choose, so help me God in heaven!
"Not such a one as you.

"Retired within my bower I sit
"My cloth to cut and sew,
"While you — you mount your prancing steed,
"And off to council go.

"I sit at home and pride myself,
"With taste to deck my board,
"While you — you rise in Council Hall,
"But cannot speak a word.

"On all these benches seat by seat
"My broider'd work I lay,
"While you with Lords and Princes sit,
"But not one word can say."

Then up at once Sir Peter rose,
The words were on his tongue;
"And now I've just the maiden found
"For whom I've look'd so long."

Great was the mirth and joy at Court,
And echoed far and wide.
As gave the Queen her waiting maid
To be Sir Peter's bride.

poems.title: The Maiden Gisselmore
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
And it was Norway's King and Queen,
So stormy were the seas,
Under the "Orkneys lay awhile
To wait a fairer breeze.
Ye maidens, leave off playing,

The King stood in his highest bower
To view the shores around,
And saw a youth with gilded masts
Who thither too was bound.

In steer'd the knight, and brown and blue
The sails his vessel bore;
His anchor on the sand he cast,
And stepp'd upon the shore.

His clothes were all of silken stuff
With golden tissue dight.
And followers bare his gilded shield
With jewels gleaming bright.

Young Alf, be stood before the king
With courteous air and dress:
"Is any bere, a knight or squire,
"Will play a game at chess?"

Sir Alf took out a chequer'd board,
That like the embers shone:
There play'd with him the king's men all,
But won a game not one.

Then up the King of Norway spake,
For vex'd at heart was be;
"Go, bid the maiden Gisselmore
"Come hither in to me."

In came the maiden Gisselmore,
And stood before the board;
"What is your royal will with me?
"Your grace bas sent me word."

"Hark thee, my little Gisselmore,
"This chess is thy delight;
"So sit thee down and play a game
"With yonder foreign knight."

Sir Alf and little Gisselmore
They sat at chess and play'd,
And aye with soft and coaxing words
He wooed the gentle maid.

They sat before the chequer'd board.
Were moving turn by turn;
"Fair maid, with right and loyal views
"Your favour I would earn.

"Hear me, my little Gisselmore,
"And plight your hand to me;
"I claim as born of noblest blood
"Equal with you to be."

"That of my brother you must ask,
"And of my other friends;
"For well you know, that not on me,
"Whom I may wed, depends."

"Your brother's leave I cannot ask,
"He lives so far away;
"Give me yourself your plighted troth,
"And you I'll not betray."

A ring, where lily twined with rose,
Into her lap he threw,
And all at once love's gentle pangs
Through her soft bosom flew.

"While yet' plough these dark blue waves,
"Three winters for me stay,
"And then to your island I'll return
"To keep our wedding day."

"I'll ask their leave of friends and kin,
"And surely wait for you;
"Nor ever any other wed,
"Although an Earl should sue."

There woo'd her Biorn of Vareness
AVith fifteen farms in fee;
She paid the knight all due respect,
But "was no longer free,"

Sir Alf sail'd o'er the salty waves
'Mid dangers not a few,
Until to a wealthy seaport town
The breeze his vessel blew.

And with a widow there he lodged,
A dame of wealth and power.
And there love-fetters bound his heart,
And vex'd him hour by hour.

The knight some love-drink surely drank.
His bride he quite forgot:
'Tis what young men too often do,
Their vows remember not.

The news was told at Norway's court.
And rumour'd far and wide;
"Sir Alf had won a widow's hand,
"And brought him home his bride."

There sat the Queen's young maidens all,
And work'd their silken seam;
The fairest of them, Gisselmore,
Her eyes were seen to stream.

She rose, the maiden Gisselmore,
And round her wrapped her cloak,
And mounting to the royal bower
To Norway's Queen she spoke.

"Lady, a while before my birth,
"My parents made a vow,
"That in the cloister I should live,
"And I would go there now.

"'Twas at an hour of urgent need,
"That they the promise gave,
"And there in cloister I would live,
"And there would find my grave."

They set her on a palfrey gray,
With gilded bit and rein,
And so to cloister led the maid.
To all her kinsmen's pain.

poems.title: Fair Ellensborg and Sir Olave
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Fair Ellensborg was gazing round,
As in her bower she stood;
"My own Sir Olave there I see
"Come riding through the wood.

"It is indeed Sir Olave's self
"In greenwood glade I see;
"Grant heaven, he prove my loyal knight,
"And hither come to me!"

Fair Ellensborg to her maiden turn'd,
And ask'd her friendly rede;
"And now what answer shall I give,
"So hard he is wont to plead?

"Tell him that long youe loved him well,
"But speak in modest tone;
"Tell him, of all who ask your hand,
"You love but him alone."

Now came Sir Olave riding in
And gaily lighted down;
And met the gentle Ellensborg
In ermine-border'd gown.

"My greeting, gentle Ellensborg!
"To me your favours yield,
"And you I'll love, and with my life
"From every danger shield."

"A sun among the lesser stars
"'Mong other men are you,
"And had you not my uncle slain,
"You should not vainly sue/'

"I'll freely gold and silver give,
"Your uncle's life to pay;
"Nay more, with friends in full Assize
"On bended knee will pray."

"My dear Sir Olave, say no more,
"But let these matters be;
"There's not another man on earth
"Is half so dear to me."

And there by stealth that very hour
They plighted them their troth,
And sware each other mutual love.
Till death o'ertake them both.

"Sir Olave, stay no longer here,
"Mount horse, and haste away;
"For if my brother Magnus comes,
"I fear a bloody fray."

With tearful eyes they bade adieu,
The loving gentle twain;
And God, their heavenly father, grant.
They soon may meet again!

Sir Olave went with hawk and hound
In greenwood glade to ride,
And in some evil hour he there
His lady's brother spied.

"Sir Olave ha! 'tis well we're met
"Alone in greenwood glade;
"The very man my uncle slew,
"And fine has never paid!"

"I'll give to pay your uncle's life
"Both gold and silver fee,
"And with my friends in full Assize
"Will pray with bended knee."

"You've not alone mine uncle slain,
"Nor ever paid the fine,
"But also won my sister's love,
"Nor cared for will of mine."

"I've won and plighted her ray troth,
"Shall her with honour treat,
"And you shall ever, while I live,
"As friend and brother meet."

With only five, his body swains,
Sir Olave left the place,
With three times five, all men at arms,
Sir Magnus gave him chase.

Sir Olave soon they overtook,
And cut to bits as small
As leaves that swept by wintry winds
From linden branches fall.

Sir Magnus left the bleeding corse.
Girt sword again to side.
And to his sister's started off
At rapid pace to ride.

And soon Sir Magnus reach'd his home,
And gaily lighted down,
And met his fond dear sister there,
In ermine-border'd gown.

"Welcome, my dearest brother, home!
"And what then did you find?
"Say, have you chased the hare today,
"Or hart or spotted hind?"

"I've neither hind nor martin slain,
"Nor any other deer,
"Than just the tame and gentle hart,
"Was wont to nestle here."

"And have you done this cruel deed?
"My dear Sir Olave slain?
"You nevermore shall live the day
"To see me glad again.

"But have you then Sir Olave met,
"And really wrought his death?
"I'll e'en to a cloister cell retire,
"And mourn him, while I've breath."

"O weep no more, nor be thine eyes
"In tears for ever drown'd;
"I'll give thee soon the richest knight
"Can in this realm be found."

"Sir Olave I would rather have
"With but his saddled dun,
"Than any else the wealthiest knight
"That dwells beneath the sun."

And spake the gentle Ellensborg,
And wrung her hands for woe;
"Brother, on you I most relied,
"Why deal me such a blow?"

With pity yearn'd Sir Magnus' heart
His sister's grief to see;
"If lovers' woe I had ever known,
"He might have lived for me."

The lady mourn'd in cloister cell
Till sorrow crazed her mind,
So much for him, her brother slew,
She daily sighed and pined.

poems.title: Young William
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Dame Margaret dwells across in Scone,
She and her daughter too;
That lovely maiden's wedding day
How many have to rue!

There wooed her Swend of Voldislef,
A knight of royal race;
But 'twas young William won her hand,
She loved his friendly face.

Though wooed her Swend of Voldislef,
So rich in gold and fee,
Yet 'twas young William won her hand,
"So kind of heart was he.

When heard young Swend of Voldislef
What news had come to town,
For sorrow up to his room he went,
And sick he laid him down. "

Up to his room he went, and lay
For very grief so low;
His mother and sister went to him,
Went often to and fro.

His mother, while alone they sat,
Would ask him, what he ail'd;
"Hast thou with any neighbour feud,
"Or ventured aught and fail'd?"

"Feud with my neighbours none have I,
"Nor been by kinsmen crossed;
"Young William weds the maid I love,
"And all my hope is lost."

"Oh! vex no more, my dearest son,
"Nor at thy wrongs repine;
"I'll show thee a richer maid than her,
"And many times more fine.

"Her counsel let a mother give,
"The best a mother can;
"Fret thou no more about a maid
"Who weds another man/'

But evil rede his sister gave;
"Go, knock him on the head;
"When once young William thou hast slain,
"His widow thou may'st wed."

His mother spake with sound good sense,
As she was wont to speak;
"The vengeance for a father slain
"A son may live to wreak."

"Pshaw!" answer'd Swend of Voldislef,
"Such fears I well may scorn:
"Tis early time to think of that,
"Ere yet the child is born.

"I ne'er shall see another chance
"To win so fair a maid:
"Please God I live, young William's luck
"Shall with his life be paid."

Young William rode to his marriage feast,
And gay the banquet there;
How wroth was Swend of Voldislef,
He little seem'd to care.

Young William took a lonely path
To journey through the wood,
And there in most unlucky hour
Sir Swend before him stood.

"Young William, bark! Why ridest thou
"To meet me here tonight,
"And knowest thou hast won the maid
"Was all my heart's delight?

"'Tis true I've won that gentle maid,
"Dear as she was to thee,
"But had the luck been thine instead,
"She ne'er had come to me.

"Fair Lisbet I have now betroth'd,
"And will not give thee place;
"There dwell in Denmark other maids
"Will not thy rank disgrace."

Fiercely Sir Swend of Voldislef
Drew out his glittering knife;
"The gentle Lisbet thou hast won,
"But that shall cost thy life."

Young William spake no more but this,
As on the ground he fell;
"If Lisbet bear a son this year,
"Call 'William' him as well.

"If Lisbet bear a son this year,
"Ye call him after me;
"Ye call his name Young William too;
"No coward he will be."

When woodland shaws were green again,
And forty weeks had run,
The lady up to her bower retired,
And bare an infant son.

The boy was born one afternoon,
They christen'd him at night,
But told Sir Swend a girl was born,
And hid the little wight.

With mother's care she rear'd him up
Till eighteen years of age,
And gave him then a tall war-horse
To serve as royal page.

Full eighteen years of age was he.
When first he bare a shield;
He vied in games with knight and squire,
And always kept the field.

Young William with a peasant stood
The bar and stone to throw,
And in their game a brawl arose.
That led to bitter woe.

Young William struck the peasant youth.
And dragged him by the hair;
"'Twere best to venge a father's death,
"And lads like me to spare!"

Young William heard, and red by turns
And deadly pale was he;
"If foully slain my father was,
"No summer-play for me!"

Young William left the tilting field.
Drew on his scarlet cloak.
And mounting to the ladies' bower,
He thus to his mother spoke.

"My greeting, dearest mother iniaei
"The truth I prithee tell;
"If foully slain my father was,
"And by whose hand he fell."

"My son, thou'rt still too young and weak
"To buckle sword to side;
"Procure that Swend of Voldislef
"Shall at the court be tried/'

Young William got a summons wrote,
And sent it round the land,
That Swend should on the following day
At court before him stand.

"I'll off" said Swend of Voldislef,
Soon as he read the deed,
"I'll to the King's house ride, and there
"Ask of my uncle rede.

"Now hark! and tell me, Uncle mine,
"What best I may begin?
"Young William summons me to court
"With all his wealthy kin."

"But hark thee, Swend of Voldislef,
"And tell me, why so sad?
"Have I not often heard thee say,
"That she a daughter had?"

"Now help me, Holy Virgin Queen!
"I then no better knew;
"A woman's craft in all my days
"I never shall see through."

"I'll lend thee a baud of trusty men,
"Take whom thou wilt or all;
"With them, dear Nephew, ride to court,
"And see what may befall."

To court went Swend of Voldislef,
And 'neath the penthouse strode;
"Now who has summoned rac to court
"This long and weary road?"

Then forth young William boldly stepp'd,
No softness he betray'd;
"My father thou hast foully slain,
"And fine hast never paid."

"No," answered Swend of Voldislef,
And spirted up the earth;
"Nor for thy father shalt thou get
"Penny or penny's worth."

Young William spake, as in the ground
He stuck his glittering sword;
"I for my father ought to get
"Both coin and civil word."

Over his helmet threw Sir Swend
A skein of silken thread;
"Prithee, young William, heed thee well,
"Thou dost not strike me dead."

It was young William, gallant youth,
His sword so glittering drew,
And Swend of Voldislef it was.
In open court he slew.

And while Sir Swend of Voldislef
Dead in the court-house lay,
Rode William off to Voldislef,
And seiz'd a lovely may.

To good Sir Nilus on the strand
The baleful tidings came;
His brother slain in open court,
His sister brought to shame.

A summons got Sir Nilus wrote
And sent it round the land;
That at the peasant court next day
Young William too should stand.

The good Sir Nilus call'd his swains,
Bade saddle up his steed;
"I'll to the King's house ride across,
"And ask my uncle's rede. —

"Oh! hear my grief, dear Uncle mine,
"Or hast thou heard the same?
"My brother kill'd in open court,
"My sister brought to shame?"

"I'll lend thee a troop of faithful men,
"Take whom thou wilt or all;
"Myself I'll ride with thee to court,
"And see what may befall."

Young William, bold and gallant youth,
Into the court-house strode,
And ask'd, who might have summon'd him
That long and weary road.

"Hear me, young William, hear the words,
"That now I have to say;
"My brother thou hast put to death;
"What blood-fine wilt thou pay?"

"As to thy brother, we are quits,
"For he my father slew:
"Thy sister I will wed today,
"And treat with honour due."

The good Sir Nilus he replied,
And these the words he said;
"Not so, young William; thou, I swear,
"The maid shalt never wed."

In wrath young William started forth,
And drew his glittering blade;
"If otherwise it cannot be,
"So lend me, God, thine aid!"

He kill'd Sir Nilus on the spot
In short and mortal strife;
And held his sword at the King's breast,
And begg'd him grant his life.

"Seize him!" with fierce and angry look
The King of Denmark cries;
"Young William seize, who dares to break
The peace of this Assize."

"Forgive me, Sire," young William said.
And drew him back with awe;
"Forgive and let me go in peace,
"I knew not Sessions law."

Young William left the justice hall,
To mount his noble dun;
"And now I'll to my mother ride,
"And tell her how I've won."

Young William on his prancing horse
Came riding through the gate,
And there the fair Dame Lisbet stood
Attired in robe of state.

"Welcome, young William, homo again!
"Welcome, my son, and say,
"What blood-fine for thy father's death
"They offer'd thee to pay."

"No fine the murderer offer'd me,
"Nor any did I crave,
"But dead is Swend of Voldislef,
"And moulders in his grave.

"Aye! dead is Swend of Voldislef,
"Sir Nilus too is dead;
I "Their sister Gertrude I've betroth'd,
I "And her I mean to wed."

The good Dame Lisbet took her son,
And clasp'd him to her breast;
"Since thou hast well thy father 'venged,
"Are all my cares at rest."

Well done, young William! luck to thee,
And all such brave young swains!
He fully venged a father's death,
And still at home remains.

poems.title: Lyborg and Her Mother-in-Law
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sir Volmor away from his home must fare,
And leave his wife to his mother's care.

Fair Lyborg was dancing, and sang the while,
Dame Ingeborg followed her full of guile.

"O wait, and ere Summer and Fall are past,
"I'll silence thy tuneful voice at last."

Fair Lyborg's maidens so gaily sprang,
And she the lay for the dancers sang.

But hardly had pass'd one other day.
Ere Lyborg on bed of sickness lay.

Fair Lyborg was sick and lay so low,
Dame Ingeborg went to her to and fro.

"O give me, dame Ingeborg, mother mine,
"A drop of water to drink, or wine."

"The wine is frozen, and will not run,
"And frozen the tap of my water-tun.

"The cellar is lock'd, and gone the key;
"I cannot tell where that key can be,"

'If frozen the wine and water too,
"Yet open the door, and admit the dew.

"Tnt open I pray the northern door;
"The breezes may yet my strength restore."

"I'll open the door to the bright noon-day,
"And leave thee to bask in its hottest ray '

"Christ, that I had a trusty friend,
"That word to my mother I could but send!"

"My mistress," her own little page replied,
"'Tis I will off with your message ride."

They knew not, but thought none other near;
Dame Ingeborg listened with eager car.

The page sprang up on his horse so high,
And rode as fast as a bird could fly.

In came the page in his kirtle red;
"Your daughter, dame Lyborg, will soon be dead.

"She prays you to haste and come tonight;
"She will not live to the morning's light."

Dame Mettelille bade her grooms, with speed
Go fetch her horses from out the mead.

The horses ran with the wain so fleet
The livelong day in the scalding heat.

The sun shone fiercely, 'twas Midsummer day,
Fair Lyborg sick and in anguish lay.

The Dame a bowl-ful of money took
And went to the loft with smiling look.

"Will any to win this sum of gold
"Put Lyborg alive beneath the mould?

So soon as the coin was duly paid,
That lily beneath the ground they laid.

Proud Mettelille came to the courtyard gate;
Dame Ingeborg near the threshold sate.

"My greeting, Dame Ingeborg, ease my fear,
"And tell me where lies my daughter dear."

"No longer ago than yesterday
"They buried thy daughter beneath the clay."

"Enough then. No further news I crave,
"But show me at once my daughter's grave."

As over the spot her mother trod,
She heard her moaning beneath the sod.

"If any would silver win and gold,
"Come help me to dig away the mould."

Fair Lyborg out of her grave they drew;
Her mother around her a mantle threw.

"O speak to me, Lyborg, my daughter dear,
"So gladly alive I see thee here:

"Now tell me what Ingeborg's death shall be,
"The wretch that alive has buried thee."

"She wish'd to have kill'd me, the hateful wife;
"But prithee, dear mother, spare her life."

"Not so: Dame Ingeborg now shall learn,
"What means it to sit in the fire and burn."

Dame Mettelille call'd her servants twain,
"Go build her a pyre on yonder plain.

"Hew boughs of the ash, and boughs of oak,
"That fiercely the tire may blaze and smoke."

Outside of the town they dragg'd the dame,
And burnt her there in the crackling flame.

Sir Volmor in haste came back from war,
The news of her sentence had spread so far.

'Twas dismal and earnest the news he learnt;
His wife was gone, and his mother burnt.

He offer'd for Lyborg gifts and gold.
But never that lily could more behold.

To gain her he five of his forts would give,
But never with him would Lyborg live.

To presents or prayers she gave no heed,
And this was his own base mother's deed.

poems.title: Childe Daneved and Swain Trusty
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
"But what shall I ever in Denmark do,
"For armour like their's too young?
"The Danish troopers will surely laugh,
"So badly I talk their tongue."
But I shall never learn good Danish,

Childe Daneved he his varlets call'd,
And bade that his horse be drest;
"I'll mount and across to Borreby,
"And be my mother's guest."

They rattled and clank'd their glittering spurs,
And off their horses sprung;
In church at Lunden in Sconeland
They heard the Vesper sung.

The Vespers they stayed in church to hear,
And masses nine beside;
And then would again Childe Daneved
His gallant good horse bestride.

But kindly the reverend Clave spake.
Their own parish priest was he;
"Now list to my prayer, Childe Daneved,
"And tarry the night with me."

"I will with nobody eat today,
"Nor drink of the sparkling mead,
"Till first I have ridden to Borreby,
"And ask'd of my mother rede."

"But list to me, dear Childe Daneved,
"There's reason for What I say;
"Our foes are lurking beyond the town,
"And surely will thee belay."

"I trust to my good and well-tried sword,
"I trust to the steed I ride;
"And next I trust to my faithful swains,
"But most in myself confide.'

"You well may trust to your own good sword,
"And trust to your gallant steed,"
"But, trust, as you will, your faithful swains,
"They'll fail you in time of need."

They scarcely had ridden beyond the town;
The childe and his mailclad band,
Than met him his foes, some thirty men.
And halted, and bade him stand.

So strong and so many seem'd his foes,
That lurking in ambush lay,
Childe Daneved's swains their furlough took,
And ran from their lord away.

They took their furlough those troopers all,
Not one of the band was true,
Except Swain Trusty, and he so fought,
As though he was hired anew.

"And I have so long your livery worn,
"So long have ridden your steed,
"And faithful I'll stand by you today,
"Nor fail you in time of need.

"I've taken your silver and gold for pay,
"And long I have shared your bread;
"I will not swerve from your side today,
"But faithfully light, till dead."

They set them together back to back
All on the greenwood lawn;
Fifteen they had slain, those two alone,
Ere peep of the morning dawn.

They sot them together back to back
Alt under the greenwood spray.
And thirty they slew, those two alone,
Great honour they won that day.

And, ended the fight, Childe Daneved,
He belted his sword to side.
And off to his mother's, with joyful heart,
He mounted his horse to ride.

As up to her house Childe Daneved
Came riding within the gate.
Out stepped his mother in costly furs
Her son at the door to wait.

"O welcome, my son, my dearest son!
"Right welcome art thou indeed;
"Now wilt thou drink of the sparkling wine,
"Or rather the luscious mead?"

"I will not eat, nor a cup will drink
"Of either your mead or wine
"Till you give Trusty, my faithful swain,
"You only dear sister mine."

"But barken to me, my dearest son,
"For what I will say is true;
"Her brother is he, so help me God!
"Her brother, as well as you."

"O list to my prayer, dear mother mine,
"Nor fraudfully tell me so;
"For where could you rear Swain Trusty up,
"That naught of it' should know?"

"I sent him, a little and tender babe,
"Away to a foreign shore;
"I heard for a truth that he was dead,
"And spake of him never more."

He made her answer, Childe Daneved,
He spake like a brave man's son;
"No reason have I to plain of that,
"And have such a brother won. —

"God bless thee, young Trusty! and here to thee
"This pledge of my troth I give.
"I never will leave thee, or play thee false,
"As long as on earth I live."

Childe Daneved, he, and Trusty too
In raiment of sable both,
Rode off to serve in th' Emperor's court.
And truly were nothing loth.

poems.title: The Compulsory Marriage
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
I heard within my lady's bower
A knight with her at play;
Of gold the diceboard and the dice,
And thus he wooed his may.

"O deign, fair maid, to hear the knight,
"So humbly to you sues,
"And you shall dress in scarlet red,
"And walk in golden shoes.

"Deign, gentle maid, to plight me troth,
"O listen to my prayer,
"And I will place upon your head
"A crown of gold to wear."

"I've to the Virgin Mary sworn,
"And plighted her my vows,
"Never with sinful man to dwell,
"Or ever be his spouse/'

"It then, so warmly as I sue,
"You scorn and flout me still,
"I'll write such runes, as spite of you
"Shall win you to my will."

"And if you really write those runes,
"And foully work my fall,
"I'll all my life complain to Heaven,
"And vengeance on you call."

He wrote the runes, such potent runes,
And threw them on her gown,
That blood sprang from her finger ends,
And tears in streams ran down.

"Tomorrow come beneath my bower
"With thirty men beside;
"I've taken now a new resolve,
"And home with you will ride."

Ere yet the lark had trill'd his song
To greet the morning hour,
Rode up the knight with thirty men
Beneath his lady's bower.

Their horses all with gold were shod.
And all with pearl bestrown,
Their saddle knobs with crystal gleam'd
And many a precious stone.

And that on which the bride should mount,
As very snow was white,
His trappings of the silken cloth
With ruddy gold bedight.

Up at her window sat the bride
To gaze on dale and down,
And saw the knight with thirty men
Come riding up the town.

"Rise ye, my maids, and dress me now
"With all the haste ye may;
"A deed, I am loth enough to do,
"I must this very day."

They dress'd her in a silken dress.
And crown of gold so red;
"Heavens, that, maiden as I am,
"I were but lying dead!"

The horse no sooner saw the bride.
So gently trained was he,
Than down, to take her on his back.
He dropp'd upon his knee.

On the good horse she seated her,
And took in hand the rein,
And swallowed then an adder draught,
Should burst her heart in twain.

That fiery adder draught she drank.
Her heart was rack'd with thirst;
"A sinful woman I 'must be,
"Or else my heart would burst."

Over the high steep bills they rode,
And through the lowly dell;
"O would that to my mother's ear
"My wishes I could tell!

"Then would I pray her that my corpse
"Not on this heathen wold,
"But buried in Saint Mary's church
"Might lie in Christian mould."

"Care for your mother, maiden fair,
"Or other friend to sigh;
"Your corpse shall not in heathen soil,
"But in Saint Mary's lie."

They rode till gilded vanes they saw
Gleaming on lofty tower;
"That castle, lady, you shall rule,
"And there shall find your bower.

"Twelve maids I'll keep, shall day by day
"Attend you out and in,
"And eight young knights shall follow you
"To bear your scarlet skin.

"No day or hour shall be too long,
"Such pastimes I shall find;
"You could not, lady, plight your troth
"To any knight more kind."

"Fair as might be to lead with you
"Such life of joy and rest,
"Yet might I rather dwell in heaven
"With Jesus and the blest,"

And straight the pearl-bespangled silk
Over the earth was strown,
And so into the ladies bower
The gentle maiden shown.

The marriage feast was baked and brew'd,
The board with dainties piled,
Yet silent walked the gentle maid,
And neither joked nor smiled.

They drank the wedding all that day,
They drank it in the best,
And then the bridefolk rose from board,
And fain would go to rest.

Up rose the maidens twelve, with silk
The grassy earth to spread,
And rose the knights, and walk'd all twelve
Behind the bride to bed.

To bridal house they followed her.
That blushing gentle fair,
Nor tarried long the wealthy knight.
But soon himself was there.

Up on the bed they lifted her.
Took off her crown of gold;
"O that I might, maid as I am,
"Be laid beneath the mould!"

They sat together on bridal bed,
The bells of heaven heard ring;
They "at an hour, and over them
They heard God's angels sing.

They heard the merry bells of heaven,
They heard the angels' song;
"Come, gentle maiden, come with us,
"And tarry not so long."

Over them both was thrown the silk,
Was thrown the sindal red,
But naught knew he, till at his side
His bride was lying dead.

"Arid all so long as I have wooed,
"Is this then what I reap?
"O heavenly Father, grant us both
"In the same grave to sleep!"

Great sorrow fill'd the bridal house
And anguish and alarm;
Dead were the bride and bridegroom both,
One on the other's arm

Great sorrow fill'd that bridal house,
And all within it cried;
Bridegroom and bride they both were dead,
One at the other's side.

They laid them in a gilded chest,
And bare them to the tomb.
Of costly marble built its walls,
And on it graved their doom

"All! were they all my friends here,
"The foes that round me stand,
"How glad were I, my darling,
"With you to quit the land!
"How glad were I, my darling!"

"And whither would you take me,
"My brave, my gentle knight?
"To sleep beside my trulove
"I surely have the right;
"To sleep beside my trulove!"

"With him then are you sleeping?
"Alas, your dream is vain!
"Go, look beneath the linden,
"For there he's lying slain;
"Go, look beneath the linden."

The lady took her mantle.
And through the wood she sped,
And underneath the linden
She found her lover dead;
Beneath the fresh green linden.

"And here then lying slaughtered,
"All smothered in your blood!
"And so at last have ended
"Your vaunts and haugluty mood!
"In this at last have ended!

"Yourself so foully slaughtered,
"My comfort and my stay;
"And I left sad and friendless
"To mourn you many a day!
"Left all so sad and friendless!"

The lady took her mantle,
And sped her through the wood,
Her father's door was open,
And weeping there she stood.
Her father's door was open.

"But is there none among you,
"Not one of gentle birth,
"Will kindly come and help me
"To lay him in his earth?
"Will kindly come and help me?"

All still they sat and silent.
There spake to her not one,
And, turning back, the lady
Went weeping all alone;
Back to her dead the lady.

Up in her arms she rais'd him
From where they left him slain,
And on his mouth she kiss'd him
Again and still again;
On his cold mouth she kiss'd him.
And then his grave she delv'd him
All with his own bright blade;
With arms as white as snow-drift
His body in it laid;
With arms as white as snow-drift.
" Some copies have open and some bolted.

"And now to some small cloister
"I'll go, my duty done,
"And wear the veil my life long,
"And be a poor black nun;
"Will wear the veil my life long."

And there with her fair fingers
The hand-bell she would ring,
And with a voice most mellow
His vigil mass would sing;
With voice so sweet and mellow.

poems.title: Tor af Havsgaard
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Det var Tor af Havsgaard,
rider over de grønne Enge;
tabte han sin Hammer af Guld,
og borte var den saa længe.
    Tor han tæmmer Fole sin i Tømme.

Det var Tor af Havsgaard,
han taler til Broder sin:
»Du skalt fare til Nørrefjæld
og lyse efter Hammer min.«

Det var Lokke Løjemand,
satte sig i Fjederham:
saa fløj han til Nørrefjæld
alt over det salte Vand.

Midt udi den Borgegaard
der axler han sit Skind,
saa ganger han i Stuen
alt for den Tossegreve ind.

»Du vær velkommen, liden Lokke!
du vær velkommen her!
hvor stander Huen i Havsgaard?
og hvor stande Landen der?«

»Vel stander Huen i Havsgaard,
og vel stande Landen der;
men Tor han haver sin Hammer mist,
fordi er jeg kommen her.«

»Ikke fanger Tor sin Hammer igjen
for Guld eller gode Ord:
femten Favne og fyrretyve
der ligger han graven i Jord.

Ikke fanger Tor sin Hammer igjen,
det maat du lide paa,
før end jeg faar Jomfru Frøjeborg
med alt det Gods, hun aa.«

Det var Lokke Løjemand,
satte sig i Fjederham:
saa fløj han tilbage igjen
alt over det salte Vand.

Midt udi den Borgegaard
der axler han sit Skind,
saa ganger han i Stuen
for Tor sin Broder ind.

»Ikke kan du din Hammer igjen
af Tossegreven faa,
med mindre vi give hannem Frøjeborg
med alt det Gods, hun aa.«

Det var Jomfru Frøjeborg,
hun blev i Sind saa vred:
Blodet af hver en Finger sprang
og randt paa Jorden ned.

Mælte det den stolte Jomfru,
hun op fra Bænken sprang:
»Ret aldrig tager jeg til Mand
den Trold saa led og lang.«

»Hør du, kjære Søster min!
du vær nu ikke saa braad!
hvor meget røde Guld giver du mig,
om jeg finder bedre Raad?

Tage vi Tor, vor gamle Broder,
saa vel vi børste hans Haar,
føre vi hannem til Nørrefjæld
alt for saa væn en Maar!«

Det var Tor af Havsgaard,
lader Brudeklæder skære;
og det var Lokke Løjemand,
skulde Brudeterne være.

Førte de den unge Brud
alt i den Bryllupsgaard;
det vil jeg for Sanden sige,
der var Guld ej for Legerne spart.

Saa toge de den unge Brud,
satte hende paa Brudebænk;
frem da gik den Tossegreve,
han bar for hende Skjænk.

En Oxekrop saa aad hun op,
vel tredive Svineflykke,
syv Hundred Brød hendes Maaltid var,
saa lyste Bruden at drikke.

En Oxekrop saa aad hun op,
vel tredive Svineflykke;
tolv Tønder Øl saa drak hun ud,
før hun kunde Tørsten slykke.

Tossegreven paa Gulvet gik,
han mon sig saa ilde kære:
»Hveden er saa, den unge Brud
hun vil saa meget tære?«

Svared det liden Lokke,
han smiler under Skarlagenskind:
»I otte Dage fik hun ikke Mad,
saa haver hun stundet til din.«

Det var gamle Tossegreve,
han glædtes ved de Ord:
»Bærer nu ind den Hammer af Guld!
bærer ham for Brudebord!«

Otte vare de Kæmper,
bare Hammeren ind paa Træ;
det vil jeg for Sanden sige,
de lagde ’n over Brudens Knæ.

Det var da den unge Brud,
tog Hammeren i sin Haand:
og det vil jeg for Sanden sige,
hun slynged ham som en Vaand.

Slog hun den Tossegreve ihjel,
den Trold baade led og lang;
saa vog hun alle de andre smaa Trolde,
at Retten maatte have sin Gang.

Det var Tor af Havsgaard,
holdt med de Trolde godt Ting:
femten Trolde og fyrretyve
de laa der i en Ring.

Mælte det Lokke Løjemand,
monne sig saa vel omtænke:
»Nu ville vi fare til vort eget Land,
mens Bruden er vorden Enke.«
    Tor han tæmmer Fole sin i Tømme.

poems.title: Sivard Snarensvend
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sivard han slog sin Stiffader ihjel
alt for sin Moders Bedste;
saa lyster ham Sivard til Hove at ride,
og Lykken saa vil han friste.
Saa listelig da render han Grammen under Sivard.

Sivard han gaar for sin Moder at staa,
med Sværd ved venstre Side:
»Kjær Moder! jeg vil nu til Hove,
om jeg fanger Hesten at ride.«

»Da skal jeg give dig Ganger god,
som vel skal bære dig fram:
jeg vil give dig den samme Hest,
som Drengene de kalde Gram.«

Ledte de frem den gode Hest,
lagde paa den forgyldene Grime:
hans Øjen de lyse som Morgenstjærner,
og Ild springer af hans Mile.

Sivard strøg af sine Handsker smaa,
hans Hænder vare meget hvide:
og selver gjorded han sin gode Hest,
paa Svende turde han ikke lide.

Selver gjorded han sin gode Hest,
paa Svende turde han ikke lide:
Grammen baade bed og slog,
og Ilden drev af hans Mile.

Sivard sættes til sin gode Hest,
han binder op Hjælm hin bjærte;
hans Moder fulgte hannem langt af By,
hun gjordes saa trang om Hjærte.

Det var Sivards kjære Moder,
fulgte hannem saa langt over Hede:
»Du vogt dig, Sivard, kjære Sønnen min,
vogt dig for Grammen hans Vrede!«

»Hør I det, min kjære Moder!
I skulle hverken sørge eller kvide:
I haver født saa rask en Søn,
som vel sin Hest kan ride.«

Det var Sivard Snarensvend,
han tog sin Hest med Spore:
Grammen han sprang ad Marken ud,
det var ikke alt af gode.

Grammen han tog ad Heden ud,
det var ikke alt af gode:
for vist er Svenden i Sadelen saar,
hans Støvler stande fulde af Biode.

I Nætter tre og Dage tre
sprang Grammen over Bjærge og Dale,
til han kom for saa højt et Hus,
de Porte var i Laas med alle.

Kongen stander paa højen Værn,
og ser han ud saa vide:
»Og hisset ser jeg en galen Mand,
sin Hest kan dog vel ride.

Hisset ser jeg en galen Mand,
sin Hest kan dog vel ride,
eller det er Sivard, min Søstersøn,
og han haver været i Stride.«

Grammen han tog da Mile for Tand,
og han sprang over de Tinde:
det vidste ingen Jorderigs Mand,
før end Hest og Mand var inde.

Der blegned Fruer og skjønne Jomfruer
under deres Skarlagenskind;
Kongen han gik saa gladelig
imod kjær Søstersøn sin.

»Jeg raader eder, alle mine Mænd!
at I gjøre Sivard godt:
jeg vil eder for Sandingen sige,
han taaler slet ingen Spot.«
Saa listelig da render han Grammen under Sivard.

poems.title: Sigvard og Brynhild
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Sivard han haver en Fole,
      den er saa spag:
han tog stolt Brynild af Glarbjærget
      om lysen Dag.
Kongen hans Sønner af Danmark.

Han tog stolt Brynild af Glarbjærget
      om lysen Dag:
han gav hende Helled Haagen
      for Stalbroderlag.

Det var Sivard Snarensvend,
red sig under Ø,
fæste han stolten Signildlil,
saa væn en Mø.

Stolten Brynild og stolten Signild,
        de Jomfruer to,
de ginge dennem til Strande,
        deres Silke at to.

»Hør du det, stolten Signildlil,
        kjære Søster min!
hvor fikst du den røde Guldring
        paa Finger din?«

»Saa fik jeg den røde Guldring
        paa Finger min:
den gav mig Sivard Snarensvend,
        kjær Fæstemand min.

Den gav mig Sivard Snarensvend,
        i Fæstensgave;
men dig gav han Helled Haagen
        for Stalbroderlag.«

Det første stolten Brynild
        den Tidend fraa,
da gik hun sig i Højeloft,
        og syg hun laa.

Stolt Brynild ganger i Højeloft,
        og syg hun laa;
alt ganger han Helled Haagen
        hende til og fraa.

»Hør du, stolten Brynildlil,
        Allerkjæreste min!
og védst du ingen gode Raad
        til Sygdom din?

Er der nu noget i Verden til,
        du Bod kan af faa:
skulde det koste alt mit røde Guld,
        du skalt det naa.«

»Der er slet intet i Verden til,
        kan raade mig Bod,
foruden Sivard Snarensvend
        hans Hjærteblod.

Der er slet intet i Verden til,
        min Hu leger paa:
foruden jeg kunde Sivards Hoved
        i Hænde faa.«

»Hvor skulde jeg Sivard Snarensvend
        hans Hoved faa!
hans Hals er haard som bianken Jærn,
        der bider intet paa.

Det Sværd er ikke i al Verden til,
        hannem bider paa,
foruden hans eget det gode Sværd,
        det kan jeg ikke faa.«

»Da ganger I eder i Højeloft
        for Sivard ind!
beder hannem laane eder sit gode Sværd
        for Ære sin!

Beder hannem laane eder sit gode Sværd
        for Ære sin!
I siger: jeg har lovet et Dystered
        for Kjæreste min.

Første han fanger eder det gode Sværd
        af Hand fra sig:
jeg beder eder for den volde Gud,
        I glemmer ikke mig!«

Det var ham Helled Haagen,
        svøber sig i Skind,
saa ganger han sig i Højeloft
        for Sivard ind.

»Her sidder du, Sivard Snarensvend,
        kjær Stalbroder min!
vilt du laane mig dit gode Sværd
        for Ære din?

Vilt du laane mig dit gode Sværd
        for Ære din?
jeg haver mig lovet et Dystered
        for Kjæreste min.«

»Og laaner jeg dig mit gode Sværd,
        hedder Adelring:
ret aldrig kommer du i den Strid,
        du skalt jo vinde.

Mit gode Sværd, hedder Adelring,
        skalt du vel faa;
men vogt dig vel for de blodige Taar,
        under Hjaltet staa!

Du vogt dig for de blodige Taar,
        de ere saa rød:
og rinde de neder ad Finger dine,
        da bliver du død.«

Det var ham Sivard Snarensvend,
        var Stalbroder tro:
laante han bort sit gode Sværd,
        sig selv til Uro.

Det var da Helled Haagen,
        det Sværd uddrog:
og det var Sivard, hans kjære Stalbroder,
        der han da vog.

Saa tog han det blodige Hoved
        under Skarlagenskind,
saa bar han det i Højeloft
        for stolt Brynild ind.

»Her haver du det blodige Hoved,
        du efter mon traa;
for din Skyld har jeg vejet min gode Stalbroder,
        det angrer mig saa.«

»Tager I bort det blodige Hoved!
        lad mig det ikke se!
for vist havde jeg ham kjærer’ end I,
        dog jeg voldte ham Ve.«

Det var da Helled Haagen,
        sit Sværd uddrog:
og det var hende stolt Brynildlil,
        han i Midje vog.

»Nu haver jeg vejet min gode Stalbroder
        og min skjønne Jomfru;
end skal jeg veje den tredje til,
        det har jeg i Hu.«

Satte han det gyldne Hjalte
        imod en Sten:
raadte da Odden af Sivards Sværd
        hans Hjærte Men.

Det var alt saa ilde,
        Den Jomfru blev fød,
der to saa ædelig Kongens Børn
        skulde blive for ød.
Kongen hans Sønner af Danmark.

poems.title: Frændehævn
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Stolt Signildlilles Brødre de toge paa Hand,
de gifte deres Søster til fremmede Land.
Hun fælded saa modige Taare.

De gifte hende bort, den væne Mø,
de gave hende over saa bred en Sø.

De gifte hende bort i fremmede Land,
de gave hende sin Faders Bane i Hand.

De loved til hende at komme
og hver en signede Sommer.

Men det stod saa i otte Aar,
stolt Signild hun aldrig sine Brødre saa’.

Stolt Signild lader brygge og blande Vin,
hun byder sine Brødre hjem til sin.

Saa hjærtelig lo da Hr. Lovmaar,
han lo ikke før i otte Aar.

Stolt Signildlil stander i Lofte,
og ser hun ud saa ofte.

Og ser hun ud saa vide,
hun ser sine Brødre ride.

Stolt Signildlil svøber sig Hoved i Skind,
hun gaar i Loft for Hr. Lovmaar ind.

»Min Herre! om det saa nu vare,
det mine Brødre kom here?« —

»Da vilde jeg gjøre mod Brødre dine,
som de vare alle Sønner mine.«

Hr. Lovmaar han tog da til at le,
den haarde Mur den revned derved,

Mælte det Barn, i Vuggen laa,
det talte aldrig før end daa:

»Det er ej for det gode,
min Fader ler ad min Moder.«

Det led fast ad Aftenmaal,
de Herrer skulde til Borde gaa.

Hr. Lovmaar satte hun op til Bord,
sine Brødre satte hun for paa Stol.

Hr. Lovmaar skjænked hun klaren Vin,
sød Mælk skjænked hun for Brødre sin’.

De vidste ej andet, end Hr. Lovmaar druk’,
da slog han det under den Bænkestok.

Stolt Signild gaar sig til Senge,
at rede under raske Drenge.

Hun redte dem Senge paa Stene,
hun vilde dem Søvnen formene.

Hun lagde ved deres Side
deres Sværd og hvasse Knive.

Det lakked fast ad Aftenmaal,
da monne alle til Senge gaa.

Den første Søvn, stolt Signelil fik,
Hr. Lovmaar af hendes Arme gik.

Hr. Lovmaar gik sig til Halle,
han vog hendes Brødre alle.

Han gik sig til Senge,
han vog de raske Drenge.

Han drog ud baade Sværd og Kniv,
han skilte dem alle ved deres Liv.

Hr. Lovmaar han tog det Dyreshorn,
han lod deri det varme Blod.

Saa tog han det Brødreblod,
han bar ind for stolt Signild god.

Hr. Lovmaar ind ad Døren tren,
stolt Signild falmer i Rosenskind.

»Siger mig, Hr. Lovmaar, kjær Herre min!
hvor haver I været om Nattetid?«

»Jeg var mig ude paa Hælde,
som jeg hørte de Høge gjælde.«

»Saa længe snakker du om Høge dine:
Herre Gud naade vel Brødre mine!«

»Du drik nu, drik, stolt Signild god!
du drik af dine Brødres Blod!«

»Saa lidet skjøtter jeg om Brødre mine,
mens jeg haver eder, min Herre, i Live.« —

Det stod saa udi otte Aar,
Hr. Lovmaar aldrig sine Sønner saa’.

Hr. Lovmaar lader brygge og blande Vin,
han byder sine syv Sønner hjem til sin.

Hr. Lovmaar stander i Højeloftssvale,
han hørte sine Sønner i Gaarden tale.

Hr. Lovmaar han svøber sig Hoved i Skind,
han ganger i Loft for stolt Signild ind.

»Stolt Signild! om det nu saa vare,
det mine syv Sønner kom here?« —

»Da vilde jeg gjøre mod Sønner dine,
som de vare alle Brødre mine.«

Hun satte Hr Lovmaars Sønner til Bords,
hun skjænked dem Mjød i dyren Skaal.

Hr. Lovmaar drak Vin og Mjød hin klare,
han tog saa lidet sit Liv til Vare.

Stolt Signild gaar sig til Senge,
at rede under raske Drenge.

Hun redte deres Senge paa Dune,
hun vilde dem Søvnen vel unde.

Hun redte deres Senge paa Bolstre blaa,
end skrev hun der Søvneruner paa.

Den første Søvn, Hr. Lovmaar fik,
stolt Signild af hans Arme gik.

Hun gik sig til Stokke,
som Sværde stod i Flokke.

Stolt Signild gaar sig til Halle,
Hr. Lovmaars syv Sønner hun kvalde.

Saa tog hun dem i gulen Lok,
hun vog dem over den Sengestok.

Saa tog hun deres Hjærteblod,
og det lod hun i Dyreshorn.

»Vaager op, vaager op, min Herre god!
I drikker af eders syv Sønners Blod!«

»Alt skulde jeg være fuld saare tørst,
om jeg skulde have til Blodet Lyst.«

Hr. Lovmaar greb efter sin brune Brand,
stolt Signild havde bundet ham Fod og Hand.

»Hold op, stolt Signild, du hug ikke mig!
ret aldrig da vil jeg svige dig.«

»Mig tykte, der var stor Svig i dig,
den Tid du vogst min Fader fra mig.

Først togst du min Fader af Liv,
og saa mine raske Brødre syv.

Saa vist skal jeg nu hævne’t paa dig,
som du haver slaget dem alle fra mig.«

Stolt Signelil drog Kniv af Ærme rød,
saa slog hun Hr. Lovmaar til sin Død.

Mælte det Barn, i Vuggen laa:
»Jeg hævner det, om jeg leve maa.«

Hun stødte til Vuggen med sin Fod,
det Barnet rulled der ud paa Jord.

»Du est af det samme Blod,
jeg véd, du bliver mig aldrig god.«

Saa tog hun det lidet Nap,
hun brød dets Hoved mod Sengeknap.

Og al den Nat hun vaagede,
de Jordeklæder hun magede.

»Nu haver jeg vejet Mand for Mand,
nu vil jeg hjem til min Moders Land.«
Hun fælded saa modige Taare.

poems.title: Grimilds Hævn
poems.author: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
poems.text:
Det var Frue Kremild,
hun lader Mjøden blænde:
det var saa mangen Helled fri,
der hun Bud efter sende.

»Du bed dem komme til Orlog!
du bed dem komme til Krig!
der skal saa mangen fri Helled
for lade sit unge Liv.«

Bød hun saa Helled Haagen,
hannem bød hun ikke til Strid:
heller til Lyst og Gammensfærd,
det var alt gjort udaf Svig.

Bød hun Helled Haagen
og Falkvor Spillemand,
Hr. Gynter og Hr. Gernot,
og flere, jeg nævne kan.

Det var Helled Haagens Moder,
hende drømte saa underlige:
det den gode Fole styrte,
der han skulde paa ride.

Frem gik Frue Bodil,
Helled Haagens Moder:
»Vogt dig vel, kjær Sønne min!
din Søster vil dig forraade.

Drømmen haver at sæde,
hvem hannem forstande kan:
kommer du til det hunske Land,
det skader saa mangen Mand.«

Svared det Helled Haagen,
han agte saa lidet paa Drømme:
»Rædde ere de Kvinderaad,
fuld ilde de Kæmper sømme.«

De Herrer rede af Gaarde
ud med den Strand saa vide:
funde de dèr den Mareminde
hvilende under Lide.

»Hør du, gode Mareminde!
du est saa vi’s en Viv:
skal jeg paa det hunske Land
forgjøre mit unge Liv?«

»Vend om, Helled Haagen!
du est en Ridder saa bold:
nok haver du i dit eget Land
Gods og Borge i Vold.

Du haver baade Guld og Sølv,
Fæster og Borge røde:
kommer du paa det hunske Land,
da bliver du raadt til Døde.«

Vred blev Helled Haagen,
og han sit Sværd uddrog:
det var den søllige Mareviv,
han Hovedet af hug.

»Her da maat du ligge død
paa den hvide Sand:
fuldvel skal jeg atter komme
fra det hunske Land.«

De Herrer ride med Strande,
som Strømmen rinder strid:
funde de dèr den Færgemand
sovende hos sin Viv.

»Vaag op, goden Færgemand!
du før os over Sund!
jeg giver dig min gode Guldring,
han vejer vel femten Pund.«

»Hav du selv din gode Guldring!
jeg maa hannem ikke eje:
aldrig kommer jeg i den Stad,
jeg bær jo for hannem Treje.

Aldrig kommer jeg i den Stad,
jeg tager jo for hannem Nød;
jeg fører dig ikke over Sund i Dag,
Fru Kremild mig det forbød.«

Vred blev Helled Haagen,
og han sit Sværd uddrog:
det var den søllige Færgemand,
han Hovedet fra hug.

Saa tog han det blodige Hoved,
han kaste det ud i Sund,
skød han Kroppen efter,
bad, de skulde findes ved Bund.

Hr. Gynter og Hr. Gernot
